title: South Korean director Yeon Sang-ho revisits AI themes in latest thriller 'Paradise Lost'
summary: South Korean director Yeon Sang-ho explores artificial intelligence in his films, including his latest, “Paradise Lost.”
story: South Korean director Yeon Sang-ho explores artificial intelligence in his films, including his latest, “Paradise Lost.”

SEOUL, South Korea -- South Korean director Yeon Sang-ho has built his films around artificial intelligence. His latest, “Paradise Lost,” revisits the theme in a psychological thriller about a mother who spends nine years with an AI version of her missing son — until the real one comes home.

Kim Hyun-joo plays Ryu So-young, whose son, Sun-woo, was abducted on a school camping trip. In her grief, she relies on an AI recreation of the boy, forever 10 years old, seen through augmented reality glasses. When the real Sun-woo, played by Bae Hyeon-seong, returns as a grown stranger, she finds herself torn between the two.
The “Train to Busan” director’s earlier AI-themed films include the 2023 Netflix film “JUNG_E” and this year’s zombie thriller “Colony," which premiered at the Cannes Film Festival.
“Paradise Lost” premiered at the Toronto International Film Festival and opens in North American theaters Friday.

The film came from an unexpected source: Yeon’s mother, a homemaker who worked as a cleaner. When she worried how hard writing stories was on her son, Yeon, who never formally studied screenwriting, told her anyone could do it.
She wrote a roughly three-page tale about a mother and son in a village, which eventually became “Paradise Lost,” titled after John Milton’s epic poem about humanity’s expulsion from paradise.
Yeon spoke with The Associated Press about the film, AI’s limits and why Asian filmmakers may be more receptive to it than Hollywood.
This interview has been translated and edited for clarity and brevity.

YEON: Relationships, mostly. Continuity in a relationship is key to seeing someone as the same person. AI Sun-woo had filled that role for nine years. But it doesn’t truly contemplate. It gives So-young suitable reactions. Can you call that a relationship? Isn’t real human identity found in relationships with people, even if it's more tragic?
YEON: I see AI as a very sophisticated manifestation of what users want. So when AI Sun-woo cries, I think it’s less his own judgment than something deep inside So-young surfacing.

AI is a manifestation of collective intelligence, so it’s hard to say it’s capable of contemplation. How that might emerge in the distant future, I don’t know. But the way to find out is very simple: If you tell AI to do something and it says, “I don’t want to,” it has started to contemplate. AI doesn’t refuse. My kids flat-out refuse.

As long as contemplation exists, can there be a paradise without pain? If only good things happened, after a week they wouldn’t be good anymore. So I never really understood paradise in Milton’s “Paradise Lost.” I felt something similar looking at AI.

YEON: I feel that way. But “AI” is such a broad term. To avoid AI, you’d have to stop searching; even search engines use it. Some cite data centers’ environmental toll, but how much of that comes from film?

English-language films had a much bigger market and far bigger budgets. Expensive films more or less had to be made for the English-speaking market. That’s crumbling as AI and many other technologies develop, and AI is accelerating it. Asia’s small market kept it from even thinking about making sci-fi. Now Asian film can take on more subjects, so I think it’s more accepting of AI.

YEON: Filmmaking sometimes needs collective intelligence. Before release, we survey 100 people at blind previews. In a way, that’s a collective intelligence test — it works on the same principle as AI.

We’ve turned “AI” into a kind of icon, but look beneath it and the question is how much collective intelligence popular filmmaking needs. I find debates that lump everything under “AI” unproductive. When the question is wrong, there can’t be an answer.

title: Herbert Blomstedt, who headed San Francisco Symphony from 1985-95, dies at age 99
summary: Herbert Blomstedt, a renowned conductor who led the San Francisco Symphony from 1985 to 1995, has died at the age of 99
story: Herbert Blomstedt, a renowned conductor who led the San Francisco Symphony from 1985 to 1995, has died at the age of 99
Herbert Blomstedt, who headed the San Francisco Symphony from 1985-95 and led orchestras in Scandinavia and Germany during a career over seven decades, died Wednesday. He was 99.
Blomstedt died at his home in Gothenburg, Sweden, according to his management agency, KünstlerSekretariat am Gasteig.

His final performance was on May 15 with the San Francisco Symphony at Davies Hall, when he entered the stage in a wheelchair and struggled to get through Gustav Mahler's Ninth Symphony, which halted for several minutes during the third movement. He was replaced for concerts the following two days and canceled future scheduled appearances this year.
“An an extraordinary role model," Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra music director Manfred Honeck said. "One of the greatest conductors and a beacon of humanity.”
Blomstedt had performances scheduled into 2027, including with the Vienna Philharmonic next June, just shy of what would have been his 100th birthday.
“Until the very end, we had hoped to celebrate his 100th birthday with a concert together,” Vienna Philharmonic chairman Daniel Froschauer said.

Blomstedt was a Seventh-day Adventist who refused to conduct rehearsals on Friday nights and Saturdays because of the Sabbath but would lead performances on those days because he considered himself a preacher of music.
“Every bar, every note is shared by us, and it’s a very intense communication,” he said of his conducting during an interview with “CBS Sunday Morning” broadcast last year. “It’s like intense sex.”
He won Grammy Awards for recordings with the San Francisco Symphony of Carl Orff’s “Carmina Burana” in 1993 and of Johannes Brahms’ “Ein Deutsches Requiem” in 1996.

“My mission is to bring good music to as many people as possible,” he said in an interview posted in 2020 by the DW Music YouTube channel. “It makes you think differently. You gave a more keen feeling for proportions and beauty.”

Blomstedt was principal conductor of the Norrköping Symphony Orchestra in Sweden from 1954-63, music director of the Oslo Philharmonic from 1962–68, principal conductor of the Danish Radio Symphony from 1967-77 and the Swedish Radio Symphony from 1977-82 and then became chief conductor of the Staatskapelle Dresden and Semperoper in Germany from 1975-85.
“Almost like turning an electrical switch for me,” he added. “When I hear the sound, it transforms me. I'm in heaven.”

Esa-Pekka Salonen, who led the San Francisco Symphony from 2020-25, said during an interview with London's Philharmonia Orchestra in 2021 that he asked Blomstedt how he was filled with joy that orchestras responded to.

“I refuse to have any stress,” Salonen recalled Blomstedt telling him. “I only do things I absolutely love. I only conduct music that matters to me and I only work with people that I like and in some cases love.”
After leaving San Francisco, Blomstedt was principal conductor of Hamburg's NDR Symphony Orchestra from 1996-98 and music director of the Leipzig Gewanhaus Orchestra from 1998-2005.
Born to Swedish parents in Springfield, Massachusetts, on July 11, 1927.
His family moved back to Sweden in 1929 and he attended Stockholm's Royal Academy of Music and Uppsala University. He studied under Igor Markevitch, then with Jean Morel at The Juilliard School.

When his scholarship at Juilliard was about to expire, he showed up without an appointment at Leonard Bernstein's apartment at The Osborne across from Carnegie Hall, rang the doorbell and left a half-hour later with a scholarship to study with Bernstein at the Tanglewood Music Center in Lenox, Massachusetts. Blomstedt was impressed with Bernstein's musicianship but disliked his exuberant podium mannerisms.
Blomstedt won the Koussevitzky Conducting Prize in 1953, made his professional debut with the Royal Stockholm Philharmonic Orchestra in 1954 and won the Salzburg Conducting Competition in 1955.
He married his wife, the former Waltraud Petersen, in 1955, and she died in 2003. He is survived by four daughters and seven grandchildren.

title: Sold-out arenas, 3.3 million viewers for Game 7: The WNBA postseason surges in numbers
summary: The WNBA Finals was the most watched since 1999 with an average of 1.88 million people viewing the seven-game series that Golden State won over Atlanta in a decisive Game 7
story: The WNBA Finals was the most watched since 1999 with an average of 1.88 million people viewing the seven-game series that Golden State won over Atlanta in a decisive Game 7
NEW YORK -- The WNBA Finals was the most watched since 1999 with an average of 1.88 million people viewing the seven-game series that Golden State won over Atlanta in a decisive Game 7.
That game averaged 3.3 million viewers, making it the most watched WNBA postseason game ever. It was up 128% from last season's clinching game between Las Vegas and Phoenix that the Aces won.
All seven games in the series were sold out, including Game 6, which was played at 12:30 p.m. EDT.
The Finals capped the WNBA’s most-watched postseason since its inaugural season in 1997, averaging 1.49 million viewers, up 27% from last year.

title: John Malkovich, a world-weary CIA man in 'Wild Horse Nine,' prefers life on the road
summary: In Martin McDonagh’s “Wild Horse Nine,” John Malkovich’s Chris is an itinerant CIA officer weary from his travels
story: In Martin McDonagh’s “Wild Horse Nine,” John Malkovich’s Chris is an itinerant CIA officer weary from his travels
NEW YORK -- In Martin McDonagh’s “Wild Horse Nine,” John Malkovich plays an itinerant CIA officer, Chris, weary from his travels. But Chris has got nothing on Malkovich's miles.

Over his 50-year career, Malkovich has performed live in 47 countries, by his count. He’s played a serial killer in Hamburg. He’s directed “Les Liaisons Dangereuses” in Paris. He’s done George Bernard Shaw in Bulgaria.

“It’s probably not by an accident that the first film I ever developed was called ‘The Accidental Tourist,’” Malkovich says, chuckling. “It just kind of happened and I went along with it. It’s a big world.”

Malkovich is best known for his screen credits, including “Empire of the Sun,” “Of Mice and Men,” “In the Line of Fire,” “Being John Malkovich” and the new “Wild Horse Nine,” in which he plays a dying CIA man on Easter Island who, after a lifetime of toppling governments and carrying out assassinations, is increasingly eager to spill the beans. The performance — mordant, droll, elegiac — is a big-screen apogee for Malkovich. He's favored to win what would be his first Academy Award.

But if Malkovich is experiencing a moment of public celebration at 72, it’s also a reminder that he has, if not eschewed the spotlight, seldom sat still long enough for it to linger. Instead, Malkovich has preferred an ever-moving, endlessly curious life on the road.

“I’m a worker, and this isn’t part of my work,” Malkovich said in an interview on his way through New York. “I rarely go to openings. I rarely see a film I’m in. I’m rarely asked to promote because I’m already gone.”

Malkovich was momentarily stationary on a recent, bright fall day. He wore a hat, not unlike his character’s in “Wild Horse Nine,” to shield his bald head from the hotel air conditioning. The threat of getting sick was his biggest worry. Days earlier, he had performed spoken word in Mexico City. By the time “Wild Horse Nine” arrives in theaters Friday, Malkovich will be in Japan, directing a play.

“I’ll go to Japan — I don’t speak a word of it. I directed ‘Leopoldstadt' in Latvian, don’t speak a word of Latvian. Well, I had five or six words, the main one was ‘cinnamon roll,’ which is two words,” Malkovich says. “I’ve just been constantly learning.”

Those experiences have taught Malkovich that countries may differ, but audiences are generally the same. They come to be compelled or amused. Mostly, he says, they come for catharsis. And he keeps giving it to them.

“You find yourself in Monte Carlo or Oklahoma City or Salé or Porto Alegre,” Malkovich says. “It’s 4 a.m., you’re up. It’s 5 a.m., you’re already in a car. This is thousands of mornings for me. I could even say maybe it’s most mornings. You don’t know anyone and you may never be back. This is my life on the road.”

Malkovich has watched some of his contemporaries lose their enthusiasm for acting, but he considers himself more interested now than when he was in his 20s. In the late 1970s, Malkovich was a charter member of the Steppenwolf Theatre Company in Chicago. Performances in plays like “True West” and “Death of a Salesman” made him one of his generation's most thrilling stage performers.

“You should learn something every day,” he says. “Somebody asked me to do a fashion line. I’ve done 24 collections. What do I know about it? (Expletive) all. The point is to learn about it, it seems to me.”

Over the last two decades, Malkovich has increasingly worked with classical music performers in hybrid stage shows that pair spoken word with orchestras and chamber ensembles. In one, the satirical “The Music Critic,” violinist Aleksey Igudesman performs classical masterworks alongside Malkovich’s deadpan readings of old, now-comical critical pans.

“I work in classical music a lot because I can help sell tickets,” Malkovich says. “OK, and what do I get from that? I get the pleasure of being on stage with unbelievably beautiful music performed by unbelievably well-trained and gifted musicians.”

Malkovich’s travels have sometimes run into local politics. Earlier this year, he pulled out of performing “The Music Critic” in Tel Aviv, Israel, after a press release falsely attributed quotes to him. Two years ago in Bulgaria, a Malkovich-directed production of Shaw’s anti-war comedy “Arms and the Man” became a target of far-right nationalist protesters who physically assaulted theatergoers.
“I think that’s all unfortunate and pretty goofy, all in all, and had nothing to do with the play,” he says.

Being on the road so often has inevitably meant sacrifice. Unable to find time in his international schedule, Malkovich twice before turned down McDonagh. But McDonagh, the playwright-turned-filmmaker of “In Bruges” and “The Banshees of Inisherin,” persisted — even if Malkovich’s intellect was intimidating.

“I was scared the first time I had a Zoom with him,” McDonagh says. “But I knew that in the silent moments you’d see acres of sorrow and regret when he’s seemingly not doing anything — when he’s just looking out of a window or listening to a Dictaphone or smoking a cigarette. That, I think, is the heart of the movie.”

When he read McDonagh’s script, which touches on CIA involvement in both John F. Kennedy’s assassination and the military coup in Chile, Malkovich found it paralleled some of his previous work: a stage adaptation of Don DeLillo’s “Libra” and a piece based on Roberto Bolaño’s “Nazi Literature in the Americas.”

“Those are the two bookends of this: Two huge national, international traumas that happened in the TV age and which are the kind of magnets that keep crushing these characters and their movement through life,” he says.

Malkovich could have easily drifted more toward movie-star iconography. It wouldn’t have been hard for him, after “Being John Malkovich,” to trade more directly on his unique screen presence and his halting, idiosyncratic line deliveries. It’s a path that Malkovich knowingly avoided, preferring to shape his own artistic life than wait around for a good part to show up.

At the Telluride Film Festival premiere of “Wild Horse Nine,” Malkovich ran into the producer Kathleen Kennedy, who produced 1987’s “Empire of the Sun,” directed by Steven Spielberg. He hadn’t seen her since.

“I probably haven’t seen Steven in all those years. OK, I had a different life. I went a different way. But without any sort of malice or distaste,” says Malkovich. “It’s just that a lot of things interested me and I pursued most of them with some degree of vigor and interest, as I do everything.”
“I always accepted in my life that doing what you want, there’s a price to that. And that’s fine. I never minded that price at all,” Malkovich says. “I’ve done exactly what I wanted, more or less.”

Malkovich grew up in a rural coal-mining town in Illinois. The big claim to fame, he says, is its proximity to a maximum-security prison. This month, like many months, he’ll be on the other side of the globe, directing a troupe of actors in a language he doesn’t understand.
“I often to put my youngest granddaughter to sleep by singing ‘One Too Many Mornings’ by Bob Dylan,” Malkovich says. “One too many mornings / And a thousand miles behind.”

title: How Anthony Ippolito talked his way into playing Sylvester Stallone in 'I Play Rocky'
summary: Anthony Ippolito took a bold step to land the starring role in “I Play Rocky.”
story: Anthony Ippolito took a bold step to land the starring role in “I Play Rocky.”

Anthony Ippolito saw the opportunity of a lifetime when he learned that Oscar-winning director Peter Farrelly was developing a film about Sylvester Stallone’s determination to write and star in the original “Rocky.” There was just one problem: Nobody had asked him to audition for “I Play Rocky.”

“So, I kind of just took it upon myself to make some stuff on my own and kind of send it to them unsolicited,” the 27-year-old actor said in a recent interview with The Associated Press ahead of the movie's limited release Friday.

It was a move that could be seen as taking a page from the book of Stallone's own improbable rise to stardom but, for Ippolito, “it didn’t really necessarily feel that way at the time, to be honest. I was just hoping somebody would see it.”
Farrelly did — and was convinced from the start.
“He sent his tape, you know, cold, and we’re like, that’s the guy,” the director recalled. “We were going to do a worldwide search, we never did it.”
Farrelly was particularly impressed by Ippolito’s ability to distinguish the man from his famous screen persona.
“This guy came fully formed — he was exactly what I was looking for because he didn’t do a caricature of Stallone or Rocky and he knew the difference,” Farrelly said.

Ippolito has already had some experience stepping into the shoes of a Hollywood icon. He previously portrayed a young Al Pacino in “The Offer,” the miniseries chronicling the making of the 1972 classic “The Godfather.” Farrelly had been a big fan of “The Offer,” and his favorite performance was the portrayal of Pacino. What he didn’t realize was that Ippolito was the actor behind it.
“That’s when I realized, ‘Oh, this guy’s good.’ I mean, I knew he was good for what we had, but I didn’t realize how this guy can transform into whatever he wants,” Farrelly said.

Both roles presented a similar challenge: portraying legendary actors at pivotal moments in their careers, before fame and success defined their public identities. He needed “to strip away the celebrity,” as he put it, looking beyond the familiar voices and mannerisms to find the people underneath. To play Stallone, Ippolito explored the hardships that shaped — and fueled — the older actor, including a difficult childhood, limited parental support and a profound sense of isolation. Ippolito described the process as partly voyeuristic with a dash of speculation.
“You’re trying to imagine moments that don’t exist in cinema at this point and kind of in between,” he said.

Equally compelling to Ippolito was Stallone’s determination. Here was a struggling actor who reportedly turned down offers in the $300,000 range for his “Rocky” screenplay rather than surrender the starring role. Fifty years later, Ippolito sees that gamble as the heart of Stallone’s story: a man willing to risk everything on a dream that Hollywood was ready to buy, but not let him live.
“It’s so incredible what he was able to do ... and the conviction that he had and his commitment to seeing his idea through all the way to the end,” Ippolito said.
For AnnaSophia Robb, who plays Stallone's first wife Sasha, Ippolito’s transformation seemed almost effortless.

“He was so subtle about the whole thing. I met him, and he’s not method or anything, but he had dedicated, you know, like a year and a half of just getting into this role,” Robb said. “So when we stepped on set, it just felt natural. It felt right.”

As buzz surrounding the film grows, Ippolito is getting his first taste of the spotlight that transformed Stallone’s life. “It’s been very, very gratifying and amazing to see the film land with certain people,” he said.
One of those people was Stallone himself, who was uninvolved in the movie other than a conversation with Farrelly. But he has seen it, as he told the AP in a September interview.
“It’s fantastic. And the kid did a great job,” he said. “This is so odd. They usually do this when you’re dead and gone.”
AP National Writer Hillel Italie contributed reporting.

title: Tony Butala, of Lettermen vocal trio known for 'The Way You Look Tonight,' dies at 87
summary: Tony Butala, co-founder of the Grammy-nominated trio The Lettermen, has died at age 87
story: Tony Butala, co-founder of the Grammy-nominated trio The Lettermen, has died at age 87
NEW YORK -- Tony Butala, co-founder of the Grammy-nominated trio The Lettermen, whose lush vocal harmonies made them one of the most popular vocal groups of the 1960s, died Sunday. He was 87.
The band's media coordinator, Tracy Clark, confirmed Butala's death to The Associated Press. She shared an official statement from the band.

“We have lost an integral member of The Lettermen family,” it read. “It is with profound sadness that we announce the recent passing of Tony Butala, founding member of the international recording artists ‘The Lettermen,’ and recipient of a Star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame. Our most heartfelt thoughts and prayers are with his children, grandchildren, siblings, the love of his life, the entire Lettermen organization and all who knew and loved him.”
A cause of death was not provided.
There will be no public viewing. Details for celebrations of life held in Wisconsin and California will be announced at a later date.

Born in Sharon, Pennsylvania, in 1938, Butala's career started in childhood. He started singing professionally at age 7, on KDKA Radio in Pittsburgh at age 8 and by age 10, he moved with his mother to Los Angeles, where he joined the Mitchell Boys Choir and appeared in classic films like “White Christmas,” “Peter Pan,” “War of the Worlds” and “On Moonlight Bay.”

In the late ‘50s, Butala co-founded The Lettermen alongside Jim Pike and Bob Engemann. The hits quickly followed: They had their first with their version of Fred Astaire’s “The Way You Look Tonight” in 1961, which peaked at No. 13 on Billboard’s Hot 100. It was nominated for a Grammy in 1962. At that award show, they also received the coveted best new artist nomination.
Over the course of the next decade, The Lettermen would place 19 more songs on Billboard charts.
Two made the Top 10, 1962’s “When I Fall in Love” and the Grammy-nominated 1968 medley “Goin’ Out of My Head/Can’t Take My Eyes off You.” Their last hit was 1971’s “Everything is Good About You.”
The beloved group toured constantly, playing colleges across the country and venues around the world.
Butala was the last surviving member of the trio's original lineup: Pike died in 2019 at age 82. The cause was complications of Parkinson’s disease. Engemann died in 2013.

Across its many decades, The Lettermen has had various lineups, replacing members who left but always remaining a trio to keep its distinctive three-part sound alive. The current lineup is made up of Donovan Tea, Bobby Poynton and Rob Gulack.
Butala stepped away from performing in 2019. And in 2020, Butala and The Lettermen received a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame.

“Tony never met a stranger,” the official band statement continued. “His life was a living example of talent, perseverance, and refinement. But above all, his true joy was entertaining and sharing his music with audiences worldwide.”

title: Jury begins deliberating at Russell Brand's rape and sexual assault trial
summary: Jurors have started deliberating in Russell Brand's trial on charges of rape and sexual assault
story: Jurors have started deliberating in Russell Brand's trial on charges of rape and sexual assault
LONDON -- Jurors began considering their verdicts on Tuesday in the trial of Russell Brand on charges of rape and sexual assault.
After three weeks of argument and evidence, judge Joel Bennathan told the jury at London’s Southwark Crown Court that they must reach a unanimous decision.
“I can only accept a verdict that is the verdict of all 12 of you,” he said.
After about an hour of deliberations, the jurors were sent home for the night with a warning not to discuss the case with anyone else.
Brand, who is free on bail, has attended court every day, accompanied by his wife, Laura Gallacher.
Six women, who don't know one another, accuse the actor-comedian of sexual misconduct between 1999 and 2009, a decade when Brand went from rising stand-up comedian to major celebrity in the U.K.

Prosecutors argued that during that time Brand was “a sexual predator” who attacked the women in a hotel room, the London offices of MTV, the toilet of a London bar, a radio station, a recording studio and his home.
Brand, 51, has pleaded not guilty to three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one count of attempted indecent assault.
Giving evidence, the entertainer acknowledged that he had been obsessed with sex as a younger man, but said his encounters were always consensual.

Brand’s lawyers argued that the claimants’ cases were undermined by the fact that they only went to police years after the alleged assaults, and following the broadcast of a 2023 documentary that contained anonymous allegations against Brand.
Brand’s lawyer, Ian Winter, said the “well of justice had been corrupted and contaminated” by the documentary.
In his closing statement on Monday, Winter said the jury must separate Brand’s treatment of women from the question of whether he committed crimes.
“It is not criminal to treat women unkindly before, during or after sex,” he said. “It is not, I am afraid, criminal to be disrespectful or rude or to act like a crazy idiot.”
He said Brand “had an immense amount of sex and none of it was unlawful.”
“Disgusting, distasteful, immoral, who cares?” the lawyer said. “It’s irrelevant to your consideration.”

Known for risqué stand-up routines and battles with drugs and alcohol, Brand rose to prominence in the early 2000s, hosting television programs and his own BBC radio show. He appeared in Hollywood films including “Forgetting Sarah Marshall” and “Get Him to the Greek” and was briefly married to pop star Katy Perry.

In recent years he has moved away from mainstream media, relocated to Florida and built a large online following with videos mixing wellness, conspiracy theories and discussions of his religious devotion.

title: How My Chemical Romance's 'The Black Parade' hit No. 1 in the US, 20 years later
summary: My Chemical Romance has hit No_ 1 on the Billboard 200 with “The Black Parade (20th Anniversary Deluxe Edition).”
story: My Chemical Romance has hit No_ 1 on the Billboard 200 with “The Black Parade (20th Anniversary Deluxe Edition).”

NEW YORK -- It's official: The influential New Jersey rock outfit My Chemical Romance has the No. 1 record in the U.S., having topped the all-genre Billboard 200 for the first time in their career. It just happens to be with an album that is two decades old.
“The Black Parade (20th Anniversary Deluxe Edition),” a new reissue of their career-defining rock opera, 2006's “The Black Parade,” is No. 1, Billboard announced Sunday.

Upon its initial release, the album cemented My Chemical Romance's shift from mainstays of the emo scene to mainstream recognition, becoming one of the most inventive bands of the 21st century. Twenty years on, it continues to resonate with nostalgic fans and new ones.

Competition was stiff. Back in 2006, the soundtrack to Disney’s “Hannah Montana” was released the same week, selling 281,000 copies in the U.S., according to Nielsen SoundScan. “The Black Parade” debuted at No. 2 with 240,000 copies. (Compare that to their previous album, 2004's “Three Cheers for Sweet Revenge,” with a best sales week of 38,000 copies, and it was a massive commercial leap for the then-still alternative band.)
“It’s hard to go up against that type of a dedicated fan base, for Miley (Cyrus), Disney and pop music,” says Paige Owens, author of “500 Essential Emo Albums.”

“The Black Parade” is also an unusual, hyperambitious release. Back in 2006, when My Chemical Romance’s contemporaries were still playing in emo tropes, the band released a rock opera for outsiders — replete with world-building, characters, narrative, costumes and spectacle, covering themes of mortality, legacy, resilience and defiance.

And sonically, it was a giant step forward: a ’70s rock-inspired release filtered through the metallic noodling of guitarist Ray Toro, the punk rock ethos of its other guitarist Frank Iero and the unmistakable tenor of frontman and mastermind Gerard Way. Comparisons to various classic rock greats, including David Bowie and Queen, were frequent. Critical acclaim followed. “All of those things are familiar,” says Jason Pettigrew, former editor-in-chief of “Alternative Press.” “But they were also recontextualized with something remarkably contemporary.”

There are a few reasons. “The Black Parade” was re-released with 20 physical variants and six bonus tracks last week, which inspires sales, encourages collectability and fosters a sense of exclusivity among fans.

According to industry data and analytics company Luminate, it earned 78,000 equivalent album units in the U.S. last week, up 653% from the previous week. That was largely driven by pure album sales, which accounted for 68,000 units, a figure up 2,082% from the previous week.

Pettigrew points to a few other factors: The band broke up for a period in the 2010s, driving interest in a reunion. They stopped releasing records after 2010's “Danger Days: The True Lives of the Fabulous Killjoys,” inspiring fans to return to their early material. But that wouldn't add up to much if “The Black Parade” “sounded like everybody else’s records,” he says. “They made the big gestures.”

In addition to the release, the band embarked on an extensive anniversary tour for the album, playing in some of their biggest venues yet. But instead of simply resurrecting the album on stage, they breathed new life into it, “expanding the lore and conceptualization behind the record,” says Owens, with new characters, set designs and even a fictional language. “I don't think we'd see the same excitement or attention around ‘The Black Parade’ if it weren’t for these live shows building off their initial vision.”

Pettigrew agrees. “They reframe their masterpiece into essentially a Broadway show with very dark undertones of the current political situation of the world,” he said. “They’ve completely raised the bar in terms of possibilities and conviction.”

It's a good question, and lately, the answer appears to be yes. In 2026 alone, Beyoncé's “B’Day,” The Beatles' “Rubber Soul” and Mac Miller's “The Divine Feminine” have all returned to the top 10 on the Billboard 200, though no catalog title had claimed the top spot until “The Black Parade.”

According to Billboard, “The Black Parade” marks the longest wait for an album to hit No. 1 after release. My Chemical Romance's 20-year stretch overtakes country star Toby Keith, whose “35 Biggest Hits” hit No. 1 in the wake of his 2024 death, nearly 16 years after the album's initial release.

Pettigrew argues both nostalgic audiences and newer, younger fans coming to the music for the first time helped power the recent sales. “Those guys had vision,” he said, and anyone can connect to their symbolism, which appeals directly to “disenfranchised people.”

Streaming platforms like Spotify and Apple Music play a role, too. Younger generations of fans have discovered “The Black Parade” years after its initial release — and many don't seem to mind that the record came out decades ago, sometimes before they were born.

“One of the silver linings of living in a streaming world is that it's very apparent that young people today do not care when something is in their hands,” said Death Cab for Cutie frontman Ben Gibbard, whose band opened for MCR on their 2025 “The Black Parade” stadium tour. “I’m a firm believer in the idea that if something is new to you, it is new.”

Gibbard says My Chemical Romance are “absolutely” the best example of a veteran band experiencing an explosion of interest decades after their biggest release. He also says his own band has benefited from new, younger audiences discovering their catalog: Death Cab for Cutie was able to play arenas instead of their usual theaters when they took their career-defining albums, 2003’s “Transatlanticism,” and later, 2005’s “Plans,” on an anniversary run.

“I was not listening to John Coltrane when I was 12 years old, but at the point that his music came into my life and started to really move me, I was just glad it was there,” he said. “I think a lot of young people seem to have that attitude.”
In the case of My Chemical Romance's “The Black Parade,” they certainly do.

title: Familiar faces rejoin 'The Book of Mormon' on Broadway: Nikki M. James, Rory O’Malley
summary: Nikki M
story: Nikki M
NEW YORK -- It's been 12 years since Nikki M. James was last in the Eugene O’Neill Theatre on Broadway starring in “The Book of Mormon.” So much has changed and yet some things are exactly the same.
“The sink in my dressing room is still clogged,” the Tony Award-winner says, laughing. “You can’t run the water that long. I don't know what it is. What's happening?”
James and fellow original co-star Rory O’Malley have returned to “The Book of Mormon” for the first time since they left when Barack Obama was just starting his second presidential term.

“It was totally surreal being on that stage again, doing a show that I love so much, hearing an audience loving it too, and having people who clearly were seeing it for the first time,” says O’Malley after his return last week.

James likened the experience to going back to your hometown after decades away and someone asking you to grab something from the deli. “You’re like, ‘Oh, sure.’ And before you know it, you’re in the car and you’ve driven there,” she says. “It’s like those pathways are all still there.”
The pair will be in the show in their old roles until Jan. 17.

“The Book of Mormon,” about two Mormon missionaries who find more than they bargained for in Uganda, including gun-toting warlords and villages infected with HIV, was a cultural juggernaut when it opened on Broadway in 2011. After they left, new cast members kept it going and this year's 15th anniversary offered a way back.

They're doing the show “in a completely different world” than the last time, says James. “The discourse around race, around religion, around comedy, about responsibility of artists and representation — all of it was different.”

The musical earned James a Tony Award and she went on to marry and have a baby, enter the Marvel Cinematic Universe and earn another Tony nomination for “Suffs.” O’Malley earned a Tony nomination and also went on to marry and have a child, winning roles in “Hamilton” and “She Loves Me.”

She and O’Malley admit they were nervous coming back, even though each had performed it well over 800 times. They've had huge career moments since but “nothing that comes close to touching this,” she says. “We know for a fact that this doesn’t happen again. So we have to treat it like the precious gift that it is.”

James and O’Malley are part of a boomlet of original actors returning to their hit shows, like Aaron Tveit coming back to “Moulin Rouge” and Leslie Odom Jr. and Christopher Jackson jumping back into “Hamilton.”
“It’s something that I hope is done a lot more,” says O’Malley. “I hope that there are more shows that have the ability to be open long enough so that people can come back and revisit it.”

James and O’Malley have changed and the show they rejoin has also changed. During the pandemic shutdown, the creators — “South Park” masterminds Trey Parker and Matt Stone, and Robert Lopez, co-creator of the equally irreverent musical “Avenue Q” — made minor changes to the script.

One notable tweak is giving James' character — the potential love interest Nabulungi, who sings the torch song “Sal Tlay Ka Siti” — more agency by becoming the one who scares off the warlords at the end.
That change now puts her on equal footing with the missionaries and means she gets to end the show center stage. “It’s a small little thing, but it makes a huge difference to me,” she says.

One of the show's highlights is O’Malley singing “Turn It Off,” a mock ode to keeping your homosexuality hidden. Raised Catholic, O’Malley has been out since he was 19 and co-founded the gay rights group Broadway Impact. “I love how far this show has let me explore my own faith journey,” he says.
The full cast of “The Book of Mormon” has stayed close with an active group text, and some from the original cast came to the theater to welcome back James and O’Malley.

“Everyone says that their theater family is like a family, and that is really true here,” says James. “We’ve been there for each other’s weddings, babies, deaths of family members, deaths of each other's parents.”

Backstage, the pair have found stickers and notes that have lasted for 15 years. There's a new tradition of putting headshots up in the stage-right dressing room tower, including one from the late Gavin Creel.

If James has her clogged sink, O’Malley rediscovered a specific smell under the stage: “I walked down there and I am immediately transported back to February of 2011 when we first moved into the theater.”

Although they rehearsed the show for two weeks to relearn everything, O’Malley hit a snag at the top of Act 2 on his first night back when he suddenly didn't know how to get on stage. He had to ask for help.
“I deleted that file a long time ago,” he says, laughing.

title: ‘You Can See Everything,’ 'Clayface' lead sleepy Halloween weekend
summary: The North American box office faced a slump this weekend.
story: The North American box office faced a slump this weekend.

The North American box office took a bit of a hit this weekend with the Halloween holiday drawing audiences away from theaters on Saturday. Ticket sales were led by the Elizabeth Holmes documentary “You Can See Everything” and the DC Studios movie “Clayface,” and aren’t likely to surpass $56 million, according to studio estimates on Sunday. That would make it the second-lowest-earning weekend of the year.

“You Can See Everything” had the slight edge over “Clayface,” with $10.6 million from 2,655 locations in its third weekend in theaters. The Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim-directed film has made $63.9 million to date against a reported production budget of $7 million and continues to generate the kind of buzz that’s hard to buy. This is the first time it’s hit No. 1, however.

“Clayface,” about the Batman villain, trailed “You Can See Everything” by only $200,684. The Warner Bros. release fell 57% in its second weekend in theaters. That brings its domestic earnings to $44.1 million against a reported $44 million budget.

Third place went to Laika’s animated film “Wildwood,” which added 150 screens in its second weekend, bringing its footprint to 3,100 theaters in the U.S. and Canada. The Fathom Entertainment release made an estimated $7.5 million, down 39% from its first weekend, bringing its running total to $25.9 million.

The comedic fantasy “Wicker,” in which Olivia Colman plays a woman who commissions a basket maker to build her a wicker husband (Alexander Skarsgård), landed in fourth place with $4.1 million. “Street Fighter,” now in its third weekend, rounded out the top five with $3.2 million.
In notable expansions, the acclaimed Sundance indie “The Only Living Pickpocket in New York” added over 1,000 locations in its second weekend and made $1.9 million, which landed it in the top 10.

Netflix also reported earnings from the theatrical release of its World War II film “The Mosquito Bowl,” which made $455,000 from 349 locations. “La Bola Negra” made slightly less, $418,000, from only 38 locations in its third weekend, bringing its running total to $1.2 million.
The domestic box office remains up over 17% from last year with nearly $8.5 billion to date.
With final domestic figures being released Monday, this list factors in the estimated ticket sales for Friday through Sunday at U.S. and Canadian theaters, according to Rentrak:
1. “You Can See Everything,” $10.6 million.
2. “Clayface,” $10.4 million.
3. “Wildwood,” $7.5 million.
4. “Wicker,” $4.1 million.
5. “Street Fighter,” $3.2 million.
6. “Resident Evil,” $2.5 million.
7. “Other Mommy,” $2.5 million.
8. “The Only Living Pickpocket in New York,” $1.9 million.
9. “Heart of the Beast,” $1.6 million.
10. “Sense and Sensibility,” $1.4 million.

title: ‘Heat’ director Michael Mann sustains ‘superficial injury’ at gun range
summary: A weapon accidentally discharged while holstered, Mann's representative says.
story: A weapon accidentally discharged while holstered, Mann's representative says.

LOS ANGELES -- Filmmaker Michael Mann was injured at a gun range on Saturday in Los Angeles. He was taken to a hospital where he was treated and is being released, his representative told The Associated Press on Sunday.
Mann sustained what his representative described as a superficial injury after a weapon accidentally discharged while holstered.

The 83-year-old filmmaker behind crime classics like “Heat,” “Collateral” and “Thief” has apparently been an experienced target shooter for decades, and the accident happened at a sanctioned gun range.

Mann continues to be quite active in Hollywood in his 80s. He most recently directed the film “Ferrari,” with Adam Driver, and is developing a sequel to “Heat,” which is supposed to begin filming early next year.

title: Director calls Broadway revival of ‘In the Heights’ at NY City Center a ‘balm for these times’
summary: David Mendizábal is directing a revival of Lin-Manuel Miranda’s "In the Heights," a musical that was Mendizábal's introduction to theater
story: David Mendizábal is directing a revival of Lin-Manuel Miranda’s "In the Heights," a musical that was Mendizábal's introduction to theater

NEW YORK -- David Mendizábal vividly remembers sitting in the audience for the final performances of playwright Lin-Manuel Miranda’s “In the Heights.” Almost two decades later, Mendizábal is directing the musical that was once his “portal to the theater.”

“It was the first time I’d ever heard or seen a world that looked and sounded like mine on an American stage,” Mendizábal told The Associated Press, referring to the 2008 musical that was a landmark for Latino representation and won four Tony Awards.

With a new cast of Latino artists, the New York City Center is presenting “In the Heights” for a limited three-week run through Nov. 15. It is the first major revival of the musical debuting at a time when, to Mendizábal, it’s vital to “show people the depth and breadth” of Latino communities.
“I think in this particular moment we need a great balm of joy, and this show brings that,” Mendizábal said.

Miranda, who also starred in the original production, recalled his experience resurrecting his barrier-breaking work. His songs and lyrics, alongside writing by Quiara Alegría Hudes, earned the original production best musical and best original score honors in its debut year.

“I’m really proud of the work Quiara and I did to make it speak across generations,” Miranda told the AP on Wednesday during a red carpet event celebrating the opening performance. “And that this generation is picking up the mantle is incredibly meaningful.”

The show’s revival comes amid ongoing federal immigration enforcement operations that have affected Dominican and Cuban families like the ones portrayed in the musical. An operation in Manhattan last month involved a Dominican national who was shot in the neck by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer, as his five-year-old son watched, prompting large protests and condemnation from local and state elected officials.

When Jenny Gersten, New York City Center’s vice president and artistic director, was deciding on the musical lineup for the gala presentation, she recalled wrestling with the question of “what would be a good balm for these times?”
The answer came quickly, Gersten said. “In the Heights is pure joy.”

The high-energy reggaeton romance is set just a 30-minute subway ride north of New York City Center, in the predominantly Latino neighborhood of Washington Heights. The story follows three simmering summer days in the lives of this community’s cast of characters: like bodega-boy Usnavi, played by Matte Martinez; his storefront salon neighbor Vanessa, played by Ashley De La Rosa; and the block’s beloved matriarch Abuela Claudia, played by Natalie Venetia Belcon.
From its three-year Broadway run to the movie-musical debut in 2021, “In the Heights” has been hailed as “an exuberant celebration of the Latino immigrant experience.”
Eighteen years after its debut, the show “still holds up,” Miranda told the AP.
“The songs still hit. Sonny’s rap is more relevant than ever. And it’s still speaking to people.”

The musical number Miranda refers to is “96,000”, the act one anthem in which the cast dreams about what they would do if they won the lottery. Sonny, who is played by Ishmael Gonzalez in the 2026 revival, dreams of investing in the neighborhood, where “the ghetto has a million promises for me to keep.”

“Sonny’s talking about gentrification, he’s talking about immigration, he’s talking about the racism within politics,” Gonzalez said in an interview on Friday. “In some ways, Sonny’s rap feels like the most present part of the show, the most present to the moment we’re living in.”
For Gonzalez, who uses they/them pronouns, the character also symbolizes the “unwavering optimism” of young Latino leaders.
“We are here, and we are a part of this country and this world. Our labor and our love upholds the spine of this country,” they said.

Chris Jackson, the actor who portrayed the character Benny in the original Broadway cast, has passed a baton of sorts to his wife, actress Veronica Vazquez-Jackson, who is playing Camilla in the 2026 revival. The two met in 2003, during one of the earliest stagings of an off-Broadway “In The Heights.”
“It’s a full circle moment of ways I can’t express,” Jackson told the AP during Wednesday’s gala celebration.
“We are literally holding the light on for so many that still aspire to be a part of this society, in our country, in our culture, and also not forgetting who they are,” Jackson said.

title: Heidi Klum reveals Halloween costume as her iconic party marks 25 years
summary: Heidi Klum underwent a bloody transformation to become a giant, gruesome severed hand for Halloween
story: Heidi Klum underwent a bloody transformation to become a giant, gruesome severed hand for Halloween

Heidi Klum underwent a bloody transformation to become a giant, gruesome severed hand for her annual Halloween party in New York on Saturday, 25 years after she began hosting the much-anticipated event.

Klum was unrecognizable, with only her eyes and mouth showing, blood dripping from her mouth as she stuck her tongue out. The top of the hand ended in a gory assortment of dangling ligaments and tendons. She had an ensemble of helpers in blood-stained hazmat suits.
The idea came to her last year to be a giant hand — specifically her own left hand, with long red nails, a thumb ring, and her engagement ring and wedding band.
“I looked at my hand and I thought, ‘Hey, I think I could fit my body in this somehow,’” Klum said.
The supermodel-turned-TV personality went viral in 2022 when she arrived at the party on the end of a fishing line, encased in a slithering worm costume.

In past years, Klum has come dressed as the Greek myth Medusa, a peacock, an 8-foot-tall (2.4-meter-tall) “Transformer,” a werewolf from Michael Jackson’s “Thriller” music video, a clone accompanied by several Klum-lookalikes, and Kali, the multiarmed Hindu goddess of death and destruction.

Klum said it took about five to six hours to get into her hand costume this year, but making it took a lot longer. She posted hints on her Instagram earlier in the day as bloodied prosthetics were applied to her face.
“Hands down, the hardest thing is carrying it,” Klum said. “It's quite heavy.”

Her husband, musician Tom Kaulitz, did not attend this year because he was on tour. But the details on her costume include a tattoo of his name on her ring finger, along with her palm lines and veins.
“A little bit of Tom is with me,” she said.

title: Carragher sorry for comments about Aston Villa that sparked club to say it was taking legal action
summary: Leading soccer pundit Jamie Carragher has apologized to Aston Villa for comments he made on a podcast that prompted the English club to say it was taking legal action against the former Liverpool defender
story: Leading soccer pundit Jamie Carragher has apologized to Aston Villa for comments he made on a podcast that prompted the English club to say it was taking legal action against the former Liverpool defender

LONDON -- Leading soccer pundit Jamie Carragher has apologized to Aston Villa for comments he made on a podcast that prompted the English club to say it was taking legal action against the former Liverpool defender.

Carragher used an expletive toward Villa fans who had criticized him for suggesting Villa manager Unai Emery should consider taking over at Manchester United if under-pressure Michael Carrick was fired.

Speaking on the Stick to Football podcast that was broadcast on Thursday, Carragher said “there is a chain in football, whether you like it or not” and that “Aston Villa will never be Manchester United.”

Late Friday, a post on Villa's account on X, signed by chairman Nassef Sawiris, read: “Aston Villa will initiate legal action against Jamie Carragher for his unacceptable insults about the club and its fans.
“Aston Villa will not allow anyone to stop our ascension in English and European football.”
Carragher responded with his own post on X on Saturday.
“I’d like to apologize to Aston Villa, the owners & their fans,” he wrote. "My language this week was clumsy & wrong.
“I can assure Villa fans it was tongue in cheek but I can understand it’s not come across that way, so apologies.”
Carragher is a leading name in soccer punditry, working for British broadcaster Sky Sports and and American broadcaster CBS since retiring from playing in 2013.
In 2018, Carragher was briefly suspended by Sky after being filmed spitting in the direction of a 14-year-old girl through his car window.

title: Beat Luke Littler: 'Queen of the Palace' Sherrock defeats darts world champ and wins $670,000
summary: A one-off Netflix broadcast called “Beat Luke Littler” offered a prize of 501,000 pounds (around $670,000) to anyone deemed a darts amateur who could defeat the 19-year-old prodigy over a single leg
story: A one-off Netflix broadcast called “Beat Luke Littler” offered a prize of 501,000 pounds (around $670,000) to anyone deemed a darts amateur who could defeat the 19-year-old prodigy over a single leg
Luke Littler beat, among others, an Australian jockey, a trash collector and a restaurant manager.
He couldn't beat the "Queen of the Palace."
A one-off Netflix broadcast called “Beat Luke Littler” offered a prize of 501,000 pounds (around $670,000) to anyone deemed a darts amateur who could defeat the 19-year-old prodigy over a single leg.

Littler, the defending world champion, needed to see off 20 opponents and had already dispatched 14 of them when he met Fallon Sherrock, who shot to fame in late 2019 when she became the first woman to beat a man at darts’ flagship world championship (in fact, she beat two men) at Alexandra Palace.

Sherrock got closer to the bullseye than Littler to earn the first shot, before a maximum 180 helped to leave her on 43 while Littler was stranded on 142. A double-20 checkout saw Sherrock claim the jackpot — the second biggest prize won in the sport’s history, only behind the winner's check of 1 million pounds ($1.33 million) at the world championship.

“It’s like an opportunity to show off the women’s stars and I feel like I’ve kind of taken the opportunity again,” she said, referring to her 2019 exploits that earned her the “Queen of the Palace” moniker and saw her get congratulatory messages from people like Sarah Jessica Parker and Billie Jean King.
“I’ve just beaten the best in the world, and I can’t say that very often."
Sherrock was allowed to compete because she is not a member of the top-tier PDC Tour so was classed as an amateur, which drew some criticism on social media.
Sherrock said she was “just so happy to overcome all the hate.”
“I mean it’s been tough,” she told Britain's Press Association. “Because obviously I do see the backlash and I do see all the negative comments.
“But at the end of the day, I fit the criteria for this. I’ve never had a tour card, and I wouldn’t class myself as a pro really, because all I do is just play darts for the enjoyment of it."
Littler played each one-leg match every 10 minutes in the event that was staged in Manchester late Friday.
Irish student Pearse Mackie, who was the eighth contestant to face Littler, was the first to have a dart for victory, but he missed bullseye.

Mark Pooke, who played Phil Taylor — widely regarded as the greatest darts player ever — in a professional match almost 20 years ago, also had darts to win in the ninth leg, but could not take out 138.
Littler said he was keen to do it all again.
“I’ve enjoyed every bit of it," he said. “The advert, the photo shoots, everything.”
See AP’s full sports coverage here

title: Margaret Qualley, Jack Antonoff file for divorce after 3 years of marriage
summary: Actor Margaret Qualley and Grammy winner Jack Antonoff have filed for divorce after three years of marriage
story: Actor Margaret Qualley and Grammy winner Jack Antonoff have filed for divorce after three years of marriage
NEW YORK -- Actor Margaret Qualley and Grammy winner Jack Antonoff have filed for divorce after three years of marriage, according to court records.
The case was filed Friday in Kings County Supreme Court in Brooklyn, New York, and is listed as an uncontested matrimonial action. Qualley is listed as the plaintiff, and Antonoff as the defendant.
Attorneys for Qualley and Antonoff did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
The couple separated in July.

Qualley, 32, is an actor known for films including “The Substance” and “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood.” Antonoff, 42, is a 14-time Grammy-winning songwriter and producer who has worked with artists including Taylor Swift, Lana Del Rey and Sabrina Carpenter. He is also a member of the band Bleachers.
The couple began dating in 2021 and married in August 2023.

title: Judge orders 3 taxpayer-funded Trump administration ads to be pulled
summary: A judge has ordered the federal government to pull three taxpayer-funded Trump administration ads from television, social media and elsewhere that she says appear to have been made for political or propaganda purposes
story: A judge has ordered the federal government to pull three taxpayer-funded Trump administration ads from television, social media and elsewhere that she says appear to have been made for political or propaganda purposes

NEW YORK -- The federal government must pull three taxpayer-funded Trump administration ads that appear to have been made for political or propaganda purposes, including one touting the president’s claim that every American will get $5,000 if Republicans keep control of Congress in the upcoming election, a judge ruled Friday.

U.S. District Judge Jennifer L. Rochon in New York sided with a coalition, including the nonpartisan watchdog Common Cause, in ordering the government to take down the advertisements entitled “$5,000 to Americans,” “Every Democrat Voted Against No Tax on Tips,” and “Cost of Socialism."

She said they must be taken off official government websites, including social media sites such as YouTube, Instagram and the like. She also ordered the cancellation of any slots, placements, reservations, or arrangements for the airing or distribution of the ads through authorized third parties, including by Trump’s flagship super PAC, MAGA Inc.
Responding to the ruling, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said: "This Biden-appointed activist judge issued a lawless order to stop the administration from sharing patriotic videos.”

Rochon ruled during a hearing in which she considered expanding a temporary restraining order she issued two weeks ago, when she banned a series of ads that glorify President Donald Trump and echo his political messaging going into the midterms.

The White House has defended the ads as public service announcements akin to what past administrations have made to promote various policies. But the recent ads differ from many past public service announcements because they aren’t aimed at helping members of the public benefit from specific government programs, according to the plaintiffs.

After Rochon issued the order, she noted that she was doing so on a Friday afternoon and that the government would have no excuse to delay taking them down immediately. Rochon was nominated to the court by then-President Joe Biden, a Democrat.
A government lawyer acknowledged that he would be able to immediately notify relevant individuals responsible for taking down the ads.

“Everyone is here. Everyone can hear my order. No one is at the theater,” the judge quipped in a reference to excuses offered by government lawyers when her recent order, which was issued during a weekend, wasn't immediately obeyed.

The plaintiffs sought the removal of at least 13 ads, but Rochon only ordered that the three be pulled, at least for now. She said there are instances in which the president's office is entitled to inform the public of its policies, justify its policies and respond to attacks on its policies.
Rochon said the plaintiffs were seeking to restrict the office in ways that were “broad and far reaching” and she found herself siding with the government on many of the ads.

But she added that irreparable harm could result to the plaintiffs if she didn't ban the ads while the court case proceeds, though she noted that she could reverse herself and restore the ads or ban additional ads after hearing more evidence in the coming weeks.

“This court can neither postpone an election nor turn back the clock,” Rochon said after concluding that the plaintiffs were likely to succeed on their claims regarding the ads and would suffer harm if they were not taken down.

“This temporary restraining order will stop the administration’s wanton disregard for the law while the court hears the full case,” said Bradley Girard, a lawyer with Democracy Forward. “Congress has made clear that partisan ads cannot be funded with taxpayer dollars, and we are proud to work with this coalition to earn today’s result.”

title: Prosecutors drop felony charge against rapper Rick Ross in domestic violence case
summary: Prosecutors have dropped a felony charge against rapper Rick Ross a month after he was arrested in Miami Beach when a woman he was living with told police he hit her
story: Prosecutors have dropped a felony charge against rapper Rick Ross a month after he was arrested in Miami Beach when a woman he was living with told police he hit her

MIAMI BEACH, Fla. -- Prosecutors have dropped a felony charge against rapper Rick Ross a month after he was arrested in Miami Beach when a woman he was living with told police he hit her, court records said.

The Miami-Dade State Attorney’s Office filed paperwork Thursday to drop a felony charge of battery by strangulation because of “insufficient evidence.” Ross, whose legal name is William Roberts II, still faces a misdemeanor charge of battery domestic violence.

Ross, 50, has pleaded not guilty to all charges, and his attorney said Friday that his client would continue to defend himself against the allegations. Ross surrendered at the Miami Beach police station on Oct. 1, two days after the woman filed a report with police, officials said. He was freed on bail several hours later.

According to an arrest report, a woman told Miami Beach detectives that she had been living with Ross when he accused her of cheating on him and struck her multiple times on Aug. 28. She said Ross also choked her with the collar of her shirt and slammed her into a wall. The woman said she was eventually able to leave the home and returned later — after Ross left — to collect her belongings.

Ross previously pleaded no contest to aggravated assault in 2017 after he was accused of forcing a man into a guesthouse at his suburban Atlanta mansion in 2015 and beating him with a handgun, according to Georgia court records. Under a Georgia first-time offender program, the court issued an order exonerating Ross of guilt on that felony count.
Ross is a longtime South Florida resident who gained prominence in 2006 with his debut single “Hustlin'.”

The rapper and entrepreneur helped put Miami on the musical map in the early 2000s, when most hip-hop fans looked to Atlanta and Houston as Southern rap headquarters. “Hustlin'” was certified platinum twice by the Recording Industry Association of America and sparked a bidding war for Ross. He eventually signed with Def Jam Records, headed by Jay-Z.

Ross’ debut album, “Port of Miami,” also went platinum, debuting at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 chart. It was the first in a series of chart-toppers, including 2008’s “Trilla” and 2009’s “Deeper Than Rap.” He has been nominated for nine Grammy Awards.
In 2008, he founded the influential label Maybach Music Group, boosting the careers of signees like Wale, Meek Mill and French Montana.
His most recent album, “Set In Stone,” was released in July.

title: What to stream: Kings of Leon, 'The Greatest,' 'Possible Love' and a 'Zelda' remake
summary: A new series about Muhammad Ali and an album from Kings of Leon are among the new streaming releases this week
story: A new series about Muhammad Ali and an album from Kings of Leon are among the new streaming releases this week
A series about Muhammad Ali and a new album from Kings of Leon are some of the new television, films, music and games headed to a device near you.

Also among the streaming offerings worth your time this week, as selected by The Associated Press’ entertainment journalists: a remake of the beloved Zelda game “Ocarina of Time,” the award-winning film “Possible Love” and a documentary about the making of “Marie Antoinette.”

— There are quite a few movies coming to streaming services this week, but perhaps the highest profile is “Possible Love,” from South Korean auteur Lee Chang-dong ( “Burning” ), which is making its Netflix debut on Nov. 6. The film, which won the grand jury prize at the Venice Film Festival, revolves around two couples in South Korea, one wealthy, one not, who are brought together by a documentary.

— Also coming to Netflix, on Nov. 7, is the absurdist comedy “Gail Daughtry and the Celebrity Sex Pass,” in which a Midwestern bride-to-be (Zoey Deutch) embarks on a journey to Los Angeles to sleep with Jon Hamm.
— Any fan of Sofia Coppola or the filmmaking process will find much to admire in “Making Marie Antoinette,” a behind-the-scenes documentary that’s streaming on Mubi on Nov. 6.

— Andrew Garfield plays a farmer who leads a peasants’ revolt in medieval England in Paul Greengrass’ “The Uprising,” streaming on Peacock on Nov. 6. In his review for The Associated Press, Mark Kennedy wrote that it “mixes fact and fiction in such an anachronistic, uncomfortable way that it undercuts the movie-maker’s initial populist scream and ceases to hold its historical power.”

— Finally, for some true independent charm, there’s the documentary “Silver Screamers” about a group of senior citizens recruited to make an amateur short horror film. It’ll make its debut on the horror streamer BloodStream on Nov. 6.
— AP Film Writer Lindsey Bahr

— Kings of Leon have unplugged. After frontman Caleb Followill broke his foot playing with his kids and picked up an acoustic guitar in recovery, he had a change of heart. The four or five electric-leaning songs that he and the band had been exploring for their latest album, “O My Beloved” out Friday, were discarded. In quickly came a clutch of new stripped-down tunes, more melancholic than bombastic, about gratitude and family. “The songs just took on a different meaning, and so all the songs that we had been working on, they no longer were as attractive to me,” Followill told the AP about their pivot. “I feel like just the whole temperature changed around us. And we realized that we’re going to make something a little more significant.”

— British rapper Skepta, one of the most globally recognized names in grime music, will release “The Fork and Knife” on Friday — his first solo full-length album in seven years. The record is one for those who exist between two cultures: In the case of Skepta, it explores what it means to be British and the son of Nigerian immigrants through garage, house, jungle, electronic and, of course, grime music.

— British singer-songwriter Rex Orange County returns Friday with his sixth studio album, “Dream Fatigue.” It’s full of his sincere, dreamy pop and this time, he’s joined by an all-star list of collaborators, including Daniel Cassar, Turnstile’s Brendan Yates, Dev Hynes, Mustafa and Jockstrap’s Taylor Skye.
— AP Music Writer Maria Sherman

— “The Greatest” is the first authorized scripted series about Muhammad Ali. Jaalen Best plays the boxing legend, with Dana Gourrier, Amin Joseph, Kai Parham and Michael Ealy among the cast. Michael B. Jordan and Jay-Z are among the show's executive producers. Created by Ben Watkins, all eight episodes of the Prime Video series come out Wednesday.

— A hit Korean webtoon with nearly 3 billion views becomes a new Disney+ and Hulu series called “The Remarried Empress.” Shin Min-a stars as Empress Navier, whose husband, Emperor Sovieshu (Ju Ji-hoon), brings home a runaway concubine to make her his new wife. Navier agrees to the divorce if she gets approval to remarry as well. The first four episodes debut Wednesday, with two more released each week through November.

— Season 2 of Netflix’s British spy thriller “Black Doves” returns Nov. 5 and picks up about a year after the events of Season 1. Keira Knightley’s Helen Webb is the wife of Britain’s new prime minister, and also a spy for an organization called Black Doves. When her handler vanishes, she is determined to find her, with Ben Whishaw’s Sam Young, a tortured assassin, at her side.

— Eviction, dead-end jobs and worsening mental health pile up for three friends (Leo Reich, Emily Fairn and Olive Gray) in Paramount+'s “It Gets Worse.” Reich created the series, and Andrew Scott and Lena Dunham guest star. All episodes land Friday, Nov. 6.
— AP Writer Alicia Rancilio

— “The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time” is unquestionably a classic, so if you’ve never played it, you’re in for a treat. If you enjoyed the original back in 1998, Nintendo would like to welcome you back with enhanced controls, overhauled graphics, full voice acting and expanded cutscenes. The Switch 2 Joy-Con lets you wield some weapons with motion controls, and you can activate the ocarina’s magical melodies by humming into the device. Many Zeldaphiles regard this time-shifting epic, in which hero Link goes from a wee lad to a grown-up hunk as he defends Hyrule from the evil Ganondorf, as the franchise’s best. The remake arrives Thursday, Nov. 5.

— “Zero Parades for Dead Spies” is British studio ZA/UM’s follow-up to the 2019 cult classic “Disco Elysium.” Like its predecessor, it’s a text-heavy role-playing adventure in which your conversational choices — and occasional dice rolls — are more important than gunplay or fisticuffs. The protagonist is an agent who gets involved in a battle among political parties vying for power in a bizarre city. Expect plenty of intrigue seen through a sarcastic lens as you take on bankers, “techno-fascists” and even “a man with a box for a heart.” Switch 2, PlayStation 5 and Xbox X/S players can join in Tuesday, Nov. 3; PC players who have been on the case since May are getting an enhanced director’s cut.
— Lou Kesten

title: King Charles III arrives in Guyana as part of official 9-day Caribbean trip
summary: King Charles III has landed in the South American country of Guyana, a former British colony that was the site of one of the biggest slave revolts in the Caribbean during the colonial era
story: King Charles III has landed in the South American country of Guyana, a former British colony that was the site of one of the biggest slave revolts in the Caribbean during the colonial era

GEORGETOWN, Guyana -- GEORGETOWN, Guyana (AP) — King Charles III arrived Thursday in Guyana, a former British colony that was the site of one of the biggest slave revolts in the Caribbean during the colonial era.
Charles landed in the South American country following an invitation from Guyanese President Irfaan Ali, who has publicly requested an apology as some Caribbean leaders press for slavery reparations.
Charles, who is on a nine-day official trip in the Caribbean, descended from the plane in a tan suit and greeted Ali, who was wearing an all-ivory Jodhpuri suit.

Guyana is a diverse country of some 840,000 people that recently became one of the world’s largest offshore oil producers after massive oil deposits were discovered off its coast more than a decade ago.
About 36% of Guyana’s population is Black while 50% is East Indian, descended from indentured servants from India brought to the South American country after slavery was abolished.
Charles last visited Guyana in 2000 as a prince.
He is scheduled to meet with Ali, business owners and elected leaders of Amerindian villages known as “toshaos” during his two-day stay in Guyana.

Hilary Beckles, head of the Caribbean Reparations Commission, said at a recent press conference that the region has never been better prepared to confront Britain and the monarchy about its links to slavery.
“The region is mobilized, the governments are mobilized," he said.
The commission was established by regional governments to make Britain and other former European slave-trading nations pay reparations for their role.
In a recent interview with ITV News, Ali said Charles has “rightfully recognized slavery as the darkest days in human history.”
“Moving to the apology is the next step,” he added. “You exploited the region. You destroyed lives. You created underdevelopment.”
The British government has consistently rejected demands for either an apology or reparations.

Charles was previously in the Bahamas and is scheduled to arrive Friday in Antigua and Barbuda for the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting and meet with leaders of 56 member states. Talks are expected to focus on climate, trade and development, but some Caribbean leaders have said slavery reparations should dominate conversations.
Coto reported from San Juan, Puerto Rico.

title: Shorter days and dark afternoons can trigger depression. Here's how to fight back
summary: People prone to seasonal depression are bracing themselves as winter approaches
story: People prone to seasonal depression are bracing themselves as winter approaches
As winter approaches and daylight hours grow shorter, people prone to seasonal depression can feel it in their bodies and brains.

The millions of people estimated to have seasonal affective disorder, or SAD, typically have episodes of depression that begin in the fall and ease in the spring or summer. One trigger for SAD is when clocks revert to standard time, which happened Sunday across much of the U.S., bringing darker afternoons. A milder form, subsyndromal SAD, is recognized by medical experts, and there’s also a summer variety of seasonal depression, though less is known about it.

In 1984, a team led by Dr. Norman Rosenthal, then a researcher at the National Institutes of Health, first described SAD and coined the term. “I believe that because it is easy to remember, the acronym has stuck,” he said.

No single cause for seasonal affective disorder has been identified. The disorder affects many more women than men, according to the NIH. Symptoms can be similar to depression, and can include persistent feelings of hopelessness or pessimism and difficulty concentrating, remembering, or making decisions.

In one effort to better understand what's going on, scientists are learning how specialized cells in our eyes turn the blue wavelength part of the light spectrum into neural signals affecting mood and alertness.
Sunlight is loaded with the blue light, so when the cells absorb it, our brains’ alertness centers are activated and we feel more wakeful and possibly even happier.

Researcher Kathryn Roecklein at the University of Pittsburgh tested people with and without SAD to see how their eyes reacted to blue light. As a group, people with SAD were less sensitive to blue light than others, especially during winter months. That suggests one possible cause for wintertime depression.

Many people with SAD respond to light therapy, said Dr. Paul Desan of Yale University’s Winter Depression Research Clinic. The therapy can involve exposure to bright light for about a half hour in the morning, powered by devices that emit light about 20 times brighter than regular indoor light.

Research supports using a light that’s about 10,000 lux, a measure of brightness. You need to use it for 30 minutes every morning, according to the research. Desan said this can help not only people with SAD but also those with less-severe winter blahs.
Special lights run from $50 to more than $400. Some products marketed for SAD are too dim to do much good, Desan said.
Yale has tested products and offers a list of recommendations, and the nonprofit Center for Environmental Therapeutics has a consumer guide to selecting a light.
If your doctor diagnosed you with SAD, check with your insurance company to see if the cost of a light might be covered.
Antidepressant medications are a first-line treatment for SAD, along with light therapy. Doctors also recommend keeping a regular sleep schedule and walking outside, even on cloudy days.

Light therapy’s benefits can fade when people stop using it. One type of talk therapy — cognitive behavioral therapy, or CBT — has been shown in studies to have more durable effects, University of Vermont researcher Kelly Rohan said.
CBT involves working with a therapist to identify and modify unhelpful thoughts.

Working with a therapist can help people take small steps toward having fun again, Rohan said. Try planning undemanding but enjoyable activities to break out of hibernation mode, including getting out and seeing a friend for coffee.
Carla K. Johnson, the principal writer of this story, retired from The Associated Press in 2025.
