title: Trump library plans on collision course with Democratic Congress
summary: President Trump is expected to spend time on plans for his presidential library, but Democrats in Congress have some questions about how it's being financed.
story: As President Trump prepares for the final two years of his presidency, he is expected to devote more attention to his presidential library, which has become a growing destination for money from companies and allies, according to current and former advisers who spoke on the condition of anonymity.

"He undoubtedly recognizes that the library development season opens now, and he will go for it," said a senior administration official. A second administration official said that in this lame-duck period Mr. Trump will focus on "all things he can control, which means: Building."
With Democrats taking control of Congress in January after a sweeping victory in the November elections, lawmakers have pledged investigations into the library's finances.
"The donors bankrolling his personal vanity project will have to answer to a new majority in Congress," Sen. Elizabeth Warren, a Massachusetts Democrat, told CBS News.

In March, Mr. Trump shared renderings of a 47-story tower on a donated plot in downtown Miami. It showed golden escalators, a full-size Air Force One and a giant statue of him raising his fist, as he did after surviving an assassination attempt in Butler, Pennsylvania, in July 2024. But then he told reporters he does not "believe in building libraries or museums" and that the building is "most likely going to be a hotel," a departure from the traditional library his foundation described to the IRS last year.

The Donald J. Trump Presidential Library Foundation, a nonprofit, registered in Florida and run by Mr. Trump's son Eric and son-in-law Michael Boulos, will fund the project. The foundation says it expects to raise $950 million by the end of 2027, including $600 million in 2027 alone, according to its October 2025 IRS application, obtained by CBS News. That far outpaces what Mr. Trump's predecessors had raised at this stage.

Tens of millions of dollars have already come from media and tech companies that settled lawsuits with him. The nonprofit is also collecting donations through a payment processing company that has Donald Trump Jr. on its board, according to a fundraising portal page. And Mr. Trump has said the luxury Boeing 747 that Qatar gave the U.S. last year — now in use as Air Force One — would go to the library, though Eric Trump and the White House have since said that plan is not final.

Some of the most recent money has come from people trying to stay in Mr. Trump's good graces. After the president threatened to cut ties with his top political advisers Chris LaCivita and James Blair over their consulting work for a pro-Russian party in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the two men donated their fees from that work to the library, The New York Post reported.

A week later, The New York Times reported that Mr. Trump had told aides and allies that his former personal lawyer, Alina Habba Mildon, should donate part of a contract worth more than $50 million to his library or another Trump-related entity. Habba Mildon's contract was with a company tied to the family of a Venezuelan businessman Mr. Trump pardoned in January, the outlet reported.

Asked by CBS News whether she planned to donate some of her fees to the library, Habba Mildon responded to the text message with a "haha" reaction. (She removed the reaction seconds later and declined to comment.)

A former Trump adviser, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, said the library is now where the fundraising action is, with the midterms over and donors already tapped for the America 250 celebrations and the White House ballroom. MAGA Inc., a super PAC run by Mr. Trump's allies, started September with more than $400 million to spend on Republicans in the midterms. Its filing due in December will show how much left it has in cash on hand.
"The library is one of the last few places he can squeeze people for money," the former adviser said. "That's what a businessman does. He just creates opportunities."

Fresh scrutiny of the library is expected after Democrats swept the House and the Senate on Tuesday. Starting in January, Democrats will have the power to subpoena records and compel testimony. Rep. Robert Garcia of California, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, issued a two-word warning on X to the administration after the election results: "Lawyer up."

"Giant corporations and foreign governments should not be able to buy influence in Washington with donations to the president's library," Warren told CBS News, adding that she will be investigating the library "and any wrongdoing will be held accountable."

The library has already drawn scrutiny over Mr. Trump's stated plan to display the gifted jet. The plane's memorandum of understanding, signed in 2025 by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Qatar's Minister of State for Defense Affairs Soud bin Abdulrahman Al-Thani, called it an "unconditional donation." But when questions were raised about the U.S. accepting and using the Qatari plane as Air Force One, then-Attorney General Pam Bondi concluded that the gift could be conditioned on transferring the plane to the library foundation by Jan. 1, 2029, about three weeks before Mr. Trump leaves office.
In August, Eric Trump told NBC News that displaying the plane was "not the plan at the moment," saying a retired Air Force One would be shown instead.

A Qatari official, speaking to CBS News on the condition of anonymity, said what happens to the plane after Mr. Trump leaves office is not Qatar's concern. "This is something the Americans need to deal with," the official said.
The White House referred questions about the library and whether any final decisions have been made about the plane or a hotel to the foundation, which did not respond to requests for comment.

"The Trump Presidential Library will be one of the most magnificent buildings in the world and a living testament to the indelible impact President Trump has made on America and its people," Davis Ingle, a spokesman for the White House, said in a statement.
Tens of millions from companies Mr. Trump sued

There have been two iterations of the library's nonprofit funding structure. The first, the Donald J. Trump Presidential Library Fund, was incorporated in Florida in December 2024, days after ABC News agreed to pay $15 million toward the library to settle a defamation suit over anchor George Stephanopoulos' inaccurate on-air claim that Mr. Trump had been found civilly liable for raping writer E. Jean Carroll. A jury found him liable for sexual abuse.

Other settlements followed. Meta agreed to pay $22 million toward the library over the suspension of Mr. Trump's accounts after the Jan. 6 Capitol riot. Elon Musk's X paid $10 million to settle a similar suit by Mr. Trump and other plaintiffs. And Paramount paid $16 million over the editing of a "60 Minutes" interview with then-Vice President Kamala Harris. Paramount reached the settlement before its merger with Skydance Media. The combined company, Skydance, is CBS News' parent company.

By then, the current foundation had been incorporated in Florida in May 2025, listing Eric Trump, Boulos and James Kiley, an attorney who has represented Mr. Trump, as trustees. The original fund was dissolved that September after failing to file a required annual report. Jacob Roth, an attorney who incorporated the first fund, declined to comment.

In March, Sens. Warren, Richard Blumenthal, and Rep. Melanie Stansbury asked the four companies for details of their payments. ABC said its $15 million was still in an escrow account held by a law firm representing Mr. Trump, where it had been since December 2024, awaiting release to the foundation. Paramount said it had paid $16 million but did not say to whom. Meta said $22 million had been "designated" for the library but did not say whether or where it was paid, and X, citing confidentiality, did not say how much of its $10 million settlement went there.

Mr. Trump's financial disclosure, filed in June, lists $56.5 million in settlement money from ABC, Meta and Paramount as paid to the foundation. It lists $8 million from X as paid to Mr. Trump himself, without saying whether some funds reached the foundation. The foundation's October 2025 filing with Florida charity regulators, which it labeled a proposed budget, projected $50 million in revenue and about $6 million in spending.

Meta and ABC declined to comment. X did not respond to a request for comment. A spokesperson for Skydance referred CBS News to the company's July 2025 statement announcing the settlement, which said the $16 million included the plaintiffs' legal fees and costs and that the remainder would go to Mr. Trump's future presidential library, with nothing paid to him personally.

The settlements are not the only large gifts. SoftBank, the Japanese investment giant, told Congress in July that it gave the foundation $50 million in January to support a library exhibit highlighting U.S.-Japan relations. Two months later, Mr. Trump's Energy Department announced it would lease federal land at a former uranium enrichment plant in Ohio to an affiliate of SB Energy, a SoftBank subsidiary, for a data center campus that the company says will be the world's largest for artificial intelligence.

A spokesperson for the Energy Department said the agency signed its lease agreement with the company on Feb. 26, about a month after SoftBank's donation to the library foundation. They added that a local development group first proposed the project in October 2024, before SoftBank acquired the lease rights in the fall of 2025. SoftBank did not respond to a request for comment.
A library or a hotel?

The library foundation's filings offer few other details about how it operates. When it registered as a charity in Florida, the foundation said its officers did not expect to be paid. But in its application to the IRS, the foundation said it would pay its leaders. It projected spending $400,000 on compensation in 2025, rising to $1.2 million in 2027. The foundation's bylaws say trustees can't be paid, but other roles can come with compensation. Eric Trump is both a trustee and the foundation's president.
The foundation told CBS News it expects to file financial disclosures covering fiscal 2025 by Nov. 15. It did not respond to a question about whether Eric Trump will be paid.
Fundraising for the library is led by Meredith O'Rourke, who has worked with Mr. Trump since 2016.

The foundation also raises money through PSQ Impact, a donation platform run by PublicSquare, a company whose board includes Donald Trump Jr. The foundation's donation page says contributions will "help preserve important archives, promote civic education, and inspire generations to come." Trump Jr. began receiving $42,000 a month in consulting fees from PublicSquare in August 2024, according to Securities and Exchange Commission filings.

A spokesperson for Trump Jr. said he was not aware of the fundraising page and had no involvement in it. PublicSquare did not respond to questions about how much has been raised through the donation page or what fee, if any, it is charging for processing.

"This is just one example of many where the Trumps are set to possibly profit off something connected to Donald Trump's presidency," said Zach Everson, a researcher for the progressive consumer rights advocacy group Public Citizen.

It remains unclear what form the library will ultimately take. Mr. Trump's suggestion that it could become a hotel is cited in a lawsuit filed in May by Miami residents, a local nonprofit and a Miami Dade College student. They argue that Florida's gift of the 2.63-acre parcel, a former college parking lot, violates a U.S. constitutional provision that bars states from giving the president financial benefits.

The land was appraised at more than $67 million, but the suit cites real estate experts who say its true market value is over $300 million. The plaintiffs note that the state's terms require only that the site include "components of a Presidential library, museum, and/or center" within five years, and do not preclude a hotel.

Other presidential libraries have been built on donated public land. Chicago leased parkland for Mr. Obama's center for $10, and Little Rock used eminent domain to assemble the site for Mr. Clinton's. But Florida conveyed its parcel outright.

The Justice Department has argued that Mr. Trump is immune from the suit. In September, U.S. District Judge Rodolfo Ruiz II, a Trump appointee, halted discovery, writing that the defendants' arguments for dismissal, including presidential immunity, "may prove to be successful." He has not yet ruled on motions to dismiss the case, and a ruling may not come until March, according to Gerald E. Greenberg, a lawyer for the plaintiffs.
If the suit is dismissed, Greenberg said the plaintiffs are likely to appeal.

"This case is really about one of the core anti-corruption provisions," Greenberg told CBS News, saying the founders "understood the dangers of people currying favor with the sovereign by giving him gifts."
"It is extremely disturbing to think of our skyline and our downtown being blighted by this monument to corruption," he added.

title: Indiana carries out first of 3 U.S. executions set for Thursday
summary: An Indiana man was executed in the first of three lethal injections scheduled for Thursday in the U.S., which would mark the second time this year that three people in the U.S. were put to death on the same day.
story: An Indiana man who admitted killing his girlfriend's two children was executed early Thursday in the first of three lethal injections scheduled for the same day in the U.S.
Jeffrey Weisheit killed the children, ages 8 and 5, by setting fire to his girlfriend's house in the Evansville area in 2010.

Weisheit died at the Indiana State Prison in Michigan City. The lethal injection started just after midnight and he was pronounced dead at 12:45 a.m., according to Noelle Russell, Indiana Department of Correction chief communications officer.
She said Weisheit's final meal was barbecue ribs and he had no final words.
Florida and Alabama were also set to carry out executions Thursday, which would mark the second time this year that three people in the U.S. would be put to death on the same day.
Alabama, Tennessee and Oklahoma conducted executions on Aug. 13.
It would be Florida's 19th execution this year under Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis, matching a record set by the state in 2025, but was the first this year in Indiana.

The death penalty has faced renewed scrutiny following the September failed execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee, although courts have rejected efforts to halt other executions since she survived two lethal doses of pentobarbital.

Pike said in a statement dictated to her lawyers and released a month after the botched execution that she's been in pain every moment since she woke up confused in a hospital. "I had not contemplated life beyond that night," she said.

Lawyers wanted Indiana Republican Gov. Mike Braun to allow Weisheit, 50, to undergo brain scans in an effort to reinforce their argument that he has a history of head injuries and mental health problems. Braun declined, and he also turned down a request to reduce the sentence to life in prison.

Weisheit's latest objection centered on the state's planned use of lethal drugs purchased from a pharmacy that is facing a disciplinary hearing next week at the Indiana Pharmacy Board. The Indiana Department of Correction said it's confident "in our ability to humanely carry out" the execution.
Following the execution, Braun issued a brief statement noting Weisheit's case was reviewed many times by state and federal courts.
"These reviews have never resulted in an overturned sentence," he said. "Today, Weisheit's sentence has been carried out as ordered by the court."

Indiana Attorney General Todd Rokita said that the execution provided "long-awaited justice for Alyssa Lynch and her brother Caleb, two innocent children whose lives were stolen in an act of unspeakable cruelty."
The execution on tap in Florida

In Florida, Jesse Guardado confessed and quickly pleaded guilty to fatally stabbing a 75-year-old woman inside her Walton County home in 2004 before stealing her jewelry box, $80 and other valuables to support his drug habit. She had helped him get a job and housing.
A federal appeals court in 2024 said Guardado, now 64, had received a "full and fair" hearing during the death penalty phase of his case.

Florida has carried out more than half the 32 total executions in the U.S. so far this year. DeSantis, who leaves office in January, has said that his goal is to bring justice to families who have waited decades for the death sentences to be carried out.
Alabama's scheduled execution

Michael Taylor, 54, faces execution in Alabama, 35 years after fatally beating an older couple with a metal bar during a robbery in their Gadsden home. Police arrested the 19-year-old Taylor with the victims' Cadillac, an hour away in Birmingham. The execution would be the state's third this year.
Death penalty opponents had urged Republican Gov. Kay Ivey to reduce Taylor's sentence to life in prison, noting his age and immaturity at the time of the killings. She declined.

"If the state kills Michael, it is not the 19-year-old who made the worst mistake of his life who it kills. But the mature, well-respected, God-fearing man sitting in that cell today," said Esther Brown of Project Hope to Abolish the Death Penalty.

The state plans to execute Taylor by lethal injection after a judge declared a nitrogen gas method unconstitutional. His attorneys objected to the last-minute switch to lethal injection since he selected nitrogen gas as his method several years ago, but a judge ruled against Taylor.

title: Did Republican efforts to redistrict the House turn into a dummymander?
summary: Republicans undertook a historic effort to redraw several states' Congressional districts mid-decade in an attempt to maintain control of the House.
story: Republicans undertook a historic effort to redraw several states' Congressional districts mid-decade in an attempt to maintain control of the House. That effort was rebuffed on Tuesday night as the GOP was on track to lose all of the districts it tried to gerrymander.

There were several reasons that states undertook what had previously been a rare practice of mid-decade redistricting. Republican efforts started when President Trump ordered Texas lawmakers to redraw their map to net up to five seats for the GOP.
But despite the all-out effort, Democrats won control of the House on Tuesday, with CBS News estimating Democrats could end up with 251 to 268 House seats.

With the House decisively swinging toward Democrats and Democrats undertaking measures in a few states to counter the GOP's efforts, Republicans are faced with the possibility of having created a so-called "dummymander," a situation in which a party tries to gerrymander, but ends up benefiting the other party.
Here's a state-by-state breakdown of how the redistricting efforts panned out:
Texas

Texas Republicans went into Election Day controlling 24 seats, while Democrats controlled 13 seats and there was one seat in a GOP-leaning district that was vacant. In redrawing the map, Republicans sought to emphasize Mr. Trump's gains in South Texas to win five more seats.
As of Wednesday, Republicans had won 24 seats and Democrats had won 14 seats, making Texas a dummymander.
Ohio

A commission comprising mainly Republicans hand-picked by GOP lawmakers redrew Ohio's map to net two more seats for their party. Republicans heavily targeted longtime Democratic Rep. Marcy Kaptur's district in the northern part of the state and Rep. Greg Landsman's Cincinnati-area district.

Heading into Tuesday night, Ohio Republicans controlled 10 seats and Democrats controlled five. Seven Democrats, including Kaptur and Landsman, won Tuesday night, and CBS News estimates another district is likely Democratic. Republicans have only won seven districts, making Ohio a dummymander.
North Carolina
Although North Carolina has a Democratic governor, Republican lawmakers have a veto-proof majority in the statehouse and pushed through a new map that attempted to oust Democratic Rep. Don Davis.

North Carolina Republicans controlled 10 House seats going into Election Day, while Democrats controlled four, including Davis' district. As of Wednesday, four Democrats had won and CBS News estimated that another five were likely Democratic. Republicans had not yet won any races, with CBS News estimating one race was likely Republican and another four were toss-ups.
If Democrats ultimately win any of the undecided races, North Carolina will be a dummymander.
Louisiana

Louisiana lawmakers redrew their districts after the Supreme Court ruled in June that compliance with Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act could not justify the state's use of race in redrawing its House district lines.

Louisiana went into Election Day with four House seats controlled by Republicans and two controlled by Democrats. The new map aimed to eliminate one of the majority Black districts that currently have Democratic representatives.

As of Wednesday, Republicans had won three districts, while Democrats had won one. CBS News estimates one district is a toss-up and the state's 5th District will be going to a runoff. If Democrats win either of those districts, Louisiana will be a dummymander.
Alabama

After the same Supreme Court decision, Alabama Republicans sought to eliminate the state's two majority Black districts, both of which are represented by Democrats. Both incumbents won reelection on Tuesday, so Republicans did not net any more than the five they already controlled, making Alabama a dummymander.
Tennessee
Tennessee lawmakers also redrew their map after that Supreme Court decision to target the lone Democratic district in Nashville.

Going into Election Day, Republicans had eight seats and Democrats had one. As of Wednesday, Republicans had won six seats and two races were set to go to a runoff, including the newly drawn 9th District in Nashville. If Democrats win one or both districts, Tennessee will be a dummymander.
Florida
Led by Florida's Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis, GOP lawmakers redrew their map to net up to four more seats for their party.

Heading into Election Day, Republicans controlled 20 seats and Democrats controlled eight. As of Wednesday, Republicans had won 16 seats, Democrats had won seven and there were five districts that CBS News estimated were toss-ups. If Democrats win any of the toss-up races, Florida will be a dummymander.
Missouri

Missouri's GOP-led legislature last year redrew their map to make one of the state's two Democratic-held districts more friendly to Republicans. But the map's legality was challenged, and a state court ruled the map could not be used unless it was approved by voters. The Supreme Court three times blocked Missouri from using the new map, leaving the 2022 congressional districts in place for Tuesday's election.
Heading into Election Day, Republicans controlled six districts while Democrats held two. Democrats flipped another district, giving them three seats to the Republicans' five.
Indiana

Mr. Trump had also pushed lawmakers in Indiana to pass a map that would edge out the state's two Democratic lawmakers and make it a 9-0 Republican delegation. Despite pressure from Mr. Trump, the GOP-led state Senate rejected the new map.
Using the same boundaries as the last two cycles, Democrats held onto their two seats and flipped a third, making the state's representation 6-3.
South Carolina

South Carolina Republicans also sought to redraw their map after the Supreme Court decision in an effort to edge out powerful Democratic Rep. Jim Clyburn and make the state's representation 7-0 for Republicans. But the measure failed in the state Senate, and Clyburn won reelection on Tuesday. Two other races are considered toss-ups.
California

In response to Texas' redistricting efforts, California's Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom put forth a ballot measure to redraw the map to gain five seats for Democrats, which was decisively approved by voters.

Heading into Election Day, Democrats held 43 districts and Republicans held nine. As of Wednesday, Democrats won in 42 districts, while CBS News estimates another six are likely Democratic. Republicans have won two districts and another two are likely Republican.
Since Democrats picked up seats in California, it is a successful gerrymander for Democrats.
Utah

A judge in 2025 rejected Utah's congressional map that favored Republicans in all four districts, and then a district court rejected the redistricting map selected by the GOP-controlled legislature and instead selected a map that would create a Democratic-leaning congressional district in Salt Lake City.
Under the new map, Democrat Ben McAdams won the 1st District in Salt Lake City by 47 points.
Virginia

Virginia voters decisively approved a ballot measure in April to redraw the congressional map to favor Democrats in 10 districts and Republicans in one. But the map was thrown out by the Virginia Supreme Court, putting back in place the map drawn in 2021.

Heading into Tuesday, Democrats held six seats while Republicans held five. Using the same boundaries as the past two cycles, Democrats won seven seats, Republicans won two and two are considered toss-ups.
Maryland

Maryland's state constitution requires that congressional districts be compact and connected, and Democratic Gov. Wes Moore and other Democratic lawmakers championed a ballot initiative to remove those restraints on redistricting.
The ballot initiative, known as Question 3, passed by 20 points on Tuesday, so Democrats are likely to redraw their map now to edge out their sole GOP representative.

title: All the House districts that flipped in the midterm elections
summary: Democrats won control of the House on Tuesday by flipping more than two dozen Republican-held seats, picking up perennial swing districts and seats that were once considered deep-red.
story: Democrats won control of the House of Representatives on Tuesday by flipping more than two dozen Republican-held seats, picking up perennial swing districts and seats that were once considered deep-red. The party's wins ranged from suburban areas in the Northeastern United States to areas of South Texas that were once viewed as increasingly GOP-friendly.

The 2026 midterm elections were also shaken up by last year's nationwide mid-decade redistricting gambit, with Texas Republicans shifting several districts rightward at President Trump's behest, California Democrats moving districts to the left and several other states tweaking their House maps for partisan purposes. Democrats notched several wins under the new maps, while the GOP's pickups have been more limited so far.
Winners in dozens of races have yet to be projected by CBS News.
Here's a look at the districts that swung from one party to another:
Upsets
In several districts, Democrats ousted GOP lawmakers who won by double digits two years ago.

Missouri's 2nd District: Democrat Fred Wellman unseated GOP Rep. Ann Wagner, who won by 12 points in 2024. Republicans tried to make the St. Louis-area seat slightly redder last year, but the new maps were tossed out in the courts. As recently as September, the Cook Political Report viewed it as solid-red.Indiana's 5th District: Republican Rep. Victoria Spartz lost to Democrat J.D. Ford in one of several election night surprises. Spartz won reelection by just over 18 points in 2024.Kentucky's 6th District: The race between Democrat Zach Dembo and Republican Ralph Alvarado for the open seat was not expected to be competitive, but the election forecasters moved the GOP-held seat toward Democrats in recent weeks. Outgoing Rep. Andy Barr won it by 26 points two years ago.Wisconsin's 1st District: Republican Rep. Bryan Steil, who was first elected in 2018, lost his race to Democrat Mitchell Berman. A Democrat has not represented the district in more than 30 years. Steil won his last reelection by just over 10 points, outperforming Mr. Trump, and the Cook Political Report rated it "Likely Republican" until late September.Nevada's 2nd District: Teresa Benitez-Thompson will be the first Democrat to represent Northern Nevada in decades, after she defeated Republican David Flippo. The seat was left open by the retirement of longtime GOP Rep. Mark Amodei, who won by a nearly 19-point margin in 2024.

Indiana's 5th District: Republican Rep. Victoria Spartz lost to Democrat J.D. Ford in one of several election night surprises. Spartz won reelection by just over 18 points in 2024.

Kentucky's 6th District: The race between Democrat Zach Dembo and Republican Ralph Alvarado for the open seat was not expected to be competitive, but the election forecasters moved the GOP-held seat toward Democrats in recent weeks. Outgoing Rep. Andy Barr won it by 26 points two years ago.

Wisconsin's 1st District: Republican Rep. Bryan Steil, who was first elected in 2018, lost his race to Democrat Mitchell Berman. A Democrat has not represented the district in more than 30 years. Steil won his last reelection by just over 10 points, outperforming Mr. Trump, and the Cook Political Report rated it "Likely Republican" until late September.

Rematches
A few Democrats won against Republicans who they'd faced before — in one case, multiple times.

Scott Perry in a rematch in the district, which is centered on the state capital of Harrisburg.Virginia's 2nd District: Former Democratic Rep. Elaine Luria defeated GOP Rep. Jen Kiggans in a rematch. Luria lost to Kiggans in 2022 after redistricting made the area more favorable to Republicans. Both parties invested in districts in the Northeast, including seats with a history of swinging from one party to another, and a competitive Pennsylvania seat that was held by an overperforming Republican for a decade.

A few Midwestern states will have dramatically different congressional delegations starting next year.

The shifts coincided with a slate of statewide Democratic wins in Texas, which elected its first Democratic senator and governor in decades.

Republican Jace Yarbrough defeated Democrat Dan Barrios in the Dallas-area district.Texas' 15th District: Democratic Tejano music star Bobby Pulido defeated incumbent Rep. The district was redrawn, replacing most of De La Cruz's voters.Texas' 23rd District: Democrat Katy Padilla Stout defeated controversial Republican pro-gun personality Brandon Herrera. The district — which includes hundreds of miles of the U.S.-Mexico border — was previously considered safely Republican, but it was left open after moderate Rep. title: Democrats win House majority with Trump approval at historic low
summary: Democrats won control of the House in the 2026 midterm elections, CBS News projects, with victories in battleground districts across the country.
story: House election results for the 2026 midterms:

Democrats won control of the House in the 2026 midterm elections, CBS News projects, with victories in battleground districts across the country. The decisive wins came as President Trump's approval rating hit 38%, historically low for a president in the midterms, in an election where 89% of voters said cost of living was a major or crucial factor in their votes. GOP House Speaker Mike Johnson announced in a call with his staff that he will not run for minority leader when the new Congress is seated. Reps. Jim Jordan and Steve Scalise told Republicans they want the job.Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, the Democratic leader, said he expects his party to win at least 255 seats after all the votes are counted. He also said no one in the caucus has raised the idea of impeaching President Trump. Democrats won control of the House in the 2026 midterm elections, CBS News projects, with victories in battleground districts across the country. The decisive wins came as President Trump's approval rating hit 38%, historically low for a president in the midterms, in an election where 89% of voters said cost of living was a major or crucial factor in their votes.

GOP House Speaker Mike Johnson announced in a call with his staff that he will not run for minority leader when the new Congress is seated. Reps. Jim Jordan and Steve Scalise told Republicans they want the job.

Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, the Democratic leader, said he expects his party to win at least 255 seats after all the votes are counted. He also said no one in the caucus has raised the idea of impeaching President Trump. "We've been relentlessly focused on affordability and on accountability," he told reporters.

All 435 seats in the House of Representatives were up for election. Democrats, who had 214 seats going into the midterms, flipped a number of GOP-held seats and proved to be competitive in battlegrounds and in some unexpected places.

Democrats won in battleground districts nationwide, in North Carolina, Pennsylvania, Texas, Michigan, New York, Ohio, Kentucky and Colorado, among other states. Several dozen races still haven't been called, including some that are surprisingly close.
Republicans in several states, including Texas and Florida, had redistricted to try to gain an edge in the elections, but redrawing ultimately did not stave off their losses.

title: 2 Native American women make history in midterms
summary: In New Mexico, former Interior Secretary Deb Haaland was elected governor, making her the first Native American woman elected to lead a U.S. state. In Minnesota, Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan became the first Native American woman senator.
story: Two Native American women made history Tuesday night in the 2026 midterm elections, winning a Senate seat and a governorship — both firsts for Native women — as Democrats swept races across the country.

In New Mexico, former Interior Secretary Deb Haaland was elected governor, making her the first Native American woman elected to lead a U.S. state. In Minnesota, Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan became the first Native American woman senator.
Haaland, a citizen of Laguna Pueblo, was already the first Native American to serve as a Cabinet secretary. She defeated Republican Gregg Hull, former mayor of Rio Rancho, in the race for governor.
Flanagan, an enrolled member of White Earth Nation, defeated Republican Michele Tafoya, a former sports broadcaster and conservative commentator.
Who are they?

Haaland has notched many firsts. She became the first Native American woman to chair a state political party in 2015 when she was elected to lead the Democratic Party of New Mexico. In 2018, she became one of the first two Native American women elected to Congress, alongside Rep. Sharice Davids of Kansas, who was reelected Tuesday. Haaland later served as former President Joe Biden's Interior secretary from 2021 until January 2025.
On the trail, she spoke about raising her daughter alone, selling homemade salsa and relying at times on food stamps.
"My story is a lot like many New Mexicans — humble beginnings," she told a Rio Rancho congregation in October.

Flanagan got her start as an organizer, then served on the Minneapolis School Board and led the Children's Defense Fund Minnesota. She was elected to the Minnesota House of Representatives in 2015 and has been lieutenant governor since 2019, where she has helped reshape Minnesota's relationship with the state's 11 tribal nations.
Raised by a single mother in Section 8 housing, Flanagan had childhood asthma that kept her in and out of hospitals. She's been an outspoken supporter of Medicaid, saying that it "saved [her] life."
What do they stand for?

Haaland ran on the cost of living, protecting New Mexico's Universal Child Care program and overhauling its child welfare system. She also blamed President Trump for cuts to federal safety net programs. She has promised to issue an executive order on day one to pause the construction of new large-scale data centers until the state Legislature passes guardrails.
Flanagan drew on her own upbringing to connect with voters who are feeling financially squeezed. She ran as a progressive, backing "Medicare for All" and national paid family and medical leave.
"Minnesota, you just beat Donald Trump again," Flanagan told supporters on Tuesday night at her election watch party in St. Paul, where White Earth leaders played a victory song on a drum.
Why does it matter?

The National Congress of American Indians, the country's oldest and largest association of tribal governments, called the wins historic milestones for Indian Country. Native American women make up approximately 1% of the U.S. population, according to U.S. Census Bureau data, but have long been underrepresented in elected office.

"Long before Native women were welcomed into the halls of government, they were leading our Nations, protecting our families, and shaping the future of Indian Country," NCAI Executive Director Larry Wright Jr. said in a statement to CBS News.

"For young Native girls across Indian Country, these victories send an important message: their voices matter, their leadership is essential, and they belong wherever possibilities are reimagined," said Wright.

He added that he hopes that representation translates into "meaningful progress," in particular, protecting tribal lands and honoring treaty obligations between the U.S. government and tribal nations.

A third Native American woman could soon join Haaland and Flanagan in making history this midterm election. In Alaska, Democrat Mary Peltola, who is Yup'ik, is in a Senate race with incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan that remains a toss-up, according to CBS News estimates. The outcome may not be decided until ranked-choice tabulation later this month.

title: DFL trifecta 2.0: Democrats win full control of Minnesota government
summary: Democrats flipped the Minnesota House and won the governor's race, returning the DFL to a trifecta after two years of divided government. The results, however, remain unofficial.
story: Minnesota Democrats won back control of both chambers of the Legislature on Tuesday, delivering the second "trifecta" in state government in four years, according to unofficial results.

The Associated Press called at least 37 state Senate seats for the Democratic-Farmer-Labor Party, which is an improvement over their one-seat majority in the 67-member chamber. DFL leaders are claiming victory in 39 districts; two races where Republicans prevailed by single digits are headed towards an automatic recount.
In the House — which was previously tied between Democrats and Republicans — the DFL has at least 77 seats, according to the AP.

With the election of DFL U.S. Sen. Amy Klobuchar to be the next governor, Democrats have total control of state government. They first won back a trifecta in the 2022 election, but their margins were much tighter.

"We are very sure that we will have a large majority — the largest majority in the House since the Obama era," said DFL House Leader Zack Stephenson late Tuesday night when votes were still being counted.
"I think it's an overwhelming display of frustration that people had with the Trump administration and with Republican governance," he said of the blue wave in Minnesota and nationally.

In 2023 and 2024 — the last time the Democrats controlled the Capitol — they passed a slate of progressive priorities, including universal free school meals, legal marijuana, abortion rights protections, paid family and medical leave, gun safety bills like a red flag law and expanded background checks and more.

The agenda for next year is still in the works and will come into sharper focus soon after each caucus meets. But both Stephenson and Senate Majority Leader Erin Murphy said affordability, especially when it comes to health care, is top of mind.

"The first thing we have to do is to address the cost of living for people, and that's not going to happen in one bill," Murphy told reporters. "We have a lot of work to do for the people of Minnesota in health care, in housing, and in child care. And those issues are going to take some time."
But when it comes to gun regulations, Democrats have already promised to pass a package that includes a ban on assault-style weapons and high-capacity magazines to Governor-elect Klobuchar's desk.

That bill passed the Senate but failed to clear the House earlier this year and it is a push from some families of Annunciation Catholic School, where a gunman killed two children and injured more than two dozen others during school mass last summer.

Klobuchar said she spent time with the parents of Harper Moyski, who was killed in the shooting at just 10-years-old, on Tuesday night before she joined the DFL Party on election night. It was what would have been her 12th birthday.

"I think the gun safety bill is going to get passed and I am so excited to be working with the leaders on this. And it certainly should be one of our top priorities," Klobuchar told reporters Wednesday.

Republicans were disappointed with the results. They believed the fraud scandal plaguing social services programs would help them break their 20-year losing streak statewide office and earn the trust of voters to lead at the Capitol.

"With another trifecta on the horizon, Senate Republicans remain committed to holding state government accountable and putting Minnesotans first," said Sen. Mark Johnson, the Republican minority leader, in a statement.

Klobuchar's election means a new negotiator at the table with lawmakers when they work to pass the next state budget next legislative session. She said she already talked to all four legislative leaders — including Republicans.
She vowed to include the minority in negotiations, even if Democrats can pass bills without GOP votes.

"I was No. 1 for bipartisan bills, No. 3 for passing bills into law — you don't get to that stage in the U.S. Senate if you don't understand the value of working with people both on the Republican side and in the same caucus that you maybe don't always agree with," she told reporters. "And I am going to put a huge priority on this as we set our priority going forward, because I believe for our state, the stakes couldn't be more high right now."

Klobuchar also said she knows she will spar with members of her own party who may be further to the left than she is. Some progressives want to raise taxes, like on social media companies, when they get power back in January. Klobuchar has said she does not want to raise any taxes.

"I see every day in my own caucus in the U.S. Senate, you're going to see people with different views," she said. "And the most important thing to me is that people know where I am coming from and the fact that I have been consistent from the beginning, including last night, in front of the entire celebration — which was an ongoing and never-ending celebration for the Democratic Party nationally and in the DFL — I actually said, spoiler alert, you're not going to like everything I do."
When asked what he thinks his caucus may not like, Stephenson said the focus Tuesday was on the celebration for Democrats commanding victories.
"We're focusing on affordability. We got a lot of things that we know we can do," he said.

title: 2 women advanced further in Navy SEAL tryouts than any in history
summary: Though the two dropped out in the third or fourth week, no woman had previously made it to the third week of the Navy SEAL endurance tests before this year.
story: Washington —  Two women attempting to become Navy SEALs advanced further through the military's grueling training pipeline than any women before them, making history despite ultimately failing to complete the demanding course at Naval Amphibious Base Coronado in California.

An enlisted sailor and a naval officer entered Basic Underwater Demolition/SEAL, or BUD/S, training several weeks ago, multiple sources told CBS News. Both had made it to the third week of training, with Hell Week, the infamous 5 1/2-day endurance test starting in the fourth week. CBS News has learned the officer was rolled back to the next class and ultimately requested to be dropped from the course before Hell Week and the enlisted sailor was medically pulled from Hell Week.
While the two women did not pass the SEAL course, they made it further than any other woman who has tried since special operations opened its doors to women in 2016.
CBS News is withholding the names of the candidates for security and privacy reasons.

Gaining access to Hell Week is a feat of its own because nearly half of all candidates, about 45%, are either removed or rolled back to the next class during training in the first few weeks prior to Hell Week, according to data compiled by the Navy between 1998 and 2023 and released through the Freedom of Information Act. Hell Week is widely considered one of the most physically and mentally demanding portions of the initial training, which lasts roughly six months.

Hell Week is designed to test the physical and mental limits of candidates. After starting in the middle of the night, candidates get about four hours of sleep over the next five days and complete tasks like carrying logs, launching boats into crashing waves, lying in cold ocean water and running around 200 miles.

A spokesperson for Naval Special Warfare Command said: "To protect the integrity of NSW Center courses and the privacy of its candidates, we don't discuss the details of any individual selection or non-selection status or where they are in the training pipeline."

Long before the Pentagon formally opened all combat positions to women in 2016, women have served alongside U.S. special operation forces. As far back as World War II, women helped gather intelligence or coordinate supply drops and combat raids for the Office of Strategic Services, the predecessor to the CIA and U.S. Special Operations Command.

In 1988, the Defense Department adopted the "Risk Rule" policy that restricted women from assignments based on their exposure to combat-related dangers, but during the Persian Gulf War, some women did experience combat though they had officially been assigned to  "non-combat" roles.

Their service in the Gulf War led Congress to repeal the combat aviation exclusion in December 1991, which allowed women to serve in combat aviation roles. In 1994, Defense Secretary Les Aspin rescinded the risk rule policy but kept in place the exclusion that barred women from serving in direct ground combat units below the brigade level.

Almost two decades later, Defense Secretary Leon Panetta rescinded the 1994 policy, removing gender-based combat assignment restrictions. By 2016, women were allowed to try out to become Navy SEALs, Army Rangers and Green Berets.

Over the last decade, thousands of women have joined infantry, armor and artillery units, but relatively few have attempted to qualify for elite special operations units, with only a handful having successfully completed the rigorous selection and training programs over the past decade.

The demands of the Navy SEAL training pipeline weeded out about 68% of candidates at various stages of training, according to Navy data between 1998 and 2023. The highest attrition occurred during the program's seven-week first phase — which includes Hell Week — where 66% of candidates were removed or rolled into another class.

Nearly half of each incoming class — about 45% — do not make it through the three weeks preceding Hell Week — some 29% voluntarily withdraw from the course. Despite Hell Week's reputation as one of the military's most punishing endurance tests, more candidates drop out during the preceding weeks than during Hell Week.

Around 21% left during Hell Week either because they asked to leave or had medical or performance issues. The figures suggest that nearly four out of five candidates who began Hell Week were able to finish it.

Attrition declined sharply during the later training stages, with 5% during the second phase, which emphasizes combat diving, and 3% during the third phase, which focuses on land warfare. Under 1% leave during the rigorous six-month SEAL Qualification Training course, which is the final leg of the pipeline before they are assigned to a SEAL team.

In 2021, a sailor became the first woman to graduate from the Naval Special Warfare training pipeline to become a Special Warfare Combat Crewman, according to previous reporting by CBS News. The Navy said that historically only about 35% of candidates attempting to join their ranks make it to graduation.

The Navy's Special Warfare Combatant-Craft Crewmen, known as SWCCs, are elite maritime operators training to operate high-speed, heavily armed boats that transport Navy SEALs into and out of hostile territory, along with other maritime missions. While they undergo separate selection and training courses, SWCCs are part of Naval Special Warfare Command.
Outside of naval special warfare, women have successfully navigated other rigorous special operation training pipelines.

Seventeen women have attempted to become Marine Raiders under Marine Forces Special Operations Command but none had passed as of 2024, according to the Military Times, which also reported that 54 women in the Air Force had entered training to join special operation jobs. Only a handful have completed the training.

In 2020, a National Guard soldier became the second woman to finish the Army's Special Forces Qualification Course and move on to a Green Beret team — the first was Capt. Kathleen Wilder in 1980, who retired as a lieutenant colonel, according to the Army Times. Less than 10 women have earned the Green Beret, according to a 2023 report from Military.com

Fewer than a dozen women have joined the historic 75th Ranger Regiment – an elite special operations Army unit that specializes in high-risk raids, airfield seizures and large-scale combat operations. Everyone who serves in the regiment has to pass the selection process and the grueling tests during Ranger School no matter the position.

One of those women is former Capt. Hailey Gibbons, a West Point graduate who completed Ranger School in 2021. She served as a logistician in the 75th Ranger Regiment until she left the military in 2023.

"If you're a logistician, if you're comms guide, military intelligence, everyone is a Ranger in that formation," Gibbons told CBS News in an interview. "And so I was like, I want to be a part of the team. I don't just want to assist the team."

Women have faced resistance from the military community in serving in combat roles and trying out for special operations, and that's still the case. As the two women were making their way through the initial weeks of BUD/S, they were criticized on social media by some former SEALs and military focused accounts.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has repeatedly questioned whether women should serve in ground combat and special operations roles, arguing that their inclusion could undermine military effectiveness and physical standards.

Shortly before he was nominated for the position, the former Fox News host and National Guard veteran said "we should not have women in combat roles" in a podcast interview with Shawn Ryan, who is a former Navy SEAL. In his confirmation hearing, Hegseth said women would have access to ground combat roles, "given standards remain high."
He offered no example of how standards had been lowered but said he's been told by service members that standards have changed "in ways direct, indirect, overt, and subtle."

Earlier this year, the Pentagon commissioned a study to review the effectiveness of women in ground combat roles. In a statement given to CBS News in January, Pentagon press secretary Kingsley Wilson said the study was "to ensure standards are met and the United States maintains the most lethal military."
Gibbons told CBS News the standards have not changed for special operations despite Hegseth's indirect claims.

"When he's saying that the standards have changed and that people have lowered standards to allow women into their formations, it's absolutely a lie because no brigade commander would sign off on that — because then they would be looked at as less than and as someone who they can't trust," Gibbons said.

title: The 2026 blue wave, in charts
summary: Compared to the 2024 presidential race, Democratic senators-elect won by larger margins in the 2026 midterms, while Republicans won by smaller ones.
story: Democrats will now control the Senate and the House of Representatives after the 2026 midterm elections. Of the 35 Senate races on the ballot, 33 have been projected so far and 20 of those went blue. Eight of them were in states that voted for President Trump in 2024. Voters in seven states flipped a previously Republican-held Senate seat to a Democrat.
Senate elections in Alaska and Mississippi are still considered toss-ups.

But even in states where Republican senators won, the margins were lower than might have been expected. For example, in West Virginia, Mr. Trump won in 2024 by 42 percentage points. In this year's midterms, Republican incumbent Sen. Shelly Moore Capito won by about 20 points — the winning margin was cut in half.

Alabama's Barry Moore won his Senate race by about 9 points in a state Mr. Trump won in 2024 by more than 30 points. In Florida, where Mr. Trump won by 13 points in 2024, GOP Sen. Ashley Moody won reelection by just 3 points. (The 2026 figures are as of Nov. 4, with 99% of votes in.)
But the opposite was true for Democratic candidates. Kamala Harris won Rhode Island in 2024 by about 14 points, but Sen. Jack Reed won reelection in the 2026 midterms by 37 points.
In fact, in states where Democrats won Senate races in the 2026 midterms, average margins were twice as large as Harris' winning margins in the 2024 presidential election.

Republicans' average margins were half as large as Mr. Trump's winning margins in 2024. In states where voters changed sides between the 2024 presidential election to the 2026 Senate elections, all went to Democrats, who gained roughly 20 points.

title: Mamdani says Democrats must keep their "foot on the gas"
summary: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani — one of the most influential members of the Democratic Party's leftward flank — said Wednesday that the left must now keep its "foot on the gas."
story: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani — one of the most influential members of the Democratic Party's leftward flank — said Wednesday that "this country has elected a new generation of leadership" in the midterms, and the left must now keep its "foot on the gas."
"Going through yesterday evening, it's a realization that it's a new dawn in America," Mamdani told reporters.
Mamdani suggested that Democrats' decisive wins in the House and Senate mean the party "can go from being on the defensive to being on the offensive."

"The defensive means trying to prevent as many New Yorkers as possible from losing their SNAP benefits or losing their health insurance," Mamdani said, taking aim at the Republican-backed One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which cut back some of those programs.
"The offensive is delivering to make life more affordable for them," continued Mamdani, whose platform is centered on lowering costs for New Yorkers.

Democrats last won a majority in the Senate in 2022. This time around, the party has flipped at least seven Republican-held seats, some of which are in deep-red territory. The party also flipped dozens of House districts.
"We have to use that power to deliver change that Americans can feel in their wallets," the mayor said.

Mamdani, who rose to the national spotlight through his mayoral campaign in 2025, flexed his influence in the primaries by endorsing three progressive House candidates in deep-blue New York City districts. All three — Brad Lander, Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier — won their respective races on Tuesday. Lander and Avila Chevalier will unseat incumbent Democrats whom they defeated in the primaries.

Valdez and Avila Chevalier are members of the Democratic Socialists of America, along with Mamdani, who said he "can't wait to count on them as partners for our affordability agenda at the federal level."

Two fellow New Yorkers who don't hail from the Democratic Party's progressive wing could play an outsized role in Congress starting next year: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, who are seeking to lead their respective chambers come January.
On Wednesday, Jeffries announced his candidacy for speaker of the House, while Schumer told reporters on the same day that he believes he will be elected as Senate majority leader.
"I think that having leaders in Washington be from our city and of our city is of incredible importance to our city," Mamdani said.

"Because for them, the struggles of New Yorkers are not intellectual concerns or ones that are being mediated through the prism of media or politics. It is one that they experience and hear from their constituents about every single day."
Mamdani said he spoke with Jeffries to congratulate him on the victories across the board and added that the two "have a good working relationship."

title: Midterm elections could zap the data center buildout, experts say
summary: Democratic victories in several gubernatorial races are likely to slow data center development across the U.S., according to tech analysts.
story: The Democrats' sweeping victories in the midterm elections on Tuesday could buoy opponents of data centers in some parts of the U.S. and slow the spread of the controversial facilities, according to Wall Street analysts.

As of Wednesday afternoon, voters had approved 38 ballot measures restricting data centers in communities across California, Illinois, Maine, Ohio, New York and other states, according to an analysis from political research firm Redbud Consulting. Residents in Harwood, North Dakota, were the only voters to approve a data center.
The election also elevates a number of state and gubernatorial candidates who made stricter regulation of data centers a key part of their campaigns.

The rapid development of data centers around the U.S. to help power artificial intelligence has provoked widespread public backlash. By a margin of more than 2-to-1, more Americans oppose than favor building a new data center in their area, a CBS News poll found this summer.
Focus on Texas

Franklin Templeton chief market strategist Stephen Dover predicted that the election results will lead to a "slowdown in data centers being built," bringing new regulations and costs for their developers.

"For tech investors, the big focus is will these midterm elections slow the pace of the planned 800 to 1,000 data centers across the U.S. fueling the AI Revolution," Yorkville Ives & Co. technology analyst Dan Ives said in a report. "The answer in our view is a clear YES."

Ives pointed to Texas, which accounts for 25% to 30% of the data center capacity expected to come online by 2030, as one state that could be affected. Democrat Gina Hinojosa, who defeated Republican incumbent Greg Abbott in the race for governor, proposed a temporary ban on data center construction during her campaign.
"Texas is the foundation of the AI buildout in the U.S.," Ives told CBS News.
Hinojosa's win over Abbott could stall the addition of 13 gigawatts of data-center power in Texas, according to Gordon Johnson, CEO and founder of the investment adviser GLJ Research.
Abbott had already suspended data center approvals, which makes it easy for Hinojosa to extend the moratorium.
"Texas already has a moratorium — Abbott built it. All the new governor has to do is keep it in place. She doesn't need a new law to keep data center permits frozen," Johnson told CBS News.
Keisha Lance Bottoms' gubernatorial victory in Georgia, the third-largest data center market, also has significant implications for the infrastructure buildout.

Bottoms, who campaigned on pausing new data center construction in the state, told CBS Mornings on Wednesday that she would immediately "sign an executive order for that pause, and then we will determine what else we need to do administratively to take that pause into effect."
Bottoms also said she plans to review tax incentives offered in Georgia that have spurred data center development.

"So, of course, we are going to have to take a look at what those agreements entail and determine what our remedies are to enact that pause, but I don't think we're going to get a lot of pushback across the state," she said. "Many local governments have already taken that first step."
Cooling an overheated sector

Market analyst Adam Crisafulli of Vital Knowledge noted that semiconductor, hardware and other stocks associated with data center construction fell sharply on Wednesday amid investor concerns over permitting delays.

Seema Shah, chief global strategist at Principal Asset Management, thinks data center developers could face additional requirements to invest in electrical grids and potentially lose tax incentives, thereby raising their costs. She added in a research note that higher development costs for new facilities could "increase the value of existing infrastructure that is already powered, permitted, and operational."

Massive investment in data centers and the artificial intelligence sector more broadly has helped propel U.S. economic growth and drive stock market gains. In the long term, however, a slower data center buildout is unlikely to hamstring the economy, Dover of Franklin Templeton told CBS News.

"It's possible to argue that the AI trade and data center buildout was getting overheated, and this could dampen some of the excessive investment that might not have a good return on capital, which investors have questioned anyway," he said. "So unbridled expansion will be tempered a bit, but probably not a lot."
Although data center moratoriums may delay construction, they're unlikely to torpedo capital spending on AI or short-circuit broader growth, according to economists.

"A more restrictive stance toward data centers would stretch the timelines of future projects, and slower construction in the medium to long term wouldn't necessarily be a bad outcome for the macroeconomy," analysts with Oxford Economics said in a report.

title: Democrats' election rout is poised to reorder federal health policy
summary: Democrats' retaking of Congress doesn't change President Trump's control of the veto pen — making the new majority's aspirations to reverse changes to Medicaid, the Affordable Care Act, and other safety net programs an uphill climb.
story: Democrats' decisive sweep of the U.S. House and Senate in Tuesday's elections will reshape the direction of federal health policy — setting the stage for oversight investigations, a legislative push to reverse cuts to the Affordable Care Act and Medicaid, and a focus on lowering costs such as insurance premiums and drug prices.

The conclusive string of victories sets up Democrats to argue that voters — who said in preelection surveys that healthcare affordability was a top concern — have given them a clear mandate to overturn historic cuts President Trump and Republicans made to public healthcare programs.

The breadth of success, including wins by Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan and other progressives, is likely to embolden some Democrats to forge ahead with ambitious policy proposals such as expanding Medicare, the federal insurance program for people age 65 and older, to cover all Americans. Their plan is to be positioned as the party that prioritizes lowering healthcare costs for the 2028 presidential election.

Party leaders, though, will need buy-in from Mr. Trump to advance any healthcare agenda. While he has veto power, he may be interested in brokering legislative deals as he seeks to cement his legacy and deflect fallout from investigations into his administration's handling of the war against Iran, mass deportations, contracting scandals, and other controversies.

Democrats were projected to win at least 237 of 435 seats in the House and at least 54 Senate seats as of Wednesday afternoon, according to The Associated Press. Several key races remained unresolved, including Senate contests in Alaska and Mississippi.

As election results continued coming out into early-morning Wednesday, Mr. Trump said in a phone interview with Politico that he had spoken with Democratic Party leaders and that voters had sent a message he must work with them "to make sure things go well for our country."
"I don't want to just be sitting there for two years vetoing everything," Mr. Trump said. "They want to see things happen, too."

But how Mr. Trump's new conciliatory position plays out in undoing GOP-led changes, such as new work requirements for many adults enrolled in Medicaid, the state-federal program for low-income and disabled people, remains to be seen. Republicans touted their overhaul of Medicaid and other changes to health programs wrought by their One Big Beautiful Bill Act as signature achievements in midterm campaigns.

Democrats, however, will have to carefully balance their policy moves against their desire to investigate a host of concerns surrounding the nation's top health official, Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has dismantled U.S. vaccine recommendations, gutted the staff of federal health agencies, and cut public health funding.

"Democrats will put forward an expansive healthcare agenda, including reversal of cuts to Medicaid and the ACA, but achieving all of that will be impossible with President Trump still in the White House," said Larry Levitt, an executive vice president at KFF, a health information nonprofit that includes KFF Health News.
New year, new Congress, new majority

An early order of business for Democrats in 2027 will likely be a legislative push to restore enhanced subsidies that reduced the price millions of people paid for Obamacare health plans. The larger subsidies were created during the covid-19 pandemic, as part of economic relief programs, but ended last year after Mr. Trump and the Republican-controlled Congress declined to extend them.

Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the current Democratic House leader widely expected to become speaker of the House, told CNN on Wednesday that the party should bring back the subsidies to help struggling families.

"My guess is it would be rolled into a broader budget negotiation or package that may or may not involve other healthcare priorities, like restoring Medicaid cuts or other things that are priorities for Democrats," said Sabrina Corlette, a co-director of the Center on Health Insurance Reforms at Georgetown University.

If they act decisively, said Leslie Dach, who chairs the Democratic-aligned advocacy group Protect Our Care, Democrats could both renew the ACA's expired subsidies and extend the enrollment period for 2027 coverage, which ends in most states on Jan. 15, shortly after the new Congress is scheduled to be sworn in.
They would need to act within days of assuming control, Dach said.

"Congress will be sworn in during open enrollment, at a time when people will be having to make difficult and horrific choices about their healthcare, given the further increases in premiums due to the Republicans," he said.
Premiums for Affordable Care Act benchmark plans are set to increase by an average of 13% for 2027, according to KFF researchers.

With Congress likely to pass another short-term government funding bill in December, the stage will be set for incoming lawmakers to also fight a battle over Medicaid spending cuts in the spring, said Rodney Whitlock, a healthcare consultant who previously worked for Republicans in Congress.

Democrats — many of whom put healthcare affordability at the center of their election campaigns — are now well positioned to place that issue at the center of negotiations with President Trump over federal spending.

"If you've got the opportunity for a battle in March over fiscal year funding — and Democrats picking and choosing what they want to make this first battle about with a unified, controlled Congress with the president — damn, doesn't it scream healthcare?" Whitlock said. "Doesn't it scream repeal or delay all the Medicaid cuts?"
Allison Orris, a partner at Manatt, advised clients before Election Day not to count on anything changing — even with Democrats in control.

"The White House ultimately will have to sign any legislation, and HR 1 was a signature accomplishment. It will cost money to undo or even just delay changes that were enacted in 2025," she said, referring to the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
What else could happen?

President Trump is likely to continue leaning heavily into executive actions to shape health policy from the White House. Democrats, meanwhile, will use their control of Congress to exercise oversight of the Trump administration and the Department of Health and Human Services.

Jeffries, the House Democratic leader, has promised the party will "hold the crooks accountable" by pursuing aggressive oversight of the Trump administration. Democrats on the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform put out a report in June previewing investigations they may launch.

Specifically, Democrats want to zero in on clandestine drug-pricing deals Mr. Trump has made with pharmaceutical companies in return for relief from certain tariffs. No contracts or paperwork on the agreements have been made public. They also claim he benefited from stock prices that rose when companies received exemptions from price negotiation in Medicare under the 2025 GOP tax and spending law.

By taking control of congressional committees, Democrats will gain subpoena power, an important investigatory tool. But it's unclear whether they can successfully pry documents from the government or companies because the Department of Justice, under Mr. Trump, is largely in charge of enforcing subpoenas. Nevertheless, subpoenas are likely to be issued regarding investigations into tariffs Trump has imposed and threatened to impose on prescription drugs.
Democratic congressional leaders will also be able to file lawsuits against the Trump administration to challenge the White House's actions.

Democrats also have telegraphed plans to probe scientific decision-making around such controversial issues as allowing more sales of flavored vapes and White House promotion of the herbicide glyphosate — and any connections these actions have had to political contributions from companies.

Other industry oversight by Democrats would likely focus on preauthorization denials by insurance companies; scrutiny of Medicare Advantage, an alternative program to traditional Medicare run by commercial insurers; and the use of artificial intelligence in medical decision-making.

Also looming is a wider discussion of universal health coverage, including partial steps such as expanding traditional Medicare benefits to include dental and hearing care and lowering the Medicare eligibility age to 60 or younger.

Expanding the program to cover all Americans faces formidable challenges, even if Mr. Trump were open to it. Much of the nation's healthcare industry — including doctors, hospitals, and insurers — would surely fight any legislative effort, and Democrats have never seriously grappled with the enormous implications of such a proposal for the federal budget, taxes, medical care, and broader society.

Other possible initiatives include implementing a federal solution to address the 10 states that have opted not to fully expand Medicaid to cover lower-income adults, as well as allowing children to remain on their parents' health insurance policies beyond age 26.

Because the new Congress is not set to be sworn in until January, a lame-duck session through year's end, for which Republicans retain the majority, will focus on funding the federal government and addressing some health programs set to expire.

One major move Congress is expected to make soon: a confirmation vote for Heidi Overton to lead the Food and Drug Administration, which has been without a top leader since May. Her confirmation is not guaranteed, however, with Democrats uniformly in opposition.

A handful of Republicans have questioned whether she will sufficiently restrict access to medication abortion, while some more moderate Republicans have expressed concerns, too — including Sen. Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, who questioned whether Overton supports the administration's changes to vaccine recommendations.
Cassidy lost his seat after Mr. Trump endorsed a Republican primary challenger, Rep. Julia Letlow, who narrowly won election to the Senate on Tuesday.

Other issues enjoy bipartisan support, such as preventing cuts to Medicare payments to doctors, scheduled to begin Jan. 1, and making fixes to the No Surprises Act, a federal law that took effect in 2022 to protect consumers with private insurance from unexpected, out-of-network charges. But movement would be a long shot.
"Everyone gets hyped up for lame ducks, and they're always a disappointment," said Doug Holtz-Eakin, an economist and the president of the conservative-leaning American Action Forum.

But come January, Washington will need to find a way to work together to make healthcare more affordable — or risk ire from voters who have consistently ranked it as one of their top issues in recent elections, noted Matt Hogan, a partner at Impact Research, a Democratic polling firm.
When put together, healthcare and prescription drug prices are the top cost concern for voters older than 50, he noted.

Reining in prescription drug prices could be an area with bipartisan support — including from Mr. Trump, who claimed ahead of the midterms that lowering some drug prices was one of his administration's greatest achievements. Both parties have proposed limits on pharmacy benefit managers, which negotiate drug prices on behalf of insurers and employers; patent restrictions for certain drugs; and the benchmarking of U.S. drug prices against the prices other countries pay.
"This is the third-straight election that's really been focused on affordability," Hogan said. "If members of Congress haven't got the message yet, I expect them to now."

KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF — the independent source for health policy research, polling, and journalism.

title: Trump asking advisers if Hegseth should go, sources say
summary: President Trump has been asking his advisers if Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth should remain in his job after Tuesday's losses.
story: Washington — President Trump has been asking advisers around him and on the phone whether Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth should stay in his job, following Republicans' catastrophic losses Tuesday night, multiple sources familiar with the matter tell CBS News.

Some White House aides have predicted some of the blame for GOP midterm losses will be trained on Adm. Brad Cooper, the head of U.S. Central Command, and Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Dan Caine, who both played big roles in guidance on the Iran war.

Still, other sources said the president hasn't decided to replace Hegseth. Before the election, Democrats were already trying to impeach Hegseth, and the likelihood of an impeachment effort could increase with Democrats holding strong majorities in both chambers.
Vice President JD Vance is blaming the war for the GOP defeat. "The reason we lost is the war," he said in a lengthy post on X Wednesday morning.

One source told CBS News that GOP Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis is being floated as a possible replacement for Hegseth, arguing DeSantis could go through Senate confirmation in the lame-duck period and then take the post when his term as governor expires Jan. 5.

Mr. Trump was asked Wednesday afternoon whether he was considering replacing Hegseth, and he told reporters, "No, I think he's doing a very good job." The president was also asked if he'd like to see Hegseth appointed to fill the seat that will be vacated by Tennessee Sen. Marsha Blackburn when she takes office as governor. "I actually think he'd be very popular if he did that," Mr. Trump said, "but I haven't heard that at all."

Asked for comment about reports that Hegseth's future as defense secretary was in question, White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly said in a statement that the president "has full confidence in Secretary Hegseth." In the statement, Kelly also praised the military operations in Iran and Venezuela and Hegseth's efforts to reverse the Biden Pentagon's prioritizing of "DEI and woke ideology."
