title: 1 dead, 2 injured in helicopter crash near Mount Everest base camp
summary: The two helicopters were ferrying trekkers who had been hiking up to Everest base camp during Nepal's popular trekking season.
story: Two helicopters collided Tuesday while trying to land just below Mount Everest's base camp, killing at least one person and injuring two others, officials said.

The aircraft were ferrying trekkers who had been hiking up to Everest base camp during Nepal's popular trekking season. Heavy snow had covered the route before the weather improved Sunday and thousands of trekkers were able to move around.
There are no roads on Everest, and helicopters are the only way to bring down trekkers and guides who become sick or exhausted in the cold and high altitude.
The helicopters crashed at Pheriche village, which is at an altitude of 13,780 feet.

A 47-year-old tourist from India was killed in the crash, according to Bhupendra Thapa, a Solukhumbhu district administration officer. Arrangements were being made to airlift the tourist's remains to Kathmandu, the Agence France-Presse reported.
A passenger from New Zealand was injured and was being transported to the capital, Kathmandu, for treatment. A Nepali pilot sustained injuries but was treated locally.
The number of people on the two helicopters wasn't clear.

The Mount Everest base camp trek lasts up to two weeks and goes from the only airstrip in the area at Lukla to base camp located at 17,380 feet. Everest's summit is at an altitude of over 29,000 feet. The trek is popular during the fall season, right after the rainy season and before the harsh winter months.

The helicopter collision is the second incident along the route to Everest Base Camp this week. On Friday, Octo. 30, a fire broke out at a hotel in Dingboche, which is known as a stop for trekkers to pause while they acclimate to Everest's high altitude.

The fire may have been sparked by a cooking gas cylinder explosion, local media reported. Guests and hotel staff were safely evacuated. No injuries or fatalities were reported. Video obtained by CBS News shows the building in flames.
Dingboche is about 2 miles from Pheriche. The two destinations are about a 40-minute hike from each other, according to trail guides.

title: Soccer player dies following on-field collision in Spain
summary: Spanish police have opened an investigation into possible involuntary manslaughter after a soccer player died following an on-field collision in a match.
story: A Spanish soccer player's death is now under investigation as possible involuntary manslaughter, after he suffered a fatal injury in an on-field collision during a match.
The country's National Police said Tuesday that proceedings were opened and prosecutors will also be involved.
Tenerife forward Jesús de Miguel died after he suffered cardiac arrest from the on-field collision in a Spanish second-division match, his club said. He was 30 years old.
De Miguel was challenging for the ball near midfield on Monday when he was struck in the chest by the onrushing Andorra goalkeeper Jesús Owono during added time.
Owono was shown a straight red card for the incident.
De Miguel was taken to a hospital and the match, tied 2-2, was abandoned after the incident.

Tenerife said in a statement to Spanish media late Monday that De Miguel suffered cardiac arrest but that his pulse was restored in the ambulance to the hospital. However, it later said his condition had "worsened neurologically" and subsequently announced that De Miguel had died at 8 a.m.
The club, located on Spain's Canary Islands, said it was "heartbroken."

"There are no words of comfort; there is absolutely nothing that can alleviate this feeling overflowing with sadness," the club wrote, in part, in a statement announcing the death on social media. "The family of Jesús de Miguel thanks each and every one of the expressions of support received, and likewise requests, from the heart, the utmost respect for their privacy in these terrible moments."
De Miguel, a Madrid native, made his professional debut in 2015 with Leganés B and has since played for a number of lower-divisions clubs in Spain. He joined Tenerife last year.

"There are no words of comfort," the club statement read. "There is absolutely nothing that can alleviate this profound sense of sorrow. We stand with his devastated family, his loved ones, and the entire Tenerife community."
The heavy collision happened when Owono rushed out of his area all the way to midfield to challenge for a long ball that De Miguel was trying to reach.
De Miguel initially curled on his knees, clutching his torso for a few seconds, before he fell over onto his back, with his arms falling to his sides.
Owono was walking off the field after being shown the red card but turned around and joined the other players rushing to check on De Miguel.
Andorra, which is owned by former Barcelona star Gerard Pique, also offered its condolences, along with other clubs, the Spanish soccer federation and La Liga.
"We wish to extend our deepest condolences to the family of Jesús de Miguel, to all his colleagues and friends, and to CD Tenerife. May he rest in peace," Andorra said in a statement.
The players of Real Madrid held a minute of silence for De Miguel during training, while fellow topflight club Espanyol postponed the presentation of its new coach.
English clubs Manchester United and Liverpool joined in offering their condolences on social media.
The Spanish soccer federation postponed two Copa del Rey matches and one Copa de la Reina match to be held later on Tuesday.
Life-threatening injuries from collisions in soccer are extremely rare.

Last year in Spain, a 19-year-old goalkeeper died from head injuries suffered during a collision in a fifth-division match. Colindres goalkeeper Raúl Ramírez had two cardiorespiratory arrests, one on the field and then in the ambulance while being transported to a hospital. He was declared brain dead two days later.
In 2001, Ukrainian goalkeeper Serhiy Perkhun was playing for CSKA Moscow when he died from head injuries received in a collision during a match.

title: Stolen watch worth $290,000 returned to store with apology note
summary: The case of the stolen Audemars Piguet timepiece took a twist when the store received a package containing the watch -- and a note saying sorry.
story: A Swiss luxury watch worth about $290,000 that was stolen from a Tokyo store last week has been returned with an apology note, according to local media.
The theft occurred when a man posing as a customer tried on the Audemars Piguet timepiece and then fled the shop in the Japanese capital while it was still on his wrist.

But the case took a twist when the store received a package containing the watch -- and a handwritten note saying sorry, the Asahi Shimbun newspaper and other media reported on Monday, citing unnamed investigative sources.
The watch's serial number reportedly identified it as the stolen item.
A name and address were also written on the package, but police believe the information is fake, the Japan Times reported.
The shop declined to comment when contacted by AFP.
Tokyo police are still searching for the man on suspicion of theft, according to the Asahi Shumbun.

In August, four luxury watches worth 200 million yen ($1.3 million) were stolen from another store in the same shopping complex. Two Chilean nationals were arrested on suspicion of theft in connection with the incident and subsequently indicted, the Japan Times reported.

After that robbery, police conducted a crime prevention session for watch store owners, advising that they only display replicas, the Asahi Simbun reported. They were also taught how to use a special lining on display cases to make them difficult to break.

title: U.S. to mediate new round of Ukraine-Russia talks, Witkoff says
summary: The envoy will also meet with European and NATO allies to discuss security guarantees for Ukraine.
story: The U.S. will mediate working-level talks between Ukrainian and Russian officials in November, U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff said Tuesday night. In a post on X, Witkoff said the discussions on Nov. 10 and 11 in Abu Dhabi would "focus on post-war security arrangements, de-escalation, humanitarian efforts, and next steps toward peace."

He added that American negotiators would meet this week with representatives from European allies and the NATO alliance, including France, Germany and the United Kingdom, to discuss future security guarantees for Ukraine, which has been one of President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's recurring demands for any deal with Russia.

"We look forward to building on the progress made in Kyiv, Oslo, and St. Petersburg toward a comprehensive, durable peace agreement that delivers lasting security for generations to come," Witkoff said.

Ukraine and Russia have held several rounds of talks mediated by the U.S. during President Trump's second term, often yielding prisoner exchanges or other low-level agreements, but Russian President Vladimir Putin, despite some controversial concessions from the Trump administration, has thus far refused to drop his demand for Ukraine to accept Russia's unilateral annexation of some territory seized over the course of the grueling war.

Zelenskyy, likewise, has consistently ruled out accepting Russia's seizure of territory by force, and many U.S. allies in Europe agree that legitimizing Putin's land grab would set a dangerous precedent.

Witkoff's latest announcement of planned talks at the working level — which generally means discussions among technocrats, not at the senior diplomatic or national leadership level — comes after a rare, localized cease-fire in the southern Ukrainian region of Kherson ended on Sunday.
The brief truce allowed humanitarian supplies into the small Russian-occupied city of Oleshky and the evacuation of an undisclosed number of residents.

The cease-fire, credited by both sides to U.S. first lady Melania Trump and Pope Leo, has raised some hope for more diplomatic progress toward ending the war sparked by Russia's ongoing full-scale invasion of Ukraine on Feb. 24, 2022.
Russia has continued pummeling the rest of Ukraine during and after the local ceasefire, however, with more strikes coming overnight into Tuesday across the country.
At least 29 people were killed in a village in the southeast Ukrainian region of Zaporizhzhia, authorities said Tuesday.
In the northeast city of Kharkiv, the regional administration said a Russian strike hit a medical facility, wounding 25 people and forcing the evacuation of around 200 patients.
Russia's defense ministry said Tuesday that it had carried out a "massive strike" on energy facilities across Ukraine, and port infrastructure in the Odesa region.
Moscow's mayor said, meanwhile, that 500 Ukrainian drones heading toward the capital were destroyed overnight.

title: More European grocery stores hit by apparent fridge-freezer hacks
summary: Grocery chains in European nations say temperatures in some stores' fridges and freezers soared over 100 degrees just weeks after a similar incident in France.
story: Grocery store chains in at least three European countries reported unexpected temperature spikes Monday in refrigerators and freezers that ruined food — the second time in less than a month that similar incidents have raised concerns about cyberattacks on increasingly interlinked infrastructure.

Netherlands-based food retailer Ahold Delhaize and Colruyt in Belgium both said an IT incident overnight had sent temperatures inside fridges and freezers in dozens of their stores in Belgium and Luxembourg soaring, while Swedish chains ICA and Coop reported similar spikes, with one outlet explicitly blaming a cyberattack, according to the Reuters news agency.

The incidents come less than three weeks after several French supermarket chains said they were hit by a cyberattack that sent refrigerator temperatures surging as high as 122 degrees Fahrenheit in hundreds of outlets.
French chains E. Leclerc, Intermarché and Cooperative U told the AFP news agency last month that they had suffered a cyberattack.

On Monday, Reuters said Ahold, the Dutch grocery store chain, had reported a cybersecurity incident to police in the Netherlands in October after detecting suspicious activity in its infrastructure. The chain realized there were temperature increases in the cooling systems on Monday, Delhaize spokesperson Sarah De Meester told Reuters.

The CEO of Belgian refrigeration company Sabcobel, which operates the systems used by Delhaize and other chains, told Belgium's national Belga news agency a cyberattack was to blame after fridge and freezer units' evaporators were switched into defrost mode.

"We began mobilizing technicians at 1 a.m. to get the situation under control," Stephan Moelans told Belga. "We've been working all night and morning to disconnect the affected units from the network."

"Over the past few weeks, we've been working very hard to protect our customers' fridges against this vulnerability," he told the news agency, but he added that many units would require physical modifications, and "that requires investment."

A handful of Swedish supermarkets also saw refrigerator and freezer temperatures soar early Monday, two chains said, forcing them to throw away spoiled food. ICA and Coop both told AFP they had no immediate information about their systems being subjected to a cyberattack.

ICA told AFP "a limited number" of its stores were affected, but it did not provide a number. One of its stores, in Sjobo in southern Sweden, posted on Facebook that its fridges and freezers had "been hacked and they set the temperature at 50 degrees" Celsius (about 122 degrees Fahrenheit).
"We are looking into what has happened and the scale of it," spokesperson Helena Johansson told AFP, adding that the company was focusing on how to help affected stores.

The Coop chain said six of its around 800 stores in Sweden had problems with their fridges and freezers and had to throw out food, with company spokesman Carlos Cancino telling AFP that the units "either stopped working entirely or have been partially impaired."
"I haven't received any information that this is a cyberattack," he said.

On Oct. 12, major French retailers said hundreds of stores were hit by a cyberattack on their refrigeration systems, which forced them to throw out food and raised concerns about food security. In that incident, refrigeration control systems from Danish manufacturer Danfoss were targeted.
There has been no claim of responsibility for any hack targeting grocery retailers in Europe to date.

Speaking after the French stores were forced to discard thousands of pounds of wasted food last month due to the still-unattributed hack, European Union food and agriculture commissioner Christophe Hansen said in a post on X that "food security requires more attention at all levels," calling the "exploitation" of vulnerabilities in such essential, networked systems a new "reality."

"Targeting equipment essential to the preservation of fresh products and to the food supply of the French people is of extreme gravity and is unprecedented," Cooperative U CEO Dominique Schelcher wrote on X last month.
Prosecutors in Paris confirmed a cyberattack and said it also hit other major chains and sparked fires as some equipment overheated.

title: Hacked alert apps send Ukrainians, Russians fake attack warnings
summary: Ukrainian and Russian emergency alert apps were hacked just hours apart, sending civilians false warnings of chemical and nuclear attacks.
story: Kyiv — Ukrainian and Russian emergency alert apps used to warn civilians of incoming missiles, drones and other military attacks were hacked hours apart on Sunday night, sending out false messages about radiation, chemical attacks and nuclear strikes.

At 10:47 p.m. local time (3 p.m. Eastern), Air Alert, a Ukrainian app developed by Ajax Systems and Stfalcon with support from Ukraine's Ministry of Digital Transformation, started sending out false warnings of radiation, chemical threats, a nuclear attack and even street fighting in Kyiv.

Some Ukrainians rely on the app to decide whether or not to take shelter ahead of incoming Russian missile and drone strikes. Many also rely on the social media platform Telegram, however, where the country's Air Force and security analysts share more specific information about incoming strikes.

The Ukrainian Air Force confirmed just 10 minutes later, at 11:02 p.m. local time, on multiple platforms, that the notifications were false. "The Air Alert app appears to have been subjected to hostile interference. There is no radiation threat!" the Air Force said in a message shared on Telegram, urging Ukrainians to remain calm and follow official updates.
Some Kyiv residents told CBS News they immediately knew the notifications were fake after checking Telegram channels.

A couple of hours later, at 2:45 a.m. in Moscow (6:45 p.m. Eastern), Russia's Emergencies Ministry app was also hacked. False alerts were sent to users in 33 regions, according to Russia's tightly controlled media, which said the messages warned of "nuclear warheads" being launched across the country and instructed residents to stock up on food for three weeks and shelter in basements.
The Russian ministry said attackers had exploited a vulnerability in its app's administrative panel, prompting officials to disconnect and isolate affected services.
Developers of the Air Alert app in Ukraine said "unauthorized interference" had occurred and temporarily disabled push notifications and the app itself.

Yurii Ihnat, a spokesman for the Ukrainian Air Force, said the hack had no impact on Ukraine's security operations and that the Air Alert app is not affiliated with the country's military command systems.
The hacks came as a temporary ceasefire expired at 10:59 p.m. Ukraine time on Sunday in and around Oleshky, a southern Ukrainian city that has been occupied by Russia since 2022.

The truce, credited by both sides to U.S. first lady Melania Trump and Pope Leo, began on Oct. 27. It allowed humanitarian aid into the city and some civilians to evacuate. Ukraine's human rights commissioner Dmytro Lubinets said both sides had observed the agreement and were discussing further humanitarian measures.

title: U.K. man returns home after 28 years walking 30,000 miles around the world
summary: Karl Bushby began what came to be known as his "Goliath Expedition" in Chile on Nov. 1, 1998.
story: Hull, England - For 28 years and one day, Karl Bushby took the long way home on an epic odyssey of human endurance back to northern England.

His adventure was made even more difficult - physically and mentally - with his two self-imposed guiding rules: he could not advance his journey with the help of any machine and he could not return home during the entire time, even if family or friends died.

It was also hardly a direct route. His journey was delayed at various times for months, if not years, by illness, visa restrictions in Russia, Moscow's invasion of Ukraine and having to swim massive bodies of water. His life was also threatened by armed gangs in the lawless Darien Gap in Central America, jail in Panama and a polar bear in Siberia.
Starting out at 29, he sported golden locks in his earliest pictures. Now 57, his beard is salt-and-pepper, and the elements and time weather his face.
On Monday, he took his final steps of an estimated 75 million to a hometown hero's welcome of claps and cheers as he walked into Hull, a gritty and proud working-class port city.

"I didn't do this alone. There was a big team, the biggest team: Earth. That's what it took to get me back," said Bushby to the assembled well-wishers in Hull, a working-class port city about 150 miles north of London.

"You wouldn't believe just how many people have been involved in this, to get us around the kinds of obstacles that we faced. We faced down governments. We faced down some of the hardest challenges. We've had to create two world records just to get back here. And I couldn't have done it on my own. So it was a world, global effort."

Bushby began what came to be known as his "Goliath Expedition" in Chile on Nov. 1, 1998. He made his way north through Central America, the United States and Canada, then crossed the Bering Sea to Russia in the world's first recorded attempt. He then carried on through Central Asia and swam for 31 days across the Caspian Sea in another reported first, in order to circumvent the war in Ukraine.

Over the past few years, he crossed Europe, and just last month, he swam from France across the English Channel, setting foot on the country of his birth where British immigration officers had set up to check his passport.

"It's almost like arriving in a foreign country," Bushby told CBS News over the weekend as he neared home. "I've worked with dollars for 28 years. I don't know the brands in the stores. So I'm going around wondering what I'm going to be buying. A couple of times I got caught out crossing the road because I'm looking in the other direction because these people drive on the wrong side of the road."
His home stretch Monday, quite literally, was a roughly 3-mile brisk walk from near Hull's town center to a quiet, sprawling neighborhood to the north of two-story, red-brick terrace homes.
Children lined the turn to his mother's home and cheered while an honor guard led the way.
Bushby pushed the cart that had been with him for about 25 years the last few steps.
He then embraced his waiting mother on the street outside her home. The cheers quieted, and the two shared a moment in this homecoming.
Bushby said he feels like a man wondering what home truly means after spending a generation around the world.

"I'm home, but it's not the home that I'm used to now for so long. And it's an odd feeling. And I almost feel guilt," he said. "Like there are other parts of the world now that feel more like home to me. And now I'm going to be faced with this weird static thing."
Now, after more than 10,000 days away, Bushby faces a different task: processing it all.
Confronted with the question of whether the world had gotten better or worse, he acknowledged the troubles but did not give up on his optimism.

"The world's in a little bit messier time; there are more wars, you know," he told CBS News. "But it's all good. At the end of the day, we've been through worse. So we all need to breathe a little bit, get through the tough times; we're going to be just fine. My bet is on us, no matter what. My bet is on humanity."
His final advice for anyone wondering if they could also accomplish something extraordinary: dream bigger.
"Yeah, you can, because I'm nothing special. Maybe we need the art of dreaming big again. People seem to dream outside of a very confined space mentally at the world that they live in," he said.

"You've got to have that little confidence. You got to realize that you're more capable than you think you are. People constantly underestimate themselves. So that's the first step, I think. Dream big. Realize you're probably capable more than you'd think. If you take nothing else from this … take that!"

title: Record bounty offered for fugitive drug kingpin "Chubby Jos"
summary: Jos Leijdekkers is one of Europe's most-wanted drug traffickers, currently hiding in Sierra Leone.
story: Dutch authorities are offering a record reward of 2 million euros ($2.2 million) for information leading to the arrest of Jos Leijdekkers, one of Europe's most-wanted drug traffickers, currently hiding in Sierra Leone.

The arrest of Leijdekkers, also known as "Bolle Jos" ("Chubby Jos"), is "the highest priority for the Public Prosecution Service and the police," said Dutch prosecutors in a statement, multiplying by 10 their previous reward.
Leijdekkers is considered to be one of the key players in the international cocaine trade.
A court in Rotterdam sentenced him in absentia in 2024 to 24 years in prison for drug shipments totaling nearly 7,000 kilos of cocaine, an armed robbery, and ordering a "liquidation."
He has also been sentenced to 79 years in prison in Belgium.
Dutch police have tracked the 35-year-old to Sierra Leone. Any information shared with prosecutors will be kept secret, the Dutch authorities said in a statement.

Justice Minister David van Weel said the increase in the reward was "necessary given the threat that Leijdekkers poses to national security, our democratic rule of law, and the international legal order."
"The Netherlands, in cooperation with the international community, is doing everything in its power to secure the arrest of Leijdekkers," the minister said in a letter to parliament.
Links to Sierra Leone

In January 2025, Dutch authorities said they were "absolutely certain" he was hiding out in Sierra Leone. The BBC reported that Dutch prosecutor Wim de Bruin said the fugitive's return to the Netherlands was of "the highest priority."

Images apparently showing Leijdekkers in the company of officials as high as President Julius Maada Bio have sparked speculation that the cocaine baron has cozied up to Sierra Leone's political class — including the president's daughter.

Suspicions that he was in Sierra Leone arose after the country's first lady, Fatima Bio, posted pictures and a video on social media that showed a man strongly resembling Leijdekkers at a religious service, also attended by President Bio.

Leijdekkers is also believed to be involved in the disappearance and death of Naima Jillal, a woman who went missing in 2019 after she got into a car in Amsterdam, according to Europol. Intercepted messages allegedly showed that Leijdekkers "played an important role in Jillal's disappearance," the agency said.

"For a long time, there was no trace of Naima Jillal, until photos of a woman believed to be her were found on a phone seized in the Marengo investigation," Europol said. "The photos show that she was most likely tortured and is probably no longer alive."

title: Paris Jackson demands $600M from father Michael Jackson's estate in legal war with longtime executor
summary: Paris Jackson accused executor John Branca of financial retaliation after she challenged his handling of Michael Jackson's multibillion-dollar estate.
story: Victoria Price told Fox News Digital that as long as there is Halloween, people will listen to the horror icon's narration in the hit song.

Paris Jackson accused John Branca, the sole executor of her late father Michael Jackson's multibillion-dollar estate, of financially retaliating against her and her siblings after she challenged his handling of the King of Pop's fortune.

Paris alleged in new court documents obtained by Fox News Digital, that she and her siblings experienced a multimillion-dollar reduction in payments while Branca maintained an "iron grip" over their inheritance.
She asked a Los Angeles court to order a $600 million distribution from her late father's estate into the family trust after accusing Branca of mismanaging the funds.
PARIS JACKSON SAYS DAD MICHAEL'S UNUSAL RULE HELPED PROTECT HER CHILDHOOD
Paris Jackson asked a Los Angeles court to order a $600 million distribution from Michael Jackson’s estate to the family trust. (Alan Chapman/Getty Images)
Branca has been the sole executor of Jackson's estate since 2009. The pop star died that year from acute propofol and sedative intoxication leading to cardiac arrest.

Branca's alleged mismanagement of estate funds included non-contractual gifts to colleagues, aggressive litigation, public attacks and a multimillion-dollar reduction in payments to Jackson's children.

"Without belaboring the point, when Paris began challenging the administration of the Estate last year through her objection to Executor Branca’s non-contractual gifts to his colleagues, her challenges were met with scorched earth litigation, public attacks, and a multimillion reduction in monies provided to her and her siblings by the Estate," her legal team wrote. "This course of conduct and administration should not continue."
Paris Jackson is the daughter of Michael Jackson and Debbie Rowe. (Swan Gallet/WWD/Getty Images)

In a separate filing obtained by Fox News Digital, Paris accused Branca of using estate resources for personal travel on private jets, improperly charging personal expenses to the estate and concealing the spending from beneficiaries.

She claimed Branca acknowledged taking multiple personal trips and reimbursed certain expenses only after she investigated them. Her attorneys characterized the conduct as "outright theft" and a breach of his fiduciary duties.
"Where the travel is of a purely personal nature, or in service of Mr. Branca's other clients or business affairs, it constitutes outright theft," the court filing stated.
Prince Jackson and Paris Jackson at the opening night of "MJ: the Musical," at Neil Simon Theatre on Feb. 1, 2022, in New York City. (Bruce Glikas/WireImage)

Paris also accused Branca of using estate funds for personal gifts, questioned more than $604,000 in credit card charges and reimbursements, and challenged $9.4 million in executor compensation, $1.4 million in payments to his law firm and roughly $835,000 in public relations expenses.

She further alleged that Branca mismanaged more than $440 million in estate cash while pursuing entertainment projects that benefited him financially, including the Michael Jackson biopic, which reportedly required tens of millions of dollars in reshoots and rewrites.
Her legal team urged the court to reject Branca's financial accounting and order him to provide a more detailed breakdown of the estate's spending.

"Once again, Ms. Jackson’s legal team raises the same hollow complaints and fails to acknowledge the unique structure of the Estate, which is operated as a dynamic business, with customary costs and expenses," a representative for the estate told Fox News Digital. "No rhetoric can hide the fact that the Executors have taken an Estate that was $500 million in debt when Michael died and turned it into the most successful Estate in history, producing $3 billion in revenue and the biggest biopic in movie history, with a box office exceeding $1 billion globally."

From left to right, Michael Jackson's kids Prince Jackson, Blanket Jackson and Paris Jackson, LaToya Jackson and Katherine Jackson attend Children's Hospital Los Angeles Receives Michael Jackson Artwork Donation ceremony on Aug. 8, 2011, in Los Angeles. (Valerie Macon/Getty Images)

As for the $600 million distribution, Paris argued that her father's estate plan entitled his children — Prince, Paris and Bigi — to trust income beginning at age 21 and portions of their inheritance beginning at age 30. She claimed the executor had never funded the trust, despite Michael Jackson's death more than 17 years earlier.

Paris Jackson accused Michael Jackson's executor, John Branca, of retaliating against her and her siblings after she challenged his handling of the estate. (Rita Barros/Getty Images)

"Michael intended for his children to become the caretakers of his legacy," the petition read. "As each child reached certain ages, Executors were to increasingly provide for each child’s independence."

Paris' filing cited more than $2.5 billion in gross estate earnings and approximately $850 million in cash or cash equivalents as of December 2024. She argued that the estate could distribute $600 million while retaining enough money to cover outstanding liabilities.

"Ms. Jackson’s counsel is well aware that the Estate is prevented from fully funding the philanthropic giving and individual trusts for the beneficiaries until several legal hurdles have been removed, including in particular the ongoing IRS litigation where they sought $700 million in taxes and penalties from the Estate," a statement provided to Fox News Digital on behalf of Jackson's estate said. "The Estate was able to secure a ruling to significantly reduce that amount, but the matter has not been settled and could still change."

Paris Jackson claimed her father’s estate plan entitled his children to trust income starting at age 21 and portions of their inheritance beginning at 30. Jackson died in 2009. (CARL DE SOUZA/AFP via Getty Images)

"Further, the claim that the executor has withheld or ‘cut' payments is a complete fabrication," the statement added. "In fact, more than $200 million has already been distributed for the benefit of Paris and the other beneficiaries. Michael Jackson’s will is clear. None of his children receive a distribution until they are in their 30s. The Estate looks forward to the time when all issues are resolved so that their trusts can be fully funded as Michael wanted."
A court hearing on Paris' request to transfer $600 million into the family trust is scheduled for Dec. 4.

Paris previously spoke about her childhood as the daughter of Michael Jackson. Behind the glitz of Jackson’s larger-than-life world, Paris said her father enforced strict rules to protect his children’s sense of normalcy.

The 28-year-old model recalled in an interview on "Call Her Daddy" that her father required his children to finish their homework and chores before enjoying weekend activities, limited their television and movie viewing, and had them wear masks in public to shield their identities from the intense spotlight surrounding his fame.
Paris said she understood that her father was famous. What she didn’t grasp was the sheer magnitude of his celebrity.

"I just didn't know how famous ... There was definitely part of me that, like when I looked out my hotel window, and it was one of the times where, like, the alias didn't work and there's just like a sea of people with signs and stuff — I'm not so naive to think, yeah, everyone experiences this, you know?" Paris said. "I just didn't understand the lengths."

title: Tony Butala, voice behind 'The Way You Look Tonight' and The Lettermen co-founder, dead at 87
summary: Tony Butala co-founded The Lettermen in the late 1950s and performed for over 60 years, earning four Grammy nominations and a Hollywood Walk of Fame star.
story: Tony Butala died at the age of 87 Nov 1. (Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images)
The Lettermen co-founder, Tony Butala, died Sunday, Nov. 1, at the age of 87.
Tracy Clark, the band's media coordinator, confirmed his death to The Associated Press with a statement, saying, "We have lost an integral member of The Lettermen family."

"It is with profound sadness that we announce the recent passing of Tony Butala, founding member of the international recording artists ‘The Lettermen,’ and recipient of a Star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame," the statement read.
"Our most heartfelt thoughts and prayers are with his children, grandchildren, siblings, the love of his life, the entire Lettermen organization and all who knew and loved him."
Tony Butala died at the age of 87 Nov. 1. (Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images)
JOHN ANDERSON, COUNTRY MUSIC HALL OF FAMER, DEAD AT 71
A cause of death was not disclosed, and there will be no public viewing. Details about celebrations of life in both Wisconsin and California will be announced at a later date.

He co-founded The Lettermen in the late 1950s with Jim Pike and Bob Engemann, and the group released its first hit, a rendition of Fred Astaire's "The Way You Look Tonight," in 1961, which earned the trio a Grammy nomination.
The Lettermen had 20 hits on the Billboard Hot 100 list. (Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images)
The band recorded 20 hits that reached the Billboard Hot 100 chart and earned four Grammy Award nominations.

Butala remained a member of the group for over 60 years, releasing hits such as "Goin' Out of My Head/Can't Take My Eyes off You," "Everything Is Good About You," "Come Back Silly Girl," "Theme from a Summer Place" and "Hurt So Bad."
Butala retired from performing in 2019. (Jean-Baptiste Lacroix/AFP via Getty Images)
He retired from performing with the band in 2019, the same year Pike died at the age of 82 from complications related to Parkinson's Disease. Engemann died in 2013.

A year after retiring, Butala attended the ceremony honoring the band with a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame. After his retirement, the band continued on with new faces, and the current lineup includes Donovan Tea, Bobby Poynton and Rob Gulack.
Butala attended the Walk of Fame ceremony honoring The Lettermen in 2020. (Axelle/Bauer-Griffin/FilmMagic)

title: Spencer Pratt says $1,200 hotel 'fortress' was cheaper than security as death threats mounted
summary: Spencer Pratt says death threats and armed security costs during the Los Angeles mayoral race made the Hotel Bel-Air the cheapest option available.
story: The 'Outnumbered' panel discusses Spencer Pratt’s claims that Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass mismanaged the Palisades wildfire response and the city’s homelessness crisis.
Spencer Pratt explained why his controversial stay at the Hotel Bel-Air was actually the cheaper option as he faced death threats while running for mayor of Los Angeles.

The 43-year-old reality star faced scrutiny in May after TMZ reported he had been staying at the luxury hotel despite appearing to suggest in a campaign ad that he was living in an Airstream trailer on the site of his California home, which was destroyed in the devastating Pacific Palisades fire.

At the time, the outlet reported that Pratt had been staying at the Hotel Bel-Air for more than a month, though "The Hills" alum disputed that characterization, saying he had spent no more than six days there during the previous month.
SPENCER PRATT’S MAYORAL RUN BACKED BY PARIS HILTON, KRISTIN CAVALLARI AS CELEBRITY DIVIDE DEEPENS
In a lengthy X post he shared Tuesday, Pratt, who lost in the June primary election, defended his choice to stay at the pricey hotel during the race.
"Why is he spending $1,200 a night? Why couldn’t he stay somewhere for $300 a night? Well, the answer to that question is not as pretty as any of us may like to hear," Pratt wrote.
Spencer Pratt defended his controversial $1,200 a night hotel stay as the cheapest option. (Getty Images)
REALITY TV STAR SPENCER PRATT GAINS TRACTION IN LOS ANGELES MAYORAL RACE AFTER FIERY DEBATE

"Most people simply presumed that I was being a bougie spoiled brat, and that I was abusing campaign funds," he continued. "They expected me to stay at a cheaper hotel, but what they don’t realize is … the Hotel Bel Air was the cheapest hotel in all of LA.

"At the time, I couldn’t explain the math to people, and my campaign staff told me I wasn’t allowed to divulge the real reason I had to stay there, but now that the election is coming to a close, I don’t need to listen to anyone anymore."
'ENTOURAGE' CREATOR BACKS SPENCER PRATT FOR LA MAYOR, SAYS CITY 'HAS COLLAPSED' UNDER CURRENT LEADERSHIP

Pratt had previously told TMZ in May that the Airstream had become unsafe, saying that the Bel Air Hotel's "armed security" made it "the only option." He claimed that supporters of his opponents, Mayor Karen Bass and City Councilmember Nithya Raman were "getting increasingly desperate and hostile" due to his performance at the May debate and strong polling numbers.
Pratt said the hotel "fortress" was less costly than round-the-clock security. (Highfive/Bauer-Griffin/GC Images)
"I can't talk about specific threats, but that lot is ... unsafe now," he said at the time.
JIMMY KIMMEL ATTACKS FIRE VICTIM SPENCER PRATT AS 'SCREAMING JERK,' LECTURES LA VOTERS ABOUT MAYORAL ELECTION
In his X post, Pratt, who ran as a Republican, elaborated on the threats that he received, which he attributed to political violence.

"Throughout the campaign, I endured numerous death threats, to the point where I had to hire full-time security," he wrote. "Anyone who’s had to hire security knows that they will always tell you to not discuss your death threats; they find that it often has the opposite effect you would expect; normal people should hear it and think ‘whoa, we need to dial back the temperature, this isn’t acceptable’, but the reality is that commie street animals get inspired, and you will end up getting copycats if you advertise your threats."
SPENCER PRATT VOWS TO LEAVE LA AND FIND 'LAST AMERICAN DREAM' IN ANOTHER CITY IF MAYORAL BID FAILS
Pratt went on to detail specific incidents he said led him to fear for his safety and that of his family.
"People were breaking into my lot in the Palisades and leaving notes on the airstream with white powder in them," he wrote.
DEM MAYOR FACES REALITY CHECK AFTER ACCUSING RIVAL OF 'EXPLOITING' PALISADES FIRE: 'ABSOLUTE TONE DEAFNESS'

The TV personality also claimed that a "lunatic" who was "hellbent on tracking me down" charged at his young son while he was boogie-boarding in the ocean. Pratt shares sons Gunner, 8, and Ryker, 3, with his wife and former "The Hills" co-star Heidi Montag, 40.

"So, I had to hire a second security detail for my family while I was away campaigning," he wrote. "I don’t know if you’ve ever had to hire 4-5 armed security professionals with blacked out SUVs, but…it’s not cheap. One of the first things they told me was that my lot in the Palisades was a security nightmare; perched mid-slope on a hill, totally exposed in a bowl, surrounded by elevated positions where a shooter could easily traipse through the wilderness of the State Park, and have a clear line of sight to every inch of my property.
SPENCER PRATT: LOS ANGELES ANGRY WITH KAREN BASS’ MISMANAGEMENT
"I wasn’t allowed to stay on that property, even if I wanted to," he added. "Enter the Hotel Bel Air."
Pratt explained that the famed LA hotel, which has hosted celebrities, presidents and royalty, is an unusually secure property due to its design.
"The Hills" alum faced backlash when it was revealed he was not living in the Airstream trailer on his Pacific Palisades lot.  (HighFive/Bauer-Griffin/GC Images)
PRATT CONCEDES LA MAYOR RACE WITH SCATHING VIDEO TEASING NEXT MOVE, BOMBSHELL INFO HE HOLDS: 'COMMIE ANIMALS'
"While $1,200 a night isn’t very unique for a decent hotel in a major city, there’s something else about the hotel that is unique," Pratt wrote.

"Unlike my turkey shoot of a lot in the Palisades, the Hotel Bel Air is surrounded with a fortress wall, with a single point of ingress, a fatal funnel that takes you over a moat, just to enter the property. You then must navigate a labyrinth of walled off bungalows, and it is very easy to get lost. Unlike normal hotels, it is a very secure facility.
"When my security team dropped me off behind the walls of the Bel Air, they felt good about leaving me alone in the secure facility," he continued.

"Had I stayed anywhere else, I would have needed to book out 3 rooms for my team to maintain overnight security, which would’ve cost an additional $3,000 per night. Paradoxically, by this calculation, I was actually saving a ton of money by staying at the secure Bel Air; even staying at a Motel 6 would’ve cost me more money, and in a campaign…money is everything."

Pratt argued that Republicans face a "permanent fundraising disadvantage" due to safety expenses.  (Robert Gauthier/Los Angeles Times)

Pratt claimed that threats of political violence disproportionately affect Republican candidates, arguing that the cost of protecting himself forced his campaign to spend money on security that his Democratic rivals could devote elsewhere. The reality star recalled that Raman appeared at a debate preparation event without visible security while he was accompanied by several armed officers.

title: John Rich says Kathy Hochul is ‘running over’ NY farmers with renewable energy agenda
summary: John Rich's country song "Dear Kathy" takes aim at Governor Kathy Hochul over renewable energy policies he says are silencing upstate New York farmers.
story: Country singer John Rich accused the New York governor of helping redefine prime farmland and creating a "chokeout" for farmers through ORES.
John Rich is blasting New York Gov. Kathy Hochul over the state’s renewable energy policies, accusing her administration of silencing farmers and overriding local officials in upstate New York.

The 52-year-old Big & Rich member has publicly joined local landowners, activists and officials who are challenging New York’s Office of Renewable Energy Siting (ORES), a state agency that reviews and permits major renewable energy and transmission projects.

Last month, Rich released his new country song "Dear Kathy," which is directed at the Democratic governor, who is running for re-election. In the song, Rich speaks on behalf of farmers and landowners who are protesting large-scale solar and wind projects on upstate New York farmland, arguing that ORES has undermined local control and put family farms, rural communities and private property rights at risk.
JOHN RICH WARNS NASHVILLE'S FAMED BROADWAY COULD GO DARK AS BUSINESSES FACE TAX ‘DEATH NAIL’
During a recent interview with Fox News Digital, Rich shared his message for Hochul, pointing to the final line of "Dear Kathy," which asks, "Why do you hate these people so much?"
"What have they ever done to you except pay taxes and put food on your table? That’s it," Rich said.
"Why do you hate these people?" he continued. "Because only somebody that has a vindictive spirit would do what she’s doing to them — or greed."
John Rich slammed New York Gov. Kathy Hochul over the state's renewable energy policies. (Jason Kempin/Getty Images; James Carbone/Newsday RM via Getty Images)

"I think greed is probably the largest driver in it because these companies that are coming in, building these huge fields. Listen, if you add up all the plans they have coming into upstate New York, it’s over 100 square miles of solar panels," Rich added.
WILLIE NELSON URGES AMERICANS TO FIGHT 'WATER THIEVING' AI DATA CENTERS DEVOURING RURAL TEXAS FARMLAND

The conflict centers on New York’s centralized permitting system for large-scale solar and wind projects. Created in 2020 under former Gov. Andrew Cuomo, ORES generally handles renewable energy projects capable of producing 25 megawatts or more. Its rules encourage developers to avoid the state’s most productive agricultural soils and require them to minimize or mitigate impacts when farmland cannot be avoided.

ORES can also waive local zoning and land-use restrictions it deems "unreasonably burdensome," a power that critics argue gives state officials too much control over farmland and leaves local communities with limited say over projects in their areas.
BROOKE ROLLINS, MONICA CROWLEY: AMERICA’S FAMILY FARMS HAVE KEPT US STRONG FOR 250 YEARS

While speaking with Fox News Digital, Rich claimed Hochul’s administration used research from Cornell University to change how prime farmland is defined. The singer argued that the move made it easier for solar and wind projects to be built on agricultural land.
WATCH: JOHN RICH SLAMS KATHY HOCHUL OVER FARMLAND DISPUTE: ‘WHY DO YOU HATE THESE PEOPLE?’

"She decided she didn’t like their definition of prime farmland because if it’s prime, it’s protected from solar and wind and projects like that," Rich said. "So they just redefined it. They just came up with a whole new equation and determined, well, based on these new numbers, there’s really no such thing as prime farmland anymore in upstate New York. So we can do whatever the hell we want to these people."
AMISH FACE NEW YORK VACCINE MANDATE IN SUPREME COURT FIGHT, MIGHT HAVE TO ‘PACK THEIR WAGONS’

"Oh, by the way, we put ORES in place. So if they try to stop us, we just run right over the top of them," he continued. "I mean, it is a complete and total chokeout that she’s put on these farmers up there."

"Some of these families have owned their farms, been in their families since before the Revolutionary War," Rich said. "You’re talking about one of the original 13 colonies, New York, and to think that 250 years later, after these same people’s ancestors had to fight off the British, now they’re standing there fighting with their own governor in the United States of America."
"It is astonishing, and I find it to be disgusting. I also think it’s probably unconstitutional," he added.
Rich said that the policies are silencing upstate New York farmers. (Getty Images)

Since taking office in 2021, Hochul has continued to advance New York’s renewable energy agenda. Her administration has promoted large-scale solar and wind development and defended the state’s approach to farmland, arguing that renewable energy projects are not taking over New York’s "best farmland" and that leasing land for solar can help farmers keep their property in their families.
When reached for comment by Fox News Digital, Hochul’s office pushed back on Rich’s criticism.

"If he really wants to help farmers, maybe he can write a song calling on his buddy Donald Trump to lift the tariffs, end his reckless war with Iran that is driving up gas and diesel prices, and rein in the ICE raids, all of which are hurting farmers here in New York and across the country," Ken Lovett, a senior communications adviser on energy and environment for Hochul, said.
DEBRA MESSING DITCHES DEMOCRAT FOR TRUMP-BACKED REPUBLICAN AS SHE SOUNDS ALARM OVER NEW YORK

Rich said he first learned about the dispute after seeing Alexandra Fasulo, an upstate New York landowner and ORES critic, discuss it on social media. The singer said he was startled by the claim that the state could sideline landowners, zoning boards, mayors and other local officials when deciding where major projects would be built.
"I said, that can’t be the case. I’m gonna go up and see this for myself," Rich recalled.
Rich argued that ORES' authority undermines "home rule," the principle that landowners and local governments should have authority over how land in their communities is used.
During his visit, Rich held two town hall meetings, including one at Fasulo’s farm, where he met with hundreds of farmers and landowners.
"We had Amish people standing in the room being silent, standing in the back," Rich said. "It looked like something out of a movie."

"And we had this discussion about ‘What are we going to do about this governor running over everybody?’" he continued. "And man, the sentiment in the room was so much frustration and feeling of bewilderment that what do you do? I mean, she's put something into gear here that just runs us over and takes away our voice."
The singer said that meeting with farmers inspired his protest song "Dear Kathy." (Anna Connors - Pool/Getty Images)
The singer told Fox News Digital that the meetings ultimately inspired him to write "Dear Kathy."

"I left there thinking to myself, I need to put this song out, ‘Dear Kathy,’" he recalled. "I need to write a song for the governor of New York on behalf of all those people whose voices she has silenced. And so that led to me with a pencil and a piece of paper and a guitar writing a letter or a song to Kathy Hochul."
WATCH: JOHN RICH SAYS MEETING AMISH FARMERS INSPIRED SONG TARGETING KATHY HOCHUL

On Oct. 28, Rich officially released the song and its accompanying music video, which highlights affected areas in upstate New York, showcasing local landowners and the Holy Trinity Monastery in Jordanville, NY, which has actively opposed large wind projects near its grounds.

"And I jokingly say in the video, 'What do you get the woman who has everything, including your freedom in her back pocket? Well, you give her the one thing she doesn't have — a country song,'" Rich said. "And so I wrote ‘Dear Kathy’ and it really was my way of speaking on behalf of those people that she will not listen to."
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Rich described "Dear Kathy" as a "fight song" for the farmers he met and emphasized that the dispute transcended party lines.
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE
WATCH: JOHN RICH CALLS ‘DEAR KATHY’ A ‘FIGHT SONG’ FOR NEW YORK FARMERS

"One interesting thing about those farmers that I met — they were Democrat, Republican, probably more Democrat than Republican, actually," he said. "And so it's not a partisan thing. Owning land is an American thing. I mean it may be one of the last things we all agree on in this country is that if you own land, if you bought that land, and you take care of that land, that's your land."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"You get to determine what happens to it or what doesn't happen to it," he continued. "And that's exactly what I felt up there. It was an across the board repudiation of Kathy Hochul and her assault on their land and on them and on their legacies."
Rich described "Dear Kathy" as a "fight song" for the farmers and landowners. (Tim Mosenfelder/WireImage/Getty Images)

"To me, as bad as that is, that was a beautiful experience actually for me to sit up there knowing that this is not a partisan deal, and I'm sitting in the room with both sides of the aisle, but everybody is in unison," Rich added.
Despite his criticism of Hochul, Rich told Fox News Digital that he would welcome the opportunity to meet with Hochul to discuss the landowners’ concerns directly.

"If Kathy Hochul wanted to sit with me and have a meeting, I would jump on the next thing smoking to be up there," he said. "I mean, I would sit down at her desk. She could bring anybody she wants and I would just ask questions. ‘Why do you think this is OK? I mean you're still an American. Don't you think that this is against the Constitution? Home rule is a real thing. You don't think that people that you govern have the right to determine what happens to their own land and not just a farm here or there, a hundred square miles of land?' I would just ask her basic questions."

title: 'Homestead' star Bailey Chase says California vaccine plans were 'final straw' that drove family out of LA
summary: Bailey Chase reveals the proposed COVID-19 vaccine mandate that drove his family from California to the mountains of North Carolina five years ago.
story: "Homestead" star  Bailey Chase tells Fox News Digital his family is now "living our best life" in North Carolina after leaving Los Angeles five years ago.
"Homestead" star Bailey Chase is opening up about the "final straw" that drove him and his family out of California for a new life in North Carolina.

During a recent interview with Fox News Digital, the 54-year-old actor, who shares daughter Waverly, 12, and 10-year-old twins Maggie and Gauge with his wife Amy, explained that concerns over how California's COVID-19 restrictions would impact his children led him to leave the Golden State behind.
"That happened five years ago in the throes of COVID," Chase said. "My wife and I picked up sticks with our three young children when they were mandating vaccines out there."

"They said they couldn't go back to school without it," Chase, who stars as former Green Beret Jeff Eriksson in "Homestead," continued. "And that was the final straw. And we've been in the mountains of North Carolina ever since living our best life."
Bailey Chase revealed that California's COVID-19 vaccine mandates for schools was the "final straw" that led him and his family to pack up and leave Los Angeles. (FilmMagic)
ZACHARY LEVI SAYS TEXAS GIVES HIM THE ‘FREEDOM’ HE COULDN’T FIND IN CALIFORNIA
Five years after trading Los Angeles for North Carolina, Chase told Fox News Digital that his life now largely revolves around his children's activities when he isn't working.
'VIRGIN RIVER' STAR BEN HOLLINGSWORTH SAYS HIS KIDS HAVE FREEDOM IN SMALL TOWN THAT 'DOESN'T FLY' IN LA

"I'm like soccer dad right now. It's soccer season, so we're going here and there," he said. "My oldest is really into ballet, and I couldn't be more proud of her and getting ready for ‘The Nutcracker’ in December, and basketball season's around the corner."
While Chase remains committed to his acting career, the "Longmire" alum said his priorities shift completely when he returns home.
CHRIS PRATT SAYS HIS FAITH WILL BE 'THE MOST IMPORTANT THING' THAT HE PASSES ON TO HIS KIDS
"I love my job, and when I'm off filming, I'm 100% focused on that. But when I'm home, I'm home," he said. "There's no greater job than being a dad."

Chase and his family currently live in Amy's hometown of Hendersonville in the Blue Ridge Mountains of Western North Carolina, about 25 miles south of Asheville. Chase has previously explained that Amy had long envisioned eventually returning to the area where she was born and raised. The actor also has ties to North Carolina after attending Duke University in Durham on a football scholarship.
'RANSOM CANYON' STAR JOSH DUHAMEL SAYS HE'D RATHER PUT MONEY INTO NORTH DAKOTA AFTER SELLING LOS ANGELES HOME

"Amy, being from the mountains of North Carolina, always had it in the back of her mind that she’d go back home one day," he said in a January 2026 interview with Duke Alumni Magazine. "We didn’t know how or when."
However, Chase recalled they decided the time was right due to California's handling of the pandemic.
Chase and his family moved to his wife Amy's hometown in North Carolina. (Getty Images)
‘TWILIGHT’ STAR KELLAN LUTZ TRADED CALIFORNIA FOR TENNESSEE LAND AND BIBLE STUDIES

"Things started to not work in LA during COVID – they shut down the schools, there were no sports for the kids," he said. "Really, no life, no work. And it became more and more obvious that we should leave LA."

"Amy’s very close with her parents, who are in N.C.," he continued. "Everything’s about seven minutes away: school, the in-laws, the grocery store, golf course, soccer field. It’s a great location. We live in a house that would not have been affordable in LA."
JANA KRAMER SAYS LOS ANGELES PRICED HER OUT OF THE CHILDHOOD SHE WANTED FOR HER KIDS
"It’s a kid’s dream," he added. "There’s a sports court and a pool. We have two golden retriever puppies, so it’s a full and lively house."

During a February appearance on the "Undaunted.Life: A Man's Podcast," Chase elaborated on the concerns that he had over California's proposed vaccine mandate for his young children's return to school.
"At that time, you know, they're 4, 4 and 6 years old," he recalled. "I got two young girls and, you know we don't need to go down that rabbit hole."
"I was like, 'No, I just don't know enough,'" he continued. "And I got one job right now, and it's to take care of these little nuggets. That's the most important job I have right now."

In October 2021, California Gov. Gavin Newsom announced plans for a COVID-19 vaccine requirement for students that he said would eventually apply to all the state's 6.7 million public and private schoolchildren.

However, the mandate was repeatedly delayed and ultimately never took effect. In February 2023, state health officials announced that they would not pursue or implement the requirement as the COVID-19 state of emergency expired at the end of that month.
The "Homestead" star said they are "living our best life." (Getty Images)
'ANT-MAN' STAR EVANGELINE LILLY SAYS SHE LEFT HOLLYWOOD BECAUSE SHE 'ALWAYS HATED BEING FAMOUS'

Chase previously acknowledged that while relocating to North Carolina was the best move for his family, leaving LA came at a professional cost after he spent 21 years building his career in Hollywood.
"I've lost out on some work by not being in L.A.," he admitted while appearing on the "Living Local" podcast in August.
"There was a big role on 'Grey's Anatomy,'" he continued. "And I understand, it's a lot cheaper for them. They just move on to the next guy and cast someone who's local to L.A."
"But what has happened is I've gotten new opportunities and different kind of jobs and some faith-based films and shows," Chase added.
The "Saving Grace" actor has also spoken openly about how he "lost touch" with God during his years in LA and shared that moving to North Carolina eventually led him back to his Christian faith.

"Moving back here, I've gotten reconnected to my faith," Chase told "Crosswalk" in January. "Just started going to church recently. It took a few years, but I really like the church where we're going to here."
"My cousin started taking us," he continued. "The girls are in youth group. They really love it."
"It's nice to be in an environment where I can openly talk about God and Jesus and without fear of criticism," he added.
WATCH HERE: ‘HOMESTEAD’ STAR BAILEY CHASE SAYS CALIFORNIA VACCINE PLANS WERE ‘FINAL STRAW’ THAT DROVE FAMILY OUT OF LA
In a 2024 Instagram post, Chase reflected on how his priorities have shifted since leaving behind "all that worry, all that stress, 20 years of hustle in LA."
"It also got me thinking if I spent as much time chasing God as I’ve spent chasing success the last 25 years, what would that look like?" he wrote.

Jesse Hutch, Kearran Giovanni, Georgie White, Emmanuel McCord, Colby Strong, Bailey Chase, Neal McDonough, Dawn Olivieri, Olivia Sanabia, Tyler Lofton and Kevin Lawson attend the "Homestead" premiere on Dec. 10, 2024. in LA. (Tommaso Boddi/Getty Images for Angel Studios)

Chase is currently starring as former Green Beret Jeff Eriksson in the faith-based streaming platform Angel Studios’ post-apocalyptic drama "Homestead," which will premiere its second season on Nov. 3.

The series follows survivors living at a fortified prepper compound in the Rocky Mountains known as The Homestead after a nuclear attack on LA plunges the country into chaos. After the bomb is detonated, Jeff escapes with his family to The Homestead, where he serves as head of security.

The actor starred in the 2024 theatrical movie "Homestead," which introduces the story and the TV series picks up directly afterward. The cast also includes Neal McDonough, Kevin Lawson Emmanuel McCord, Jesse Hutch, Betzaida Landín, Charles Esten and Dawn Olivieri.
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE
Chase told Fox News Digital that starring in the "Homestead" movie and follow-up TV show had inspired the cast to start prepping for a potential apocalypse.
Chase is currently starring as former Green Beret Jeff Eriksson in the show. (Angel Studios)

"'Homestead' has changed all of our lives and the first thing I did when I came home after the film was arm my home more," he said. "And then right before season two, Hurricane Helene hit here in the mountains of North Carolina. And I now have a brand-new generator and some other things."
When asked if most Americans would be able to survive a major disaster, Chase predicted that it would be more challenging for people who live in bigger cities.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
"They're overpopulated and there aren't enough resources," he said. "So for those who are a little bit more in the country, their odds are a lot higher."
Chase also starred in the 2024 "Homestead" movie. (Angel Studios )
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE
"Those are the kind of people who hunt and fish and can go out and find their own game," Chase added. "So if I'm laying odds, I'm betting on those guys."

While reflecting on what drew him to "Homestead," Chase explained that his focus on faith and family has also influenced the projects he chooses, noting that the show offers a different message than much of what is coming out of Hollywood.
"I take my job as being a father as the best job and most important job that I'll ever have. And I do take it seriously," Chase told Fox News Digital.

"And how that translates to me being an actor, that's why I'm so proud of ‘Homestead’ and the story that we get to tell, because it reflects my own personal values," he continued. "We got men and women and boys and girls, and it's about promoting faith, family, community and being there for your brother."
"Not all the shows that Hollywood's putting out does that, so I feel truly blessed to be part of a show that delivers a message that I believe in so deeply to my core."
"Homestead: The Series" season two premieres Nov. 3 on Angel with new episodes released weekly on Tuesdays.

title: 'DWTS' judge Carrie Ann Inaba speaks out on lift controversy after Val Chmerkovskiy suspension
summary: Carrie Ann Inaba revealed she and Jenna Johnson "hugged it out" after the lift rule controversy and Val Chmerkovskiy's suspension from "DWTS."
story: The "Boy Meets World" alum says partner Pasha Pashkov has helped her embrace confidence on and off the dance floor.
Carrie Ann Inaba addressed recent controversies on "Dancing With the Stars" with one swift social media post.

Inaba embraced Jenna Johnson in one image captured during the Oct. 20 show, the same episode where Johnson's husband, Val Chmerkovskiy, was suspended after sharing an inappropriate image online aimed at the judge.
During last month's episode, Inaba criticized Johnson's lifts, to which the dancer received a reading after she pushed back.
VAL CHMERKOVSKIY SUSPENDED FROM 'DANCING WITH THE STARS' OVER WILL SMITH OSCARS SLAP REFERENCE
Carrie Ann Inaba talked about how negative comments hurt her mental health. (Getty Images)

"I have not spoken about what happened because of professional courtesy for those who are still competing, and we actually have standards and practices that keep us separated," Inaba wrote on Instagram.

"I think it’s important for everyone to know that Jenna and I hugged it out after the Super Bowl show. Jenna was an absolute professional about it, and two women worked through the moment. It came to my attention later that Jenna was deeply hurt. So I also offered to speak with her at anytime."
JOHN STAMOS TOLD 'DANCING WITH THE STARS' PRODUCERS TO NEVER ASK HIM TO JOIN THE SHOW AGAIN

She added, "I have also offered to discuss the lift rule and how I enforce it. @ sharnaburgess made a great video explaining lifts, assists and which dances allow and don’t allow them. I think in the future, a new lift rule should be created for next season."
Inaba received criticism in the past for docking points over lifts, with fans claiming she picks and chooses when to apply her rule.

"I think in the future, a new lift rule should be created for next season," she commented. "I think a session of with all the dancers and the judges in a room together to discuss the history of how and why Len Goodman, our original producers and I defined the lift rule and the what the purpose is which is safety and fairness. [sic]"
CARRIE ANN INABA SHARES HER STRUGGLE TO MANAGE HIDDEN, INVISIBLE ILLNESS: 'IT'S REAL'
"The show has evolved tremendously, the way the show is cast has also changed, and so has our audience and the way they consume the show."
"DWTS" judge Carrie Ann Inaba admitted to being harder on the female contestants. (Getty Images)
Inaba added, "So, working together to create a better understanding between the dancers and the judges and our audience is important to me, as we move forward and is something I have asked for."

title: Chris Pratt went from living in a van to Hollywood stardom after chance encounter changed everything
summary: Chris Pratt recalls the moment Rae Dawn Chong walked into Bubba Gump Shrimp Company and offered him a role that launched his Hollywood career.
story: The actor opened up to Fox News Digital about fatherhood and admitted he hopes to learn from both his own father’s strengths and mistakes while raising his children.
Chris Pratt's journey to becoming one of Hollywood's go-to action stars started with him living in a van in Hawaii.

In a recent post on X, the 47-year-old actor reflected on his beginnings: "Before Hollywood, I was living in a van in Hawaii and waiting tables at Bubba Gump Shrimp Company," revealing that a chance encounter working one night changed his life.

"One day, the incredible Rae Dawn Chong walked into the restaurant, and naturally, I went up to her table and said, 'Hey, you’re a movie star! What are you doing here?'" he recalled. "She asked if I could act, and I said, 'F- - - yeah, put me in your movie!'"
Since he didn't have a phone, he gave Chong his friend Mike's number, who told him a few days later that someone had called for him.
Pratt reflected on the early days of his career in a recent social media post. (Mike Coppola/Getty Images)
NICKI MINAJ, ANNA NICOLE SMITH AND MORE STARS WHO GOT THEIR START WAITING TABLES AT RED LOBSTER

"I called her back, and sure enough, she was serious," he wrote. "I drove over to pick up the script, went back to Mike’s house, and read all 120 pages three times in a row. First script I’d ever read. My character's name was Devon, and I remember thinking, 'Sweet! I could totally play a Devon!'
After the audition, he recalled Chung telling him he "could act and offered me the part."

While he lived in Hawaii, the movie was filming in Los Angeles, which made Pratt a little nervous, as he had "about $60 to my name, a bag of clothes, and some rollerblades." He then found out that Chung would fly him out to Los Angeles for production.

"I remember thinking right then and there, my life just changed forever. I'm going to be an actor," he wrote. "That little movie was 'Cursed Part 3,' a low-budget horror comedy that opened the door to Hollywood for me. I'll forever be grateful to Rae for taking a chance on a kid working at a shrimp restaurant. Everybody starts somewhere, and this is where it all began for me."
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE
Pratt had $60 to his name when he was offered a part in his first movie. (Dimitrios Kambouris/Getty Images)
Pratt's role in "Cursed Part 3" led to bigger projects, including his breakout role playing Andy Dwyer in the hit NBC show, "Parks and Recreation."

He then landed the role of Peter Quill, or Star-Lord, in the Marvel movie, "Guardians of the Galaxy," playing the character in the film's two sequels, as well as in "Avengers: Infinity War" and "Avengers: Endgame."
Pratt credited James Gunn for changing his life. (Charley Gallay/Getty Images for Disney)

When speaking to Moviefone in May 2023, Pratt shared he is "grateful" for "Guardians of the Galaxy" director James Gunn for casting him as the lead in the movie, saying, "He's changed my life" and the life of his children.

"He found a working actor who had already at that point done way better than most people who come out to town. I wasn't a waiter any longer, I was a series regular on a show. I was getting recognition," he said. "He brought me to a whole new level that ultimately changed the entire way the industry saw me. I no longer was auditioning. That was the last audition I ever had. So he changed my life."
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Pratt went on to star in a number of successful projects. (Alberto E. Rodriguez/Getty Images)

Since becoming a Marvel superhero, Pratt has starred in the "Jurassic World" franchise, voiced characters in "The Lego Movie" and its sequel, "The Super Mario Bros. Movie" and its sequel and "Onward," and has starred in the TV series "The Terminal List" since 2022.
He has also starred in a number of standalone blockbusters, including "Passengers," "The Magnificent Seven," "The Tomorrow War" and many others.

Chris Pratt stars in "The Terminal List." (Marni Grossman/Prime)
Pratt was married to actress Anna Faris from July 2009 to August 2017, when they announced their separation. They share one child together, a son named Jack, 14.
He then married Katherine Schwarzenegger in June 2019, and they share three children together; Lyla, 6, Eloise, 4, and Ford, 1.

"It's an incredible blessing to be a father. It's also a lot of hard work. And so I think I just want to teach them that ... I don't know, I want to do my best," he told Fox News Digital in October. "I basically want to get right everything my dad got right and get right everything my dad got wrong. And I'm sure I'll screw up both, you know?"
Pratt called being a father a "blessing." (Pablo Cuadra / Getty Images)

title: Michael Douglas says Jack Nicholson 'has disappeared' from the Hollywood spotlight
summary: Michael Douglas claims Jack Nicholson is enjoying "walking around in his slippers" after essentially disappearing from Hollywood following 2010 film.
story: Michael Douglas discusses surviving stage 4 cancer, maintaining a lasting marriage and his close relationship with son Cameron. The Oscar winner has written a new memoir, "One Helluva Ride."
Michael Douglas admitted his longtime friend, Jack Nicholson, has essentially "disappeared" from the spotlight.
Douglas, 82, reflected on his storied career and missed opportunities while discussing his new memoir, "One Helluva Ride."
When asked who he never had a chance to work with, Douglas noted that he "would have liked to have acted with Jack," according to The Independent.
"He's not working any more. He's well," Douglas said. "He has disappeared. I know that."
JACK NICHOLSON'S DAUGHTER CALLS OUT HOLLYWOOD'S STATUS-CHASING ELITE IN SCATHING NEW ESSAY ABOUT MODERN LA
Michael Douglas admitted Jack Nicholson has "disappeared" after decades of work. (Getty Images)

The "Wall Street" actor added, "I still see him, but he is fine. He is up there by his house and walking around in his slippers. It happens. He deserves it. I understand. He is a few years older than me, but I understand."
Nicholson, 89, is rarely seen in public and was last credited on the 2010 film "How Do You Know."
PARIS JACKSON SAYS DAD MICHAEL’S UNUSUAL RULE HELPED PROTECT HER CHILDHOOD
Last week, Crystal Hefner exposed secrets about the Playboy Mansion and its star-studded roster of attendees.
Hefner, 40, name-dropped one Hollywood heavy-hitter who was known for his frequent trips to the Holmby Hills home during an episode of her "After the Mansion" podcast.
Michael Douglas recently released his memoir, "One Helluva Ride." (Getty Images)
"I think a lot of celebrities came because they were just curious, and others used it as their personal country club," she said.
"They used to call it Jack Nicholson’s drive-thru at one point because he would drive up, grab some food or whatever else he could get there and leave."
Nicholson's daughter, Lorraine, once shared her own experiences at the famous mansion where she spent her childhood playing with Hef's sons, Marston and Cooper.

"People assume that my father took me to the Mansion, but they assume wrong," she wrote in a 2024 essay for Vanity Fair. "In fact, I can venture with confidence that I spent more time there than my father ever did."
Jack Nicholson and actress Rebecca Broussard had two children: Lorraine and Raymond Nicholson. (Mirek Towski)

Lorraine wrote about growing up as the daughter of somewhat controversial parents, and noted that her friend's parents were "not so keen on letting their children come over to Jack Nicholson's house."

"For the Hefners, I imagine it was nice to know that my father would never be like the other fathers, lingering a little too long after their children were dropped off, marveling, open-mouthed and fully clothed, at the way the refracted light danced on the roof of the grotto," Lorraine wrote.

"They didn’t have to worry about these things, because my father was on the list. Which meant that he could show up at the Mansion, without an invitation, at any time."
Rebecca Broussard and Jack Nicholson welcomed Lorraine into the world in 1990. They dated for five years before ending their relationship in 1994. (Getty Images)

Crystal also admitted her late husband was obsessed with Hollywood lore and stardom.
"One thing that mattered most to Hef was fame," she shared.

"Any celebrity was treated extremely well whenever they visited. He would have Bill Maher for chats, hang with Berry Gordy of Motown and then you’d see plenty of other people there. Buzz Aldrin, the original Catwoman."
Crystal Hefner claimed Jack Nicholson was often at the Playboy Mansion. (Ralph Dominguez)
She added, "I always liked the non-womanizer celebrities. They always felt more safe."

Crystal began dating Hefner when she was 21 years old. The couple got engaged in 2010 when she was 24 and the Playboy founder was 84.
They called off their wedding just days before the ceremony in 2011 but later reconciled. Crystal and Hefner married in 2012 and remained together until his death in 2017. He was 91.
Hugh Hefner died in 2017. He was 91. (Charley Gallay/Getty Images for Playboy)
She explained that during Hef's "final years," she did her best to "treat him with respect and dignity."
Crystal wanted the media mogul to "still feel like he was respected and revered all the way until the very end."

"The entire mansion existed to cater to Hef's needs, women included," she said. "He would cry during the romantic scenes of the old films and just look over at me to help him. Or maybe it was a performance to encourage me to believe his feelings were real."

title: Jenny McCarthy living in a tent while battling ‘paranoid’ fears after mold poisoning diagnosis
summary: Jenny McCarthy says mold and mycotoxin poisoning left her living in a tent after two years of surgeries, infections and a desperate search for answers.
story: Donnie Wahlberg and Jenny McCarthy told Fox News Digital that they prefer ordering take-out and watching the faith-based TV show for date nights.
Jenny McCarthy's two-year health nightmare left her physically exhausted, emotionally shaken and so fearful of mold exposure that she traded her home for a tent in a desperate attempt to heal.
The former TV host revealed that her ordeal began in 2024 and spiraled into a series of painful infections, surgeries and unexplained symptoms during an episode of "The Jenny McCarthy Wahlberg Show."

"Okay, I have been dying to tell you this story because the last two years of my life have been absolutely fricking insane. Insane, okay?" McCarthy told her viewers. "Some of you guys already know that I’ve been dealing with mold and mycotoxin poisoning. I’ve talked about pieces of it before."
BRANDI GLANVILLE SPEAKS OUT ON COMPLEX DIAGNOSIS AND $6K MONTHLY MEDICAL BATTLE

Jenny McCarthy revealed she had been living in a tent after a grueling two-year health battle left her fearful of mold exposure and increasingly paranoid about her surroundings. (WireImage/Getty Images)
McCarthy claimed the whole ordeal began in 2024 with a toothache.

"And somehow that led me down a rabbit hole of doctors, surgeries, teeth being pulled, mysterious growths popping up in places you are not expecting, implants literally falling out, and eventually realizing my immune system was fighting something so much bigger," she said.
McCarthy's health spiraled into a series of medical complications, including severe dental infections, repeated surgeries, jawbone damage and recurring eye cysts.

The former "The View" co-host also battled debilitating leg cramps, facial swelling, worsening food allergies and insomnia before undergoing testing that she said revealed mold poisoning. McCarthy claimed the condition had compromised her body's ability to fight infections, leaving her physically and emotionally exhausted.
