title: 5 habits that could help keep you out of a nursing home, from an orthopedic surgeon
summary: Dr. Vonda Wright shares five daily habits that help older adults maintain independent living, starting with skeletal longevity and muscle strength.
story: Dr. Vonda Wright, a surgeon and longevity expert, reveals her top strategies for staying out of a nursing home and preserving mobility.
Three in four Americans aged 50 and older would like to remain in their homes as they age, according to the AARP — and preserving that independence starts with daily habits.

Dr. Vonda Wright, a double board-certified orthopedic surgeon, author and authority on active aging and mobility, who is based in Orlando, Florida, said there are three main problems that can make it difficult for older adults to age in place.
Those include difficulty getting up from a chair and caring for themselves, memory problems, and incontinence that makes it hard to manage personal hygiene.
FORGET THE GYM: A 30-SECOND TEST MAY BE ONE OF THE BEST INDICATORS OF LONGEVITY
"The missing piece in most conversations between mental health, physical health and independence is your skeletal longevity," Wright said.
Three in four Americans aged 50 and older would like to remain in their homes as they age, according to the AARP. (iStock)
Staying independent with age requires attention to the entire musculoskeletal system, including the muscles, bones and tendons, according to the surgeon.
Wright shared the following habits as most important for maintaining independence outside of a nursing home.
No. 1: Keep moving
The human body "craves mobility," Wright said.
"When you think about it, it's our first skill. We learn to walk when we're 1," she pointed out.
WEEKLY WEIGHTLIFTING SWEET SPOT MAY BE LINKED TO LONGER LIFE, STUDY FINDS

For older adults, staying active can help preserve the ability to handle everyday tasks independently. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention suggests low-impact activities such as walking, cycling and water exercise.
"Even when your hips hurt, even when your knees hurt, you should move on the ground, or get in a pool in chest-high water," Wright suggested.
Staying independent with age requires attention to the entire musculoskeletal system, including the muscles, bones and tendons, according to the surgeon. (iStock)
While the doctor does not recommend exercising through a new injury or severe pain, she pushed back against the belief that rest is the best way to address pain.
PEOPLE LIVING PAST 100 IN ONE TINY VILLAGE SHARE 3 DAILY HABITS

"Rest doesn't cure anything. When you have, for instance, arthritic knees, do you know what can help? Building the muscles around your knees, building the muscles in your hips to support your knees," she said. "So rest is not the answer for feeling better — staying strong and mobile is."
No. 2: Build muscle
Strength training can help older adults maintain the ability to get out of a chair, climb stairs and carry groceries — everyday tasks that support independent living.
There is never an age or skill level when it’s too late to build muscle, according to Wright.
FITNESS EXPERT REVEALS 6 THINGS PEOPLE OVER 35 SHOULD DO AFTER WORKOUTS TO STAY STRONG

"Even if you feel like you've declined or your parents have declined, there is no age or skill level when we can't become more mobile, when we can't build muscle or reconnect the neuromuscular pathways," she said.

It’s even possible to build muscle sitting in a wheelchair, she noted. "Some of the very first research done by Dr. Maria Fiatarone at Tufts University showed that even at 90 years old, you can regain function."
"There is no age or skill level when we can't become more mobile, when we can't build muscle."

In that small 1990 study, nine nursing home residents who completed eight weeks of high-intensity resistance training increased their muscle strength by an average of 174%, and also showed improvements in muscle size and mobility.
For older adults, staying active can help preserve the ability to handle everyday tasks independently. (iStock)
The National Institute on Aging recommends that older adults perform muscle-strengthening activities at least two days a week, targeting all major muscle groups, with recovery time between sessions.
Some options include resistance bands, hand weights and body-weight exercises. Beginners are advised to start gradually and seek guidance from a doctor or physical therapist as needed.
No. 3: Eat enough to support strength
Older adults tend to eat less, which can undermine efforts to maintain energy and build muscle, Wright warned.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"It’s something I see even happening to my 86-year-old parents; they're just eating less and less," she said. "And we cannot fuel the muscle we want to build [and] the energy we need without a protein-forward, adequate-calorie diet."
"The most common mistake I see seniors making as they age is assuming that aging is an inevitable decline from vitality to frailty."
Although older adults may require fewer calories, they still need enough nutrients to support their health, according to the National Institute on Aging.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

To help maintain muscle, the agency recommends that older adults consume protein-rich foods throughout the day, including seafood, dairy, fortified soy products, beans and lentils. Specific calorie needs will vary based on each person’s weight and activity level.
No. 4: Drop the mindset that decline is inevitable
Wright urged older adults to challenge assumptions about what they can and can’t do as they age.
The surgeon urged older adults to challenge assumptions about what they can and can’t do as they age. (iStock)
"The most common mistake I see seniors making as they age is assuming that aging is an inevitable decline from vitality to frailty," she said.
"They just assume that a certain number of birthday candles predisposes them to sitting on a couch the rest of their life. The reality is that there is no age or skill level when you're done."
No. 5: Have open conversations
Wright suggested that people should start working toward future independence during their busy working years.

"We need to start thinking about that in our busiest times of life, in our 30s, our 40s, our prime times of working," she said. "It’s part of a long-term, lifetime plan to live where you want to live, with whom you want to live, when you want to live there."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The doctor recommends that adults directly ask their aging parents what assistance they need and to explore available support, including community programs.
Although older adults may require fewer calories, they still need enough nutrients to support their health, according to the National Institute on Aging. (iStock)
In many cases, she said, parents do not want to be a burden to their adult children, so they never ask for anything.
"I think this is a time for really open, frank conversations," Wright said. "What do you want help with? How can I help you? How could we get help for you if possible?"
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

As an example, Wright said her elderly parents live with her family. When she noticed their meals started to suffer while she was traveling, she arranged for support to help them continue managing their lives.
"I have half of their meals delivered every week because I'm not going to be home to shop or cook," she said. "They remain independent, but with assistance. And that's what works for us."

title: Paper straws could be doing more harm than good, study suggests
summary: A South Korean government-commissioned life cycle assessment found paper straws scored 6.33 times higher than plastic on a cancer-related measure.
story: 'Fox & Friends' co-hosts react to a new study raising concerns about the environmental impact of paper straws while revisiting President Donald Trump's decision to bring back plastic straws.
Paper straws have been marketed as a more environmentally friendly alternative to plastic, but a new South Korean assessment suggests they may carry a greater pollution-related health burden.
South Korea’s Ministry of Climate, Energy and Environment commissioned the assessment from the Korean Society for Life Cycle Assessment, according to news reports.
Researchers compared how paper, plastic and other disposable straws could affect human health and the environment, from production through disposal.
POPULAR ARTIFICIAL SWEETENER LINKED TO POTENTIALLY DANGEROUS HEART RISK
Paper straws scored 6.33 times as high as conventional plastic straws in an estimate of cancer-related harm from pollution generated during production and disposal, according to South Korean reports.
The score estimates potential harm from pollution generated from production through disposal — not chemical exposure or cancer risk from drinking through a straw, the researchers noted.
The assessment compared how paper, plastic and other disposable straws could affect human health and the environment, from production through disposal. (iStock)
The assessment reportedly compared four straw types: paper, conventional plastic, biodegradable plastic and bio-based polyethylene, or bio-PE.
Researchers assessed 16 environmental impacts, assuming about 74% of discarded straws were incinerated and 26% went to landfills, based on South Korean waste statistics.
MICROPLASTICS DETECTED IN MOST HEART ATTACK PATIENTS' BLOOD IN STARTLING NEW STUDY
Conventional plastic straws performed best in 10 of the 16 environmental categories, but no straw type came out ahead in every category.
The study did not measure whether chemicals leach from straws into drinks and did not assess health outcomes among people who use them.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Researchers recommended that stores provide disposable straws only upon request, according to The Korea Herald.
Paper straws scored higher than conventional plastic straws on one modeled measure related to cancer-causing effects, according to reports. (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)
Lawmaker Kim Wi-sang, whose office received the report, later criticized plastic straw restrictions, arguing that alternatives had failed to deliver their promised environmental benefits.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
President Donald Trump has also criticized paper straws, calling them ineffective and arguing that they may pose health risks.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

In February 2025, he signed an executive order directing federal agencies to stop buying and providing paper straws and to develop a national strategy to end their use, according to a White House press release.
"I was tired of having straws melt in my mouth," Trump previously said.
The study’s findings do not prove that drinking through a paper straw increases a person’s cancer risk. (iStock)

Fox News Digital previously reported on health concerns raised by Florida lawmakers, including a 2023 University of Antwerp study that detected PFAS, or "forever chemicals," in 27 of 39 straw brands tested, most often in paper straws.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Separately, 360° Foodservice, a European food-service packaging association, previously said its member companies have a no-PFAS clause and set requirements for food-contact safety.
Fox News Digital reached out to the Foodservice Packaging Institute and 360° Foodservice for comment.
Deirdre Bardolf is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital.

title: Get $20K 'trophy arms' at home without spending a dime, NYC fitness trainer says
summary: A New York City trainer shares the twice-weekly arm workout and high protein diet strategy behind sculpted "trophy arms," no $20,000 needed.
story: Marfred Suazo, better known as "Fonz the Trainer," said many of his clients want 'trophy arms' and shared his top strategies for achieving that look.

With some women reportedly spending up to $20,000 to achieve sculpted "trophy arms," a New York City fitness trainer says a targeted at-home routine and proper nutrition can offer a more affordable alternative.
Marfred Suazo, better known as "Fonz the Trainer," said he often has clients aiming to get what he calls the "holy grail" of arms.
Building trophy arms doesn’t require daily workouts, but exercise selection, controlled movements and nutrition matter, according to Suazo, who runs a program called the Decade Strong Blueprint.
BIGGEST WASTE OF MONEY IN YOUR HOME GYM MAY SURPRISE YOU, FITNESS EXPERT SAYS

"A lot of people talk about tone and things like that, but I think the best thing — the epitome of an arm — is having it well-balanced and well-framed into the body and having the right proportion from the shoulders to the triceps and biceps," he told Fox News Digital.
A New York City fitness trainer says a targeted at-home routine and proper nutrition can help people achieve "trophy arms." (iStock)
The goal should be proper proportion to a person’s frame rather than size, Suazo emphasized.
A structured approach can help people make the most of their workout time, according to the trainer.
10-MINUTE FITNESS HABIT CAN HELP ADULTS OVER 40 MAINTAIN MUSCLE AND STAY STRONG

"Most of us don’t have so much available time to do it, so we want to do it as smartly and as effectively as possible," he said. "A more planned-out training protocol will get you to that point where you really start seeing the arms develop and change in shape."
Suazo shared the following tips for building stronger, more defined arms.
No. 1: Choose the right exercises

Suazo recommends combining exercises that work multiple muscle groups, such as pullups, rows and chest presses, with movements that target specific areas, including lateral raises and triceps extensions.

"We’re building muscle with these bigger movements, these compound movements, and then just fine-detailing everything else with lateral raises, triceps extensions and overhead triceps extensions," he said.
Building sculpted "trophy arms" doesn’t require daily workouts, but exercise selection, controlled movements and nutrition matter, according to the trainer. (iStock)
No. 2: Find the right frequency
Suazo recommends training the arms twice a week, noting that chest and back workouts also work those muscles.
"Two to three times a week, I think, is more than enough."
JUST 10 MINUTES OF DAILY FLOOR EXERCISES MAY IMPROVE BALANCE AND AGILITY, STUDY FINDS
Adults should do muscle-strengthening activities that work all major muscle groups at least two days a week, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
Muscle-strengthening activities can include lifting weights, using resistance bands or performing body-weight exercises such as pushups.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
It’s also important to allow muscles time to recover. The National Institutes of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases advises against working the same muscles on consecutive days.
No. 3: Focus on controlled movement
Some common mistakes include rushing through exercises and failing to use a "full range of motion," Suazo said.
"Full range of motion" refers to a comfortable range performed with good technique, without forcing a painful movement.

The trainer recommends combining exercises that work multiple muscle groups — such as pull-ups, rows and chest presses — with movements that target specific areas, including lateral raises and triceps extensions. (iStock)
Suazo emphasized deliberate, controlled movements rather than simply rushing to reach a target number of repetitions.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"Moving with intention is the biggest thing, where you’re really fatiguing the muscles, and you’re getting growth and stimulus out of them," he advised.
Lighter weights can also challenge the muscles when the exercises are sufficiently demanding, Suazo added.
"We’re building muscle with these bigger compound movements."
Make nutrition count
Nutrition also plays a role in getting the desired results, Suazo said.
"You use the gym and all your training programs to really shape the arm as best as possible and build the areas that you want. To reveal these things, you can only do that with proper nutrition."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Protein helps the body build, maintain and repair muscle, according to the National Institutes of Health’s Office of Dietary Supplements.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Suazo recommends three to four meals a day, with protein included throughout the day.
"You want to have protein-conscious meals a few times per day," he said. "This will help reveal all the hard labor that you’re doing in the gym to develop a tremendous physique aesthetically."
Melissa Rudy is senior health editor and a member of the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to melissa.rudy@fox.com.

title: E. coli outbreak lands 3 in hospital, health officials investigate link to pumpkin patch
summary: Three children are in intensive care after an E. coli outbreak potentially linked to Brookshire Farms pumpkin patch in San Luis Obispo, California.
story: Dr. Tyler Evans, an infectious disease physician and founder of Wellness Equity Alliance in California, speaks with Fox News Digital about E. coli infections linked to a California pumpkin patch that closed just days before Halloween.
Three children are in intensive care with E. coli infections as health officials investigate a possible link to a California pumpkin patch that closed just days before Halloween.

Five cases of Shiga toxin-producing E. coli infection have been confirmed, potentially originating from Brookshire Farms in San Luis Obispo, according to an Oct. 27 advisory issued by the County of San Luis Obispo Public Health Department.
The suspected exposure period is Oct. 16 through Oct 26.
FDA WIDENS CYCLOSPORA OUTBREAK INVESTIGATION TO SIX MORE STATES AS CONFIRMED CASES TOP 6,000
Health officials advise that anyone who visited the pumpkin patch between those dates should monitor for gastrointestinal symptoms.
Three children are in intensive care with E. coli infections as health officials investigate a possible link to a California pumpkin patch that closed just days before Halloween. (Getty Images)
"We are working diligently to identify the source of these infections to protect the health of our community," said County Health Officer Dr. Christy Mulkerin in the news release.
"We encourage anyone who may have been exposed and is experiencing symptoms consistent with E. coli infection to seek immediate medical attention."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Typical symptoms of E. coli include cramping, severe abdominal pain, bloody diarrhea and signs of dehydration, which usually begin within three to 10 days of exposure.

Young children under 10 are typically at the highest risk for complications, which can include hemolytic uremic syndrome, a serious condition that damages blood cells and can lead to kidney failure, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
"We are working diligently to identify the source of these infections to protect the health of our community," said County Health Officer Dr. Christy Mulkerin in the news release. (iStock)
Dr. Tyler Evans, an infectious disease physician and founder of Wellness Equity Alliance in California, warned that diarrhea can lead to dehydration and fatigue.
"The diarrhea is really the key component here, and the stomach cramps," he told Fox News Digital.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Evans said younger children and older adults can be particularly vulnerable, emphasizing the need to closely watch children younger than 5.
Typical symptoms of E. coli include cramping, severe abdominal pain, bloody diarrhea and signs of dehydration, which usually begin within three to 10 days of exposure. (iStock)
Speaking generally about potential exposure routes in pumpkin patches, Evans said E. coli can spread when bacteria from feces reach someone’s mouth.
He pointed to potentially contaminated food or water, animal contact and person-to-person transmission as possible transmission routes.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Evans also noted that not all E. coli bacteria cause illness. The confirmed cases in this investigation involve Shiga toxin-producing E. coli.
"One of the most effective ways that we can prevent this is washing your hands," the doctor added.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The farm has voluntarily closed as a precaution while investigators work to identify the source of the infections, determine whether the cases are connected and assess whether others may be at risk, according to the county health department.
Brookshire Farms told Fox News Digital it was reserving comment pending test results from the county health department.
Melissa Rudy is senior health editor and a member of the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to melissa.rudy@fox.com.

title: Common developmental condition linked to higher risk of Parkinson's-related disorders
summary: Older adults with autism were diagnosed with parkinsonism at more than double the rate of the general population, a study of 57 million Americans found.
story: Dr. Chadrick Lane, a neuropsychiatrist and director of the geriatric and neuropsychiatry clinic at UT Southwestern Medical Center in Dallas, Texas, said humor can be a helpful wellness tool for those navigating the Parkinson's journey.

Older adults diagnosed with autism face a significantly higher risk of developing Parkinson’s disease-related movement disorders compared to the general population, according to a large new study published in the journal Autism.
Researchers analyzed Medicare and Medicaid claims data covering nearly 57 million Americans aged 45 and older between 2017 and 2019.
Individuals on the spectrum, as well as those with intellectual disabilities, were diagnosed with parkinsonism at much higher rates than those without autism.
HOW EATING HABITS COULD INFLUENCE PARKINSON’S DISEASE RISK, ACCORDING TO EXPERTS

Parkinsonism refers to a range of neurological conditions characterized by certain movement symptoms, including tremors, muscle rigidity, balance difficulties and slowed voluntary movement, according to the Parkinson’s Foundation.

While earlier research suggested an overlap between autism and motor decline later in life, it was unclear whether those problems stemmed from the condition or from antipsychotic medications, which are widely known to trigger Parkinson’s-like symptoms as a secondary side effect.

A nationwide study of nearly 57 million Americans aged 45 and older revealed that adults with autism and intellectual disabilities are diagnosed with Parkinson’s-related movement disorders at rates far exceeding those in the general population. (iStock)

To determine whether medications explained the link, researchers excluded people who took antipsychotics from the analysis. They still found higher rates of Parkinson’s-related diagnoses in neurodivergent populations.

In the general population control group, the prevalence of parkinsonism was roughly 1.57%. The prevalence rose to 3.83% among adults with autism alone, 4.32% for those with an intellectual disability alone, and 4.86% among individuals diagnosed with both autism and an intellectual disability.
PARKINSON’S PATIENT’S YEARS-LONG TREMOR VANISHES WITHIN MINUTES OF NEW ULTRASOUND TREATMENT

"A critically important new contribution of this study is increased incidence rates of parkinsonism for autistic people in middle and older adulthood, which suggests that these cases aren’t simply a byproduct of lifelong motor challenges," Greg Wallace, lead author and a professor in the Department of Speech, Language and Hearing Sciences at The George Washington University in Washington, D.C., said in a press release.
The study represents the first time scientists have tracked the incidence rate, or the risk of newly emerging cases over time, among older autistic individuals.
The risk of parkinsonism persisted even after researchers completely eliminated individuals taking antipsychotic medications, ruling out common drug-induced side effects as the sole driver. (iStock)
"It is therefore important for clinicians to establish clear baselines of motor skills and challenges during adulthood that can be tracked over time," Wallace added.
Dr. Lee Murray, a neurologist based in Jackson, Tennessee, said this study clarifies previous research that suggested patients with autism are at a higher risk of having Parkinson's.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"This study takes into account the use of antipsychotic medications that can cause a Parkinson's look (resting tremor, stiffness, shuffled gait, stooped posture, softened voice), which is a different pathology than stereotypical or idiopathic Parkinson's disease," Murray, who was not involved in the study, told Fox News Digital.
"This study showed patients with autism that was associated with intellectual disability seem to have the greatest association with concomitant Parkinson's."

The neurologist cautioned that autism encompasses a wide range of symptoms and severity, so the findings don't mean that people with milder cases face a significantly higher risk of Parkinson’s disease.
"It certainly is an interesting correlation, although it does not imply that someone with autism is certain to develop Parkinson's," Murray added.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"From a clinical perspective, it's helpful to review medications with the autistic patient's physicians and, if possible, try to avoid medications that may cause a Parkinson's appearance."
Despite the scope of the data, the authors noted several key limitations of using insurance records.
A major limitation of the research stems from its reliance on Medicare and Medicaid billing records, which carry risks of diagnostic coding errors. (iStock)

The investigation relied on billing and diagnostic codes submitted through Medicare and Medicaid, which can contain errors or reflect differences in how clinics and medical providers diagnose conditions.
The reliance on claims data also means researchers could not assess the severity of individual motor symptoms or examine the role of lifestyle factors, genetics and family history, they noted.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Additionally, the data only captured adults who were enrolled in public insurance programs, potentially leaving out older individuals who rely strictly on private health insurance.
"Patients with autism can have atypical movements that can be misdiagnosed as Parkinson's if the examiner is not accustomed to diagnosing it."

Because people on the autism spectrum may already struggle with coordination, repetitive behaviors or executive functioning challenges, experts say early indicators of Parkinson’s disease can be missed or mistaken, potentially delaying essential care.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"Patients with autism can have atypical movements that can be misdiagnosed as Parkinson's if the examiner is not accustomed to diagnosing it," Murray confirmed.

The researchers emphasized the need for physicians, long-term care facilities and family caregivers to closely monitor older autistic patients for motor decline so interventions can begin as early as possible.
Khloe Quill is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital. She and the lifestyle team cover a range of story topics including food and drink, travel, and health.

title: White House official details what gets Trump’s attention in intelligence briefings
summary: President Trump receives photos of drug seizures during briefings and presses officials on protecting individual victims amid the sweeping cartel crackdown.
story: Federal authorities detail a Homeland Security Task Force operation targeting the Trinitarios gang, whose alleged members were charged in connection with murders and other violent crimes. (Department of Homeland Security via X)

EXCLUSIVE: President Donald Trump may be briefed on sprawling cartel networks and massive drug seizures, but sometimes it's the story of a single American crime victim that captures his attention, a White House official told Fox News Digital.

The official described how Trump can shift from discussions about major criminal organizations to an individual harmed by crime, pressing officials about what more the federal government can do to protect everyday Americans.
"I could be talking about very grand cartel stuff, which he's very interested in," the official said, explaining that the president may instead focus on one person hurt by criminal activity.
WHITE HOUSE HIGHLIGHTS 'STEEPEST' EVER DECLINE IN US CASUALTIES FROM CARTELS AMID BOAT STRIKES
According to a White House official, President Trump will pivot during intelligence briefings to hear about how everyday Americans are affected by crime. (Getty Images)

The official said Trump receives regular briefings that include photographs of narcotics seized by federal agents. While the president takes pride in successful enforcement operations, the official described his reaction as quickly turning to the amount of work still ahead.

The president's response to the photographs, according to the official, is to ask what more can be done to stop the flow of drugs into American communities. Trump also pressed for federal agencies to work together as the administration seeks to dismantle entire criminal organizations rather than simply arrest their leaders as agencies have done in the past.
That approach is at the center of a campaign that has brought together more than 20 federal agencies under the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) initiative.

According to figures provided by the White House, the task forces made nearly 12,000 arrests during fiscal year 2026, seized approximately 161 metric tons of drugs, $482 million in criminal assets and nearly 13,000 weapons.
ICE ARRESTS MORE THAN 100 ALLEGED GANG MEMBERS IN SINGLE WEEK, INCLUDING VIOLENT MS-13, TDA SUSPECTS: DHS

Weapons taken from 26 Trinitarios gang leaders, members and associates are laid out on a table during a press conference at the Moakley Federal Courthouse in Boston on June 9, 2026. (Boston Globe via Getty Images)

The administration also reported 676 criminal organizations disrupted in figures provided to Fox News Digital. The task forces have 6,585 active investigations, including more than 1,000 targeting major drug kingpins and 814 targeting designated Foreign Terrorist Organizations.

The task force operates nationwide, bringing together federal law enforcement agencies with hundreds of state, local and international partners. Its public website, HSTF.gov, outlines the initiative's mission, participating agencies and enforcement efforts targeting cartels, transnational gangs and other criminal organizations.

Behind those numbers, the official described an effort to break down longstanding divisions among federal law enforcement agencies that previously pursued overlapping investigations with varying degrees of cooperation.
DOJ TOUTS HUNDREDS OF GUN, DRUG ARRESTS AS ST LOUIS SURGE OPERATION ENDS: 'VIOLENCE IS NOT INEVITABLE'

A photograph showing Trinitarios gang members rests behind a table filled with items taken during the arrests of 26 Trinitarios gang leaders, members and associates for their alleged involvement in five murders and 19 attempted murders in Essex County during a press conference at the Moakley Federal Courthouse on June 9, 2026. (Boston Globe via Getty Images)
The official said more than 1,800 cartel-related narcotics task forces previously operated across the country, with varying degrees of coordination.
Agencies including the FBI, DEA and Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) could pursue overlapping targets, occasionally competing to bring indictments first.
Interagency disagreements sometimes left investigations stalled for years, the official said.

Under the new approach, the National Coordination Center brings together the Departments of Justice and Homeland Security, with support from military and intelligence partners, to resolve conflicts and coordinate investigations across jurisdictions.
DRUG CARTEL KINGPIN AMONG TARGETS IN SWEEPING TRUMP CRACKDOWN ON ALLEGED MEXICAN CORRUPTION NETWORK

Items taken from 26 Trinitarios gang leaders, members and associates arrested for their alleged involvement in five murders and 19 attempted murders in Essex County are laid out on a table during a press conference at the Moakley Federal Courthouse in Boston on June 9, 2026. (Boston Globe via Getty Images)
"Now we're all indicting together," the official said.
Rather than focusing exclusively on high-value targets, investigators are pursuing the transportation networks, distributors, collectors and money launderers that keep criminal enterprises operating.
The official explained that taking down a cartel leader does not necessarily dismantle the organization because others can quickly assume leadership.
"There's five more people ready to step up as soon as we take out one," the official said.
A sweeping federal investigation into the Trinitarios gang in Massachusetts illustrates the kind of coordinated law enforcement effort the administration is pursuing.
In June, federal prosecutors announced racketeering conspiracy charges against 26 alleged gang leaders, members and associates in connection with five murders and 19 attempted murders.

The announcement brought the total number of Trinitarios members charged in related investigations over two years to 56. Prosecutors alleged the gang's involvement in 11 murders and 30 attempted murders since 2017.

Court documents describe chapters operating in the Boston area whose members allegedly engaged in drug trafficking, kidnappings and witness intimidation. Investigators also alleged the gang recruited minors attending local schools, sometimes using younger members to conceal weapons or serve as lookouts.

The investigation involved HSI, the FBI, DEA, ATF and state and local law enforcement partners. The investigation began before the HSTF initiative, and the charges remain allegations against defendants who have not been convicted.
The task force's reach also extends to drug trafficking operations moving narcotics across state lines.
In Louisiana, federal prosecutors announced five cases involving more than a dozen defendants and hundreds of kilograms of narcotics.

Near Breaux Bridge, investigators discovered approximately 147 kilograms of methamphetamine concealed inside modified ice cream freezers. In another case near Lafayette, authorities found approximately 100 kilograms of cocaine hidden inside an 18-wheeler's cab.

The White House official also pointed to Tren de Aragua, the Venezuelan criminal organization that drew national attention during the 2024 presidential campaign, as an example of the administration's broader strategy.

Fox News Digital extensively covered allegations of Tren de Aragua activity at apartment complexes in Aurora, Colorado, including accounts from local officials and residents who described violence and intimidation.
Trump subsequently made Aurora a recurring focus of his criticism of the Biden administration's border policies.

The official recalled Fox News Digital's reporting on the controversy and argued that the administration's coordinated enforcement campaign has weakened the gang's ability to operate openly in the United States.
"I'm not saying they're completely gone here, but they are so on their heels because we have this concerted effort taken," the official said.
"You don't see them bragging in the social media anymore," the official added.

In May, the Justice Department announced charges against more than 25 defendants in a nationwide Tren de Aragua crackdown spanning six federal judicial districts. Authorities reported seizing more than 80 firearms, approximately 18 kilograms of narcotics and more than $100,000.
The official described the crackdown as an example of the administration's effort to pursue criminal organizations at multiple levels, rather than concentrating solely on their leaders.
The administration is seeking to apply that same approach to more deeply established criminal networks, including the notorious Sinaloa Cartel.
The official said the task force's ultimate objective is not simply accumulating arrests or celebrating drug seizures, but reducing the ability of criminal organizations to threaten Americans.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

For Trump, the official said, even major seizures can serve as reminders of the work still ahead. The president may take pride in enforcement results, but the official described his attention as quickly turning to how much more needs to be done to stop narcotics from reaching American communities.
Jasmine Baehr is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital, where she covers politics, the military, legal debates surrounding life and family policy, as well as faith and culture.

title: Kamala Harris urges Dems to 'be ruthless' with power after midterms, demands Trump accountability
summary: Former Vice President Kamala Harris, former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton and former President Bill Clinton offered their thoughts on the heels of the midterm elections.
story: Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton warned that Democrats will squander their victory in the midterms if they don't stay focused on delivering for voters.

After Democrats swept control of Congress in the 2026 midterm elections, former Vice President Kamala Harris, former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton and former President Bill Clinton offered their views about how the party should use its newfound power.

Harris called for Democrats to ruthlessly leverage their powers to provide "economic relief" and to hold President Donald Trump's "administration accountable for their deep-seated corruption." Hillary Clinton said that "The post-Trump era begins now," while her husband offered a more conciliatory message, and even called for reining in America's national debt.

"On Election Day, the American people spoke loud and clear: they are done with the corruption, incompetence, and callousness coming from the White House and the capitulation of Republican leaders," Harris declared in part of a Wednesday post on X.
KAMALA HARRIS BREAKS WITH LEFT FLANK, WARNS DEMS THAT IMPEACHING TRUMP IS 'NOT A GOOD IDEA'

Former President Bill Clinton, former Vice President Kamala Harris and former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton attend the inauguration ceremonies in the U.S. Capitol Rotunda on Jan. 20, 2025 in Washington, D.C. (Shawn Thew-Pool/Getty Images)

"Now, the work begins to actually deliver results. The American people have elected Democrats across the country in federal, state, and local races who must be ruthless in using every lever of power to deliver economic relief for working families and hold this administration accountable for their deep-seated corruption," she asserted.

Hillary Clinton declared in a Wednesday post on X, "Last night, Americans made a clear call for accountability and affordability. A body politic cannot recover until its harms have been treated and its wounds have been healed. Crimes against our people and our Constitution must be answered for. The historic abuses of the last two years must be prevented from happening again."
She was the 2016 Democratic presidential candidate who lost to Republican Donald Trump.
DEMOCRATS' HISTORIC WINS IN TEXAS HIGHLIGHT TAKING CONTROL OF CONGRESS IN MIDTERM BLUE WAVE
President Donald Trump delivers remarks during a campaign rally at the Ocean Center Arena on Oct. 30, 2026 in Daytona Beach, Fla. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)

"American families should be able to thrive, not just survive. Every child should have the chance to live up to his or her full potential. The American Dream must be more than a mirage. I am confident Democrats can deliver both, and much more. The post-Trump era begins now," Clinton wrote.
Bill Clinton, America's 42nd president, suggested that Democrats have been handed the chance to "rebuild trust."

"The American people have given us clear direction: to put their needs ahead of the chaos and corruption coming out of Washington. That means helping families with the cost of living and protecting their health care. It means ending senseless wars and tariffs that drive up prices. It means getting our national debt under control. And it means holding those in power accountable to the people they serve," he said in part of a statement issued on Wednesday.
HILLARY CLINTON WARNS DEMS MAY SQUANDER MIDTERM VICTORY IF THEY FAIL TO STAY FOCUSED AFTER ELECTION

Former President Bill Clinton and former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton walk through the event area during the 48th Bank of America Chicago Marathon, on Oct. 11, 2026 in Chicago, Ill. (Jacek Boczarski/Anadolu via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"Last night’s victory gives us an opportunity and a responsibility to rebuild trust. We should do so with humility and determination, and an open hand, not a clenched fist, to those who didn’t vote for our candidates," Clinton said.
The White House and Republican National Committee did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's comment requests on Thursday.
Alex Nitzberg is a writer for Fox News Digital.

title: Republicans turn on Trump after devastating midterm losses hand Democrats control of Congress
summary: GOP insiders blame Trump after Election Night's blue tsunami flipped both chambers, with Democrats scoring seven Senate and 27 House pickups.
story: President Donald Trump weighs in on Republicans’ midterm losses, the war with Iran and working with a Democratic-controlled Congress.
Seismic political change is coming to Washington, D.C., and as Republicans sift through the wreckage that was Election Night, fingers are pointing in several directions over who’s to blame.

The blue tsunami Tuesday tore the GOP’s coalition asunder, flipping the balance of power in both chambers heading into the final two years of the Trump administration. And as Republicans search for where things went awry, GOP operatives and insiders told Fox News Digital that it starts at the top with President Donald Trump.

"Look, first and foremost, this is a Trump loss," Dan Eberhart, an oil drilling chief executive officer and prominent Republican donor, told Fox News Digital. "He wanted to be — he wanted people to consider him on the ballot. And unfortunately, as a Republican, that's what we got."
LIZ PEEK: THERE MAY BE A SILVER LINING IN TRUMP'S BRUTAL MIDTERM DEFEAT
President Donald Trump listens at a campaign rally at the Ocean Center in Daytona Beach, Fla., on Oct. 30, 2026. (Jacquelyn Martin/AP)

In the Senate, Democrats scored seven pickups on Election Night, with outstanding races in Alaska and Mississippi still waiting to be called. And in the House, Democrats roared back into power with 27 pickups and with several races still outstanding.
The Iran war, ignoring the economic hurt squeezing voters, attacking sitting Republicans and more are on the list of grievances from Republicans reeling in the days after.

The Senate map, in particular, was at one point favorable for Republicans and viewed as an uphill battle for Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and Democrats to put a dent in the GOP’s thin, 53-seat majority.
But Trump’s decision to go on a "primary revenge tour and antagonizing senators," a GOP aide told Fox News Digital, among several other issues, opened up the field for Democrats to pounce.
Indeed, Trump’s handpicked candidates were pummeled in races that were once safe bets for Republicans.
DEM FLIPS KEY SENATE SEAT IN BATTLEGROUND NORTH CAROLINA AS COOPER DEFEATS TRUMP ALLY

His backing of Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, Sen. Darline Graham, R-S.C., and fight with Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., last year that ultimately led to his retirement and created an opening for Democrats in the Tar Heel State, proved fatal for the GOP, coupled with stunning losses in Maine, Kansas, Ohio and Iowa, kneecapped any chances Republicans had of keeping power in the upper chamber.

"Trump ignored affordability completely," another Republican aide told Fox News Digital. "Ousted good members a la Cornyn, Tillis who knew how to win tough races, and poisoned the base’s opinion of our majority with his SAVE Act/filibuster bulls---."
"We had a great map, and he hijacked [it]," they continued.

In the House, where Democrats are on pace to potentially win upward of 250 seats, Fox News Power Rankings projected that Trump’s tariffs and the war in Iran were significant drivers for voting blocs leaving the GOP.
TRUMP'S GAMBLE ON KEN PAXTON BACKFIRES AS DEMOCRAT PULLS OFF HISTORIC TEXAS SENATE UPSET
The U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., is seen on Nov. 3, 2026. (Aaron Schwartz/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
One House Republican complained that GOP leaders were too focused on "bluster" rather than "doing the job," though they did not mention Trump by name.
"All the name changes were so unnecessary — Gulf of America, Lake of America, Department of War," the GOP lawmaker said.

A second House Republican rattled off a lengthy list of shortcomings, including the quality and character of "certain candidates," Trump’s immigration enforcement, tariffs, general affordability issues, historic midterm headwinds, and "departure from traditional conservatism in favor of populism."
Meanwhile, people in Trump’s orbit blamed the candidates themselves.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Trump outside advisor Alex Bruesewitz posted on X that "most Republican candidates this cycle were uninspiring, lazy, and thoroughly ineffective communicators."
"I’m not all that surprised by some of these outcomes," he said.
Meanwhile, some are expecting a massive shift in Trump’s base of support in Congress as he heads toward a lame duck likely punctuated by investigations and stalled agendas.
"I think Trump being a lame duck starts today," Eberhart said. "You know, if I'm up in the [2028] cycle, I'm waking up today, I'm against the arch. I'm against the ballroom. I want space from Trump."
Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

title: Ted Cruz says 'blue tsunami' took over Texas after Democrats swept statewide races
summary: Sen. Ted Cruz called the 2026 midterms a "blue tsunami" after James Talarico defeated Ken Paxton and Gina Hinojosa unseated Greg Abbott in Texas.
story: A panel joins ‘The Will Cain Show’ to break down Democrats’ sweep of the House and Senate, major victories in Texas and Hakeem Jeffries’ bid to become the next House speaker.

Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, delivered a scathing assessment on Wednesday of Republicans' sweeping midterm election losses, describing the results as a "blue tsunami" and warning that his party had lost touch with voters, particularly in the Lone Star State.
In a lengthy post on X, Cruz acknowledged that Republicans had suffered historic defeats, losing control of both chambers of Congress while Democrats swept statewide races in Texas.
"2026 was not simply a blue wave; it was a blue tsunami. It was an a-- kicking," Cruz wrote. "It was not simply a bad 2006 midterm election. It was a Watergate-level repudiation."

His blunt assessment came after a landmark Democratic breakthrough in traditionally Republican strongholds across the country, including in his home state, where Democrats won every statewide race, ending decades of Republican dominance.
FLORIDA'S DESANTIS DESCRIBES GOP MIDTERMS WIPEOUT AS 'CLOSE TO AN EXTINCTION-LEVEL EVENT' FOR REPUBLICANS
Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, delivers remarks on the second day of the Republican Midterm Convention at the American Airlines Center in Dallas, Texas, on Sept. 10, 2026. (Laura Brett/Sipa USA)
"Nowhere are the consequences of this election greater than Texas," Cruz wrote. "In the Lone Star State, we lost every single statewide election."
"Texas is blue. That is a hard sentence to utter. But Texas, today at least, is blue," he continued.

Democrats scored two major victories in Texas, with James Talarico defeating Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton in the U.S. Senate race — marking the first Democratic Senate victory in the Lone Star State in nearly four decades — and state Rep. Gina Hinojosa unseating longtime Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, according to the Fox News Decision Desk.
TRUMP'S GAMBLE ON KEN PAXTON BACKFIRES AS DEMOCRAT PULLS OFF HISTORIC TEXAS SENATE UPSET
Democratic Senate nominee Texas state Rep. James Talarico speaks at an election night event in Austin, Texas, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. (Eric Gay/AP Photo)
Cruz argued that Republicans' political defeat stemmed from their failure to address growing frustration over the cost of living, as voters continued struggling with everyday expenses.
"Food is too high, gas is too high, diesel is too high, insurance is too high, life is too high," he wrote.
"Understandably, people were pissed off, and elected Republicans didn't do enough to address their very real pain," Cruz said.
He also criticized tariffs and the prolonged war with Iran, arguing that both had contributed to voter frustration.
CONSERVATIVES STUNNED BY 'CATASTROPHIC' MIDTERM BLUE TSUNAMI, BLAME TRUMP'S IRAN WAR, HIGH GAS PRICES

Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated longtime Republican Gov. Greg Abbott in Texas' 2026 gubernatorial election, marking a historic Democratic victory in the traditionally Republican stronghold, according to the Fox News Decision Desk. (Danielle Villasana/Getty Images)

He said Republicans had lost support among blue-collar workers, young voters, farmers, ranchers and Hispanic voters, while evangelical Christians failed to turn out with the same enthusiasm as in previous elections, concluding that his party had "alienated rural America."
Cruz said he called Talarico after the election to congratulate him on his victory.

"Last night, I called James Talarico. I congratulated him on his very impressive victory," Cruz wrote, adding that the two had a "pleasant conversation" and that he was willing to work with the Democrat on issues benefiting Texas.
Despite the sweeping losses, which also included Democratic wins in the state's lieutenant governor and attorney general races, Cruz expressed optimism that Republicans could regain ground in Texas.
DEMS SEIZE THE SENATE AS BLUE TIDAL WAVE CRASHES DEEP INTO TRUMP COUNTRY, TOPPLES GOP STRONGHOLDS
Sen. Ted Cruz speaks during a roundtable discussion at the U.S. Capitol on March 3, 2025, in Washington, D.C. (Kayla Bartkowski/Getty Images)
"But hear me now: we will bring Texas back," he wrote. "Texas will be red again."
Throughout the campaign, Talarico cast himself as a moderate dedicated to representing Texans rather than Democratic interests in Washington.

Paxton, along with President Donald Trump and other national Republicans, labeled Talarico a "communist" and a vegan in barbecue-loving Texas, pointing to his support for the transgender community while in the Texas Legislature and a floor speech in which he said God was "nonbinary."
"We have not suddenly become a bunch of tofu-eating, gun-banning, tutu-wearing pinko commie liberals," Cruz wrote. "That ain’t us. Texas is still Texas."
"We will rebuild as a true blue-collar party, not by embracing socialism, but by being real free-market conservatives," he continued, predicting a political comeback for Republicans.
"It is dark right now, but it is always darkest before the dawn, and morning is coming," he said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Fox News Digital's Alex Miller, Elizabeth Elkind and Amanda Macias contributed to this report.
Michael Sinkewicz is a writer for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to michael.sinkewicz@fox.com

title: Erika Kirk channels Charlie with blunt message to conservatives after GOP midterm losses
summary: Erika Kirk invoked her late husband Charlie Kirk's words, urging conservatives to stay positive and avoid infighting after election setbacks.
story: Turning Point USA CEO Erika Kirk shares an inside look at TPUSA's headquarters in Arizona, detailing its 'Chase the Vote' campaign and activism kits designed to mobilize young conservative voters.
Erika Kirk had a message for conservatives reeling from Republican election setbacks, and she turned to her late husband Charlie’s words to deliver it.
"I miss Charlie so much every single day, but especially on a day like today," she wrote.
"He always said that when things are going well, we need to stay humble. And when things aren’t going the way we want, we need to stay positive, keep our faith, and get back to work."
ERIKA KIRK URGES CONSERVATIVE STUDENTS NOT TO BACK DOWN IN FIRST SCHOOL YEAR SINCE CHARLIE'S ASSASSINATION
Charlie Kirk and wife Erika appear on stage during the Turning Point USA Inaugural Eve Ball at the Salamander Hotel in Washington, D.C., Jan. 19, 2025. (Samuel Corum/Getty Images)
The widow of Turning Point USA CEO and founder Charlie Kirk said her husband had built a political operation meant to endure both victories and defeats.

"Charlie’s vision for Turning Point Action was always bigger than one election," she wrote. "He wanted a permanent, year-round operation with the people, relationships, and resources to compete in every cycle.
INSIDE CHARLIE KIRK’S EFFORT TO DEVELOP THE NEXT GENERATION OF CONSERVATIVE VOICES
"He knew there would be victories and setbacks because he had experienced both and that’s why he built for both."
Kirk also thanked the staff, students, volunteers and ballot chasers who worked during the election cycle.
ERIKA KIRK SAYS PRESIDENTIAL LIBRARY-STYLE TRIBUTE TO CHARLIE KIRK IS 'IN THE WORKS' AS TPUSA EXPANDS

Conservative political activist Charlie Kirk, founder of Turning Point Action, speaks during a meeting on the campus of the University of Arizona in Tucson Oct. 17, 2024.  (Olivier Touron/AFP via Getty Images)
"I know Charlie would be unbelievably proud of each and every one of you, and I am, too," she wrote.

In a lengthy post on X, Erika Kirk said Republicans saw once comfortable races tighten or flip as candidates she described as democratic socialists campaigned on the cost of gas, groceries and housing.
FLORIDA CONGRESSMAN DIAGNOSES GOP'S BLUE TSUNAMI LOSSES: 'WE FAILED TO MAKE THEM THINK WE CARED ABOUT THEM'

"A rising stock market doesn’t mean much when nearly half of Americans don’t have a 401K and just want to put gas in their trucks, put food on the table, and provide a good life for their families," she wrote.
Erika Kirk paired her warning with a defense of free enterprise, arguing conservatives must understand why voters looked elsewhere without embracing the policies their opponents offered.
CALLING DEMOCRATS ‘COMMUNISTS’ WON’T WIN GEN Z — REPUBLICANS NEED A BETTER OFFER
"We can disagree with the solutions voters were offered while still recognizing why they were looking elsewhere for answers," she wrote.
Erika Kirk warned conservatives against turning on one another as she urged them to take voters’ frustrations seriously.
JASON CHAFFETZ: FIVE TIMELESS POLITICAL LESSONS THAT GOT LOST IN 2026
President Donald Trump joined Charlie Kirk's widow, Erika, on stage at Charlie Kirk's memorial service in Arizona Sept. 21, 2025. (Eric Thayer/Getty Images)

"The biggest mistake conservatives can make right now would be to allow this moment to become another exercise in finger-pointing, in-fighting, or trying to secure their own political preservation," she wrote.
"That does not solve the problems the American people are demanding be solved."
Erika Kirk said exit polls showed voters were concerned about the economy and the war in Iran.
FOX NEWS VOTER POLL: 2026 MIDTERM ELECTIONS USHER IN A BLUE WAVE AS DEMOCRATS WIN CONTROL OF CONGRESS
She said those concerns echoed what Turning Point had been hearing from students around the country for months.
"This isn’t a surprise to us because we’ve heard the same concerns from our students around the country for months and we’ve been concerned about it too," she wrote.
JONATHAN TURLEY: SOCIALISM IS BACK IN STYLE, AND DEMOCRATS ARE BUYING THE PITCH

Erika Kirk, widow of Turning Point USA founder Charlie Kirk, speaks during a Turning Point USA event at the Pavilion at Ole Miss at the University of Mississippi in Oxford, Miss., Oct. 29. (Jonathan Ernst-Pool/Getty Images)
Erika Kirk rejected socialism as an answer, arguing it places economic power in government hands rather than allowing individuals and families to build prosperity.
She said that approach conflicts with the free enterprise, individual liberty and opportunity at the heart of the country.
But she also warned that Americans will not simply stick with a party out of habit.

"Americans are not looking for labels and don’t subscribe to unquestioned party loyalty anymore either," she wrote. "They will support the candidates who can both speak to their concerns and deliver on what THEY need and dream about for their families."
Charlie Kirk and wife Erika and their two children at Christmas in December 2024. (Charlie Kirk via Facebook)
She identified affordable homes, safe communities and greater opportunity for the next generation as the promises voters want fulfilled.

Erika Kirk said the organization would study the results, listen to voters and spend the next two years making the case that conservative policies and free markets can address the problems Americans face.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
She pledged to continue building relationships in communities across the country and preparing for "2028 and beyond."
"Our principles haven’t changed and neither has our mission," she wrote.
"Onward."
Stepheny Price is a Writer at Fox News with a focus on West Coast and Midwest news, missing persons, national and international crime stories, homicide cases, and border security.

title: Florida congressman diagnoses GOP's blue tsunami losses: 'We failed to make them think we cared about them'
summary: Firebrand GOP Florida rep says party must prepare for difficult two years, says Republicans bear responsibility for loss as a team
story: Rep. Randy Fine says Republicans failed to understand what Americans wanted, even as Sunshine state GOP slate bucked the national trend.

As Republicans sift through the wreckage of a devastating election night that handed Democrats control of both chambers of Congress by large margins, one Florida Republican who bucked the national trend says the GOP fundamentally misread the electorate.

In an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital, Congressman Randy Fine — who expanded his own winning margin by five points despite the national backlash — offered a candid assessment of his party's shortcomings and warned that Republicans must now prepare for an "ugly two years" battling Democrats over immigration and other contentious issues.
Representative Randy Fine, a Republican from Florida, outside the US Capitol in Washington, DC, US, on Thursday, Dec. 18, 2025. (Graeme Sloan/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

While Republicans held their ground in Florida, winning the governor's mansion, the Senate race, and maintaining their 20-8 edge in the US House, nationally the GOP got crushed under the weight of a blue tsunami.
ILHAN OMAR HIT WITH EXPULSION THREAT AS GOP LAWMAKER VOWS TO BOOT HER FROM CONGRESS OVER DOJ PROBE
Congressman Fine presents no easy answer to the GOP's divergence in fortunes between Florida and the rest of the country:

"You know, I think that's a hard question to answer. What I would say, I can speak to my race, and I'm actually one of the few Republicans in the country whose margin increased from my last election. I won my special election after having $14 million spent against me. I won it by 14 points. I won last night by 19 points. And so what I can tell you is what worked for me.

"My constituents want a fighter, someone who says what they believe. They know it's not driven by polls or anything else and fights for them, whether it's fighting for their constituent service issue or fighting on illegal immigration or fighting to bring money to the district. And that's why I went up so much. I took my race seriously because I knew the winds were against us.
"And so, Florida, I think just people know how good we have it and they don't want to screw up the state. I think that's why we won all 20 of these races."
Fine refuses to single out anyone in GOP leadership for the electoral outcome, and believes the Republicans must approach each election cycle as a unified team:

Florida Republican gubernatorial candidate, Rep. Byron Donalds, R-Fla., gestures as he arrives to an election rally with U.S. President Donald Trump at Alico Arena on the Florida Gulf Coast University campus on Oct. 23, 2026 in Fort Myers, Fla. (Alex Wong/Getty Images)

"Well, look, I'm not a finger pointer, but what I would say is this. We're a team and the team lost. And so then the whole team bears responsibility and that includes me. I mean, while I did well, my team lost, and I'm not going to be here pointing the fingers at anybody.
FROM CAMPUS RADICALS TO BEIJING'S AI SABOTAGE: REP RANDY FINE SAYS 'US FIGHTING TO SAVE WESTERN CIVILIZATION'

"I think that what we did is we failed to understand what the American people wanted. I think we failed to make them think we cared about them. Now, I didn't fail in my district, but I think nationally people came to believe that we weren't interested in them and that's wrong.
"We were, but we failed to communicate it, and maybe that's part of my special sauce is I know how to communicate better than many of these people."
With Democrats firmly in control of both chambers of Congress, Fine anticipates two years of playing defense, and a continuous fight to explain why Democrats' policies will be harmful to the country:

"I don't know that we're going to push the agenda. I think what we're going to be is we're going to be on defense. We're going to have to fight back. And you know, as my father told me this morning, he goes, 'Randy, you've been a fighter your whole life. You were built for the fight.'

"So we're going to be having to fight against stupid policies that they will be pushing. And it's going to be an ugly two years, but we're gonna have to explain why all of the things that they said they would do during the campaign are so bad. We obviously didn't succeed in doing that. But as they put those policies forward, we're going to have to make the argument for why they would damage America."
Immigration is the single issue that Fine identifies as having the greatest potential to harm the country:

"I think they will seek to reopen the border and allow illegals to flood in. I think they will seek mass amnesty, rewarding all of the illegals that are here. And I think they will stop any requirement for people who come to this country to assimilate. They believe in the ‘third worldification’ of America. And that's going to be the number one thing we have to fight back against."
Florida and Texas painted a particularly stark contrast in electoral outcomes. Fine suggests the Sunshine state GOP was better prepared to face headwinds:

"Well, I think maybe our candidates at the top of the ticket were better. You know, Byron Donalds is an incredible spokesman for the conservative movement. Ashley Moody is a multiple-time winner statewide. And I think Texas allowed itself to slide on a lot of these things.

"They had a big influx of illegal immigrants. And they also really didn't fight back against the Islamification of their state in a way that we have in Florida. Demographics are destiny. And I think, to some degree, Texas was overtaken by that yesterday."
Fine has long been an outspoken critic of Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, and believes he represents a danger to the country:

"Of all the races last night, that one breaks my heart the most. I mean, someone who literally supports Muslim terror, someone whose family is embedded in so many aspects of Muslim terror. Someone who's really a danger to this country being elected to the United States Senate. It's an unspeakably horrible thing, a historically bad thing. Someone who doesn't support the United States. Someone who supports the Muslim Brotherhood.
Democratic Senate Candidate Abdul El-Sayed speaks during a campaign town hall at Cadillac High School on October 10, 2026, in Cadillac, Michigan. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

"It breaks my heart. I'm not from Michigan, I don't know what they were thinking, but it's a terrible, terrible, terrible day. Look today for me has been a hard day. You know I won my election last night, I was super excited. My margin went up. It's unheard of in this cycle and so I'm super excited, then I watched the bottom fall out of the election results and realized so many good people lost today.

"So it's a challenging day for me, the high of winning so decisively with the low of realizing the battle that we have ahead of us, but God puts us where he wants us to be and I'm a fighter and I am ready for the fight."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Finally, as it appears that either Jim Jordan or Steve Scalise is likely to be the next House Minority Leader, Fine declined to weigh in:

"No, I mean, these are discussions. I've not spoken with either Scalise or Jordan at this point. They've got a lot of phone calls to make, and we'll get to that when we get to that. But it won't be Mike Johnson. He's taken himself out of consideration."
David Unsworth reports on Latin America. You can follow David Unsworth on Twitter @LatinAmerUpdate

title: Vance courting disgruntled Trump voters to form ‘new right’ alliance after Republican bloodbath, sources say
summary: JD Vance blamed the Iran war for the GOP's midterm losses and laid out four tasks he says will bring disaffected Republican voters back to the party.
story: Midterm election developments unfold as Donald Trump addresses reporters at the White House following key congressional races. Plus, former RNC chairwoman Ronna McDaniel discusses the GOP's performance.
EXCLUSIVE: Vice President JD Vance is seeking to forge a new alliance with disaffected Trump voters ahead of the 2028 election cycle, Fox News Digital has learned.

Vance took control of his own messaging Wednesday morning in the wake of a brutal Republican midterm beatdown, breaking with President Donald Trump on foreign policy and America's relationship with Israel.

A source familiar with post-election happenings told Fox News Digital that there was a White House meeting Wednesday morning aimed at aligning the entire administration officials on post-midterm messaging. A second source familiar described the meeting as a regular senior staff meeting.
Vice President JD Vance called out Democrats on Friday, saying that the midterms will be a referendum on "common sense versus pure unadulterated crazy." (Getty Images)
VANCE'S SCATHING IRAN WAR POSTMORTEM PUTS POTENTIAL 2028 GOP SHOWDOWN IN FOCUS: 'EVERYONE KNOWS WHY'
"The reason we lost is the war," Vance's post said. "The president himself said so last night."

"If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest," he went on.
"But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there."

In the post, Vance said a pollster and "one of the smartest people I know in politics" laid out four tasks that would bring voters back to the GOP — end the war in Iran, focus on the cost of living and inflation, put America first, and "change our relationship with Israel."
JD VANCE DECLINES TO ENDORSE NETANYAHU DESPITE TRUMP'S STRONG BACKING

A Trump administration official who spoke with Fox News Digital said that the four tasks are Vance's rallying cry to the "new right," broadly defined as a coalition of Republicans that aligns with the president's original "America First" movement — staying out of foreign conflicts, making America an affordable place for Americans to raise families, and closing the borders.
But those voters, they said, also believe that Trump is too aligned with Israel on foreign policy matters.
Vice President JD Vance points to President Donald Trump at the Republican convention Thursday, Sept. 10, 2026, in Dallas. (Alex Brandon/AP Photo)
Among some on the political right, the war in Iran is intrinsically tied to Israel's influence in the Middle East, and Trump's relationship with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
TRUMP TOLD DONORS 'WE NEED TO ELECT JD,' SOURCE CONFIRMS, AS HE WEIGHS VANCE OR RUBIO IN 2028

The official made it clear that Vance’s message is not a separation from Trump, à la former Vice President Mike Pence who denounced Trump after the Jan. 6, 2021, riot at the capitol. Rather, they said, he is aiming to send a clear message to Republicans who support Trump and disagree with or feel betrayed by his foreign policy.
And that message is: "Vance is our guy."
The White House did not return Fox News Digital's request for comment at time of publication on the meeting or Vance's post-election messaging.
The vice president has not strayed much from Trump and the White House's preferred messaging for the past two years — though he has been one of the few voicing concern over the ongoing war in Iran.
Despite his friendship with Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, reports and comments from the vice president himself have expressed how his stance on the Iran conflict differs.
Trump acknowledged earlier this year that Vance was "maybe less enthusiastic" about attacking Iran from the jump.
TRUMP 'COULDN'T TRANSFER THE LOVE' OF HIS SUPPORTERS TO OTHER REPUBLICANS AMID HISTORIC MIDTERM LOSS
Vance is widely considered a top GOP presidential candidate in 2028 — along with Trump's Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
So far, Democrats stand at 54 Senate seats to Republicans' 44, after sweeping wins in typically red Texas, ruby-red Kansas and other Republican strongholds like South Carolina.
DEMS SEIZE THE SENATE AS BLUE TIDAL WAVE CRASHES DEEP INTO TRUMP COUNTRY, TOPPLES GOP STRONGHOLDS
Votes are still being counted into Wednesday in a tight race in Alaska, that could see Democrats winning yet another seat in the Senate and widening their majority over the GOP.

The outcome of the midterms could have massive implications for the 2028 election, and Republicans are grappling now with how to face one of their biggest-ever challenges in trying to flip back the upper chamber despite a widened gap throwing them deep into a minority in January.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Needing only 218 to control the House, Democrats on Wednesday afternoon had won 237 seats, with more projected to filter in as ballots are counted and races are called.
Peter D'Abrosca is a politics reporter at Fox News Digital.

title: Fox News/NORC Study: Voters look to 2028 focused on the economy
summary: As the 2028 race for the White House looms, grocery prices, gas costs and healthcare top what voters want newly elected officials to tackle first.
story: President Donald Trump weighs in on Republicans’ midterm losses, the war with Iran and working with a Democratic-controlled Congress.
After the midterm elections, attention will turn to the 2028 race for the White House. What is on voters’ minds as they look ahead to the next presidential election?

Most Republicans want the next president to follow President Donald Trump’s policies, if not his style. Nearly 4 in 10 MAGA Republicans want Trump’s successor to emulate both, and about half want the next president to follow his policies alone. Non-MAGA Republicans are less enthusiastic: 45% want his policies to continue, but only about 15% of non-MAGA Republicans want a president with the same style.

Independents prefer something entirely different: 6 in 10 want the next president to break with both Trump’s policies and his style. Likewise, few Democrats want to see either his style or his policies repeated.

Even as the Democrats have won control of the Senate and the House of Representatives, and Trump finds his approval rating at 39%, a bloc of voters remains loyal to the president and is likely to influence the 2028 campaign. While half of voters want a successor who does not emulate his style or follow his policies, 26% want a president who will carry on his policies, and another 12% want the next president to copy his policies and his style.
FOX NEWS VOTER POLL: 2026 MIDTERM ELECTIONS USHER IN A BLUE WAVE AS DEMOCRATS WIN CONTROL OF CONGRESS
Fox News/NORC study results show the views of registered voters nationwide on political, economic and policy issues. (Fox News/NORC)

Looking ahead, voters across party lines say improving economic conditions is the most important issue for the country to address over the next five years. Six in 10 voters feel they are holding steady financially while about 3 in 10 feel they are falling behind. Few, about 1 in 10 voters, feel they are getting ahead financially. Voters who describe their own financial situation as less than satisfactory, or say they are falling behind, are more likely to name the economy as the top issue.

What should Tuesday's winners prioritize once sworn into office? When asked what is most important for newly elected officials to work on first in 2027, 3 in 10 voters want elected officials to address grocery costs. About 2 in 10 want action on gas prices, and a similar share say they should work on healthcare and prescription drug costs.
Slightly fewer are concerned about housing costs, while about 1 in 10 want officials to address electricity and other utility costs.

Voters are closely divided on whether the country can look forward to better days or if the good days are behind us. And it’s linked to how they’re feeling financially. About two-thirds of those who say they are getting ahead financially are optimistic about the future. However, about two-thirds of voters who are falling behind financially think the country’s best days are in the past.

Beyond the economy, priorities diverge. About 1 in 5 Democrats point to access to affordable healthcare, while about a similar share of Republicans say protecting individuals from government overreach is the top issue. About 1 in 10 independents say the country should address the affordability of healthcare, and about the same share say government overreach.

Voters are divided over AI’s effect on the U.S. economy during the next 10 years. About 4 in 10 say it will be harmful, while 3 in 10 expect benefits. About 1 in 10 expect AI to make no difference, while slightly more, about 2 in 10, are unsure. About 4 in 10 expect AI to negatively affect the environment and the arts and entertainment industry.

About half of voters want substantial changes in how the country is run. Party identification shapes how much change voters want and which branches of government they think most need reform. Democrats are about three times as likely as Republicans to want complete upheaval of how the country is run. Half of democratic socialists favor complete and total upheaval, compared with about 1 in 10 MAGA Republicans.
Fox News/NORC study results show the views of registered voters nationwide on political, economic and policy issues. (Fox News/NORC)

In the 2024 Fox News Voter Analysis conducted for the presidential election, most Republican voters said they wanted substantial change or total upheaval. Now, with a Republican in the White House and their party controlling both houses of Congress, they are less eager for major change.
FOX NEWS VOTER POLL: HOW DEMOCRATS TOOK CONTROL OF THE SENATE
Fox News/NORC study results show the views of registered voters nationwide on political, economic and policy issues. (Fox News/NORC)

Overall, 4 in 10 voters think Congress should be substantially reformed, including three-quarters of MAGA Republicans and half of non-MAGA Republicans. Democrats are less likely to say Congress needs reform, but half say the executive branch should be improved. Few voters in either party want changes to the Constitution. Democrats are more likely than Republicans or independents to say the Supreme Court needs reform.
Fox News/NORC study results show the views of registered voters nationwide on political, economic and policy issues. (Fox News/NORC)

Voters across party lines support term limits for Congress and Supreme Court justices. Democrats favor abolishing the Electoral College, but Republicans and independents are less enthusiastic. Most Republicans support limiting mail voting to people physically unable to vote in person. MAGA Republicans are more supportive of limiting mail voting than non-MAGA Republicans (63% vs 40%). Democrats oppose the idea, regardless of whether they support the Democratic Socialists of America.
AMERICANS CLASH OVER SUPREME COURT EXPANSION AS FIGHT OVER 9 JUSTICES HEATS UP: ‘LET’S PACK IT NOW’
Fox News/NORC study results show the views of registered voters nationwide on political, economic and policy issues. (Fox News/NORC)

The expansion of artificial intelligence has triggered some public backlash against AI data centers. Voters are divided on whether AI will help or hurt during the next 10 years. More Democrats say the technology will be harmful while more Republicans expect benefits.
Fox News/NORC study results show the views of registered voters nationwide on political, economic and policy issues. (Fox News/NORC)

Among Republican voters, MAGA Republicans are more enthusiastic about AI than non-MAGA Republicans. Forty-five percent of MAGA Republicans believe AI will help the U.S. to compete with other countries, and another 4 in 10 feel AI will do more to help the economy.

Among Democrat voters, supporters of democratic socialism and those who do not support the movement are similarly likely to feel AI will help aspects of American society. However, supporters of democratic socialism are more likely than other Democrats to feel AI will do more to hurt than help.

Overall, 6 in 10 voters are extremely or very concerned about the effect of data centers on the price of utilities in the communities where they are being built. About half are concerned about the effect of data centers on pollution of natural resources, land development or the health of the local population, regardless of whether they live near a data center. Democrats are more concerned about the effects of data centers than Republican voters, again, regardless of their proximity to the facilities.

Voters across party lines support requiring companies to pay for electric grid upgrades needed for their data centers, increasing government regulation of AI, and limiting AI in schools. Most Democrats and independents oppose building a data center in their community. Most voters also oppose local construction, whether their county already has a data center.
AMERICA’S MULTI-BILLION TECH BOOM COMES INTO FOCUS AS 7 KEY STATES PUT IT TO A MIDTERM TEST
Fox News/NORC study results show the views of registered voters nationwide on political, economic and policy issues. (Fox News/NORC)
The economy is a top issue for most voters, yet 4 in 10 say they could support a candidate whose economic views differ from their own.

After the economy and jobs, nearly 6 in 10 voters see healthcare as an important issue, and about 6 in 10 would not support a candidate who disagrees with them on healthcare policy. About half could not back a candidate whose views on Israel and the Palestinians differ from theirs. Overall, about 6 in 10 say they could never support a candidate they disagree with on abortion, guns, or immigration.
Explore the results here: https://civichealth.norc.org/crosstabs.html
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
