title: Under-the-radar implication of Dem blue wave means 'zero' chance GOP accomplishes critical goal, experts warn
summary: Ron DeSantis warns that Tuesday's Senate losses effectively end Trump's chances of replacing Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito with conservatives.
story: Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis sounded off Wednesday on Republicans' massive nationwide losses, while analysts consider whether his vocal responses are positioning him for a nationwide run.

Republicans’ sweeping losses Tuesday could reshape the Supreme Court for years, prominent conservatives warned, arguing that Democrats’ new Senate majority may block President Donald Trump from replacing Justices Clarence Thomas or Samuel Alito with conservative successors.

"Assuming Republicans lose the seats where prediction markets have the Democrats at 90+% to win, that would produce 55 Democrat Senate seats," Florida Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis wrote on X on Tuesday night in a post that was viewed almost 4 million times.

"Chance of confirming a worthy successor to Justice Thomas and/or Alito during President Trump’s term: Zero. Chance of confirming a worthy successor during a hypothetical GOP admin 2029-2033: probably zero (GOP won’t be able to recapture enough seats in 28)."

Democrats took control of the Senate Tuesday night and hold 54 seats as of midday Wednesday, and DeSantis was joined on social media by several others explaining that Alito, 76, and Thomas, 78, will be almost impossible to replace with equally conservative appointees.
AMERICA SAW THE BLUE WAVE COMING — BUT DRASTICALLY UNDERESTIMATED THE EXTENT OF THE DEM TSUNAMI

Democrats took control of the Senate on Tuesday night, making it unlikely Republicans will be able to replace Supreme Court Justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito with conservative successors. (AP Photo/Yuki Iwamura; Tim Evans/AFP via Getty Images)

Ed Whelan, a conservative legal expert who clerked for the late Supreme Court Justice Antonin Scalia, wrote on X that Trump is now effectively blocked from appointing federal judges or Supreme Court justices during the final two years of his term.

"If a Republican is elected president in 2028, that president will not be able to appoint any justices or judges until Republicans regain the Senate," Whelan wrote. "Given the deep hole, that might not happen until 2033. "
Whelan also explained that a justice resigning during the upcoming "lame duck" session is highly unlikely and Republicans would have a hard time securing 51 votes.
TRUMP CHEERS ALITO STAYING FOR ANOTHER SUPREME COURT TERM: 'ONE OF THE GREATEST OF ALL TIME'

Supreme Court Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas wait to leave the stage after the inauguration ceremonies in the Rotunda of the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Jan. 20, 2025. (Chip Somodevilla/AFP via Getty Images)

"If Sherrod Brown wins Ohio seat, he gets sworn into Senate in early December, so Senate becomes 52R-48D," Whelan wrote. "Collins and Murkowski would be unlikely to support anyone Trump would nominate. John Cornyn, Thom Tillis, and Bill Cassidy aren’t going to be eager to do Trump any favors. And there are other senators—e.g., John Curtis of Utah—who would be leery of anyone Trump would be eager to push through."
Others on social media echoed similar sentiments.

"In 2033, Clarence Thomas will turn 85 and Samuel Alito will turn 83," conservative author Hans Mahncke posted on X in response to DeSantis. "There is no reason to believe they won't still be going strong on the bench. But the larger point is absolutely valid. No one lives forever, and if these two great men are not eventually replaced by genuinely conservative justices, America will go the way of the rest of the Western world."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The U.S. Supreme Court on Feb. 20, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Heather Diehl/Getty Images)
"Again, the consequences of tonight's election for the Supreme Court are staggering," Denny Burk, the dean of Boyce College at the Southern Baptist Theological Seminary, posted on X.
Andrew Mark Miller is a reporter from Pasadena, California, who has been with Fox News Digital since 2021. You can reach him at AndrewMark.Miller@fox.com.

title: GOP's midterm defeat sparks bold claims from foreign leaders who've clashed with Trump
summary: Pedro Sánchez says Americans voted against hate and climate denial as European leaders react to the Democratic Party's 2026 midterm victories.
story: Chief congressional correspondent Chad Pergram joins 'The Faulkner Focus' to discuss the progressive agenda after Democrats sweep the midterms.

The GOP's sweeping midterm losses are drawing a positive response from several foreign leaders who have clashed with President Donald Trump, with some expressing hope that Democrats' victories could lead to a shift in U.S. policy on major global issues.

Democrats secured majorities in both the U.S. House of Representatives and the Senate in Tuesday's elections, setting the stage for a shift in congressional power in January and prompting reactions from officials in Europe, the Middle East and Africa.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez took aim at Trump's policies in a Wednesday X post, suggesting that American voters had rejected the president's political agenda and predicting that a similar shift would soon take place in Spain.
"Yesterday, American society voted against policies that only make people poorer," Sánchez wrote. "Against hate. Against sexism. Against climate denial and against elite privilege."
AMERICA SAW THE BLUE WAVE COMING — BUT DRASTICALLY UNDERESTIMATED THE EXTENT OF THE DEM TSUNAMI

A voter marks their ballot in the Kern County Elections Office on November 3, 2026 in Bakersfield, California. Americans go to the polls in consequential midterm elections, where control of the House and the Senate is at stake for the remainder of President Donald Trump's second term in office. (Mario Tama/Getty Images)

Sánchez has been an outspoken critic of U.S. and Israeli military operations against Iran, accusing Washington in March of "playing Russian roulette" with millions of lives. His opposition to the war and disputes with Trump over NATO defense spending have contributed to tensions between Madrid and Washington.
"We are not going to be complicit in something that is bad for the world and is also contrary to our values and interests, just out of fear of reprisals from someone," Sánchez said.

Prime Minister of Spain Pedro Sánchez Pérez-Castejón arrives at Huis ten Bosch Palace for a dinner hosted by the King and Queen of The Netherlands during the NATO Summit 2025 on June 24, 2025, in The Hague, Netherlands. (Patrick van Katwijk/Getty Images)

"Wild result in the USA last night! I'm cautiously optimistic on Europe's behalf," European Parliament Vice President Christel Schaldemose wrote in a Wednesday X post. "Not because everything now changes for the better, but because it could benefit the support for Ukraine, the green transition, and relations with the rest of the world."

Schaldemose criticized Trump’s interest in Greenland in January 2025, also suggesting that Europeans should "stand up for ourselves both in terms of the economy the global economy but also in terms of digital policy and the climate."
Britain's newly appointed Prime Minister Andy Burnham delivers a speech outside 10 Downing Street after taking office, in London, Britain, July 20, 2026. (REUTERS/Temilade Adelaja)

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Wednesday that the election results presented an opportunity for world leaders to work together to ease cost-of-living pressures and resolve the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, Sky News reported.

"Well, President Trump has accepted the results, and I feel the world has an opportunity now to unite around the issue that is affecting us all - and that's the cost-of-living," Burnham said. "That has been the issue that I have put front and centre in my first three months in Downing Street, and we've made moves, but I can't get people's cost of living pressures down until the conflict in the Middle East is resolved."

Trump said in July that he had a "very good" conversation with Burnham about trade and security issues, although the two governments have since differed over Israeli settlement activity in the West Bank. In September, Britain announced plans to strengthen sanctions targeting settlements and prevent British companies from assisting settlement construction, drawing criticism from U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee.
Americans have been grappling with higher costs as the war in Iran has caused energy prices to surge. The U.S. affordability crisis was a major issue for voters heading into this year's midterms.
Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad ‌Baqer Ghalibaf claimed in a Wednesday social media post that U.S. voters "said NO TO WAR" amid cost-of-living concerns.

"Conscience or the cost of living, Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message," Ghalibaf said, according to the Independent. "If the US govt betrays their public will to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our NO comes with a Nightmare."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Japan's Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara emphasized during a Wednesday press conference that the Japan-U.S. alliance "remains the cornerstone of Japan's foreign and security policy regardless of the outcome of the elections," Kyodo News reported.

Additionally, South African President Cyril Ramaphosa told reporters on Wednesday that he thinks the Democratic Party’s victory in the midterms will "introduce a new era in world relations," Reuters reported.

Trump confronted Ramaphosa during a May 2025 White House meeting, playing video footage that he claimed showed evidence of widespread violence against White South African farmers. Ramaphosa disputed Trump's allegations of persecution, while subsequent fact-checks found that some of the footage had been mischaracterized.
Trump claimed in a Tuesday night Truth Social post that if his name appeared on the ballot in the 2026 midterms the GOP would have "won IN A LANDSLIDE!"

Trump nevertheless congratulated Democrats on their victories and expressed a willingness to work with the incoming congressional majorities, while emphasizing that he would retain the power to veto legislation he opposes.

"They'll send over things that are insane, and I'll veto them," Trump told Fox News' Bret Baier on Tuesday night, adding that the two parties would eventually have to work together to get legislation passed.

title: DeSantis calls GOP midterm losses 'extinction-level event' — and explains why Florida survived
summary: Outgoing Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis called GOP losses an "extinction-level event" while highlighting Florida as the party's lone bright spot.
story: Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis sounded off Wednesday on Republicans' massive nationwide losses, while analysts consider whether his vocal responses are positioning him for a nationwide run.

Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis warned Wednesday that Republicans have been nearly wiped out nationally after devastating election losses, while highlighting his state as the lone remaining GOP stronghold among the 10 most populous states as speculation builds about his political future in 2028.

Tuesday was an otherwise brutal night for the GOP, as the Trump movement faces major questions amid setbacks in longtime Republican strongholds such as Kansas and Texas, while holding Senate seats in West Virginia and deep-red Wyoming and South Dakota.

"This is close to an extinction-level event for Republicans… out of the 10 largest states in this union, only one state will have Republican control of their state, the state of Florida," DeSantis said at a Wednesday news conference.
DEMOCRATS SEIZE MAJORITY OF GOVERNORS’ OFFICES IN ELECTION-NIGHT SHIFT
DEMS SEIZE THE SENATE AS BLUE TIDAL WAVE CRASHES DEEP INTO TRUMP COUNTRY, TOPPLES GOP STRONGHOLDS

"We've built up a record of achievement. We've earned trust from a number of our voters that, even in the worst situation that you can imagine politically, we were able to hold the line," DeSantis added.
Fox News Digital reached out to DeSantis for comment.
Orlando-based political strategist and pollster Doug Kaplan told Fox News Digital that DeSantis appears to be eyeing a lasting role on the national stage.
"I think last night was a big night for DeSantis. If you're looking at winners on the Republican side, then I think he's found his lane if he wants to run for president in 2028," he said.

Kaplan characterized DeSantis' comments as an "opening salvo" in an effort to distance himself from the Trump-led status quo in the Republican Party, though he acknowledged the staying power of Trump's MAGA movement among GOP primary voters.
DeSantis also highlighted his own push for the election-cycle buzzword "affordability" in Florida.
Amendment 3 passed with about 62% of the vote Tuesday. It increases homestead property tax exemptions from $50,000 to $250,000 by 2028.

"The existence of Amendment 3 on the ballot is one of the reasons Florida averted the fate of other red states. It drew more voters to the polls," DeSantis said, highlighting an issue on which Republicans still won decisively.

Kaplan predicted Vice President JD Vance and Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, may also follow DeSantis’ tack. Both men saw their party take major losses in their home states, he noted, citing Vance’s former Senate seat going to Democrat Sherrod Brown.

DeSantis highlighted losses in Cruz’s home state but did not reference the senator: "Texas has been the most significant Republican state this century. A Democrat sweep of statewide races — and possible capture of the legislature — takes away one of the anchors of the modern GOP. A huge loss," DeSantis said, echoing his point that Florida remains the only one of the 10 most populous states with a Republican governor.
AMERICA SAW THE BLUE WAVE COMING — BUT DRASTICALLY UNDERESTIMATED THE EXTENT OF THE DEM TSUNAMI
Gov. Ron DeSantis speaks during a press conference at Florida International University on Aug. 26, 2026, in Miami. (Al Diaz/Miami Herald/Tribune News Service via Getty Images)

He pointed to stunning upsets that included Kansas, Texas, Georgia, North Carolina, South Carolina and potentially Mississippi — which hasn't elected a Democrat to the U.S. Senate since segregationist Sen. John Stennis' last term in the 1980s.

"If Mississippi goes down, that will give Dems 56 Senate seats," DeSantis said. The Magnolia State emerged as perhaps the biggest surprise of the morning, with Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith trailing Scott Colom, a Democratic state district judge from Lowndes County, by about one-tenth of 1% in a race most Republicans didn’t even have on their radar.
Former Miami Mayor Francis Suarez, a Republican whose now-Democrat-run city maintained a 3-1 Republican advantage in its congressional delegation, credited DeSantis with helping set the stage:

"We had a great outcome, right? And I think the 1.5 million-vote registration advantage that Gov. DeSantis took four years to build was actually the firewall that prevented Florida from going down the same path as Texas or Michigan," Suarez told FOX Business’ "Big Money in the Morning" on Wednesday.

"Republicans need to simplify their message. They need to be message discipline like Democrats were in this cycle. And then they got to find young, articulate, attractive candidates like the Democrats have found."

Speaking with "Straight Shooter" host Stephen A. Smith on Election Night, DeSantis similarly argued that voters supported conservative policies on some ballot measures while rejecting Republican candidates, suggesting a disconnect between the party's agenda and its appeal to voters.
Former senior Senate advisor and political strategist Mary Marslender told Fox News Digital that DeSantis is doing what any successful governor would in this scenario.

"He’s taking a victory lap on a winning record. That doesn’t means he’s distancing himself from Trump or the MAGA movement. DeSantis successfully focused on state-level results: tax relief, public safety and electoral success, all while underscoring Florida’s position as a reliable conservative stronghold," Marslender said.
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis speaks with President Donald Trump as he arrives at Southwest Florida International Airport in Fort Myers, Fla., on Oct. 23, 2026. (Reuters)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"If congressional members in Washington could have done the same, we would have seen a very different outcome these midterms. We should expect to hear more from DeSantis on Florida’s proven results and his approach to governance in the run up to 2028."

"I think the timing of Governor DeSantis's comments is pretty clear. Republicans have to confront some very difficult election results and now make a decision on how to make forward," said Elizabeth Pipko, a former RNC national spokesperson.
"He shares a lot of great ideas with President Trump... It will be interesting to see if they choose to work together in some way and how that leads into 2028."

For DeSantis, who will leave office in January after his unsuccessful 2024 presidential bid, the question is whether Florida's success will remain a state-level victory lap or become the foundation for a renewed national political role ahead of 2028.
Born and raised in Allentown, Pennsylvania, worked in both the New York and Washington bureaus for Fox News since 2013.

title: House Dem who defied Hakeem Jeffries scores upset win in pro-Trump district
summary: Marie Gluesenkamp Perez ran a heated race against John Braun in a district Donald Trump carried in 2024.
story: 'The Big Money Show' panel analyzes President Donald Trump's economic messaging on the campaign trail and reviews the latest Fox News polls in the Ohio and Texas Senate races ahead of the midterm elections, where cost of living remains a top concern for voters.
A Democratic lawmaker who publicly defied House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., twice beat the odds to win re-election in a district that President Donald Trump carried in 2024.
Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, D-Wash., defeated Republican Washington State Sen. John Braun to win a third term in the House of Representatives, The Associated Press reported.
It's an important victory for House Democrats in their quest to claw back the majority in Congress, but one that could also create drama for party leaders on key votes over the next two years.
JEFFRIES THREATENS 'SERIOUS RESPONSE' AFTER DEMOCRATS HELP GOP ADVANCE ANTI-SOCIALISM VOTE
Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, D-Wash., arrives for a vote series at the U.S. Capitol on Sept. 25, 2024, in Washington, D.C. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

Gluesenkamp Perez, who has been known to buck her party on votes in the past, infuriated her fellow Democrats twice in September when she sided with Republicans on procedural votes that helped GOP leaders rescue their agenda from conservative rebellions.
If not for her and Rep. Jared Golden, D-Maine, siding with Republicans on those two votes, the House GOP's agenda would have been paralyzed.

The first time earned her a rare public rebuke from Jeffries, who called it a "breach of trust." Other left-wing lawmakers called for her to be removed from the powerful House Appropriations Committee over the move.

But one could argue that Gluesenkamp Perez's public defiance of her own party was critical for her political survival. Trump won her district by roughly 3 percentage points in 2024, and she first won her seat by defeating an incumbent House Republican.

President Donald Trump looks on during the trophy ceremony after the U.S. Team wins 17-13 following the Sunday's Singles on day four of the Presidents Cup 2026 at Medinah Country Club on Sept. 27, 2026, in Medinah, Ill. (Luke Hales/Getty Images)
Washington's 3rd Congressional District includes rural areas and the city of Vancouver, and smaller coastal towns in the southwest portion of the state.
HOUSE DEMS OVERWHELMINGLY REJECT ANTI-SOCIALISM RESOLUTION AFTER 2 MODERATES DEFY JEFFRIES

Part of what bolstered Gluesenkamp Perez in her previous two races was her opponent, Joe Kent, suffering from electability issues because of his association with far-right groups. He was later named Trump's director of the United States National Counterterrorism Center, but resigned over disagreements on Middle East policy.
This time, however, the race was expected to be much closer, with Braun running as a more mainstream GOP candidate.
Joseph Kent, director of the National Counterterrorism Center, during a House Homeland Security Committee hearing in Washington, D.C., on Dec. 11, 2025 (Daniel Heuer/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Braun is a former Navy captain who also helps run his family's company, Braun Northwest, a manufacturer of emergency vehicles.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
More than $20 million was spent on their race, according to The Washington Standard, a sign of its critical position for both parties.
Elizabeth Elkind is a politics reporter for Fox News Digital leading coverage of the House of Representatives. Previous digital bylines seen at Daily Mail and CBS News.
Follow on Twitter at @liz_elkind and send tips to elizabeth.elkind@fox.com

title: Florida's DeSantis describes GOP midterms wipeout as 'close to an extinction-level event' for Republicans
summary: Outgoing Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis called the midterm elections results a "close to an extinction-level event" for Republicans around the U.S.
story: Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis sounded off Wednesday on Republicans' massive nationwide losses, while analysts consider whether his vocal responses are positioning him for a nationwide run.

Outgoing Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said Wednesday that the Republican losses in the midterm elections are "close to an extinction-level event" for the party "in many parts of the country, as we have seen probably in the last 100 years."

DeSantis spoke after Republicans lost control of both the House and Senate on Election Day. Rep. Byron Donalds, a Florida House Republican, won the contest for DeSantis' seat despite other GOP candidates losing their gubernatorial races around the U.S.

"Here's the thing. Democrats are unpopular. They were able to win based off the sentiment that exists in the country right now. They did not earn a mandate to indulge all their left-wing fantasies. And they're going to be in there governing, and we'll see what ends up happening," DeSantis said.
"But this was not a positive view of the Democrats. This was a rejection of Republicans in Washington," he added. "And Democrats just happened to be the beneficiary."
TRUMP-BACKED BYRON DONALDS MAKES HISTORY AS FLORIDA'S FIRST BLACK GOVERNOR
Gov. Ron DeSantis holds a press conference regarding Hurricane Isaias on Oct. 8, 2026. (USA Today Network via Reuters)

DeSantis, who has not ruled out a 2028 presidential bid, said, "In January, when everyone in office leaves, who were either term-limited or got voted out of the 10 largest states in this union, only one state will have Republican control of their state, the state of Florida.

"Last night we witnessed — to call it a wave, I don't think would be fully accurate — it's the political equivalent of a meteor strike that went all around the United States. Blue states, red states, everything in between," DeSantis said. "And the one state that was able to hold the line and withstand that is right here in the free state of Florida.

"If you look at our chief rival, in a healthy sense, the state of Texas, and I would say over my lifetime, Texas has been the crown jewel of Republican politics. I think we've been the leader for Republicans and conservatives since I've been governor. But if you go over the whole generation, no one holds a candle on the Republican side to the Lone Star State. And yet, not only did they lose a very highly publicized U.S. Senate race, they lost everything," DeSantis continued.
BLUE WAVE SWEEPS DEMOCRATS INTO POWER

"The governor, attorney general, all the other statewide. They lost four Republican Supreme Court justices on the Texas Supreme Court. They may even lose the Texas Legislature or one house or even both. Let's just be clear that that is going to hurt, not just for the next two years. That's something that can reverberate for the next decade or more," he also said. "And if the Republican Party doesn't have Texas as an anchor, then we are not going to be viable nationally going forward."
DeSantis predicted that in the 2028 election cycle, "You are not, as Republicans, going to be able to retake the Senate under this current map just two years from now.
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis speaks with President Donald Trump as he arrives at Southwest Florida International Airport in Fort Myers, Fla., on Oct. 23, 2026. (Reuters)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"And with all the House seats that have been done, probably not viable to take that back as well. So this is really going to have an impact," DeSantis added. "Two years, four years, six years, maybe even longer before Republicans could exercise unified control in Washington again like we've enjoyed over the last two years."
Greg Norman is a reporter at Fox News Digital.

title: Why removing your data online may still leave your family exposed
summary: Data broker opt-out forms may not protect your family. People search sites can still expose your info through a spouse's or parent's profile.
story: Data privacy expert Brittany Kaiser says restrictions on data center development could force American companies to process information abroad, raising concerns over where sensitive data ends up.

You removed your information from data broker sites. You submitted the opt-out forms, did the work and maybe even felt good about it. Here's what you may have missed: Your family members' personal information could still be exposed. And because their profiles may point directly back to you, some of your information could remain accessible, too.

That's the problem with approaching family data broker removal one person at a time. People-search sites often connect relatives through shared addresses, public records and family relationships. In fact, the Federal Trade Commission warns that even after you opt out, your information may still appear in reports about relatives, neighbors or associates. Here's how those connections can leave your household exposed and what you can do about them.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
WHY CAREFUL PEOPLE STILL END UP ON DATA BROKER SITES
Data broker sites can connect family members through shared addresses and public records, potentially exposing personal information even after someone opts out. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Your family is already connected in these databases

Data broker profiles often contain more than one person's information. They can include family relationships that help connect individual records. Search for yourself on people-search sites such as Spokeo, Whitepages, BeenVerified or Intelius. Depending on the site and available records, you may find a section identifying possible relatives or associates.

That list could include your spouse, adult children, parents or people who once shared your address. Some connections may even be outdated or incorrect. For someone trying to learn about your household, those details can provide a starting point. Now consider what happens when you remove your own listing. Your name might disappear from the site's direct search results, but your spouse's profile could still identify you as a relative. Your parent's listing might include an address where you previously lived. As a result, removing one profile may leave behind information that points to the same person.
How one remaining profile can expose your household
Family connections can create privacy gaps in several ways. Here are three examples worth checking.

Married couples often share address histories, property records and other identifying information. When one spouse removes a people-search listing, but the other remains visible, the remaining profile may still reveal their shared address, possible relatives and other household details. Some people-search reports may also include property ownership or estimated financial information, although the details vary by service. For a scammer, a spouse's publicly available information could provide another way to identify or contact someone whose direct listing has been removed.

This is one of the scenarios that concerns me most. Many adults help their parents manage online accounts and avoid scams. Yet they may overlook the personal information already available through people-search sites. An older parent's profile could include previous addresses, relatives' names and other public-record details collected over many years. That information may help criminals make a scam sound more believable. Consider the grandparent scam. Someone calls an older adult, pretends to be a grandchild facing an emergency and demands money immediately. The FTC warns that scammers may already know personal details about their targets or the family members they impersonate. Reducing publicly available information can remove some of the details criminals might use to support their stories.

The reverse can happen, too. Parents may remove their own information without checking whether their adult children have searchable profiles. A young adult's address history, voter registration information or other public records may contribute to people-search listings. Those listings can also identify possible relatives. Someone searching for that adult child could potentially discover connections to their parents and other family members. For example, a scammer might use a child's name and location to make a fake emergency call to a parent sound more credible. That's why checking only one generation of your family may leave important privacy gaps.
A SCAMMER HAS YOUR NAME, PHONE NUMBER AND ADDRESS. WHAT CAN THEY ACTUALLY DO?
Older relatives may have searchable online profiles that reveal personal details and family connections scammers could exploit. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Why removing one profile may not be enough

Data brokers collect information from multiple sources, including public records, publicly available online information and other data brokers. Even after a successful opt-out, some information can reappear when a site obtains updated records. Meanwhile, another people-search service may still have a copy of the same details. The FTC specifically warns that opting out of people-search sites does not remove the underlying information from government public records. It also recommends checking periodically for new listings. That's why I recommend taking a household approach to personal data removal rather than concentrating on one individual.
How a family data removal service can help protect your household

Manually removing personal information from data broker sites takes time. Doing it for multiple family members adds even more work, especially when you have to check whether profiles have returned. That's why I recommend considering a family data removal service that can manage the process for several household members at once.

These services can automatically submit removal requests to hundreds of covered data broker and people-search sites, depending on the provider. Some offer family plans that protect multiple people under one subscription. They can also send recurring removal requests when personal information reappears, helping maintain protection without requiring every family member to handle the process individually.

Look for a service that provides ongoing removal requests, covers multiple family members and lets you track progress. While no service can erase every public record or guarantee complete removal from the internet, ongoing data removal can significantly reduce the amount of personal information available about your household. By protecting several family members together, you can help close privacy gaps that individual removals might leave behind.
Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com.
People-search databases can link relatives across multiple profiles, making it important to check and remove exposed information for the entire household. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
What a family privacy audit looks like
Before you can reduce your household's exposure, you need to understand what information is already available.

With their knowledge and permission, search for each adult's name on several major people-search sites. Look at more than the primary profile. Check whether the listings identify relatives, current addresses or previous locations. Keep in mind that people-search databases can contain inaccurate information. A listed relationship does not automatically mean the connection is correct.

Check whether your parents or older family members have searchable profiles. If they need help, walk them through the available removal options or assist them with their permission. Pay particular attention to addresses, phone numbers and family relationships that could be useful in an impersonation scam. Also remind them to verify unexpected emergency calls by contacting family members through numbers they already know.

Adult children may have their own people-search listings, even when they have never knowingly signed up for one. Check whether those profiles reveal current addresses, previous residences or connections to other family members. Then help them understand how to request removal and why they should check again later.

After identifying exposed profiles, you can submit opt-out requests individually or use a service to manage the process. For households with several adults, I recommend considering a family data removal service that can protect multiple people under one subscription. These services can automatically submit removal requests to hundreds of covered data broker and people-search sites, saving you the time and effort of handling each family member's information separately.

Because listings can reappear, look for a service that offers recurring removal requests, ongoing monitoring and progress tracking. This helps reduce the amount of personal information that strangers and scammers can find about your family. The goal is to make it harder for someone to connect individual profiles and build a detailed picture of your household.
Kurt's key takeaways

I've talked a lot about removing personal information from data brokers, but there's another side to this that deserves more attention. You can spend hours cleaning up your own online profile and still have your name, address or family connections exposed through someone else's listing. That's what concerns me. Most people have no idea how much information about their families can be pieced together from publicly available records.

I think protecting your household should be part of any serious privacy plan. Start by checking what information appears about your spouse, parents and adult children. If you find exposed details, take steps to remove them. I recommend using an ongoing data removal service, especially when you're trying to protect multiple family members. It can handle requests across hundreds of covered sites and keep checking for information that returns. You may never be able to erase every public record, but you can make it harder for strangers and scammers to put together a detailed profile of your family.

title: Apple's first touchscreen MacBook comes at a price
summary: Apple's first touchscreen MacBook Pro starts at $2,899 with a PROLED XDR OLED display, but the non-touch M6 model costs $900 less at $1,999.
story: People try out the new MacBook Pro with a touchscreen following the launch by Apple CEO John Ternus in Los Angeles, on Oct. 28, 2026. (REUTERS)

Apple has finally given the MacBook Pro something many people have wanted for years: a touchscreen. The company unveiled its first touchscreen MacBook Pro on Oct. 28, introducing a new way to interact with its laptop. It also brings a stunning OLED display, a thinner design and some serious processing power. However, there's one detail that might make you think twice before reaching for your wallet. The new touchscreen MacBook Pro starts at $2,899.

That's a lot of money for a laptop, even by Apple's standards. So, what exactly are you getting for that price? More importantly, will touching your MacBook's screen make enough of a difference to justify an upgrade? Let's look at what Apple has introduced and who might benefit most.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
8 BIGGEST THINGS WE LEARNED FROM APPLE'S 2026 EVENT
Apple's first touchscreen MacBook Pro lets users interact directly with the display, bringing familiar iPhone and iPad gestures to the Mac. (Apple)
Apple finally brings touch to the MacBook Pro

For years, Apple maintained that the Mac worked best with a keyboard and trackpad. Meanwhile, Windows laptop owners have enjoyed touchscreen options for a long time. Apple even experimented with touch controls through its Touch Bar, but that feature never replaced the traditional laptop experience.

Now Apple has changed course. Its new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display lets you interact directly with the screen. You can scroll through websites with your finger or pinch to zoom into photos. Apple also lets you drag content between windows and interact with supported creative apps.

Think about how often you instinctively touch your laptop screen, especially after spending years using an iPhone or iPad. Now that gesture will actually do something on the new MacBook Pro. Apple also redesigned the hinge to keep the display steadier when you touch it. That's a thoughtful addition because nobody wants a screen wobbling every time they tap a button.

However, this remains a traditional laptop. It doesn't fold into a tablet, and it doesn't support Apple Pencil. You'll still use the keyboard and trackpad for much of your work. That may disappoint anyone hoping to replace both a MacBook and an iPad with one device.
The OLED display could be the bigger story

While everyone is talking about the touchscreen, Apple's new display technology might have an even greater impact on your everyday experience. The company calls it the PROLED XDR Display, and it uses tandem OLED technology. Unlike traditional laptop screens that rely on a backlight, OLED pixels produce their own light. That allows the display to show deep blacks alongside bright highlights without the same backlight glow.

Apple says the new screen reaches up to 2,000 nits of peak brightness for both HDR and SDR content. It also delivers a claimed 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio and supports refresh rates up to 120Hz for smoother motion. Those numbers sound impressive, but what will you actually notice?
Apple CEO John Ternus mingles at the launch of a new MacBook Pro with a touch screen in Los Angeles on Oct. 28, 2026. (REUTERS)

Photos should look more vibrant, especially when you're viewing pictures taken on your iPhone. Movies can show more detail in dark scenes. If you edit videos or work with photography, the improved color accuracy could be especially useful.

Apple has also added an antireflective coating to help reduce glare. An optional nano-texture finish provides additional reflection control for people who work in bright environments. For someone who spends hours looking at a laptop screen, these improvements could be more valuable than touch alone.
A touchscreen MacBook Pro with serious processing power

Apple isn't holding back on performance. The new touchscreen MacBook Pro comes with either an M5 Pro or M5 Max processor. Both target people who need more processing power than a basic laptop typically provides. If you're editing high-resolution video or working with large photo libraries, these chips are designed to handle that workload. Apple also offers configurations with up to 128GB of unified memory and 16TB of storage. However, those upgrades can drive the price considerably higher.

The new MacBook Pro runs macOS 27 and includes Apple Intelligence alongside Apple's upgraded Siri AI. It also brings Dynamic Island to the Mac for the first time. That familiar feature from the iPhone sits near the top of the display and gives you access to live updates and useful controls. For video calls, Apple includes a 12-megapixel Center Stage camera. Meanwhile, an upgraded six-speaker system promises deeper bass. The laptop also includes Thunderbolt 5 connectivity and an HDMI port, which should appeal to people connecting external displays.
12 BIGGEST APPLE WWDC 2026 TAKEAWAYS YOU NEED TO KNOW
Apple's new touchscreen MacBook Pro comes in 14-inch and 16-inch models, with prices starting at $2,899. (Apple)
Apple's new MacBook Pro is thinner and lighter

One concern with touchscreen laptops is whether all that additional technology makes them heavier. Apple says it has managed to move in the opposite direction. The new 14-inch touchscreen MacBook Pro weighs about three pounds, roughly half a pound less than its predecessor. The 16-inch model comes in at four pounds, approximately 0.7 pounds lighter. Both models also feature slimmer designs. That should make carrying a MacBook Pro between meetings or packing one for a trip a little easier.

Apple promises up to 24 hours of battery life, depending on the configuration and usage. That's an impressive claim for a machine with this much performance and such a bright display. However, we'll need independent testing to see how battery life holds up during real-world work.
How much does Apple's touchscreen MacBook Pro cost?

Apple has positioned its touchscreen MacBook Pro firmly in premium territory. The 14-inch model with the M5 Pro chip starts at $2,899, while the 16-inch version starts at $3,399. If you want the more powerful M5 Max processor, prices jump to $4,499 for the 14-inch model and $4,799 for the 16-inch version. And remember, those are starting prices for each configuration. Adding more memory or storage can increase the total substantially.

There is another important detail. Apple introduced a separate 14-inch MacBook Pro with its newer M6 chip on Oct. 27. That model starts at $1,999, but it uses a Liquid Retina XDR Display without touch support. That means you're looking at a $900 difference between Apple's entry-level M6 MacBook Pro and its least expensive touchscreen model. Of course, the more expensive version also includes an M5 Pro processor and the upgraded OLED display. These are different performance configurations, so the additional $900 doesn't represent the cost of touch alone.

For another perspective, the previous 14-inch MacBook Pro with the M5 Pro chip started at $2,499. That makes the new touchscreen version $400 more expensive than its comparable predecessor. Still, this gives you a meaningful choice. You can buy a powerful new MacBook Pro for considerably less if you don't need to interact directly with the screen. We've previously reported on how rising AI chip costs have pushed Apple prices higher. This latest introduction adds another premium option to an already expensive lineup.
Will your favorite Mac apps work with touch?

Apple says many existing Mac apps will respond to touch immediately because macOS can translate finger taps into mouse clicks. That should make basic interaction straightforward, even before developers fully optimize their software. However, Apple's bigger ambition involves creative applications. The company demonstrated touch controls in Final Cut Pro that let editors manipulate clips directly on the screen. Musicians can use Logic Pro to play virtual instruments with their fingers.

Apple also expects third-party apps, including Adobe Lightroom and Microsoft Office applications, to take advantage of the new touch capabilities. That sounds promising. Still, a touchscreen doesn't automatically make every app easier to use. Tiny buttons and crowded menus can be frustrating when you're trying to select something precisely with a finger.

Early hands-on reports suggest that touch works smoothly for common gestures. However, some smaller macOS controls can still be awkward to tap. Those are preliminary impressions rather than findings from extended testing. It will be interesting to see how quickly developers adapt their interfaces and whether people continue using touch regularly after the initial excitement wears off.
The new PROLED XDR Display combines OLED technology with touch controls. (Apple)
Should you upgrade to Apple's touchscreen MacBook Pro?

This is the question I'd ask before spending nearly $3,000. If you already own a relatively recent MacBook Pro that handles everything you throw at it, I wouldn't rush to replace it solely for touchscreen capabilities. A mouse or trackpad still gives you excellent control, especially when you're working on detailed projects.

However, if you edit video professionally or spend your days working with photos, the OLED display could make a real difference. The improved portability also makes the new model appealing to people who regularly travel with demanding workloads. For everyday activities like email and web browsing, a less expensive MacBook Air or standard MacBook Pro will probably be more than enough.

Before making that decision, take a look at our guide explaining how to know when it's time to replace your Mac. A computer that still performs well may have several good years left. You can also explore our best laptops for 2026 at CyberGuy.com to compare other options before committing to Apple's premium model.

One more suggestion: If you're considering the touchscreen MacBook Pro, visit an Apple Store when it becomes available on Nov. 6. Spend some time using the touchscreen alongside the keyboard and trackpad. That hands-on experience could tell you more than any specification sheet.
Pro tip: Don't forget to protect your new MacBook

If you're spending nearly $3,000 on a new MacBook Pro, protecting that investment should be a priority. While macOS includes built-in security features, Macs can still face malicious downloads and online scams. I recommend keeping your software updated and using strong antivirus software for an additional layer of protection. Strong antivirus software can help detect malware and warn you about dangerous websites before they cause trouble. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.
Kurt's key takeaways

I have to give Apple credit for finally bringing a touchscreen to the MacBook Pro. It feels like a feature that should have arrived years ago, especially when we're all so accustomed to touching the screens on our phones and tablets. I'm also impressed by what Apple is promising with its new OLED display. For people who work with visual content, that could be the most compelling reason to upgrade.

But here's where I hesitate. At $2,899, Apple is asking a lot for a feature that many competing laptops have offered for years. And with the standard M6 MacBook Pro starting at $1,999, there's a pretty compelling argument for saving that extra $900. I want to see how useful touch becomes in everyday work before calling this a must-have upgrade. My advice is to try it in person before spending the money. A touchscreen sounds great, but the real test is whether you still reach for it after the excitement wears off.
Would you pay nearly $3,000 for a touchscreen MacBook Pro? Let us know why or why not by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: 7 holiday shopping scams to watch for this season
summary: Black Friday deals are already drawing scammers who use fake delivery notices and gift card payment requests to steal your personal financial information.
story: Cybercrime losses reached nearly $21 billion last year, prompting Kurt Knutsson to warn of increasingly sophisticated AI scams. He joins 'Fox & Friends Weekend' to break down the FBI data, highlighting that investment fraud alone cost victims $8.65 billion.

Black Friday is still weeks away, but the holiday shopping season is already picking up. Stores are promoting early deals, our inboxes are filling with sales emails, and chances are you're already thinking about gifts for family and friends. Scammers are getting an early start, too.

Holiday shopping scams are designed to blend in with legitimate promotions and messages. A tempting discount could lead to a fake online store. A delivery alert might ask you to confirm your address or pay a small fee. And an email about a problem with your order could be an attempt to steal your payment information.

The tricky part is that these messages often arrive when you're already looking for deals or expecting packages. Before you click or enter your credit card information, here are seven holiday shopping scams to watch for and simple ways to protect yourself.
DO NOT CLICK FAKE 'ACCOUNT RECOVERY' AMAZON EMAIL

Why holiday shopping gives scammers an opening

During the holidays, it is normal to receive messages from unfamiliar stores. You may also be expecting several deliveries at once. Meanwhile, sales and shipping deadlines create pressure to act quickly. Scammers take advantage of those distractions. A fake message becomes more convincing when it matches something you are already expecting. That's why one of the best ways to avoid holiday shopping scams is to verify unexpected messages through a company's official website or app rather than responding directly.
The deal that's too good to be true

You see a social media ad for a name-brand coat, popular gadget or designer handbag at 80% off. The photos look professional, and a countdown clock warns that the deal is about to expire. Big discounts happen during the holidays. However, unusually low prices on popular merchandise can signal a scam. Some fake stores collect your payment and send nothing. Others deliver cheap counterfeits or products that look nothing like the advertisement.

The copycat online store

Fake shopping websites can look remarkably convincing. Scammers copy brand logos, product photography and website layouts to make their stores appear legitimate. Sometimes, the biggest clue is hiding in the website address. A fake store might add words such as "outlet" or "sale" to a familiar brand name. Others use subtle misspellings or unfamiliar web addresses.

One important detail: A padlock icon or HTTPS connection does not guarantee that a shopping website is legitimate. It means the connection is encrypted. Scammers can use encrypted websites, too. When in doubt, type the retailer's official address into your browser or open its trusted app.
The fake delivery notice

"Your package could not be delivered. Please confirm your address." Messages like this appear through text messages and emails, often claiming to come from the U.S. Postal Service, UPS or FedEx. Because you may have packages on the way, the message can seem believable. Scammers frequently direct you to a fake tracking page. There, they may ask you to enter your address, credit card number or other personal information. Some demand a small redelivery fee.

The problem with your order email

Another common scam involves an email claiming that your payment failed, your shopping account has been locked or a purchase needs immediate confirmation. Some messages go further. They claim someone made an expensive purchase using your account and provide a phone number to call if you want to cancel it. That number may connect you directly to a scammer. The gift card payment request

Gift cards make convenient holiday presents. Unfortunately, scammers also like them because the money can be difficult to recover once the card numbers and PINs are shared. A scammer may pretend to be a seller, employer or family member who urgently needs financial help. Some even claim to represent government agencies or utility companies.

The charity appeal that pulls at your heart

The holidays are a popular time for charitable giving. Scammers know that emotional appeals can encourage people to donate quickly. Fake charities may use names that resemble familiar organizations. Others take advantage of natural disasters or heartbreaking stories to solicit donations. Some scammers impersonate legitimate charities and direct donations to fraudulent payment pages.

The marketplace bargain that disappears

Online marketplaces and local resale groups can be useful places to find holiday bargains. However, they also attract scammers posing as legitimate sellers. A seller might advertise a popular item at an unusually low price, then demand payment before you can inspect it. Others try to move conversations away from the marketplace to avoid its protections. Fake payment confirmations and requests for additional shipping fees are other warning signs.

Avoiding holiday shopping scams starts with a few simple habits. These precautions can help protect your finances and personal information.

How security software can help protect holiday shoppers

Good habits are your first line of defense, but nobody spots every scam every time, especially during the busy holiday season. That's where reliable security software can provide an extra layer of protection. Look for software that offers real-time protection against viruses, malware, spyware and ransomware. Some security solutions also include scam detection tools that can help identify fraudulent text messages, fake shopping websites and suspicious links. These features are particularly useful when scammers impersonate familiar retailers or delivery companies.

A built-in password manager is another valuable feature. It can generate and securely store strong, unique passwords for your shopping accounts. That helps reduce the risk of someone accessing multiple accounts if one password is compromised.

AI-powered scams are also becoming more convincing. Fake celebrity endorsements, manipulated videos and fraudulent holiday giveaways can make questionable offers appear legitimate. Some security products now include AI-powered scam detection and deepfake detection tools to help identify certain types of manipulated content. However, these capabilities vary by product, device and platform.

While security software cannot stop every scam, combining it with secure payment methods, account alerts and careful shopping habits can help protect your money and personal information throughout the holiday season.

Cybercriminals are creating convincing retail websites and social media advertisements to lure shoppers with unusually low prices during the holiday season. (Fernando Gutierrez-Juarez/picture alliance via Getty Images)
Kurt's key takeaways

I love finding a great holiday deal as much as anyone. But I've learned that the best way to avoid getting scammed is to be a little skeptical when something looks unusually attractive or demands an immediate response. Scammers are getting better at copying familiar stores and creating convincing messages. They're also using AI to make fraudulent offers look more believable. That's why I recommend checking purchases directly through retailers you trust and using security tools that can help flag suspicious activity. title: iPhone Duo vs Galaxy Z Fold 8: Is $2,000 worth it?
summary: Apple's iPhone Duo reportedly outlasted the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 by over three hours in battery tests, but its weight and repair costs raise concerns.
story: Apple's newly unveiled foldable iPhone Duo sparks significant consumer interest despite a hefty $1,999 starting price tag. On 'Varney & Co.', Taylor Riggs explains the premium device's unique dual-screen capability and ultra-thin design. Host Stuart Varney admits he plans to purchase the high-end smartphone, which can cost up to $3,000 for the two-terabyte storage model.

How much would you pay for a phone that turns into a small tablet? Apple is betting the answer is nearly $2,000. After seven years of watching Samsung build folding phones, Apple has finally entered the race with its first-ever foldable iPhone.

The new iPhone Duo, which went on sale Oct. 23, opens like a book to reveal a 7.6-inch screen. Its biggest competitor, Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8, offers the same screen size and a remarkably similar design. However, Samsung's phone is lighter and costs about $100 less.

Apple has some interesting advantages of its own, including impressive battery performance and a clever screen designed to reduce glare. But there are compromises on both sides, including a repair bill that might make you think twice about carrying either phone without protection. So, has Apple finally cracked the folding phone formula, or does Samsung still have the better idea?

8 BIGGEST THINGS WE LEARNED FROM APPLE'S 2026 EVENT
Apple's first foldable iPhone, the iPhone Duo, takes on Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8 with longer battery life, a glare-reducing display and a higher price tag. (Annice Lyn/Getty Images)
Apple enters the foldable phone race seven years late

Samsung introduced the original Galaxy Fold in 2019. Those early devices came with plenty of growing pains, including concerns about screen durability. Since then, Samsung has steadily improved its folding technology.

Apple took its time. In fact, we covered one of the company's early ideas in our article about Apple's foldable iPhone patent in 2023. Now the iPhone Duo is finally here, and Apple has made some interesting design decisions. The phone features a polished titanium frame, Apple's A20 Pro processor and a large inner OLED display. It also introduces a redesigned version of iOS built around the folding experience.

Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8 takes a different approach. It uses Qualcomm's Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 chip and Samsung's One UI 9 software, which has evolved through several generations of folding phones. That experience gives Samsung an advantage in some areas. However, Apple has already managed to outperform its rival in early battery testing.
iPhone Duo vs Galaxy Z Fold 8 price: Prepare for sticker shock

Let's get the painful part out of the way. The iPhone Duo starts at $1,999 for 256GB of storage. The 512GB model costs $2,199, while the 1TB version jumps to $2,599. If you really want to splurge, Apple's 2TB model costs an eye-watering $3,199.

Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8 starts at $1,899.99 for 256GB. The 512GB version costs $2,099.99, while the 1TB model reaches $2,499.99. That puts Samsung roughly $100 below Apple at comparable storage levels. Of course, Samsung has another advantage. Its Fold 8 has been on sale since August, so retailers and carriers have had time to introduce promotions.

However, I'd look closely at those deals before celebrating the savings. Some carrier offers require a qualifying trade-in or a lengthy commitment to monthly bill credits. There's also a larger question. When you're already spending nearly $2,000, will saving $100 really determine which phone you choose? I suspect the answer comes down to what happens when you actually hold them.
Apple's folding iPhone has a weight problem

One of the first things you'll notice about these phones is how similar they look. Both fold horizontally like a book, with smaller screens on the outside and expansive displays when opened. But there's a noticeable difference in weight. The iPhone Duo weighs 8.96 ounces, compared with 7.09 ounces for Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8. That's almost two ounces heavier for Apple's phone.

If you've ever carried a heavy smartphone in your pocket all day, you know how noticeable that can become. The difference could be even more apparent when you're holding the phone open for extended periods. Samsung also wins on thickness. Its Fold 8 measures about 0.38 inches thick when closed, while the Duo measures 0.44 inches. Apple counters with a rounded titanium design that may feel more comfortable in your hand. Samsung uses sharper edges and a flatter appearance.

There's also something worth thinking about. Both phones have relatively small outer screens. Apple's measures 5.4 inches, while Samsung's comes in at 5.5 inches. Those screens are perfectly usable for everyday tasks. However, they're considerably smaller than the displays on many conventional flagship phones. You could end up spending $2,000 on a device that requires an extra step whenever you want a bigger screen. That's why I'd recommend trying both in person before buying. The phone that feels exciting for five minutes in a store needs to feel comfortable after five hours in your hand.
The iPhone Duo display has a clever trick

Both folding phones open to reveal 7.6-inch OLED screens with adaptive refresh rates up to 120Hz. Each also offers peak outdoor brightness of 3,000 nits. The real difference comes down to how those displays handle reflections.

Apple developed a nano-texture finish for the Duo's inner screen. It creates a matte appearance that helps reduce glare and makes the fold crease harder to see. Anyone who has struggled to read a glossy screen near a sunny window might appreciate this approach.

Samsung's screen has a more traditional glossy finish, which can make colors appear richer. Some early iPhone Duo reviews suggest Apple's matte display sacrifices a little contrast and vibrancy to achieve its reduced reflections. Neither approach will appeal to everyone. However, Apple has another interesting feature coming.
Apple Pencil support could give the Duo an edge

The iPhone Duo now supports the Apple Pencil (USB-C) through iOS 27.2, which Apple released on Oct. 26. That means you can sketch or annotate documents directly on the folding screen. The feature already works in the software's release candidate.

Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8 does not support the S Pen. Samsung removed the feature as it pursued thinner folding designs. There is one catch with Apple's approach. The Duo works only with the USB-C Apple Pencil. Even if you already own an Apple Pencil Pro, you won't be able to use it with this phone.

The USB-C version also lacks the pressure sensitivity available on more advanced Apple Pencil models. Still, this could be useful for someone who regularly signs documents or prefers handwritten notes.
Samsung still understands multitasking better

Here's where those seven years of Samsung experience become apparent. Let's say you're on a video call and someone sends you an important document. You want to review it without interrupting the conversation. Then you need to check your calendar. Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8 can handle several apps on its larger screen. You can run three apps in split-screen mode, and Samsung also offers pop-up windows for additional flexibility. The Fold 8 supports Samsung DeX, too, giving you a desktop-style experience when connected to compatible external displays.

Apple has introduced Split View on the Duo, allowing two apps to run side by side. That's a first for the iPhone, and it should make the larger screen far more useful. However, Apple's approach remains more restrictive than Samsung's. Split View uses a fixed arrangement, and you don't get the same floating-window flexibility. There's another issue that early iPhone Duo owners are discovering.
Some iPhone apps aren't ready for the bigger screen

Apple redesigned iOS 27 for the Duo, which ships with iOS 27.1. Its own apps have been adapted to use the folding display. However, some third-party apps haven't caught up. Early reviewers found that certain apps display large black bars or awkward layouts when opened on the bigger screen. That could be frustrating when you've paid so much for additional screen space.

Fortunately, developers can update their apps to support the Duo's design. Some popular apps have already received updates, and more are expected. For now, though, Samsung has a more established folding software experience. I would also pay attention to which apps you use most. A larger screen loses some of its appeal when your favorite apps still behave as though they're running on a much smaller phone.
Apple's battery life delivers a welcome surprise

Folding phones have a difficult job. They need enough battery power to run a large display without becoming too bulky. Apple's iPhone Duo uses two internal batteries and an A20 Pro processor designed for efficient performance. Samsung equips its Galaxy Z Fold 8 with a 4,800mAh battery and Qualcomm's Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 chip.

Both processors offer plenty of power for demanding apps. However, early independent testing suggests Apple has a surprising advantage when it comes to battery life. In one battery test involving continuous web browsing over 5G, the iPhone Duo reportedly lasted 13 hours and 20 minutes, compared with 10 hours and 6 minutes for Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8. That's more than three additional hours for Apple.

Another independent test produced encouraging results for the Duo. While streaming video over Wi-Fi with the larger screens at maximum brightness, Apple's foldable reportedly lasted 18 hours and 15 minutes, compared with 16 hours and 30 minutes for Samsung. Although the tests used different methods, both suggest Apple has managed to squeeze impressive battery life out of its first folding phone.

Apple officially claims up to 31 hours of video playback using the inner display. However, that figure comes from controlled laboratory testing, so everyday results will vary depending on how you use the phone.

Charging is another consideration. Apple says the Duo can reach 50% in about 20 minutes with a compatible wired charger. Samsung supports 45W wired charging and fast wireless charging. For anyone who spends long days traveling or regularly finds their battery running low before dinner, Apple's early results are encouraging.
THE IPHONE DUO IS OFFICIALLY HERE — GET IT FOR NO MONEY DOWN AT T-MOBILE
The iPhone Duo starts at $1,999, roughly $100 more than Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8, as Apple enters the foldable smartphone market. (Jung Yeon-je/AFP via Getty Images)
A $2,000 folding phone still comes with camera compromises

For nearly $2,000, you'd expect a phone with an incredible camera. And while both of these foldables take excellent photos, there's a catch. Apple's iPhone Duo has two 48MP rear cameras, while Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8 has two 50MP cameras. Neither has a dedicated telephoto lens, which means you're giving up some of the zoom capabilities found on other premium phones.

Think about trying to get a close-up shot of your child playing soccer or capturing something interesting in the distance while on vacation. Apple's Duo offers 2x optical-quality zoom by cropping into its main sensor. Samsung uses a similar approach, with digital zoom for subjects farther away. Both can handle everyday photos, but if you love getting those close-up shots, an iPhone 18 Pro Max or Galaxy S26 Ultra may be a better choice.

Here's where Samsung throws another option into the mix. Its Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra starts at $2,099.99, just $100 more than Apple's Duo at their regular starting prices. For that extra money, you get a 200MP main camera and a dedicated telephoto lens with 3x optical zoom. That's worth considering if you want a folding phone but aren't willing to give up a more versatile camera. And with Samsung already offering discounts on some models, you may not even have to spend more.
Apple has some fun camera features Samsung can't match exactly

Ever try taking a group photo and realize you're the one missing from it? Apple's Smart Take could help with that. Just prop open the iPhone Duo, get into the picture and let its AI recognize when everyone is posing. The phone automatically snaps the photo, so there's no racing against a timer or asking someone else to take the shot.

Then there's Duo Preview, which lets the person you're photographing see themselves on the outside screen. That could save you from hearing, "Wait, let me see that one," after every picture. Apple also came up with Kid Cue, which plays Peanuts animations on the outer display to get children to look toward the camera. If you've ever tried getting a toddler to cooperate for a family photo, you can probably appreciate that one.

Samsung has a few tricks of its own. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 can show people a preview on its outer screen, and you can prop it partially open for hands-free photos. That comes in handy when you want to be in the picture instead of always being the one taking it.
The most expensive iPhone Duo surprise could come after you buy it

Now let's talk about something that deserves far more attention than it usually receives. Repairs. Apple rates the iPhone Duo IP68 for dust and water resistance, while Samsung gives the Galaxy Z Fold 8 an IP48 rating. That gives Apple stronger protection against dust under standardized laboratory testing. However, neither rating guarantees that a folding screen or hinge will survive years of rough treatment. These phones also contain more moving parts than conventional smartphones. And if something goes wrong, the repair costs can be substantial.

There's another reason to think carefully about durability. As we reported in our article, Apple confirms iPhone Duo screen problems after launch. Some owners experienced cracks along the inner screen near the hinge within hours or days of purchase, sometimes during initial setup. Apple acknowledged an issue affecting a small number of devices and directed affected customers to contact AppleCare for replacements. The company hasn't identified the cause or disclosed how many phones are affected. An AppleCare+ subscription isn't required to request a replacement for this acknowledged issue. Still, it's something I'd consider before spending nearly $2,000 on a first-generation folding iPhone.

According to Apple's published repair estimates, replacing the iPhone Duo's damaged inner display costs $999 without AppleCare+. That's roughly half the cost of the entry-level phone. Apple also lists an estimated $1,499 charge for certain other damage repairs. There is some relief for minor screen damage. Apple's replaceable inner display cover layer costs $49 to replace without AppleCare+, provided the damage is limited to that layer. AppleCare+ can significantly reduce eligible repair charges. For example, an inner display repair is listed at $99 under the coverage, subject to the plan's terms. Of course, the coverage itself adds to the cost of ownership.

Samsung's folding phones also have specialized displays and hinges that can be expensive to repair. However, repair pricing varies by model, damage and coverage. This is one area where I'd encourage anyone considering either phone to look beyond the advertised purchase price. After all, a $2,000 phone is expensive enough without worrying about what happens if it slips out of your hand and you're suddenly facing a repair bill approaching $1,000.
Another iPhone Duo change could surprise travelers

Apple has made the iPhone Duo eSIM-only worldwide. That means you won't find a physical SIM card slot. Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8 supports both eSIM and a physical nano-SIM card, although configurations may vary by market.

For most people in the United States, this probably won't be an obstacle. Major carriers support eSIM, and many international providers offer digital plans. However, if you travel frequently and prefer buying physical SIM cards at your destination, Samsung gives you more flexibility. It's worth checking whether your preferred mobile provider supports eSIM before buying the Duo.
iPhone Duo or Galaxy Z Fold 8: Which should you buy?

If you've been waiting years for a folding iPhone, Apple's Duo is an appealing first attempt. It offers excellent early battery performance, an impressive display and the convenience of staying within Apple's ecosystem. However, I wouldn't overlook Samsung. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 is significantly lighter, costs a little less and offers more flexible multitasking. Those advantages could become increasingly important once the excitement of owning a new folding phone wears off.

And here's something else to consider. If most of your day involves texting or checking email, you may spend far more time using the smaller outer screen than you expect. The larger display becomes especially useful when you frequently review documents or watch videos while traveling.

Before buying either phone, think about how much time you would realistically spend with it unfolded. Also, if you're considering switching between Apple and Samsung, take a look at our guide on how to transfer data to a new iPhone or Android at CyberGuy.com. It can help make the move considerably easier.
HERE ARE SOME TIPS ON HOW TO ORGANIZE PHOTOS WITH KEYWORDS ON YOUR PHONE

Apple's iPhone Duo and Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8 feature 7.6-inch folding displays, but differences in weight, battery life and multitasking could influence buyers. (Nikolas Kokovlis/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
Kurt's key takeaways

I have to give Samsung credit. Seven years ago, folding phones seemed like an expensive experiment, and I wasn't convinced they'd ever catch on. But Samsung stuck with the idea, and now Apple has finally joined the party. I like what Apple's done with the iPhone Duo, especially the display and those impressive early battery results. Still, I keep coming back to the price. Nearly $2,000 for a phone that's heavier than Samsung's and doesn't have a dedicated telephoto camera? That's a tough sell. And the possibility of a $999 inner screen repair would certainly make me nervous.

I also wouldn't count Samsung out just because Apple has entered the race. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 is noticeably lighter, and Samsung has spent years figuring out how to make that larger screen useful. Being able to run more apps at once is a nice advantage, especially if you're someone who likes getting work done on your phone. And let's face it, a lighter phone is something you'll appreciate long after the excitement of showing everyone how it folds has worn off.

If I were spending this kind of money, I'd want to see how Apple's first folding iPhone holds up after a few months of everyday use. I'd also want to hold both phones before deciding. But here's what I keep wondering. How often would I really open that larger screen? If I ended up using the smaller outside display most of the day, I'd have a hard time convincing myself that spending $2,000 was worth it.
Would you really spend $2,000 on a folding phone, or do you think Apple and Samsung are charging us more to solve a problem we never had? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.
