title: Florida police unveil $148K flying patrol vehicle
summary: Florida Polytechnic University's Jetson ONE eVTOL police vehicle named Astro still awaits FAA authorization before officers can fly operational patrols.
story: Florida Polytechnic University's Astro flying patrol vehicle takes to the skies above campus as police explore how electric aircraft could support emergency response. (Florida Polytechnic University)

You may be used to seeing police cars cruising through your neighborhood or helicopters flying overhead. But what if an officer could respond to an emergency in a small electric aircraft that looks like a giant drone? That idea is getting closer to reality in Florida. The Florida Polytechnic University Police Department in Lakeland has introduced a flying patrol vehicle that the university has nicknamed Astro. Jetson, the company behind the Jetson ONE personal flying machine, built the single-seat aircraft.

According to the university, it's the first U.S. law enforcement agency to add this type of piloted electric aircraft to its fleet. Jetson calls it a world first. However, Astro still needs FAA authorization before officers can use it for operational police patrols. Here's how Astro works and why police believe this unusual aircraft could change the way they respond to emergencies.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
FLYING SPORTS CAR HIDES ITS WINGS AS PRODUCTION GETS CLOSER
Astro is Florida's new flying patrol vehicle

Astro gets its name from the dog in the classic cartoon The Jetsons. The aircraft even looks like something George Jetson might have parked outside his house. Astro uses electric vertical takeoff and landing technology, commonly called eVTOL. As a result, it can lift straight into the air without needing a runway. Unlike a conventional police helicopter, Astro has a compact frame that folds for easier transport and storage. The aircraft features an open cockpit surrounded by a lightweight frame.

Eight electric motors power its eight propellers. Meanwhile, a four-axis joystick allows the pilot to control its movement. Florida Polytechnic University selected the Jetson ONE to explore its potential for law enforcement. The aircraft arrived during summer 2026. Since then, police personnel have completed flight training, according to Jetson. That includes Police Chief Aaron Murray. Jetson also identifies the aircraft by its registration number, N911FP. The number references emergency services and Florida Polytechnic University. Jetson tells CyberGuy that Astro is a standard Jetson ONE with police lights added. Officers use a handheld radio, and the aircraft has mounts for action cameras. The company says a pilot-controlled searchlight could be added in the future.
How fast can the flying police vehicle go?

Astro may look compact, but its advertised performance is impressive. According to Jetson's published specifications, the aircraft can reach speeds of 63 mph. That's fast enough to cover short distances across a large campus without following roads or dealing with traffic. However, battery life limits how long it can stay airborne. Jetson estimates approximately 20 minutes of flight time per charge, making Astro better suited to short missions than extended patrols. Jetson tells CyberGuy that the aircraft takes approximately 90 minutes to recharge using a 240-volt connection. Charging through a standard household outlet takes about three hours. However, officers can swap batteries between flights. This allows them to return to the air sooner if fully charged replacements are available. Each flight still lasts approximately 20 minutes.

Jetson confirms that the 210-pound maximum includes the pilot, police gear and any emergency supplies. The company says this is a hard limit, which could restrict how much equipment an officer can carry. Jetson also advertises several safety features. The company says Astro can continue flying even if one motor fails. It also has an automatic landing system and a ballistic parachute designed for emergencies. Jetson lists the vehicle at $148,000 before taxes and additional fees, making it a significant investment for a police department.
How police could use Astro during emergencies

Florida Polytechnic University wants to explore whether Astro can help officers respond when roads become difficult to navigate. Consider what happens after a major Florida storm. Roads may flood, debris can block access and emergency crews may struggle to reach certain locations. Once weather and flying conditions allow, a small aircraft that takes off vertically could help officers survey the damage.

Police Chief Aaron Murray believes Astro could help officers monitor the campus and reach places that traditional vehicles cannot easily access. The department also wants to investigate using it to deliver emergency supplies. "Advanced air mobility is a technology on the rise, and we can either choose to be proactive or reactive as it develops," Murray said.

The university also plans to collaborate with regional law enforcement agencies on potential emergency-response missions. However, Astro carries only its pilot. It cannot transport an injured person or bring someone back from a rescue mission. Because the 210-pound limit includes the officer and everything onboard, the amount of emergency supplies Astro can carry depends on the pilot's weight and equipment.
PILOTLESS CARGO AIRCRAFT COULD CHANGE HOW PACKAGES MOVE
The single-seat Jetson ONE aircraft can reach speeds of 63 mph and stay airborne for approximately 20 minutes per charge. (Florida Polytechnic University)
The FAA hurdle facing Florida's flying police vehicle

There's an important regulatory issue before Astro can become a regular part of police operations. Jetson developed the ONE as a recreational aircraft designed around the FAA's Part 103 ultralight rules. Those rules allow qualifying ultralight vehicles to operate without traditional aircraft or pilot certification. However, Part 103 limits their use to recreational or sporting purposes. Police patrols fall outside those permitted uses. FAA guidance specifically identifies aerial surveying and patrolling as activities that cannot operate under Part 103.

Jetson says Florida Polytechnic University needs additional federal authorization involving FAA Part 91 rules to use Astro for public-safety missions. When the university announced the aircraft in mid-October, it said the approval process was in its final stages. At that time, officials expected approval in November or December. The university has not publicly confirmed when regular operational police patrols will begin.
Students will help develop the flying police aircraft's future

Astro has another role beyond its potential police duties. It will serve as a hands-on research platform for Florida Polytechnic University students. The university launched an aerospace engineering degree program in fall 2026. As a result, students will have an opportunity to study electric aircraft technology while learning about the challenges of operating it.

Faculty members and students plan to use Astro's flight data for research and senior engineering projects. Reports also indicate that the university is exploring virtual training simulations for police officers. This could provide useful information about how small electric aircraft perform during specialized missions. It may also help future engineers identify limitations that need attention before wider adoption.

Florida is also expanding its involvement in advanced air mobility. The nearby SunTrax transportation testing facility in Auburndale has a dedicated aerial test track for emerging aircraft technology. Testing under Florida's participation in a federal advanced air mobility pilot program is expected to begin by the end of 2026. That statewide testing effort is separate from Astro's pending authorization for police operations.
Could more police departments start using flying vehicles?

Astro raises an interesting possibility for law enforcement agencies looking for alternatives to traditional helicopters. Police helicopters require significant resources to purchase and maintain. A smaller electric aircraft could eventually offer another option for certain missions, especially when an officer needs a quick view of an area from above.

However, Jetson's aircraft also has substantial limitations. Its short flight duration means officers would need to plan missions carefully. Swappable batteries could support repeated flights, but officers would still need to land between missions to replace them. Weather conditions and airspace restrictions could further affect operations. There's also the question of whether a single-seat piloted aircraft provides enough benefits compared with a drone, which can conduct aerial surveillance without putting an officer in the cockpit.

Even so, Jetson sees the police department's purchase as an important step toward expanding personal electric aircraft into professional use. The company says its entire 2026 and 2027 production is sold out. It is now accepting orders for 2028, with a listed price of $148,000. Jetson also expects Astro to appear at the public UP.Summit event at Kennedy Space Center in Florida on November 7 and 8.
A closer look at Astro reveals its compact design, open cockpit and police markings, with eight electric motors powering the $148,000 aircraft. (Florida Polytechnic University)
What this means to you

You probably won't see flying patrol vehicles operating above your neighborhood anytime soon. However, Astro offers an early look at how public-safety agencies might use small electric aircraft. After a major storm, an officer flying over blocked roads could potentially assess damage and help emergency crews understand where assistance is needed. The same technology might eventually support searches for missing people, although Astro's usefulness still needs to be demonstrated during actual police operations.

There's another side worth considering. As police departments explore aerial technology, questions about privacy will become increasingly important. People may want to know when officers can fly above their property and whether aircraft will collect or record information. Those questions deserve attention alongside the aircraft's potential benefits. For now, Florida Polytechnic University has an opportunity to study a new approach to emergency response while working toward the necessary federal authorization.
Kurt's key takeaways

I've been following Jetson's flying aircraft for several years, and seeing one enter a police department's fleet is an interesting development. When I first covered the Jetson ONE, the attraction was the idea of people being able to fly their own electric aircraft. Now we're seeing a possible use beyond recreation. I can understand why a police department would want this technology, especially in Florida, where storms can leave communities cut off from emergency services. But I'm also interested in what happens after the excitement wears off. Twenty minutes of flight time leaves little room for unexpected delays, and there's still the question of whether an officer flying overhead offers enough advantages over a drone to justify the expense. I'm encouraged that the university plans to study those questions before putting Astro into regular service. And I think communities should have a say in how police use these aircraft, particularly when it comes to privacy.

Would seeing police officers flying above your neighborhood make you feel safer, or would you worry about having another set of eyes watching from the sky? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: ChatGPT now lets you lock private chats with a PIN
summary: OpenAI's new locked chats feature lets you protect ChatGPT conversations with a PIN, Face ID or Touch ID, but there are key privacy limitations.
story: OpenAI Chief Global Affairs Officer Chris Lehane addresses the investigation into an OpenAI hack on an Australian government Medicare portal. During an interview with Lawrence Jones, Lehane explains the context of the July security incident and shares findings from their ongoing review. He also reacts to a new Fox News poll showing 71 percent of Americans oppose local AI data centers.

Ever handed someone your phone or let them use your computer to show them something, then suddenly worried about what else they might see? Maybe you've been using ChatGPT to work through a personal issue or plan a surprise for someone. Your conversation history can reveal quite a bit.

Now, OpenAI is giving you a way to keep certain conversations out of sight. The company just introduced Locked Chats, a new feature that lets you protect individual ChatGPT conversations with a four-digit PIN. On supported devices, you can also use Face ID, Touch ID or your phone's unlock method.

That sounds reassuring, especially as more people turn to artificial intelligence for personal advice. However, there are a few privacy limitations worth understanding before you start locking everything down. Here's how the feature works and how to set it up.

Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. FAKE CHATGPT BILLING EMAILS CAN STEAL YOUR LOGIN
OpenAI's new Locked Chats feature adds another layer of privacy for people using ChatGPT to discuss personal or sensitive topics. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
What are ChatGPT Locked Chats?

OpenAI's new Locked Chats feature allows you to protect selected conversations without deleting them. Once you lock a chat, it moves into a separate area under Projects > Locked chats. The conversation disappears from your regular chat history, pinned chats and standard search results. Its title and contents stay behind your PIN until you choose to open them. You can even continue the conversation later without moving it back into your regular history.

Think about how useful that could be if you share a computer with your spouse or occasionally let someone use your phone. Perhaps you're researching an anniversary surprise and don't want the details popping up in your sidebar. Now, you have a way to keep that conversation separate.

There's one important detail if you already use ChatGPT Projects. Locking a conversation removes it from its original project. As a result, the conversation loses access to that project's instructions, files and memory. Even if you unlock it later, the conversation returns to your regular history rather than its previous project.

The feature is rolling out gradually to ChatGPT Free, Go, Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise and Edu users. It works on the web, in the iPhone and Android apps and in the new ChatGPT desktop apps for Mac and Windows. OpenAI says ChatGPT for Healthcare does not support Locked Chats.
How to lock a ChatGPT conversation with a PIN
You can lock an existing conversation in a few steps. The process is similar whether you're using ChatGPT on your computer, iPhone, Samsung Galaxy or Google Pixel.
Note: If you don't see Lock chat, the feature may not have reached your account yet. OpenAI is releasing it gradually. Some conversation types also cannot be locked.

Open ChatGPT and sign in to your account.Find the conversation you want to protect.Open the conversation's three-dot menu (•••).Select Lock chat.Select Lock chat again to confirm.If this is your first time, select Create a PIN.Enter a four-digit PIN.Enter the PIN again to confirm it.
Open ChatGPT and sign in to your account.
Find the conversation you want to protect.
Open the conversation's three-dot menu (•••).
Select Lock chat.
Select Lock chat again to confirm.
If this is your first time, select Create a PIN.
Enter a four-digit PIN.
Enter the PIN again to confirm it.
Your conversation will move into Locked chats. The PIN belongs to your OpenAI account, so you can use the same PIN across supported devices where you're signed in.
Note: If you don't see Lock chat, the feature may not have reached your account yet. OpenAI is releasing it gradually. Some conversation types also cannot be locked.
META AI LAUNCHES PRIVATE INCOGNITO CHAT
ChatGPT users can now select "Lock chat" from a conversation's menu to protect it with a four-digit PIN and hide it from regular chat history. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
How to use Face ID or Touch ID for ChatGPT Locked Chats

Typing a PIN every time you want to open a personal conversation can get tiresome. Fortunately, OpenAI supports biometric authentication on compatible iPhones and device authentication on supported Android phones.

Open the ChatGPT app.Open the sidebar and tap your profile icon to access Settings.Select Security and login.Tap Account PIN.Turn on Use Face ID or Use Touch ID, if available.Follow any prompts to enable authentication.
Open the ChatGPT app.
Open the sidebar and tap your profile icon to access Settings.
Select Security and login.
Tap Account PIN.
Turn on Use Face ID or Use Touch ID, if available.
Follow any prompts to enable authentication.
You can now use supported biometric authentication to access locked conversations on that iPhone. Your four-digit account PIN remains available as a backup.
Samsung Galaxy and Google Pixel users follow the same steps inside the ChatGPT app. The available authentication method depends on your phone and its settings.

Open the ChatGPT app.Go to Projects.Select Locked chats.Enter your four-digit PIN when requested.Select Use device unlock when prompted, if available.Follow your phone's instructions to enable authentication.
Open the ChatGPT app.
Go to Projects.
Select Locked chats.
Enter your four-digit PIN when requested.
Select Use device unlock when prompted, if available.
Follow your phone's instructions to enable authentication.

Once enabled, you can use your supported device unlock method to access protected conversations. Depending on your phone, that may include fingerprint recognition or another available authentication method.
This setting applies only to the device where you enable it. Turning on device authentication on your Galaxy or Pixel does not automatically enable it on another phone.
How to open a locked ChatGPT conversation
Once you've protected a chat, you'll probably want to return to it. Fortunately, OpenAI keeps your locked conversations in one dedicated location.
Open ChatGPT.Go to Projects.Select Locked chats.Enter your four-digit PIN or use supported device authentication.Select the conversation you want to reopen.
Open ChatGPT.
Go to Projects.
Select Locked chats.
Enter your four-digit PIN or use supported device authentication.
Select the conversation you want to reopen.

You can continue chatting as you normally would. Opening the conversation temporarily gives you access without permanently removing its protection. You can also start a brand-new conversation directly inside Locked chats. After opening that area with your PIN, simply enter a new message. It will remain in the protected section. However, there's a limitation worth knowing. OpenAI doesn't allow you to archive, pin, move or share a conversation while it's locked. You'll need to permanently unlock it before using those options. Anyone who can open a locked conversation can also copy its contents.
Will ChatGPT lock your conversations again automatically?

Yes, although the timing depends on your device. On iPhone, Samsung Galaxy and Google Pixel, OpenAI says access ends automatically after you've been away from a locked chat or the Locked chats area for one minute. The same one-minute rule applies when the app runs in the background.

On the web, refreshing the page or closing the tab ends access. The desktop and web versions also relock after you've been away from the authorized window. If you want to secure everything immediately, select Lock now.

There's another detail worth knowing. A conversation may remain visible in the browser tab immediately after you lock it. Similarly, another device that's already running ChatGPT might temporarily display an older conversation title until it refreshes. So, check your screen before handing over your device.
How to move a locked ChatGPT conversation back to regular history
You may eventually decide that a conversation no longer needs extra protection. You can return it to your normal history without deleting its contents.

Open Projects > Locked chats.Enter your PIN or use device authentication.Open the conversation you want to restore.Select the three-dot menu (•••).Choose Unlock chat , or Unlock on iPhone.Confirm by selecting Unlock chat.
Open Projects > Locked chats.
Enter your PIN or use device authentication.
Open the conversation you want to restore.
Select the three-dot menu (•••).
Choose Unlock chat , or Unlock on iPhone.
Confirm by selecting Unlock chat.
The conversation returns to your regular history and can eventually appear in ordinary search results again.
The privacy limits of ChatGPT Locked Chats

Here's where I want you to pay close attention. Locking a conversation can stop someone casually browsing your chat history. However, OpenAI makes clear that Locked Chats do not provide end-to-end encryption or create a separate encrypted vault. The company also says locking a chat does not change how long it retains your information. Your existing Improve the model for everyone setting remains unchanged, too.

Memory introduces another consideration. If ChatGPT remembered something before you locked a conversation, that information can still exist in regular Memory. Once the chat is locked, new information remembered from subsequent messages stays within the Locked Chats memory area. Other locked conversations can use that information, but regular chats do not receive those new memories automatically. Locked chats can also draw on existing regular Memory when it's enabled.

There's also a potential surprise involving shared links. If you previously shared a conversation through a link, locking it does not revoke that link. Anyone with the existing link may still access the content that was previously shared. You must delete the shared link separately to stop that access.

Files come with their own limitations. Documents and other files uploaded or created inside a locked conversation receive the same protection as the chat itself. However, files already stored elsewhere in ChatGPT's Space or brought in from connected services keep their existing access permissions. Locking a conversation won't automatically protect those separate files.

For workplace accounts, existing organizational retention and compliance policies still apply. OpenAI says Enterprise and Edu conversation logs can include locked chats through its compliance tools. Workspace administrators cannot unlock your chats or reset your PIN, but authorized compliance systems may still access applicable conversation data.

These are important limitations if you're discussing financial information or other highly personal subjects. I would still avoid uploading passwords, Social Security numbers or complete banking credentials to a general ChatGPT conversation.
How to stop ChatGPT from using your new chats for AI training

If you're concerned about how OpenAI handles your conversations, there's another privacy setting you should review. Turning off Improve the model for everyone prevents your new conversations from being used to train OpenAI's models. These instructions apply to personal ChatGPT accounts. OpenAI says content from ChatGPT Business, Enterprise and Edu workspaces is not used to train its models by default.
Here's how to do it.
On the ChatGPT website
Open ChatGPT and sign in.Click your profile icon to open your account menu.Select Settings.Click Data controls.Select Improve the model for everyone.Turn the setting off.Select Done.
Open ChatGPT and sign in.
Click your profile icon to open your account menu.
Select Settings.
Click Data controls.
Select Improve the model for everyone.
Turn the setting off.
Select Done.
On iPhone, Samsung Galaxy and Google Pixel
Open the ChatGPT app.Open the sidebar.Tap your profile icon to access Settings.Select Data controls.Turn off Improve the model for everyone.
Open the ChatGPT app.
Open the sidebar.
Tap your profile icon to access Settings.
Select Data controls.
Turn off Improve the model for everyone.

Your new conversations will no longer be used for model training after you turn off this setting. They can still remain in your chat history, so you'll need Locked Chats or another option to keep them out of view. For additional privacy controls across other AI services, see my guide on how to opt out of AI data collection in popular apps.
ChatGPT Locked Chats vs. Temporary Chat: Which should you use?

OpenAI already offers a feature called Temporary Chat, which serves a different purpose. Temporary Chats don't appear in your regular history or create new memories. OpenAI also excludes them from model training while they remain temporary. However, the company may retain temporary conversations for up to 30 days for safety purposes. Depending on your settings, a Temporary Chat can also use existing personalization information.

Locked Chats make more sense when you want to save a conversation and return to it later without leaving it exposed in your normal history. You can keep adding messages, and the conversation stays behind your PIN.

So, if you're having a one-time discussion you don't need to save, Temporary Chat may be the better choice. If you're working through something personal over several days, Locked Chats gives you a way to maintain that conversation with additional access protection.
ChatGPT's Temporary Chat feature keeps conversations out of regular history, offering an alternative for discussions you don't need to save. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
What happens if you forget your ChatGPT PIN?

This is one detail I really don't want you to overlook. Resetting a forgotten PIN permanently deletes all your locked chats, along with memories stored only within those chats and files or other content protected only by the previous PIN. OpenAI says the deletion cannot be undone. Even its support team cannot recover that protected content. If you remember your current PIN and simply want to change it, you can do so without losing your conversations.

Open ChatGPT.Go to Settings.Select Security and login.Select Account PIN.Under Change PIN, select Change on the web or desktop, or Change PIN on iPhone or Android.Enter your current PIN.Create and confirm your new four-digit PIN.
Open ChatGPT.
Go to Settings.
Select Security and login.
Select Account PIN.
Under Change PIN, select Change on the web or desktop, or Change PIN on iPhone or Android.
Enter your current PIN.
Create and confirm your new four-digit PIN.

If you've forgotten your PIN, you can also reset it from Settings > Security and login > Account PIN. However, you'll need to verify your identity and confirm the permanent deletion of your protected chats and associated content before creating a replacement PIN.

One more thing: OpenAI doesn't allow every conversation to be locked. The exclusions include Temporary Chats, archived chats, group chats and conversations created from shared links. Chats involving scheduled tasks, meeting recordings or background tasks are also excluded. The same applies to conversations with responses saved as project sources. Some Health, Codex and Work conversations have additional restrictions. If the Lock chat option doesn't appear, your conversation may not qualify.
Kurt's key takeaways

I like that OpenAI is finally giving people more control over which conversations appear when someone opens ChatGPT. As AI becomes a place where people work through personal decisions, there's a real need for some discretion. Being able to hand someone your phone without exposing an entire conversation history is a useful improvement. Still, I would treat Locked Chats as a convenience and access-control feature rather than a guarantee of confidentiality. The four-digit PIN helps keep curious eyes away, but your broader privacy depends on the information you share and the settings you've chosen. And that leaves me wondering whether OpenAI should eventually offer something stronger for conversations people consider deeply private.

Would you trust ChatGPT with your most personal conversations if they were protected by a PIN, or should OpenAI offer stronger privacy protections before you feel comfortable sharing? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: Fake party invite scam: Can you trust a friend's reply?
summary: A phishing email disguised as an Evite fooled a man even after he emailed his friend to verify it, revealing how compromised Gmail accounts aid scams.
story: Clicking links in a fake party invitation email can install malware that gives criminals remote access to your computer and personal information, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson explains.

An invitation from a friend lands in your inbox. Something feels off, so you do the responsible thing. You email your friend to make sure the invitation is legitimate. A reply comes back confirming everything. You would probably feel comfortable clicking at that point, right?

That's what makes a recent email from John in Westlake, Ohio, so unsettling. He received a suspicious Evite and decided to investigate. However, the response he received raised even more questions. John has since confirmed with his friend that the emails were part of a scam. His experience reveals a potential weakness in how we verify suspicious emails, especially when someone else's inbox may be compromised.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
FAKE CHATGPT BILLING EMAILS CAN STEAL YOUR LOGIN
When an unexpected invitation raises suspicions, taking a moment to verify the sender can help you avoid falling for a phishing scam. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
A suspicious Evite gets an unexpected reply

John received what appeared to be a fraudulent Evite from a friend. After reading our previous warnings about fake Evite emails, he decided to email his friend directly rather than click the invitation. What happened next made him even more suspicious.
Here's what John wrote:

"I received what I thought was a fraudulent eVite from a friend. Thanks to your previous posts, I strongly suspected that this was a phishing attempt. So, I independently emailed my friend and asked if the eVite was legitimate. I got the response below."
Hi John
This is from me, and I sent it, Sorry for the confusion,
Thank you
"It appears that the scammers either set up an auto-response on the Gmail account or manually responded to my email. The punctuation was wrong, so I didn't consider the response legitimate."

John thought the reply sounded unlike his friend and wondered whether someone had gained access to the account. He later contacted his friend again and confirmed that the emails were a scam. John also shared the actual Evite-branded invitation, which advertised a "Dinner Gathering & Celebration" and included a "View Invitation" button. Its polished design resembled a legitimate event invitation, showing how easily someone could mistake a fraudulent message for the real thing.
WHY VERIFIED SOCIAL MEDIA ACCOUNTS CAN STILL LEAD YOU INTO A SCAM
The Evite-branded invitation John received appeared to advertise a dinner celebration, but he later confirmed with the supposed sender that the emails were fraudulent. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
How a fake party invite scam could manipulate email replies

Most people know they should be cautious about unexpected links. In fact, we've repeatedly encouraged readers to verify suspicious messages before taking action. That remains excellent advice. However, there's an additional concern when the email account you're contacting may already be under someone else's control.

The Federal Trade Commission warned in May 2026 about fraudulent invitations that imitate popular services such as Evite and Paperless Post. These messages may appear to come from someone you recognize. When you try to view the invitation, a fake website can ask for your email password or a verification code.

If criminals obtain access to that account, they may send more fraudulent invitations to the account owner's contacts. The messages can appear to originate from a legitimate email address, making them especially convincing. Now consider what happens when someone replies to one of those invitations asking whether it's real. If a criminal still controls the sender's inbox, that person could potentially intercept the question and send a reassuring answer. A recipient might then believe the invitation is safe because a familiar email address confirmed it.
Could scammers set up automatic Gmail replies?

John wondered whether someone had configured an automatic response inside his friend's Gmail account. Technically, that's possible. Gmail allows users to create email templates and filters that automatically respond to certain messages. Someone with unauthorized access could potentially misuse that feature or simply respond manually while impersonating the account owner.

Although John confirmed the emails were fraudulent, we still don't know how the reassuring reply was generated. There's no technical evidence yet showing whether someone accessed his friend's account, configured an automatic response or used another method to impersonate him. What John's experience does demonstrate is that a reassuring email reply can accompany a confirmed scam.
What Evite says about the fake invitation scam
We reached out to Evite about John's experience and asked whether the company was aware of this type of scam. In a statement provided to CyberGuy, Evite said:

"We're not currently seeing a rise in phishing scams, however, staying aware is always important, which is why we're constantly monitoring and providing tools to help users spot the fakes at evite.com/blog/etiquette/how-to-spot-phishing-email-scam/ . The best way to tell the difference is that a scam is generic, but a real gathering today is highly specific. Real hosts are over-communicating, sharing everything from parking instructions and dress codes to very specific themes like 'Strawberry' or 'Western.' That level of detail is what makes a modern invite harder to fake and gives guests the confidence to say 'yes' without second-guessing.
Evite advice? Check the details. If it just says 'You're invited' with a link, be cautious. A real Evite host today is telling you where to park and what to wear."

Evite's advice is worth keeping in mind, although scammers can also create convincing invitations with specific event details. That's why it's important to take additional precautions before clicking an unexpected invitation.
If scammers gain access to a friend's email account, they could potentially respond to your questions and make a fraudulent invitation appear legitimate. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
How to protect yourself from fake party invite scams
A few changes to how you verify unexpected invitations can help prevent a suspicious email from becoming a much bigger problem.

If an invitation seems unusual, contact the sender using a phone number you already have. You can also reach out through another established communication channel, provided you have reason to trust that account. Avoid using phone numbers included in the suspicious invitation. A criminal could provide a fake contact number designed to make the story sound legitimate.

Be cautious if an invitation asks you to enter your email password or share a security code before revealing event details. A phishing website may use those requests to steal account access. If you expect an invitation from a particular service, open its official app or visit its website directly. Check whether the invitation appears in your account rather than following an unfamiliar link.

Pay attention if a familiar contact suddenly uses an unusual writing style or gives an answer that doesn't fit the conversation. Unexpected requests to click another link should make you even more cautious. However, don't rely entirely on spelling mistakes or punctuation. Criminals can write convincing messages, while legitimate emails may contain errors. The safest approach is to confirm the situation through another trusted method.

Fake invitations can sometimes lead to malicious downloads rather than stolen passwords. In certain attacks, criminals disguise remote access software as something you need to install to view an invitation. Strong antivirus software can help identify dangerous downloads and block known malicious websites on supported devices. Keep your operating system and security software updated so you receive the latest available protections. If you accidentally downloaded an invitation file, avoid opening it. Run a security scan using trusted software. If you entered login credentials on a suspicious website, change them through the legitimate service immediately. If you suspect someone has accessed your Gmail account, review its settings for changes you didn't make. An attacker may use forwarding or automated email rules to interfere with incoming messages.
On a computer, follow these steps:

Open Gmail and click the Settings gear.Select See all settings .Open Filters and Blocked Addresses.Review the filters and look for unfamiliar rules, especially ones that automatically send templates or handle incoming messages unexpectedly.Check Forwarding and POP/IMAP for forwarding addresses or access settings you don't recognize.Open General and review any automatic vacation response that may be enabled.
Open Gmail and click the Settings gear.
Select See all settings .
Open Filters and Blocked Addresses.
Review the filters and look for unfamiliar rules, especially ones that automatically send templates or handle incoming messages unexpectedly.
Check Forwarding and POP/IMAP for forwarding addresses or access settings you don't recognize.
Open General and review any automatic vacation response that may be enabled.
If you discover unfamiliar settings, investigate them and remove unauthorized changes. You should also secure your Google account and review recent sign-in activity.

A strong, unique password helps protect your email. You should also enable two-factor authentication or use a passkey where supported. Passkeys provide stronger protection against phishing because they are tied to legitimate websites or apps. Visit your Google Account security settings at myaccount.google.com/security to review recent activity and connected devices. If you suspect unauthorized access, change your password using a trusted device and sign out unfamiliar sessions. A password manager can help you avoid reusing passwords across accounts. That way, one exposed password is less likely to compromise another service.

Scammers often use personal information found online to make fraudulent messages sound more convincing. Data brokers collect and sell details such as your email address, phone number and information about your family. A personal data removal service can help reduce that exposure by requesting that participating data brokers remove your information. Although no service can erase everything or prevent a friend's email account from being hacked, limiting what's available online may make it harder for criminals to personalize scams. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting Cyberguy.com

When you encounter a fraudulent invitation, use your email provider's phishing-reporting tools. In Gmail, open the suspicious message, select the three-dot menu and choose Report phishing . You can also report scams to the Federal Trade Commission at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. If the message appears to come from a friend, contact that person using another trusted channel. They may need to secure their account and alert other people who received similar invitations.
What to do if your friend confirms their email was hacked

If your friend confirms that someone accessed their account, avoid interacting with the invitation. Save the suspicious message as evidence and report it to your email provider. You may also want to check whether you received any follow-up messages containing unfamiliar links.

Encourage your friend to begin account recovery through their email provider's official website. They should review their account activity and remove unauthorized access. If the scammer sent invitations to other contacts, your friend should warn those people through a communication method they still control. For Gmail users, Google provides instructions for securing a hacked account. Acting quickly may help prevent additional messages from reaching trusted contacts.
Kurt's key takeaways

John's email made me reconsider a piece of advice I often give. I've always encouraged people to contact someone they know when a suspicious message arrives. I still believe that's smart advice, but how you reach that person is important. If their email account has been compromised, you could end up communicating with the scammer instead. Personally, I'd rather pick up the phone and call a number I already trust. I'm glad John trusted his instincts and followed up with his friend. He received a reply saying the invitation was legitimate, yet he kept questioning it. That extra effort helped him confirm the scam. We can't assume every strangely worded email comes from a hacker, but we also shouldn't ignore something that feels wrong. Scammers count on us trusting familiar names and email addresses. John's experience shows why a little extra verification can be worth the effort.

title: Microsoft AI beats doctors in simulated diagnosis test
summary: Microsoft's AI diagnostic system identified 83% of complex medical cases in a study, more than doubling the 36% accuracy of generalist doctors.
story: Laura Ingraham examines the impact of artificial intelligence on healthcare, questioning whether AI will replace doctors. A major public hospital system CEO plans to replace radiologists with AI for breast cancer screening, aiming for cost savings. Dr. Marc Siegel, Fox News Senior Medical Analyst, advocates for AI as a tool to enhance, not replace, human doctors, stressing the irreplaceable value of personal interaction and physician oversight for diagnoses.

Ever leave a doctor's appointment with more questions than answers? Maybe you've gone through several tests, only to hear that your doctor still isn't sure what's causing your symptoms. That uncertainty can be exhausting, especially when you want answers. Now, Microsoft says its new artificial intelligence system could help doctors solve some of medicine's toughest diagnostic puzzles. And the early numbers are impressive.

In a study published on Oct. 22 in the journal Science, Microsoft's AI diagnostic system correctly identified 83% of complex medical cases, compared with 36% for generalist physicians who could consult reference materials. That's more than twice the accuracy under the study's testing conditions.

However, there's an important catch behind those numbers. The research took place in a simulation, and the doctors weren't specialists working together on difficult cases. Still, the findings raise a fascinating question about how artificial intelligence could change your next visit to the doctor.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
AI MAY SPOT DEADLY HEART RISK IN A ROUTINE ECG
Microsoft's MAI-DxO system uses multiple AI agents to evaluate symptoms, recommend tests and work toward a diagnosis. (Microsoft AI)
How Microsoft's AI diagnostic system works

Microsoft calls its technology the MAI Diagnostic Orchestrator, or MAI-DxO. The system uses multiple AI agents that work together much like a panel of doctors discussing a difficult medical case. Instead of jumping to an immediate answer, the AI begins with limited information. It asks follow-up questions and considers which medical tests might help identify the problem. Then, its AI agents challenge one another's conclusions as new information becomes available.

Think about someone who has unexplained fatigue and several unusual lab results. A doctor might consider one possible explanation before ordering additional tests. Microsoft's system can examine multiple possibilities and reconsider its initial assessment as the evidence changes. That approach could prove especially useful when symptoms overlap across different diseases.

According to Microsoft's published findings, researchers evaluated the technology using 304 complex medical cases from The New England Journal of Medicine . These cases often involve unusual illnesses that challenge even experienced physicians. The results were striking. MAI-DxO correctly diagnosed approximately 83% of those cases. Generalist physicians working alone achieved 36% accuracy when they could use reference materials. Without those resources, their accuracy dropped to 22%. Researchers also tested the system using historical emergency department cases. There, the AI achieved approximately 80% accuracy, compared with 47% for the physician comparison group.
Why the AI versus doctors comparison needs a closer look

Before anyone starts canceling doctor appointments, there's something important to understand about this research. The physicians in the comparison were generalists, including primary care doctors and general internists. They evaluated cases individually, even when they had access to medical reference materials.

However, hospitals typically involve specialists when patients develop particularly difficult medical problems. Those specialists may work together and review additional evidence before reaching a diagnosis. Microsoft did not directly compare its system against teams of medical specialists.

There's another important detail. Microsoft's AI was evaluated across 304 complex cases, while physicians worked through a smaller set of 56 cases held out from the system's development process. That means the headline percentages don't represent two groups completing exactly the same number of cases.

That limits how broadly we can interpret the findings. The researchers also relied on existing medical cases rather than treating patients in real time. While those cases provide a useful challenge, actual medical care can be far more unpredictable.

Patients sometimes struggle to describe symptoms. Medical records may contain gaps, and physical examinations can reveal clues that never appear in a written case summary. The simulation also relied on an AI system to supply information from existing case reports. When certain details weren't available, it could generate plausible responses. That helped researchers create diagnostic conversations, although those interactions cannot fully reproduce the uncertainty doctors encounter with actual patients.

Furthermore, reaching the correct diagnosis represents only part of caring for someone. Doctors must determine the appropriate treatment and understand how individual circumstances affect medical decisions. The study's authors also work for Microsoft, making independent testing especially important before hospitals consider relying on the technology for patient care. For now, Microsoft's results show how well the technology performed under controlled testing conditions. Whether it can deliver similar benefits during everyday patient care remains an open question.
HIDDEN CLUES COULD HELP PREDICT A WOMAN’S BREAST CANCER RISK YEARS IN ADVANCE
Microsoft's research suggests AI could eventually help doctors diagnose difficult medical conditions more accurately while keeping patients involved in their care. (iStock)
What makes Microsoft's medical AI different?

You might be wondering how this technology compares with ChatGPT or other AI assistants that already answer medical questions. The underlying AI models play a major role in Microsoft's system. In fact, the researchers tested models developed by OpenAI, Google, Anthropic and other companies.

One finding deserves attention. OpenAI's GPT-5 correctly solved approximately 79% of the complex cases when researchers used a basic prompt without Microsoft's orchestration system. Adding MAI-DxO increased accuracy to approximately 83%. That's an improvement, although the underlying AI model already performed remarkably well.

With the newer GPT-5.5 model, the gains were larger on complex cases. Microsoft's orchestration system raised accuracy from approximately 72% to nearly 87% in that comparison. However, the additional system provided little improvement on emergency department cases using the strongest models. These results suggest that much of the diagnostic capability comes from powerful AI models themselves. Microsoft's approach can improve its performance further, depending on the model and medical problem.

Meanwhile, Microsoft CEO of AI Mustafa Suleyman has described the company's larger ambition as "medical superintelligence." The idea involves developing AI systems capable of eventually exceeding today's strongest medical teams in clinical reasoning and coordination. Microsoft is also collaborating with Mayo Clinic on AI technology that could eventually help clinicians anticipate how a patient's medical condition might develop. Those ambitions extend well beyond the capabilities demonstrated in the current study.
Could Microsoft's AI help lower medical costs?

Anyone who has received a surprisingly expensive medical bill knows how quickly diagnostic testing can add up. Microsoft believes its technology could eventually help doctors make better decisions about which tests patients actually need.

During the study, researchers assigned estimated costs to diagnostic procedures. They then measured whether the AI could reach accurate conclusions while avoiding unnecessary testing. In one cost-conscious configuration, MAI-DxO achieved approximately 81% accuracy on complex cases while generating an estimated $2,241 in diagnostic costs per case. The physicians using reference materials averaged approximately $4,725 in estimated diagnostic costs.

However, some configurations designed to maximize AI accuracy generated higher testing costs. The savings depended partly on how researchers adjusted the system. It's important to understand what those dollar amounts represent. Researchers estimated the cost of diagnostic workups, including medical testing and standardized visit expenses. These figures do not represent actual patient bills or the cost of operating the AI. They're estimates based on the simulation, so researchers still need to determine whether the savings would hold up in real hospitals. Nevertheless, reducing unnecessary procedures while preserving diagnostic accuracy could offer significant benefits if future clinical trials confirm the results.
Microsoft prepares to test its AI in real hospitals

The next challenge involves moving beyond simulated medical cases. Microsoft has announced a partnership with Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston to evaluate MAI-DxO in clinical environments. Under the planned research, consenting patients will continue receiving standard medical care. They will also interact with Microsoft's AI system as researchers compare its recommendations with physicians' independent assessments. Importantly, doctors will remain responsible for patient treatment.

The study should help researchers understand how well the AI performs when it encounters actual patients and the unpredictable circumstances of a busy hospital. Meanwhile, Microsoft faces competition from other technology companies pursuing similar goals. Google recently published a study in The Lancet involving its own conversational medical AI system, called AMIE. In that study, 98 patients interacted with Google's AI before urgent primary care appointments. Physicians monitored the conversations in real time, and none required a safety-related interruption under the study's predefined criteria.

Participating clinicians also reported that the AI-generated information often helped them prepare for appointments. Although the research was relatively small, it provided an early look at how conversational AI might work alongside doctors. Microsoft's upcoming clinical evaluation will offer another opportunity to examine whether these systems can perform reliably outside controlled simulations.
Doctors review medical scans as researchers explore whether AI could help identify complex illnesses and reduce unnecessary testing. (iStock)
What this means to you

For now, Microsoft's AI diagnostic system remains a research technology. You cannot rely on it as a replacement for a medical appointment. However, these findings offer a possible preview of where health care could be headed. If AI systems continue improving, your doctor might eventually have access to a powerful digital assistant that can review difficult cases and suggest overlooked possibilities. That could be especially helpful for people who have spent months trying to understand unexplained symptoms.

AI might also help clinicians evaluate test results more efficiently. In the future, that could reduce unnecessary procedures and potentially shorten the time patients spend waiting for answers. Still, accuracy alone should never determine whether a hospital adopts AI for patient care. Doctors need to understand when these systems make mistakes. Patients also deserve clear information about how their medical data gets used and who reviews AI-generated recommendations.

We've previously reported on how more Americans are turning to AI for health advice. That growing interest makes careful use even more important. If you're already asking an AI chatbot about symptoms or medical test results, use its responses to prepare questions for your doctor. Avoid treating those responses as confirmed diagnoses. And before uploading medical records into any AI service, review how the company handles sensitive health information. Ultimately, the most useful role for this technology may be helping physicians reach better decisions while keeping patients involved in their care.

Want to put AI to work for your own health? Watch the free replay of my CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways AI Can Help You Get Better Healthcare at cyberguy.com/cyberguylive/classes/, where I share practical ways to prepare for doctor visits and make sense of complicated medical information.
Kurt's key takeaways

I find these results both exciting and a little unsettling. Anyone who has watched a loved one struggle through a difficult diagnosis knows how frustrating it can be to wait for answers. If AI can help doctors catch something they might otherwise miss, I'm all for it. But let's be careful about declaring AI better than doctors based on simulated cases. I want to see how this technology performs with actual patients before we put too much trust in it. What interests me most is the possibility of giving doctors another set of highly capable eyes. A second opinion can change everything, and AI could make that available much faster. Of course, protecting sensitive medical information needs to be part of the equation, too.

title: Identity thieves don’t need your password anymore; here are 6 new account takeover threats
summary: Account takeover threats go beyond stolen passwords as criminals exploit session cookies, SIM swaps and MFA fatigue to bypass your login security.
story: Experts now say passkeys, like biometrics and face ID, are the best way to protect our digital lives.

You may think of a stolen password as the main way someone gets into your account. But online criminals have learned that they do not always need to steal the password itself. They may hijack an active login session, convince you to approve a sign-in, take control of your phone number or use malware to collect information from your device.

Passwords are still important. However, they are only one part of the security system protecting your identity. Here are six ways criminals may try to get around traditional password protection and the practical steps you can take to protect yourself.

Cybercriminals can access online accounts without stealing passwords by hijacking login sessions, exploiting security approvals or abusing connected apps. (Felix Zahn/Photothek via Getty Images)
1. Stolen login sessions

When you sign in to a website, the service often creates a session that tells it you have already proved who you are. Your browser or app may keep that session active so you do not have to enter your password every few minutes. Criminals can sometimes steal the digital tokens or cookies associated with these sessions. If the service accepts the stolen information, an attacker may gain access without entering your password or completing another verification step.

How to protect yourself: Review the devices and active sessions connected to your accounts. Sign out of anything you don't recognize and check for suspicious login activity. We've previously explained how to check for unfamiliar devices and remove them from your Apple, Google and Microsoft accounts.

If you suspect unauthorized access, change your password using a trusted device and revoke other sessions when the service allows it. Remember that removing a device from an account list does not always terminate an active login session.
2. SIM swaps and phone account fraud

Your phone number is often connected to email, banking, payment and social media accounts. Criminals may try to convince a mobile carrier to transfer your number to a SIM card or eSIM they control. If the transfer succeeds, they may receive calls and text messages intended for you, including certain account verification codes. A sudden loss of cellular service can be an early warning sign, especially when there is no known local outage. Other signs include an unexpected carrier notification about a device change or a password reset message you did not request.

How to protect yourself: Ask your carrier about an account security PIN, number transfer lock and port-out protection. These protections vary by carrier. For sensitive accounts, use a passkey, security key or authenticator app when available. Unlike text verification codes, authenticator app codes generally do not depend on your phone number. If text messages are your only available second authentication method, keep them enabled. They still provide more protection than relying on a password alone.
ARE BANK TEXT CODES ENOUGH TO PROTECT YOU?
Stolen session cookies and malicious browser extensions can give hackers access to sensitive accounts, even when strong passwords are in place. (Britta Pedersen/picture alliance via Getty Images)
3. Fake login approvals and MFA fatigue

Multifactor authentication, or MFA, adds another layer of protection to your accounts. However, criminals sometimes target the person receiving the security request. One tactic is MFA fatigue, also called push bombing. An attacker who can trigger authentication requests repeatedly sends approval notifications, hoping you eventually tap "Approve" to make them stop. Criminals may also impersonate technical support or a financial institution and ask you to read aloud a one-time security code.

How to protect yourself: Never approve a login you did not initiate or share a verification code with someone who unexpectedly contacts you. If repeated prompts appear, deny them and check the account through its official website or app. Change your password if you suspect it has been compromised. When available, choose phishing-resistant authentication, such as a passkey or security key. App-based approvals that require number matching can also offer additional protection against accidental approvals.
4. Malware and risky browser extensions

An infostealer is malicious software designed to collect information from a device. Depending on its capabilities, it may steal browser-stored passwords, session cookies, payment information or other sensitive data. These programs can arrive through fake software updates, pirated applications, suspicious email attachments, malicious advertisements or compromised browser extensions. Some malware operates quietly, which means you may not immediately notice anything unusual.

How to protect yourself: Keep your operating system, browser and security software updated. Avoid downloading software from unfamiliar websites and review browser extensions regularly. If you suspect malware has compromised a device, use a separate, trusted device to secure important accounts. Run a security scan with strong antivirus software and remove suspicious software. For a serious infection, professional assistance or reinstalling the operating system may be necessary. Avoid signing back into sensitive accounts until you are confident the device is secure.
5. Malicious apps with access to your accounts

Some criminals do not need to steal your password or infect your device. Instead, they may trick you into giving a connected application permission to access your information. For example, a fake productivity tool might ask to read your email, access your contacts or manage files in your cloud storage. You may encounter a legitimate-looking permission screen asking you to approve those requests. If you grant access to a malicious app, it may be able to retrieve information through the permissions you approved. In certain cases, that access can continue even after you change your account password.

This technique is sometimes called OAuth consent phishing. In a September 2026 warning, the FBI explained that criminals can trick people into granting malicious applications access to their accounts. That access can remain active even after a password change unless the victim revokes the application's permissions.

How to protect yourself: Review the third-party applications connected to your Google, Microsoft and other important accounts. Look closely at what each application can access. Remove permissions for apps you no longer use or do not recognize. Be especially careful with applications requesting access to email, contacts, cloud files or account management features.
Passkeys can help, but they are not the whole answer

Passkeys can significantly reduce the risk of traditional password phishing. They use cryptographic credentials associated with your device, security key or password manager. Unlike a password that you type into a website, a properly implemented passkey is tied to the legitimate website or service. That makes it much harder for a fake login page to steal the credential. However, passkeys do not eliminate every security risk. Criminals may still target an already authenticated session, an infected device, a malicious connected application or an account recovery process.

How to protect yourself: Use passkeys when your important accounts support them. Protect your devices with a strong screen lock and keep recovery information current. If a service offers backup recovery codes, store them securely so you can regain access if your primary device is lost or damaged.
Why changing your password may not be enough

Changing a compromised password is important, but it may not automatically remove every form of unauthorized access. Some services revoke existing sessions after a password change, while others require you to sign out of devices separately.

A criminal might also have established another route into your account, such as an app-specific password, an unauthorized connected application or a new recovery method. Your email deserves particular attention. Someone with access to your inbox could create forwarding rules that quietly send copies of your messages elsewhere.

Review security settings for unfamiliar recovery addresses, connected devices, forwarding rules and app permissions. Remove anything you did not authorize. Also, check whether your password was reused elsewhere. If it was, replace those passwords with unique credentials. A password manager can make this easier without requiring you to memorize every login.
What to do if someone gets around your password
If you suspect an account takeover, act quickly. Start with the account that controls access to your other accounts, usually your primary email.
Here's where to focus:

Secure your email: Use a trusted device to change your password, revoke suspicious sessions and check recovery information.Review connected apps: Remove unauthorized permissions and app-specific passwords.Check your phone account: Contact your mobile carrier immediately if you suspect a SIM swap or unauthorized number transfer.Protect financial accounts: Review recent transactions and contact your bank or card issuer about suspicious activity.Watch for identity theft: Examine your credit reports for unfamiliar accounts or inquiries. Consider placing a fraud alert or credit freeze.Preserve evidence: Save security alerts, screenshots, transaction records, case numbers and dates of conversations with financial institutions.
Secure your email: Use a trusted device to change your password, revoke suspicious sessions and check recovery information.
Review connected apps: Remove unauthorized permissions and app-specific passwords.
Check your phone account: Contact your mobile carrier immediately if you suspect a SIM swap or unauthorized number transfer.
Protect financial accounts: Review recent transactions and contact your bank or card issuer about suspicious activity.
Watch for identity theft: Examine your credit reports for unfamiliar accounts or inquiries. Consider placing a fraud alert or credit freeze.
Preserve evidence: Save security alerts, screenshots, transaction records, case numbers and dates of conversations with financial institutions.

A credit freeze is free and can help prevent criminals from opening new credit accounts in your name. You must contact all three major credit bureaus — Equifax, Experian and TransUnion — to freeze your reports at each bureau. If you believe someone has stolen your identity, visit IdentityTheft.gov for a personalized recovery plan from the Federal Trade Commission.
The value of watching beyond the login

Strong account security is essential, but identity misuse can happen outside the original account. A criminal might use exposed personal information to apply for credit, take over a mobile account or attempt financial fraud without triggering a traditional password alert. That's where an identity theft protection service can provide another layer of monitoring.

These services can monitor certain financial accounts, credit activity and exposed personal information for signs of suspicious activity. Some also provide identity restoration specialists who can help you navigate the recovery process if your identity is stolen. Features vary by provider and plan, and no service can prevent every form of identity theft.

For additional peace of mind, consider a service that offers monitoring, timely alerts and recovery assistance. See my picks for the best identity theft protection services at Cyberguy.com to compare your options and find the right coverage for your needs.

Once a month, review active sessions for your main email and financial accounts. Remove devices you no longer use and check whether your recovery information or connected app permissions have changed. Pay attention to unexpected login alerts, changes to your mobile account and new financial activity. A short monthly security check can help you spot suspicious changes before they become a larger problem.
FAKE CHROME UPDATE SCAM COULD INFECT YOUR COMPUTER
SIM swap scams allow criminals to take control of phone numbers and intercept verification codes used to protect banking, email and social media accounts. (Donato Fasano/Getty Images)
Kurt's key takeaways

For years, I've told people to use strong passwords and turn on two-factor authentication. I still stand by that advice. But what concerns me now is how criminals can get into accounts without ever knowing the password. Think about someone quietly reading your email through a connected app you forgot about or using a stolen login session to access information you've worked hard to protect. You might change your password and assume everything is fine, while that access remains open.

That's why I recommend checking which devices and apps have access to your most important accounts. Start with email and your mobile carrier, because losing control of either can create problems with your financial accounts. And while identity theft monitoring services can help alert you to certain suspicious activity, they work best alongside strong account security. A few minutes reviewing your settings today could save you a great deal of trouble later.

title: Elon Musk's Starlink could be your next cellphone carrier
summary: SpaceX is reportedly pursuing access to 80,000 cell sites to turn Starlink into a major wireless carrier rivaling Verizon, AT&T and T-Mobile.
story: President Donald Trump praised Elon Musk at the Golden Age of American Innovation Summit, recounting how the SpaceX founder rapidly deployed Starlink to hurricane-ravaged North Carolina. Trump says the technology restored critical communications and helped save hundreds of lives.

Ever look at your cellphone bill and wonder why you're paying so much when you still can't get a decent signal? Maybe calls drop inside your house or your phone loses service during a road trip. It's frustrating, especially when the big wireless companies keep promising better coverage.

Now, Elon Musk wants to give you another option. His company, SpaceX, is reportedly pursuing access to at least 80,000 cell sites across the United States. The goal is to turn Starlink into a major wireless carrier that could compete directly with Verizon, AT&T and T-Mobile. If Musk pulls this off, the way you choose your cellphone service could change.

AMAZON LEO SATELLITE INTERNET TAKES ON STARLINK

You’ll learn how to secure your phone and personal information, find better travel deals, avoid common scams, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
