title: The November 2026 Read With Jenna Pick Is a Book About Found Family and Forgiveness
summary: The Read With Jenna book club pick for November 2026 is Sweet Pea by Kit de Waal.
story: For her November 2026 Read With Jenna pick, Jenna Bush Hager chose a book about compassion, everyday kindness and unexpected twists of fate that bring people together.
Jenna said “Sweet Pea” by Kit de Wall is a “beautiful reflection of found family and finding hope in the face of fear and loneliness.”

“Paulette is 29 when her dream life falls apart, leaving her with a newborn baby and no idea what to do next. Through motherhood and an unexpected bond with a grandfather and grandson connected to her past, she discovers the strength to embrace forgiveness and second chances.”
For Jenna, this book is a “testament to how our lives can be transformed when we refuse to turn away from love.”
"Sweet Pea" by Kit de Waal
Speaking to TODAY, De Waal said “Sweet Pea” began as a book with six characters’ voices. As she wrote, she thought, “I want more Paulette.”

When the 1970s-set novel opens, Paulette is a woman from St. Kitts living in London and working as a nurse. She’s madly in love with Denton, a man she knows won’t give her everything she wants — but she’s still hoping he might. Then comes a disaster.

“I knew it was her story. The only way it was going to work is if I took her out of that crowded space and gave her her own identity and gave her room to breathe and could properly tell her story,” she said of Paulette.
“Sweet Pea” is a story where there is no villain, De Waal said. “People are trying to do their best,” she said. “In life, there’s very few actual bad guys.”

Instead, the action kicks off with a devastating car accident that binds Paulette’s life with another family’s. Eventually, she takes Nellie, the the son of a woman affected by the accident, under her wing, if reluctantly.

“There’s a reason people act and behave the way they do, and I really wanted to explore when good meets good, when bad meets bad, when the accident meets the other accident. I like exploring the gray areas of life.”
De Waal said, while reading, she hopes people think of who the Nellie of their lives might be.
“Who’s the person that I see that needs something? Could you do something? Can you extend some kindness?”

title: ‘DWTS’ Disney Night Ends With Unexpected Bottom 2 and Emotional Elimination
summary: It was Disney Night on ‘Dancing With the Stars’ Season 35. Find out the scores and who got eliminated during the Nov. 2 episode.
story: “Dancing With the Stars” channeled the happiest place on Earth during Disney Night.
The Nov. 2 episode of “DWTS” was magical as the eight remaining couples performed routines inspired by Disney stories and stage adaptations — with a Broadway twist.

Cynthia Erivo joined Carrie Ann Inaba, Bruno Tonioli and Derek Hough as a guest judge. Additionally, co-hosts Alfonso Ribeiro and Julianne Hough had their turn on the dance floor with the return of team dances.

Last week ended in a double elimination, with Jackson Olson and Tyler Cameron getting eliminated. This episode saw one couple receive immunity in next week’s dance-off round, while another was eliminated at the end of the episode.
Read all about what went down during the Nov. 2 episode of “DWTS,” including the dances and scores of each couple.
Disney Night Kicks Off With Dynamic Broadway-Inspired Opening Number
The opening performance of the Disney Night on “DWTS” was Tony worthy!
The troupe and pros knocked it out of the park as they performed a Broadway-inspired routine to “Circle of Life/Nants Ingonyama” from “The Lion King.”

There was also a performance of “Belle” from “Beauty and the Beast” with Kyra Belle Johnson, “Seize the Day” from “Newsies,” “The Greatest Show” from “The Greatest Showman,” and “Friend Like Me” from “Aladdin.”
The Couples Make the Perfect Disney Pairs
Amber Glenn was the first star to dance, embodying Hercules and even leading Pasha Pashkov during their routine. The judges applauded her strength and called it the perfect opening.

Maura Higgins embodied Tinker Bell as she and Mark Ballas went all out during their jive to “You Can Fly! You Can Fly! You Can Fly!” from “Peter Pan.” However, the judges felt the routine was a bit low energy — and Maura agreed that the dance style made her feel like she was in “Tinker Hell.”

Tatyana Ali and partner Jan Ravnik brought the passion during their contemporary routine. Carrie Ann said the actor gave her chills and applauded her performance. She also gave Tatyana her first 9 of the season.

“Get this man on Broadway, stat!” was the feedback Derek Hough gave Harry Shum Jr. after his contemporary routine. Cynthia said she was “flabbergasted.” After nabbing a perfect score, they were at the top of the leaderboard and, so far, had immunity for next week.

Ezra Frech was praised for making “the impossible, possible,” getting high remarks from all four judges. Julia Stiles, who had been experiencing pain from a rib injury, had been hard on herself but proved that she still had skin in the game.

Jenna Dewan delivered a “feast” for the eyes, with Bruno saying her routine was “‘Dancing With the Stars’ at its best.” She and Val Chmerkovskiy got their first perfect score of the night. Also at the top of the leaderboard, she would compete with Harry for immunity.
Last but not least, the judges admired Connor Wood’s dedication, yet gave notes on his technique.

What Happened During the Team Dances?

title: How Has Social Media Impacted ‘Dancing With the Stars’? Derek Hough Shares His Thoughts
summary: Derek Hough shares the pros and the cons of social media when competing and judging on “Dancing With the Stars.”
story: “Take it From Me” is a TODAY series where experts use their wisdom to explain trends or make recommendations within their fields. In this edition, Derek Hough shares the impact social media has on “Dancing With the Stars.”
“Dancing With the Stars” has evolved over the 21 years it’s been on the air, but the addition of social media has taken it to another level.
Derek Hough, current Season 35 judge, tells TODAY.com that having an online community “has been a huge engine and why the show is so unbelievably popular again.”

“DWTS” has seen a rise in ratings week to week, especially after Dedication Night, which scored 7.36 million viewers, according to ABC. The episode was a season high and the show’s best non-finale episode in six years.
And then there’s the discourse on the social platforms that keep the show a trending topic. However, Hough says, being so popular on social media “comes at a cost.”
“It comes with the negativity, and that’s always been there,” the dancer says, first touching on the judges’ role to deliver constructive criticism.
“The judges (are in) an unpopular position out of the gate because you’re never going to make everybody happy,” he says. “You either overscore somebody or you underscore somebody.”
He understands that viewers will rarely say, “I agree with that.”
“We accept that. We understand that. That’s the judges’ role. We’re like the vinegar in the salad dressing,” he adds.
Hough, though, believes social media takes a toll when you’re the one competing.

“But with the pros and the celebrities, who are working so hard, they’re putting themselves out there. They’re already terrified and vulnerable,” he says, noting that the backlash they receive online “breaks my heart.”
He knows from personal experience. Before he was sitting at the judges table, Hough was a pro for 17 seasons. He’s won a record-breaking six Mirrorball trophies.

“I’ve been a part of the show, where the show has been such a beautiful and positive place,” he reflects. “And here’s the thing, there’s still discourse on the show and we might critique somebody and say something, whatever it is, but it’s within the context of the show.”
“But then it’s the outside stuff that can get a little noisy,” he says.
He believes the negativity impacts the celebrities more than the pros, who have the opportunity to compete multiple seasons.

“But for the celebrities, this is their one shot,” Hough, also a Mucinex Recharge brand ambassador, says. “And I always want them to have a great experience and a positive experience, even if we’re critiquing them, even if they’re not getting the scores they want.”

Hough isn’t the only one who has strong opinions about how social media has impacted “DWTS.” Current pro Brandon Armstrong previously told TODAY.com that the inclusion of Instagram and TikTok has done a “180 on my job.”
He said that while he originally got hired because of his dance, choreography and teaching skills, “Nowadays, it’s your social media presence” that is also a factor.

“Your ability to be on social media is 50% of the battle because if you can’t generate a fan base and generate votes, it really doesn’t matter how good of a dancer you are, because that’s only 50% of the equation,” he says.
There are no requirements, he said, on how much content the competing couples are expected to produce. Though, he believes it does help when you need the votes to stay another week.
“Ultimately, what it takes to win is you have to have the vote,” Armstrong said. “You have to have the backing of the people that watch the show.”
And for that, they turn to social media.

title: The Surprising Way ‘Sister Wives’ Star Janelle Brown Found Out Kody Quit the Show
summary: “Sister Wives” star Janelle Brown reacts to the surprising news that ex-husband Kody Brown decided to quit the TLC series after appearing on the show for the past 16 years.
story: “Sister Wives” star Janelle Brown is reacting to the surprising news that ex-husband Kody Brown decided to quit the TLC series after appearing on the show for the past 16 years.

When the reality television show returned for its 21st season on Oct. 4, Kody Brown and his wife Robyn Brown were absent. It was confirmed in a trailer released prior to the premiere that the couple will not participate in the new season and that the episodes will instead focus on Kody Brown’s ex-wives: Janelle Brown, Christine Brown and Meri Brown.

Although the Season 21 premiere addressed his choice to not participate in the show for the first time since it began, Janelle Brown shared a more in-depth response to his absence in a recent interview with People, revealing how she learned of his departure.
“I actually got an email that they weren’t coming back, and I’m like, ‘Oh, wow. OK,’” she told the magazine.
Janelle Brown added that she has not spoken to the couple since filming Season 20, when they sold the property where they used to live.
“I don’t know anything about what’s going on in their lives. And so yeah, I’m like, ‘OK, I guess this is what we’re doing now,’” she said.
Reflecting on Kody Brown leaving the show, she explained that “it felt like the end of an era” but also a fresh start.

“I feel like going forward now, there’s so many beautiful things happening for all of us. And I think it’s nice that we can focus on that and not so much all the conversations that were happening because of things that Kody would say,” Janelle Brown continued.
The reality television star confirmed she and Kody Brown separated in December 2022, after nearly 30 years together. They share six children, including son Garrison who died in 2024.
While speaking to People, Janelle Brown revealed how their children reacted to Kody Brown quitting “Sister Wives.”
“They really were surprised,” she said. “But again, most of my children don’t really have a relationship with their father, so it was kind of just news really.”

As for her thoughts about her ex and Robyn Brown — his only remaining wife after breakups with Christine Brown in 2021 and Meri Brown in 2014 — Janelle Brown said she hasn’t reached out to them, but she wishes them well.
Even though the two will not be featured in Season 21, Janelle Brown teased that they will still be mentioned frequently.

“Well, I think that we needed to make sure people understood why they weren’t there,” she shared. “So I do think we had to kind of emphasize that in the first episode. I definitely think that goes away as the season progresses.”

She added, “But this is important, people have been watching the show for a long time and we needed to make sure that they understood that those two people were not going to be on their TV every night.”
Janelle, Christine and Meri Brown all voiced their opinions on Kody Brown exiting the series on camera in the first episode of Season 21.

“I don’t know how to process it all. I’m just going to be honest. No idea how I feel about this whole thing,” Christine Brown told cameras. “It’s just bizarre they’re done ... I don’t know what it means. I have no idea.”
At the end of Season 20, Kody Brown’s relationships with his exes were strained. He said he planned to complete a “pilgrimage” to “apologize” to Janelle, Christine and Meri Brown.
After showing the apologies in the premiere, Janelle Brown questioned the sincerity.
“I feel like the apology tour was, in the end, something he was trying to redeem himself with, and I don’t think it was necessarily that sincere because there’s been no contact since,” she said.
The premiere ended with the three ladies moving past their issues with each other and coming together to sort through family photos.

title: Tour the Original TODAY Studio with Host Dave Garroway in 1952
summary: Original TODAY host Dave Garroway took viewers on a tour of the studio during the show’s first episode in 1952.
story: As TODAY marks its 75th anniversary, the TODAY Archive is revisiting legendary interviews, stories that moved us and other iconic moments from our 75 years on the air. These are the segments that shaped TODAY and created a lasting legacy. Today, we look back at original host Dave Garroway taking viewers on a tour of the studio during TODAY’s first episode on Jan. 14, 1952.
How times have changed.

When TODAY premiered Jan. 14, 1952, the set looked just a wee bit different from what we all know today. At the time, the newsgathering operation included electric typewriters, telephoto machines, chalkboards and a wall of newspapers.
During that premiere episode, the program’s first anchor, Dave Galloway, took viewers behind the scenes to see how TODAY came to life.
What Did Dave Garroway Show Viewers?
In the black-and-white clip, Garroway gave “a little tour,” showcasing how the news program got up and running.

“Let me take a little tour with you, if you’re not busy for a second, and find out some of the tools and some of the people who work on the news as it comes in,” Garroway said. “This is in no sense a studio. This is really a working news center. The news actually is written and put together here in front of your eyes, and will be every morning.”

Garroway then made the rounds, introducing announcer Jack Lescoulie, who was armed with a cigarette while sitting at a desk where some of the news and features were created by “pretty girls like Mary Kelly,” who was on the phone with the weather bureau.
Garroway also marveled at an innovation in front of Kelly that we know as an electric typewriter.
“This is a fantastic machine,” he said before hitting keys that he said made it sound like a machine gun.
Dave Garroway Talked to Overseas Reporters

The tour went on to show tape recorders and a telephoto machine before Garroway said hello to overseas news editor Buck Prince, who revealed calls from London and Frankfurt were standing by. This prompted Galloway to chat with correspondent Romney Wheeler in Britain.
“Here in London, we are pleased and proud to be part of this exciting new experiment,” Wheeler said as he talked about some ships in a storm on the English coast.
Galloway then talked with a Frankfurt reporter, who said the snow in that part of the world was a big story.
Dave Garroway Shared the Goal of TODAY

After hanging up, Galloway reminded viewers that “we can take you to anyplace in the world.” He then introduced news editor Jim Fleming, who he said would provide updates 15 minutes before and after the hour.
Garroway revealed machines that took in the news that appeared on the set, as well as newspapers from all over the nation hanging up to explain just what TODAY’s mission is.

“This is not a program from New York to you someplace, if you don’t live in New York,” he said. “This is a program from America, to America, so that the guy in one city knows what the people in other cities are feeling and thinking. That’s why we fly in the newspapers from most important American cities every day.”

title: Heidi Klum’s Husband Was Missing From Her Halloween Festivities. Here’s Why
summary: Halloween is supermodel and television personality Heidi Klum’s big day.
story: Halloween is supermodel and television personality Heidi Klum’s big day. And at her side is usually her husband, rocker Tom Kaulitz.
But this year, the Tokio Hotel frontman was noticeably missing from her annual epic bash, which marked 25 years of Klum’s #Heidiween festivities.

Speaking to Entertainment Tonight, Klum, dressed as a giant, severed version of her own left hand, revealed that Kaulitz had to skip the party at restaurant Cathédrale in Manhattan because of his band’s ongoing tour in Europe. But Klum made sure to include a loving nod to her beau.

“That’s my engagement ring and my wedding band,” Klum said, pointing out the giant set of rings on her costume’s ring finger. “My husband he couldn’t be here today because he’s on tour right now, and I’m going to join him on tour. But he couldn’t be here today, so you know he’s always with me.”
Klum also showed reporters that her hand costume included a “Tom” tattoo, matching the one she has on her actual hand.
Kaulitz, who wed Klum in 2019, is the supermodel’s third husband. She was previously married to singer Seal from 2005 to 2014, and stylist Ric Pipino from 1997 to 2002.

In years past, Kaulitz, whose band is performing in Hamburg, Germany on Nov. 1, has played an important role in bringing the fantastical concepts behind Klum’s costumes to life. For example, in 2022, Klum dressed as an enormous earthworm. Kaulitz was the disturbing fisherman who had attached the gruesome worm to his line. So sweet!
Last year, Klum dressed as the mythical creature Medusa while Kaulitz was one of the monster’s unfortunate victims who had turned to stone.
Klum has often referred to Kaulitz the love of her life. The two met at a mutual friend’s birthday party, she told Ellen Degeneres in 2018. And for Klum, it was pretty much love at first sight.

“It was to the point, so bad, that I couldn’t even look at him,” Klum recalled to the comedian. “You know when you’re immediately attracted to someone that you’re like, ‘Oh, my gosh, I can’t look at him!’ So, I had to sit next to him, instead of across, because then I would’ve had to look at him the whole time.”

title: ‘SNL’ Revives Tom Hanks’ Iconic David S. Pumpkins for Halloween Cold Open
summary: David S. Pumpkins, the wacky, random weirdo brought to life by none other than actor Tom Hanks, made his return to the “Saturday Night Live” stage Oct. 31 for an extra special Halloween cold open.
story: He’s back! Any questions?
David S. Pumpkins, the wacky, random weirdo brought to life by none other than actor Tom Hanks, made his return to the “Saturday Night Live” stage Oct. 31 for an extra special Halloween cold open.
The jack-o-lantern suit-wearing, singing character, who last made his appearance on the sketch comedy show four years ago, gave it his all — like he always does.
“I’m David Pumpkins, maaaaan!” Mr. Pumpkins exclaims, eliciting cheers from the studio audience.

In the sketch, cast members Jeremy Culhane and Grace Reiter take a spooky mausoleum tour, guided by Kenan Thompson. While they’re first greeted by some quintessential scary characters like the infamous Lizzie Borden, the ride takes a weird turn when they run into David.
David S. Pumpkins —  flanked by his two dancing skeleton friends, played by cast member Mikey Day and former “SNL” alum Bobby Moynihan — performs his signature Halloween routine.
Though Culhane and Reiter attempt to get a little clarity around who the heck this David guy really is, they’re given little explanation. They’re simply told that he’s a “Halloween guy.”

David S. Pumpkins’ shenanigans is interrupted by Donald Trump, played by James Austin Johnson, who rants about the upcoming midterms. He’s joined by Nicki Minaj, played by Saidah Belo-Osagie, and former press secretary Katie Zacharia, played by Veronika Slowikowska.
David S. Pumpkins speaks again at the end of the cold open to deliver the final iconic line: “Live from New York, it’s Saturday Night!”

Mr. Pumpkins first charmed — and annoyed — audiences when he made his debut in 2016 during an episode that was hosted by Hanks himself. The sketch, “Haunted Elevator” included David S. Pumpkins’ signature cartoon-y dance music and moves, supported by Day and Moynihan.
Since, the Halloween Guy has made a handful of appearances on the show. Each time, no one really understands why he’s there. And that’s OK!

title: Wave of bomb threats against European airliners triggers diversions and tarmac searches
summary: A passenger ​plane ⁠flying from Dublin ⁠to Rome was on Thursday ⁠diverted ‌to a French air force base after a bomb ‌threat.
story: LONDON — A wave of bomb threats against passenger airliners caused chaos in the skies and airports of Europe on Thursday, the latest of such incidents this week that have prompted emergency landings and security sweeps on runways.

No explosives have so far been found, and it is not clear who or what is behind the security threats made against at least 14 airliners. But the threats have caused disruption to Europe’s airspace and some of its busiest airports.

One of the first reports involved Aer Lingus Flight EI402 from Dublin to Rome, which changed course near Paris and diverted to a French air force base, the airline said. There, all 151 passengers and six crewmembers were evacuated while a bomb squad inspected the aircraft, French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu’s office said in a statement.
Confirmed flights threatened Thursday

Aer Lingus EI402 from Dublin to Rome — received bomb threat over France, made emergency landing at air base and inspected by bomb squad, according to airline and French officials.Finnair AY1761 from Helsinki to Rome Fiumicino — escorted into Rome by Italian air force jets, bomb squad search found no explosives, airline said.Finnair AY1471 from Helsinki to Vienna — also received bomb threat, likewise no explosives found, according to airline.LOT Polish Airlines LO235 from Warsaw to Brussels — crew made midair checks after receiving threat, "additional screening" once in Brussels found no "suspicious items," airline said.LOT Polish Airlines LO331 from Warsaw to Paris — "affected by a potential threat" but searches of passengers and luggage found nothing, Polish officials said.Ryanair FR3606 from Copenhagen to Sofia and Ryanair FR6410 from Madrid to Sofia — both landed normally following bomb threat, no explosives found, according to Bulgarian Transport Ministry.Ryanair FR1730 from London Stansted to Sofia — also received a bomb threat and diverted to Plovdiv, the Bulgarian Transport Ministry said.Wizz Air WMT3064 from Milan to Bucharest — airport said it was notified of the bomb threat as flight was arriving, bomb squad found nothing.Czech police say four unidentified flights headed for Prague have also received threats.
Aer Lingus EI402 from Dublin to Rome — received bomb threat over France, made emergency landing at air base and inspected by bomb squad, according to airline and French officials.
Finnair AY1761 from Helsinki to Rome Fiumicino — escorted into Rome by Italian air force jets, bomb squad search found no explosives, airline said.
Finnair AY1471 from Helsinki to Vienna — also received bomb threat, likewise no explosives found, according to airline.
LOT Polish Airlines LO235 from Warsaw to Brussels — crew made midair checks after receiving threat, "additional screening" once in Brussels found no "suspicious items," airline said.
LOT Polish Airlines LO331 from Warsaw to Paris — "affected by a potential threat" but searches of passengers and luggage found nothing, Polish officials said.
Ryanair FR3606 from Copenhagen to Sofia and Ryanair FR6410 from Madrid to Sofia — both landed normally following bomb threat, no explosives found, according to Bulgarian Transport Ministry.
Ryanair FR1730 from London Stansted to Sofia — also received a bomb threat and diverted to Plovdiv, the Bulgarian Transport Ministry said.
Wizz Air WMT3064 from Milan to Bucharest — airport said it was notified of the bomb threat as flight was arriving, bomb squad found nothing.
Czech police say four unidentified flights headed for Prague have also received threats.
From there, reports of threats in the skies over Europe arrived at dizzying pace, triggering searches by cabin crews and then again by airport security once on the ground.
Security operations were launched at airports in Prague, Copenhagen and Warsaw, with passengers at the last seeing the military and police sniffer dogs patrolling the tarmac.

A Finnair flight from Helsinki was escorted by Italian air force jets to Rome’s Fiumicino Airport “following anonymous reports of a suspected bomb threat,” according to a spokesperson for the city’s airport authority. Bomb disposal experts found nothing.

title: ‘Looks like Mars’: Toxic smog from Indonesia wildfires sparks health crisis, protests
summary: Wildfires in Indonesia are blanketing the country and other southeast Asian nations in toxic smog, prompting widespread protests.
story: Almost every day for months, Indonesian schoolteacher Natanael Undas has gazed up at smoke-filled skies in apocalyptic shades of yellow and orange.

“It looks like Mars, like we’re living on another planet,” said Undas, whose home in central Kalimantan province is at the heart of devastating wildfires generating toxic smog in Indonesia and across Southeast Asia.

Although his family keeps the windows shut at all times, the noxious smoke penetrates the house anyway, sending Undas’ 2-year-old daughter into constant sneezing fits amid a spike in respiratory illnesses in haze-affected regions.

Wildfires are nothing new in Indonesia, whose forests and peatlands are set ablaze each year as family and commercial farms clear land using traditional “slash and burn” methods. But the fires this year are far worse than usual, said Undas, who has been documenting Indonesia’s air quality on Instagram since 2014, as heat and drought aggravated by a “super” El Niño weather pattern make this the country’s worst fire season in over a decade.

The unrelenting haze from the fires has affected millions of people in the region since they started in July, closing schools in multiple countries and spurring arguments about who is to blame. Indonesian protesters have accused their government of insufficient action, while other countries are threatening prosecution.

On Wednesday, hundreds of Indonesian students and members of civil society groups protested in the capital, Jakarta, and other cities against the policies of President Prabowo Subianto, including his resistance to declaring the fires a national disaster.
“We want transparent and independent investigations about these wildfires,” protester Natasha Ruvantina told NBC News. “And also, we want a long-term prevention strategy.”
The Indonesian government said in a statement Wednesday that it recognized the students’ concerns, adding that it was prosecuting companies linked to the fires and sending aid to affected provinces.

The fires have also caused frustration in countries such as neighboring Singapore, where air pollution this month reached its highest level since 2015, when Indonesian wildfires were also intensified by El Niño. Singapore officials have threatened to prosecute companies seen as responsible for the devastation, and on Tuesday the foreign ministers of Singapore and Indonesia said they were considering a joint task force to combat illegal land burning.
“We will use the full force of the law to make sure those who profit from fire must answer for the fires,” Indonesian Foreign Minister Arrmanatha Nasir said.
Indonesia’s neighbors and other countries have been accused of contributing to the problem.

In a report this month, the Indonesian environmental organization Walhi named 66 companies with links to Singapore and 27 companies with links to Malaysia that it said were associated with fire hot spots. On Thursday, the Indonesian government said police had identified 20 corporations suspected of being involved in the fires, including four from Singapore, Malaysia and South Korea.

title: Melania Trump to host Russia and Ukraine representatives at the White House in a rare meeting
summary: First lady Melania Trump will host representatives from Russia and Ukraine at the White House on Thursday, her latest diplomatic initiative after an unprecedented humanitarian ceasefire she helped broker between the warring sides.
story: First lady Melania Trump will host representatives from Russia and Ukraine at the White House on Thursday, her latest diplomatic initiative after an unprecedented humanitarian ceasefire she helped broker between the warring sides.

The meeting comes as the Trump administration pushes for progress in broader peace negotiations, with the United States set to lead renewed trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, next week. The losses suffered by Republicans in the midterm elections dealt a setback to President Donald Trump and his foreign policy, injecting yet more uncertainty into the American approach to the conflict.
“This event represents an extraordinary moment in American history,” the White House said in a statement announcing Thursday’s meeting.

It appears that this will be the first time both sides will meet face-to-face at the White House. It is unclear what exactly the gathering was designed to achieve and whether the president or any of his envoys would attend.
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

title: U.S. Marine dies in Japan during training, military says
summary: The person, who has yet to be named, died Tuesday in Okinawa, the 3rd Marine Division said.
story: A U.S. Marine has died in Japan following a “training incident,” the military said in a statement Wednesday.

The unnamed Marine was undertaking training at Camp Schwab in Okinawa, Japan’s southernmost prefecture, the statement said. The area is home to a large U.S. military presence and bases that serve as a regional hub in the Indo-Pacific.

The Marine, who was with the 3rd Marine Division, died Tuesday and will not be named until 24 hours after the individual’s family has been notified, the 3rd Marine Division said in a statement Wednesday.
For Subscribers
“It is with heavy hearts that 3rd Marine Division announces the death of a Marine following a training incident at Camp Schwab, Okinawa, Japan, on Nov. 3, 2026,” the statement said.
“The circumstances surrounding the incident remain under investigation,” it added. “We express our deepest condolences to the family and loved ones of our Marine.”
For Subscribers

Okinawa was under U.S. occupation following World War II until it was handed back to Japan in 1972. Today, the U.S. population on the island is nearly 80,000, with nearly 30,000 being active-duty troops from all four branches of the armed forces, though the Marines make up the bulk of the forces.

Separately, Secretary of State Marco Rubio last month pledged to cooperate with Japanese authorities investigating allegations that a ​U.S. Marine murdered a woman in Okinawa. The case sparked widespread protests and led to a U.S. military curfew and mandatory training in standards and discipline.
Lt. Gen. Benjamin Watson, commander of the III Marine Expeditionary Force, said at the time that serving on the Japanese island “comes with responsibility.”

title: U.S. will stop $4B in aid to Israel at the end of the year, Trump says
summary: Oil prices slid in response to the deal, which the president said was Netanyahu’s idea.
story: President Donald Trump said Tuesday that he has made a deal with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for the U.S. to stop sending $4 billion in aid annually to Israel.
It was not immediately clear which exact funding Trump meant.
Trump said that he and Netanyahu “made a deal months ago that we’re stopping” and that the money would get “cut off at the end of the year.”

Trump said in a phone interview with “Fox & Friends” that the idea was Netanyahu’s — Netanyahu has previously floated tapering American aid over the next decade. Netanyahu’s office declined to comment Tuesday.

“We’ll help Israel if they need it — you know they’ve been a great ally,” Trump said, adding that the Israeli government was “fine with it, because, you know, they have become a very successful country” and “they don’t need” the money.

Trump was speaking while voters were heading to the polls for the midterm elections. U.S. military aid to Israel and Israel’s use of American weapons in Gaza and the West Bank have been among the most contentious issues during the campaign.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

Trump appeared to acknowledge a political dimension to the decision, saying, “The left uses the $4 billion payment that everybody knows about, when it’s no secret, as a signal of unfairness, and we can’t allow that to happen.”
“I don’t like that, because, you know, it’s too easy. It’s almost too easy a target,” he said.

“Why should we suffer the slings from lunatics like an El-Sayed when they don’t need it?” Trump added, referring to Abdul El-Sayed, the progressive Democratic Michigan Senate nominee, who has forcefully criticized Israel and U.S. foreign policy during the campaign.

The price of Brent crude oil slid 3%, to $101 a barrel, in response to Trump’s comments, its lowest in more than three weeks, as investors and traders viewed the comments as possibly further evidence that the Iran war could be ended without escalation. It ticked back up to $103 at noon ET.
The initial drop added to oil’s biggest one-day decline in three months Monday, after Trump told NBC News that he was not planning to attack Iran after the midterms.
Complex aid picture

The U.S. has agreed to give Israel $3.8 billion annually as part of a “memorandum of understanding” signed in 2016 during the Obama administration. The agreement, which took effect in October 2018, specifies $3.3 billion a year in military financing grants and $500 million a year for joint missile defense. It is due to expire in 2028.
Almost all of that money must be spent on purchases from the U.S.
But the total amount is much higher, with American military aid to Israel greatly boosted following the Hamas-led attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, and the subsequent Israeli assault on Gaza.

In the two years after Oct. 7, the U.S. spent at least $21.7 billion in military aid to Israel, according to a paper by William D. Hartung, a senior research fellow at the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft, a think tank based in Washington.

title: U.S. military carries out limited strikes on Iran’s Qeshm Island
summary: The strikes, which appeared to be limited as opposed to a full return to hostilities, came on the eve of crucial American midterm elections.
story: The U.S. military carried out limited strikes Monday on Iran’s Qeshm Island, according to two U.S. officials.

The officials said the U.S. attacks, which came on the eve of crucial U.S. midterm elections and as the Middle East is anxious about the possibility of a return to all-out war, were not a resumption of major combat operations in Iran. They described the attacks as self-defense in response to Iran’s ongoing efforts to target maritime shipping and U.S. assets.
The U.S. continues to intercept drones and missiles that are targeting shipping every day, one of the U.S. officials said.

The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps has routinely targeted and shot at U.S. manned and unmanned aircraft over the Strait of Hormuz and in the area over the past few weeks, one of the U.S. officials said.
The U.S. is occasionally striking Iranian missile launchers in self-defense when the Revolutionary Guard shoots at U.S. aircraft, the official said.
Iran tried to target a U.S. aircraft again, leading to the U.S. strike on Qeshm to take out the launcher, the official said, calling it part of ongoing operations.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
A third U.S. official said, “This was a defensive measure for Iranians using surface-to-air missiles against U.S. assets.”
Iranian state media reported that five explosions were heard Monday on Qeshm Island.
President Donald Trump had said the U.S. would not launch strikes on Iran before Tuesday’s midterm elections.

Asked on “Fox & Friends” what would happen once the elections were over, Trump said he wasn’t looking to “kill lots of people,” but “if we have to, we’ll have to.” The latest strikes were “just a minor attack,” he said while insisting the situation does not constitute a war.
The unpopular Iran war and the resulting impact on U.S. gasoline prices and other parts of the economy have been a vulnerability for Republicans as they try to keep control of Congress.

The administration was last known to have carried out some attacks in early September, but thousands of U.S. troops remain in the waters off Iran to maintain a naval blockade aimed at preventing tankers carrying Iranian oil from getting to the global market. A third aircraft carrier and thousands of additional troops are also on their way to the Middle East.

Earlier Monday, Vice President JD Vance offered measured optimism that a deal can still be struck to prevent Trump from following through on his threat to potentially order new strikes on Iran after the midterm elections.

title: Supermarkets across Europe hit by new fridge cyberattacks
summary: The incidents caused temperature spikes and spoiled food at stores in Sweden, the Netherlands, Belgium, Ireland, Luxembourg and Estonia. It follows a similar cyberattack in France last month.
story: Supermarkets across Europe were hit Monday by a new wave of apparent cyberattacks affecting fridges and freezers.
The incidents caused temperature spikes and spoiled food at stores in Sweden, the Netherlands, Belgium, Ireland, Luxembourg and Estonia.

They follow a cyberattack in France last month, in which, police said, hackers seized control of cooling units at hundreds of supermarkets, raising temperatures as high as 122 degrees Fahrenheit and causing fires and food losses.
Authorities have not indicated who could have been behind the incidents. There were no claims of responsibility.
The continent is confronting broader security fears stemming from Russia’s war in Ukraine.
The new cyberattack highlights how digital threats can increasingly affect people’s everyday lives, the European Commission said Monday.

title: Fake alerts warn of nuclear danger as Ukraine and Russia report emergency app hacks
summary: The dueling accusations came just as a rare humanitarian ceasefire between the two sides ended, raising fears of intensified fighting.
story: Nuclear danger, radiation threat and street combat: Ukrainians received a wave of messages Sunday night that raised alarm with a series of grave — and baseless — warnings.

Authorities said the country’s emergency alert application had been targeted in a cyberattack, and hours later Russia said its own alert system had also been hacked. The dueling accusations came just as a rare humanitarian ceasefire between the two sides ended, raising fears of intensified fighting rather than a move toward broader peace.

Residents in Ukraine have become used to the unsettling alerts that buzz their phones with news of incoming Russian missiles and drones — a service millions rely on to seek shelter before the attacks hit their cities. But the warnings Sunday night immediately stood out.

title: Israel’s president says parties need to engage with ‘open heart’ to avoid fresh election
summary: “Creative solutions” are needed to prevent another round of elections, Isaac Herzog has stressed, after no faction emerged with an obvious path to power.
story: Israeli President Isaac Herzog has urged the country’s political parties to enter negotiations on forming a new government with an “open heart,” as he prepares to consult with factions on a path forward after an uncertain election result.
Last week’s elections saw Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc denied a majority, with the parties in his ruling coalition claiming 53 seats in Israel’s 120-member Knesset.
Parties in the bloc aligned with Netanyahu’s main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, won 48 seats, leaving neither man with an obvious path to forming a government.

The balance of power is held by parties representing Israel’s minority Arab community, which nearly doubled its representation in Israel’s parliament with 19 seats. But both Netanyahu and Eisenkot had ruled out working with them prior to the vote.

Netanyahu has since continued to attack the Arab parties, accusing them of holding stances on Gaza and the West Bank he considers unacceptable. Eisenkot, however, has indicated he is open to working with anyone who agrees to four conditions on Israeli sovereignty and opposition to Hamas, potentially opening a path to a deal that could propel him to power and avoid fresh elections.

While Netanyahu is the leader of the single largest party, it is up to Herzog — largely a ceremonial figure — to decide who has the first shot at forming a government. He will hold initial consultations with party officials Wednesday, beginning a delicate process that could last weeks.

“I hope the representatives will come with an open mind, and today I add: with an open heart,” Herzog said in a statement Sunday. “Come to listen and to be heard, to share ideas, and to find creative solutions to prevent another round of elections.”

Netanyahu, who is set to remain in his post as a caretaker until a new government can be formed, has claimed Arab parties used foreign backing to “steal” the elections, without providing evidence. Israeli intelligence agency Shin Bet has said it is investigating possible foreign interference in the election but that the probe was not intended to “cast aspersions” on any specific group.
Arab party leaders have strongly denied any wrongdoing, while Herzog pushed party leaders to accept the election result.

“During an election campaign, candidates naturally and predictably climb to lofty positions,” Herzog said in his statement. “But the elections are over. The election results are a fact. They are a reality. And now is the time to call on all our leaders to stop climbing and face this reality.”

The four conditions Eisenkot set out for prospective partners include recognizing Israel as a Jewish state, committing to the values of its independence, accepting mandatory military service for all Israeli citizens and recognizing Hamas as a terrorist organization.

“Every Knesset member who is willing to sign on to these principles is a potential partner on the path to establishing a new and better government for Israel,” he said in a statement Saturday. “The door to the government we will form will be open to every public representative who accepts these principles and is ready to rise to the occasion.”
Netanyahu, meanwhile, said Sunday that it was “forbidden” to form a government with Mansour Abbas, head of Arab-led party Ra’am.

He said on X that Abbas wants to establish a Palestinian state with East Jerusalem as its capital and evacuate Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territories, citing an old Ra’am policy platform.
During the campaign, Netanyahu’s Likud party repeatedly alleged that Eisenkot would usher the Arab parties into power.
In one of several AI-generated videos posted by Netanyahu, Eisenkot was portrayed astride a wooden Trojan horse, with Abbas and left-wing politician Yair Golan inside.
Abbas said Friday that he was coordinating with other Arab leaders on “the prospects for forming a government to replace the one led by Netanyahu.”

Eisenkot’s anti-Netanyahu bloc contains a broad array of ideologies and views on the issue, ranging from Golan, who has publicly advocated for a deal with the Arab parties, to Avigdor Lieberman of the right-wing Yisrael Beiteinu party, who continues to oppose working with them.
With that much friction, a stalemate and more elections remain a real possibility.

Fawaz Gerges, a professor of international relations at the London School of Economics, told NBC News that Israel still appears stuck, adding that Eisenkot’s conditions for the Arab parties are effectively asking them to “forsake their identity.”
“I don’t think we will see the opposition led by Eisenkot forming a government in Israel,” he said. “So what we have now is a deadlock.”
For the major Israeli parties, it is a choice “between Israel as a democratic state or Israel as a Zionist exclusive society,” he said.
But Yossi Mekelberg, a senior consulting fellow with the Middle East and North Africa Program at U.K. think tank Chatham House, sees flexibility that could yield a breakthrough.
Parties “make all these promises before the election, and it is obvious that you break at least some of them after the election,” he said.

title: Minor detained after U.S. warned Russia of possible Moscow terrorist attack, FSB says
summary: The FSB said it “verified” the information received from U.S. law enforcement, and “as a result of these operations, a Russian minor was detained,” Russia’s Tass news agency reported.
story: Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) ​said it had received information from ‌the U.S. through established partner channels about preparations for a terrorist attack ​in Moscow.

The FSB said Sunday that it had “verified” the information received from U.S. law enforcement and that “as a result of these operations, a Russian minor was detained,” Russia’s Tass state news agency reported.

It said that a person “had posted photos on the short-video platform TikTok showing himself wearing tactical gear—including a balaclava, a cap, protective eyewear, and headphones—while holding an object resembling an automatic weapon.”
For Subscribers

A search of his devices revealed a “subscription to a neo-Nazi channel on the messaging app Telegram, and a significant number of search queries concerning past terrorist attacks, mass shootings, and other acts of violence,” Tass reported, citing the FSB.

The U.S. Embassy in Moscow ⁠said that it was “aware of ​a credible threat of a mass casualty ​event” Saturday at Moscow’s Tsaritsyno Museum Reserve and that the U.S. government was ​coordinating with Russian authorities.
For Subscribers

The Tsaritsyno ​Museum Reserve, a palace museum and park complex ‌south ⁠of Moscow, was temporarily closed Saturday and access to the park was restricted, the RIA news agency ​reported, ​citing Russian ⁠law enforcement agencies.

The Russian tabloid Baza reported that the venue was evacuated toward the end of an organ concert, which was cut short with about 10 minutes left in the program. A separate concert dedicated to the folk traditions of the North Caucasus region was subsequently canceled, the newspaper reported.

In March 2024, the U.S. Embassy warned ​that extremists had imminent plans ​for ⁠an attack in Moscow. Days later, gunmen attacked the Crocus City Hall ⁠concert ​venue outside Moscow, killing ​more than 140 people.

title: Stores looted in German riots as Gen Z activists protest living costs, military service
summary: Police said Molotov cocktails were thrown at the emergency services, as protests grew in Germany following weeks of unrest in France.
story: Rioters looted stores and set fires to barricades in Frankfurt on Saturday as protests across Germany demanded lower living costs and better education.

Tens of thousands of people across more than 30 cities took to the streets, including in the capital Berlin and financial hub Frankfurt, in protests organized by the campaign group Gen Z Regelt (Gen Z Takes Charge).
The activists demand spending on schools, climate protection and housing, and are against plans to return to mandatory military service.
But the largely peaceful protests, which coincided with Halloween and came weeks after some of the worst rioting in decades erupted in neighboring France, turned violent in some areas.

“In ⁠the city center, windows have been smashed at several shops,” Frankfurt police said on X. “Molotov cocktails are also being thrown at the emergency services. We urge all bystanders to avoid the ​city center or to leave the area.”

title: Massive protests sweep Europe over cost of living and strained public services
summary: Massive protests were sweeping Europe on Saturday as part of demonstrations driven by the cost of living and deficient public services, with police bracing for potential violence after recent looting and riots.
story: Massive protests were sweeping Europe on Saturday as part of demonstrations driven by the cost of living and deficient public services, with police bracing for potential violence after recent looting and riots.
Germany, France, Spain and Italy are among the nations where demonstrations were being held on Halloween following a recent wave of Gen Z-led marches across the continent.

French officials said they would deploy 70,000 police on Saturday following some of the worst rioting in decades, which erupted in cities across the country after student protests about the state of education evolved into wider demonstrations about the cost of living and social security.
As the demonstrations began Saturday afternoon in Paris, protesters were pictured holding a banner that read: “We do not need tear gas for our future to be blurry.”
Videos vetted by NBC News show large crowds and fires burning in Marseille.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

Some 320,000 people demonstrated across France on Saturday, including 70,000 in Paris, according to the French Interior Ministry. Authorities reported more than 560 arrests nationwide by Saturday night.

While the protests have been largely peaceful, police arrested 1,300 people last week after an estimated 410,000 took to the streets in cities across the country. Stores, public buildings and businesses have also been damaged since the protests erupted last month.

“Everyone is ​on deck to ensure an extremely firm response to any trouble,” Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said at a news conference earlier this week as he set out security arrangements, adding there was “a very high ⁠risk” of unrest.
Measures introduced last week to protect shops would be reinforced, he said, and demonstrations would not be permitted “in city centers, where there is a risk of public disorder.”

title: U.K. PM open to slave trade apology but rules out financial reparations
summary: U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said that he is open to am apology for his country’s role in the slave trade, but ruled out financial reparations.
story: LONDON — British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said that he is open to a formal apology for his country’s role in the trans-Atlantic slave trade, but ruled out financial reparations as King Charles III continued his tour of the Caribbean.
Burnham’s comments show a marked shift in stance for the U.K.,  which has consistently rejected demands for either an apology or reparations.
They came as he is due to attend the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in Antigua and Barbuda next week. Charles, as head of the “family of nations,” will preside over the event.

“We are offering a structured dialogue with those affected by the transatlantic slave trade,” Burnham wrote in an op-ed in The Guardian newspaper published Friday. “Listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of the British state will form an important part of this process, and I am open to them.”
But Burnham ruled out financial reparations, saying the British people of today who “played no personal part” in the slave trade could not be held liable.

The trans-Atlantic trade in enslaved people was central to European colonialism and the growth of the British Empire, as millions of Africans were trafficked to the Americas to grow and harvest cash crops, while being subjected to violence, torture, sexual abuse and the denial of basic human rights.
Mia Mottley, the prime minister of Barbados, said on X that he welcomed the prime minister’s openness to a formal apology.
Jamaica’s prime minister, Andrew Holness, also posted on X, writing: “Open-minded dialogue is always a good place to start addressing difficult issues.”
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
Jamaica recently took its case for reparations to Charles, and the case has since been referred to the United Kingdom’s highest court of appeal.
Caribbean nations had urged Britain to acknowledge its role in the slave trade ahead of Charles’ visit to the Bahamas and Guyana last week.
Charles last week visited Clifford Park, where in 1973 he granted the Bahamas independence after 300 years of British rule.
Members of the Bahamas’ Rastafarian community and others lined a nearby road to protest.
“Pay us what you owe us!” one woman cried out. “I stand in memory of the horrors and the atrocities committed against Black people.”

In his first public remarks on the island nation, Charles said: “It is only right that we should acknowledge the great suffering and injustices of the past in these islands and beyond, even as we rejoice in the successes of the present.”

title: U.S. set to deport Afghan refugees to Pakistan, despite risk they’ll be returned to Taliban
summary: The Trump administration is preparing to deport dozens of Afghan immigrants and asylum-seekers to Pakistan on the first flight of its kind, a senior administration official told NBC News — a move critics say could put their lives at risk.
story: The Trump administration is preparing to deport dozens of Afghan immigrants and asylum-seekers to Pakistan on the first flight of its kind, a senior administration official told NBC News — a move critics say could put their lives at risk.
The proposed deportation flight, which has not been publicly announced, could take place as early as Monday, according to rights advocates and families of detainees.

Among those facing deportation are relatives of Afghans who worked with the U.S. military in its 20-year war against the Taliban, which is now back in power. The deportees could face severe repercussions should Pakistan return them to Taliban-ruled Afghanistan as is widely expected.

Afghans driven from their country by war and political instability have been welcomed by the U.S. for decades, including tens of thousands who fled the country following the chaotic withdrawal of U.S.-led forces in 2021. President Donald Trump halted admissions for Afghans and other refugees when he returned to office last year as part of a broader immigration crackdown.

His administration has deported thousands of people to countries that are not their own, many of them in Africa, in what immigration lawyers say is an effort to skirt international laws against returning asylum-seekers to the countries they fled from. The legality of these so-called third-country deportation agreements is set to be debated by the Supreme Court in December.

It is not clear what kind of formal agreement the U.S. may have with Pakistan, but the senior administration official said the U.S. charter flight would not be able to land there without the Pakistan government’s knowledge and approval. The deportation plan was earlier reported by Bloomberg and The New York Times.
Bloomberg cited a federal government official familiar with the plans as a source for its report, while The New York Times cited three U.S. officials.

Shawn VanDiver, president of the San Diego-based advocacy group AfghanEvac, said it had confirmed that in recent days, at least 80 Afghans have been moved to Louisiana from 34 other ICE facilities around the country, 19 of them without legal representation.
He said it was possible that there were hundreds of Afghans at the Central Louisiana ICE Processing Center, which has served as a hub for ICE detainees before their deportation from the U.S.

If the U.S. sends Afghan detainees to Pakistan, they are not likely to be there long. Pakistan, which has hosted millions of Afghan refugees for decades, launched a sweeping crackdown in 2023, pressuring hundreds of thousands of Afghans to leave the country and forcibly deporting others.

They are arriving to an Afghanistan battered by multiple humanitarian crises, including widespread malnutrition, as well as an ongoing military conflict with neighboring Pakistan and a dramatic rollback of women’s rights under the Taliban’s hard-line Islamic policies.
VanDiver said the Trump administration would most likely be aware that Afghans sent to Pakistan would be at high risk of being returned to Afghanistan.
“You don’t have to be that smart to figure out that they’re sending them to Pakistan so that Pakistan will finish the job,” he said.

Regardless of whether they worked with the U.S. military, VanDiver said, any Afghans flown from the U.S. would be viewed with suspicion by the Taliban and at risk of persecution, imprisonment or worse.
That does not appear to be a major concern for the White House, said the senior administration official, who declined to be identified because they were not authorized to speak to the media.
“The administration’s position is, ‘These individuals do not have status in our country, therefore we don’t really care what happens to them,’” the official said.

VanDiver and others say the Trump administration’s treatment of Afghan allies could also have long-term consequences for U.S. national security by discouraging people in other countries from working with U.S. forces in future conflicts.
Asked whether the Trump administration was concerned about that, the official said, “I don’t think they care.”

The White House referred a request for comment to the Department of Homeland Security, whose spokesperson said the agency could not confirm removal operations “for operational security reasons.” ICE did not respond to a request for comment.
A State Department spokesperson said the agency had “no plans to announce.”

“We reaffirm our position that all countries must be able to manage their borders and immigration processes in a manner that ensures the safety, security and prosperity of their citizens,” the spokesperson said.
Pakistan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and its embassy in Washington did not respond to requests for comment.

The senior administration official said the Afghans on the flight could include people with deportation orders, people who were turned down for asylum and people whose temporary protected status was terminated by the Trump administration. Many of the Afghans facing deportation requested asylum after crossing into the U.S. from Mexico, VanDiver said, and some of their cases are still pending.
‘We just sat there and cried’

Charlotte, a U.S. citizen whose Afghan husband has been in ICE detention since early 2025, said he had been moved to the Louisiana facility from Pennsylvania this month and told he would be deported in early November. She declined to be identified by her full name out of concern that her husband could be targeted by the Taliban.

Charlotte said she and her husband, whose asylum case has been pending for nine years, were visiting family in Maryland last year when he accidentally crossed into West Virginia and was pulled over. Though he was carrying his valid Illinois driver’s license, he did not have his work permit with him.

“When he was pulled over,” she said, “the sheriff actually said, ‘I’m an ICE agent. You’re going to immigration custody. I don’t care if the charges are dismissed, or I don’t care if you have a five-year work permit or Social Security card. I don’t care if you’re legal. Trump’s administration just took over — you’re going directly to immigration custody.’”

Charlotte sold their home in Illinois and moved to Maryland with their son, now 6, in order to be able to visit her husband at the ICE facility where he was held in Pennsylvania, about 100 miles away.
“I lost my nice house, our car, we left everything behind,” she said.
Over the next 20 months, when she took her son to see his father at the Moshannon Valley Processing Center, they were always separated by plexiglass.
“They never let him hug him one time,” Charlotte said. “We just sat there and cried every time.”
But at least they knew where he was and that he was OK, she said. Now that he’s in Louisiana, she said, “we can’t even visit or even say goodbye, he’s over 1,200 miles away.”

With her husband potentially being sent to Pakistan or Afghanistan — a country he hasn’t been to since 2016 — the uncertainty is even greater; Charlotte said he is growing his beard to comply with the Taliban’s strict rules for men’s facial hair.
“I’m just terrified that he’s not going to be safe,” she said, “or he’s going to be held in the jail and there’s nothing I can do.”
Charlotte said she believed her husband had been targeted for deportation because of a past conviction for a nonviolent crime that has since been resolved.
“I still don’t think this should end our entire life, for a child not to see his dad,” she said.
“He’s completely devastated and traumatized,” she said of their son. “He wants to fight. He wants to go protest. He wants to speak to Donald Trump. He basically knows so much more than he should.”

The preparations for the deportation flight come nearly a year after a shooting in Washington that killed one National Guard member and seriously injured another. The suspect, an Afghan national who served alongside U.S. troops in Afghanistan and was evacuated to the U.S. in 2021, had been granted asylum by the Trump administration. Immigration restrictions were tightened after the shooting.

VanDiver said the Trump administration may also be using the Pakistan flight as a test case for Camp As Sayliyah, a U.S.-run camp in Qatar where more than 1,000 Afghans who had been slated for resettlement in the U.S. have been stranded since Trump returned to office last year.

Asked about VanDiver’s claim, the White House referred a request for comment to the Department of Homeland Security, whose spokesperson again said the agency could not confirm removal operations “for operational security reasons.”

According to AfghanEvac, the camp was housing 287 men, 319 women and 433 children as of July. Most of them have been approved for U.S. resettlement after extensive vetting, and many of the adults worked alongside U.S. forces in Afghanistan.
The group at Camp As Sayliyah also includes 150 relatives of U.S. military service members, AfghanEvac said.

The State Department said earlier this year that everyone would be removed from the camp by March 31, a deadline that was later extended to Sept. 30. In September, the Trump administration delayed its closure by another nine months, The Associated Press reported.
Earlier this year, the administration  considered sending the Afghans at Camp As Sayliyah to the Democratic Republic of the Congo, which is experiencing the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history.

In a statement on Friday, AfghanEvac accused the Trump administration of planning the Afghan deportation flight as the country is distracted by next week’s midterm election, “hoping no one is watching.”
“The government won’t say where these flights land, because it knows what happens to the people on them when they do,” the group said. “A government confident in what it is doing does not hide it.”

title: Italy’s PM deploys troops as nation faces widespread strikes and port blockades
summary: ROME — Tens of thousands of people took to the streets of Rome, Milan and other Italian cities Friday as part of nationwide demonstrations against the cost of living and high military spending.
story: ROME — Tens of thousands of people took to the streets of Rome, Milan and other Italian cities Friday as part of nationwide demonstrations against the cost of living and high military spending.
The demonstrations were largely peaceful but an NBC News crew saw police use a water cannon on protesters and groups of police charging to disperse protesters in Rome on Friday night.

After several weeks of violent protests in Italy and throughout Europe, more widespread disruption is expected after the Unione Sindacale di Base (USB) and other trade unions called on workers in both the public and private sectors to strike and protest.

The demonstrations in Italy appear to have been partly inspired by those in France, where some of the worst rioting in decades erupted in cities across the country after student protests about the state of education in the country evolved into wider actions about the cost of living and social security.

Elsewhere in Europe, a huge encampment of tents has occupied a square in Madrid since late last month, and thousands of people in Portugal have taken to the streets in the city of Lisbon. Tear gas and water cannons were also used on black-clad protesters in Brussels.

In Rome, many waved communist and Palestinian flags, as well as signs against the Iran war. Some let off pink smoke bombs. There was a jovial mood among the demonstrators as they lined up before the march, as has often been the case early on at previous protests, only for violence to break out later.
Giovanna Di Matteo, a member of the left-wing Potere al Popolo! party, said she was protesting against the government that “did nothing for the people of this country.”

The government had spent money on the military “while they cut on welfare, they cut on services and people cannot reach the end of the month,” she said. “They have no money for their houses, they have no money for gasoline and everything.”

Luca, a 20-year-old medical student said the protesters felt they were “still not being heard, that everything is still the same,” and the government didn’t “care about our voice, about our voices, and about the future of this nation that is our nation.”

“We have been completely screwed by the fact that the wages do not keep up on inflation and the wages in general do not keep up with the cost of living,” added Luca, who asked to have his last name withheld out of fear of repercussions from law enforcement.
Major demonstrations also took place in other cities and towns across Italy.

They came after a number of protests in recent weeks have turned violent. Groups of masked protesters looted stores in Milan and elsewhere and threw projectiles at police, who responded with tear gas and water cannons earlier this month.
Italian police were out in force again Friday with riot brigades, drones and helicopters visible in the skies above the Rome protest.

Their presence was heavy after protesters stormed Rome’s historic Colosseum on Saturday, while in the south, farmers and truckers have blockaded highways and ports to protest high fuel prices which have risen since the United States and Israel launched the war against Iran.
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, who has made law and order a key tenet of her administration, said she had “great respect” for peaceful protesters on X earlier this month.
But her right-wing government has since introduced tougher penalties for rioters, including financial liability for parents whose children take part in vandalism and looting.
“There is nothing revolutionary about vandalizing and stealing. Vandalism and theft are not protest, they are criminality,” Meloni said on social media after unveiling the legislation.
The government also said it would deploy 500 army troops alongside the police in Milan until the end of the year.

title: U.S. approves $2.1 billion sale of Patriot interceptors to Ukraine
summary: The Trump administration approved the sale of $2.1 billion in Patriot air defense systems to Ukraine on Friday, the State Department said in a statement.
story: The Trump administration approved the sale of $2.1 billion in Patriot air defense systems to Ukraine on Friday, the State Department said in a statement.
The State Department said 500 Patriot missiles are being purchased for Ukraine with donations from Canada, Germany and Norway through a U.S. program and that no American funds were involved.

“This proposed sale will support the foreign policy and national security objectives of the United States by improving the security of a partner country that is a force for political and economic stability in Europe,” the department said in a news release.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said repeatedly in recent weeks that Patriot missile systems are essential for defending against Russian attacks.

“Our soldiers have been very strong this year. Then we really build, try to build air defense shield to defend our civilians, but always a big deficit with Patriot missiles and other kind of air defense,” Zelenskyy told NBC News’ “Meet the Press” two weeks ago.
The Ukrainian leader had accused the Pentagon of delaying the delivery of the interceptor missiles that other countries have purchased for Ukraine.
For Subscribers
The announcement of the sale comes as President Donald Trump has recently ramped up criticism of Zelenskyy and described him as an obstacle to efforts to end the war between Russia and Ukraine.
For Subscribers
Zelenskyy also recently noted that Ukraine was left further exposed because of restrictions on the Starlink satellite internet service.

Ukraine said Saturday that both Starlink, run by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, and its military variant, Starshield, were fully functional after a long outage, two days after Trump indicated Musk had been asked to “put it back.”

title: Outcry prompts ‘Call of Duty’ to cut Seoul tragedy footage
summary: American video game publisher Activision said Friday that it was removing controversial footage from its newly released “Call of Duty” game after an outcry in South Korea over the inclusion of real-life footage from a deadly 2022 Halloween crowd crush in Seoul.
story: American video game publisher Activision said Friday that it was removing controversial footage from its newly released “Call of Duty” game after an outcry in South Korea over the inclusion of real-life footage from a deadly 2022 Halloween crowd crush in Seoul.

Last week’s global release of “Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4” came days before the Oct. 29 anniversary of the disaster in the South Korean capital’s nightlife district of Itaewon, where a crowd of tens of thousands of partygoers surged beyond control in a narrow alley, causing nearly 160 deaths.

The game, which takes place amid a fictional North Korean invasion of the South, features about 10 seconds of heavily edited footage of the tragedy to illustrate what the aftermath of a Pyongyang attack might look like, though it does not refer to the Itaewon crowd crush directly.

Groups representing families of the crowd crush victims had demanded that the footage be removed, saying it was appalling that the game had directly reproduced actual scenes of people performing CPR “while victims lay on the cold streets amid chaos and desperation.”

“If the game developer has even the slightest sense of respect and empathy for the victims of the Itaewon disaster, it should promptly take corrective action,” the Itaewon Disaster Bereaved Families Association and Itaewon Disaster Citizens’ Countermeasures Committee said in a joint statement Friday.
The California-based game publisher, Activision, apologized in a statement and said the footage would be completely removed through a game update scheduled for release Nov. 12.

“This game is a fictional work created to provide a realistic and immersive experience,” the company said, according to the South Korean public broadcaster MBC. “In using actual news footage in the game, we never intended to evoke any tragic incident, including the Itaewon disaster, or to trivialize the suffering associated with such tragedies.”

The controversy came as grieving families are still waiting for answers about authorities’ failure to prevent the disaster four years ago. Nearly two dozen officials have been charged in the investigation, which is still underway, while three former police officers have been jailed.
On Thursday, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung vowed that his government would “uncover the truth.”

title: Evacuations begin in Ukraine under localized ceasefire brokered by Melania Trump
summary: An evacuation mission was underway in a Russian-occupied city in Ukraine, during a truce brokered by first lady Melania Trump and with Pope Leo XIV’s involvement.
story: A landmark evacuation and humanitarian aid mission was underway Friday inside a devastated Russian-occupied city in Ukraine, during a localized ceasefire brokered by first lady Melania Trump and with the involvement of Pope Leo XIV.

Ukrainian officials have described the operation in Oleshky as one of the most significant pauses in fighting since Russia launched its full-scale invasion more than four and a half years ago. Humanitarian teams from both sides were on the ground early Friday, with the first lady posting to X that they were “delivering aid and preparing the convoy for civilian evacuation.”
However, any sense that the ceasefire might yield wider progress in the war was tempered by Russian missile strikes on other cities ahead of what is predicted to be a bitter winter for Ukraine.
Some Ukrainians in the city were also worried about where they would end up after being evacuated.

Though Oleshky is just across the Dnieper River from Ukrainian-held Kherson, the planned escape route to Ukrainian-controlled territory runs through Russia and its ally Belarus. Some residents told Sky News they feared they would not be allowed to continue into Ukraine, leaving them weighing whether to board the buses or remain in the devastated city.

title: Patrick Stewart and Ian McKellen: A friendship that surpassed the stage and screen
summary: “He wore his heart on his sleeve, which made him a man to rely on, to admire and in my case, love,” McKellen said in a statement on Stewart’s death.
story: To many, Patrick Stewart and Ian McKellen represent a formidable mutant rivalry in the “X-Men” films or two of theater’s pre-eminent Shakespearean actors, but behind the curtain the pair shared something even more enduring: a friendship that spanned decades.

Stewart died Wednesday at age 86 following a diagnosis of Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia. McKellen, Stewart’s artistic brother-in-arms, remembered him Thursday as “the most respected and beloved actor of his generation on either side of the Atlantic.”
“He wore his heart on his sleeve, which made him a man to rely on, to admire and in my case, love,” McKellen said in a statement on social media.
The pair — about a year apart in age — met at England’s esteemed Royal Shakespeare Company, with Stewart joining in 1966 and McKellen in 1974.

title: Final election results show neither Netanyahu nor rival can immediately form government
summary: Parties led by Israel’s Arab minority made historic gains, winning a combined 19 seats in a race in which Palestinians with Israeli citizenship headed to the polls in record numbers.
story: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s right-wing bloc won 53 seats in Israel’s 120-member Knesset, results released by election officials Thursday showed, well below the 68 it had controlled at its peak in the previous parliament.
The bloc supporting Netanyahu’s main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, won 48 seats in an extremely tight race, meaning neither secured the 61 seats needed to form a government.
The count is complete, but the results still need to be certified and submitted to President Isaac Herzog on Wednesday.
Herzog will then consult with party chairs and choose a candidate ⁠he thinks has the best chance to form a government.

Parties led by Israel’s Arab minority made historic gains, winning a combined 19 seats in a race in which Palestinians with Israeli citizenship headed to the polls in record numbers Tuesday, many hoping to oust Netanyahu and far-right members of his coalition, including Bezalel Smotrich, his finance minister, and National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir.

Both leading blocs have ruled out the possibility of forming a government with the two main Arab parties, Ra’am and the Joint List. But their rise as potential kingmakers has brought the complex realities faced by Palestinian Israeli nationals into fresh focus.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

Ahead of the election, Netanyahu and other members of his coalition amplified allegations of foreign election interference, referring Arab parties to the domestic security service, the Shin Bet, for investigation over allegations of Qatari intervention.

Qatar denied the allegations. Mansour Abbas, the head of Ra’am, said his party had “no connection” to such conduct and urged a full investigation. He also accused Netanyahu of a “campaign of incitement and delegitimization” against Arab citizens.

Dean Livne, the acting director general of Israel’s Central Elections Committee, said in a published letter sent to a member of parliament that there was “no basis for allegations of systematic violations of electoral integrity.”
Before the election, both Netanyahu and Eisenkot ruled out forming a government with the Arab parties.

But Yair Golan, the head of the smaller left-wing Democrats party, called for a government formed “in partnership” with Arab parties. “We must no longer accept Netanyahu’s racist division between Jewish votes and Arab votes,” he said Wednesday on X.

The majority of Palestinians with Israeli citizenship are the descendants of those who remained within what became Israel during the war that led to the country’s founding in 1948. At the time, hundreds of thousands more fled or were expelled from their homes. Palestinians refer to this as the “Nakba,” which means “catastrophe” in Arabic.
